en: Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle One,
compiled by Bodhisattva Sthiramati;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Having realized the ultimate principle of true purity within all assemblies, you have transcended the ocean of noble conduct to reach the further shore;
having attained mastery over all phenomena, your skillful means of transformation and guidance are inconceivable.
Possessing immeasurable, rare, and supreme virtues, you are the foundation for the mutual benefit of both self and others.
I pay homage to the Great Awakened Honored One, To the peerless, sublime Dharma, and the assembly of noble ones.
I pay homage to the masters who expounded this treatise, And those who, having personally received the holy intent, analyzed it.
Through understanding the sūtras and their commentaries, I have now applied diligent effort to synthesize them.

Now, within this verse, I offer praise for their supreme qualities without error and prostrate with deep reverence, making offerings to the Three Jewels as well as to the two masters—the author of this treatise and the commentator on its sūtra—each according to their respective merit.
Why is this so? Because it is the basis upon which this treatise relies and that which gives rise to it.

The Buddha, the Bhagavat, is the equal basis for all the teachings, such as the sūtras; he is the foundation from which a portion of the teachings arises, having awakened by himself to the true nature of all phenomena without a teacher.
Immediately following this, the assembly of noble disciples who study in accordance with the Dharma and take the Dharma as their refuge do so because it flows from the Dharmadhātu.

Both masters who commented on the Sūtra likewise accorded with the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata; taking as their basis that portion which is unerring in hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they composed these treatises accordingly.

The first two verses reveal six aspects of the supreme qualities of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: namely, the meanings of essence, cause, fruit, activity, endowment, and differentiation.

Regarding "those who have realized the ultimate principle of true purity," this reveals the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that is to say, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas takes the *tathatā* of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in all its aspects as its essential nature.

"Those who have transcended the ocean of noble practices and ascended to the other shore" clarifies the meaning of the cause; that is to say, the Buddha’s bodhi arises from the causes of having fully cultivated and practiced the noble practices of all aspects throughout immeasurable and innumerable great eons across the ten stages, beginning with the Stage of Extreme Joy.

"Attaining mastery over all phenomena" clarifies the meaning of the fruition; that is to say, having permanently severed all afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and their remaining habitual tendencies, one realizes the fruit of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)—endowed with boundless and marvelous qualities—and thus exercises sovereign mastery over all phenomena.

"Miraculous skillful means for transformation and guidance" clarifies the meaning of activity (*karman*); that is to say, by means of immeasurable methods of subduing—such as supernatural powers, prophetic declarations, instructions, and manifestations—which transcend the sphere of all [limited] wisdom, one leads those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed so that their mental continuum becomes pure.

"Immeasurable, rare, and supreme qualities" clarifies the meaning of "conjunction," which refers to being conjoined with the jewel-like dharmas of supreme great compassion, powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, produced by various boundless and difficult ascetic practices that transcend the limits of conceptual thought and calculation.

The phrase "the basis for the benefit of both self and others" clarifies the meaning of their distinction; that is to say, the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya), the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya), and the Essential Body (svābhāvikakāya) of the Tathāgata serve as the respective bases for the benefit of self and others.
As for "basis" (*āśraya*), it carries the meaning of "body" (*kāya*) and "substance" (*ātman*); there is no difference between them.
Regarding the basis for benefiting both oneself and others, this is explained from the perspective of what is preeminent.
That is to say, the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is supreme in its self-benefit, because within great assemblies it is able to receive the foremost, vast, and profound Dharma-treasure.

The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is supreme in benefiting others, for it can arise continuously throughout all worlds in the ten directions—just like various feats of craftsmanship and other transformative acts—in order to establish what must be done for sentient beings.

The *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body) refers to the *dharmakāya* common to all Sugatas; because it takes as its essence the *tathatā* (suchness) of the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) from which all most subtle obscurations have been eliminated, it is the most supreme for the benefit of both oneself and others, since by realizing this body, one attains the other bodies.
These three bodies of the Buddha represent the meaning of differentiation.
It should be understood that within this context, the merits of the Dharma and the Saṃgha are also praised.
As for the Jewel of the Dharma, it is comprised of meanings such as its intrinsic nature, causes, and results.
The Jewel of the Saṃgha arises from following and training in this [teaching];
thus, so that students may be free from all fears, I shall now initiate this treatise by establishing its essential nature.
The *Vastu-saṃgrahaṇī* and the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* each consist of four parts:
the inclusion of the three categories, the truths, the dharmas, the attainments, and the treatises;
as well as the number, the causes, the grasping of characteristics, the establishment, and the sequence.
The detailed analysis of the meanings and metaphors, and the summary verses, should be understood.
Question:
For what reason are the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth explained at the beginning of this treatise?
Answer:
It is because one wishes to enable the student to attain skillfulness regarding the various points of analytical investigation, such as the causal factors and so forth. Why is this?

By means of this skillfulness, one is able to attain two kinds of praised benefits: namely, the praised benefit of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the praised benefit of formal discussion and definitive analysis (*viniścaya*).
Regarding "mental attention that praises and benefits," this refers to being well-conducive to the increase of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Being well-conducive to the increase of *śamatha* means having attained skillfulness in these various points of analytical investigation and thereby becoming free from doubt.
Because the mind is easily concentrated, right observation manifests before one in whatever single object one delights in.
As for "skillfully conforming to and increasing vipaśyanā," it means observing all objects of knowledge through immeasurable gateways, thereby swiftly bringing right wisdom to ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding "discussing, determining, praising, and benefiting": because one has thoroughly mastered such points of investigation, one achieves mastery over all questions and answers and attains fearlessness toward all opposing doctrines.
Question:
How many types are there for each of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana)?
Answer:

There are five aggregates (*skandha*), namely: the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

There are eighteen elements (*dhātu*), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

There are twelve bases (āyatana), namely: the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; and the mind-base and the mental-object-base.
Question:
For what reason are there only five aggregates?
Answer:

This is for the purpose of manifesting the five kinds of self-entities (*ātman-vastu*): namely, to manifest the self-entity of the body and its requisites, the self-entity of experience, the self-entity of speech, the self-entity that performs all dharmas and non-dharmas, and the self-entity that is the substratum upon which those depend.
Among these five, the first four are the objects of "mine," while the fifth is the object of the "self-characteristic.

Regarding the "bodily equipment," this refers to the meaning of the internal and external form-aggregates (*rūpa-skandha*) and the enjoyment of the other aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*), which will be explained under the section on characteristics.

Regarding "the entity of the self that serves as their basis": this refers to the meaning of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the entity characterized by a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) which serves as the basis for the body, its faculties, and so forth. Why is this so?
Because worldly sentient beings mostly conceive of the aggregate of consciousness as the self, while they conceive of the other aggregates as "mine" (*ātmīya*).
Question:
For what reason are there only eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
Answer:
Because the body, its equipment, and so forth, possess the nature of sustaining the experience of the six modes of activity in the past and present:
"body" refers to the six faculties, such as the eye;
"equipment" refers to the six objects, such as form.
The "sixfold experience of the past and present" refers to the six consciousnesses.
The "capable sustainers" refer to the six faculties and the six objects, which can sustain the six consciousnesses because they serve as their respective bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*).
The six consciousnesses of the past and present are able to maintain and experience [their objects] because they do not abandon their own characteristics.
One should know that the eighteen [dhātus] are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being able to maintain.
Question:
For what reason are there only twelve bases?
Answer:
Because only the body and its instruments can serve as the gateway for the growth and development of the six types of future experiential enjoyment.

That is to say, just as the sixfold aspect of enjoyment in the past and present is sustained by the eye and the other [faculties], so too the sixfold aspect of enjoyment in the future has the faculties and their objects as its gateways for growth and development.

Regarding the term "only" (*kevala*): it means that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are established based solely upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and not based upon the sixfold consciousnesses characterized by experience.
Question:
What is meant by the "appropriation aggregates" (*upādānaskandha*)?
Answer:
They are called the aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha) because they are conjoined with clinging.
"Clinging" refers to the desire and greed present within the aggregates.
For what reason is sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) called "clinging" (*upādāna*)?

It is because it draws forth and does not relinquish the aggregates (*skandha*) of the future and the present; thus, the longing for the future and the attachment to the present constitute sensual desire, which is termed "clinging."

Craving (*chanda*) has the characteristic of seeking; greed (*lobha*) has the characteristic of attachment. Because craving seeks a future personal existence as its means, it draws forth the future aggregates (*skandha*) to arise in the present.
Because one uses attachment to the present self-body as a means, one grasps at the present aggregates so as not to let them go;
therefore, these two are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Question:
For what reason are there factors associated with grasping (*sopādāna*) mentioned among the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer:
It should be explained in the same manner as the aggregates (*skandha*).
One should know that because the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are associated with grasping (*upādāna*), they are called "dharma-s with grasping" (*sopādāna-dharma*).
Question:
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of form?
Answer:
The characteristic of manifesting transformation is the characteristic of form.
This is of two kinds:
first, transformation through contact; second, manifestation through spatial direction.
Regarding transformation through contact: this refers to the fact that when one is touched by hands and feet, or even by mosquitoes and snakes, it immediately undergoes transformation and decay.

Regarding "that which is manifested by way of location": this refers to the manifestation of such-and-such forms or this-or-that form through a specific location; or it refers to various mental constructions produced either by a concentrated mind or by discursive thought that is not in a state of concentration.
"Location" refers to the place directly before one.
"Such and such forms" refers to images of the same category as the objects of knowledge, such as skeletons and so forth.
"This and that form" refers to the distinctions of shape and color.
"Various mental constructions" refers to conceptualizing according to [perceived] characteristics.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of feeling?
Answer:
The characteristic of experiencing is the characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*).

That is to say, by means of feeling, one experiences the various maturations (*vipāka*) obtained from pure and impure karma: through pure karma, one experiences the maturation of pleasure; through impure karma, one experiences the maturation of suffering; and through both pure and impure karma, one experiences the maturation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Why is this so? Because the ālayavijñāna, which is the resultant maturation (*vipāka*) induced by pure and impure karma, is always associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Only this feeling of equanimity is the actual substance of maturation; since the two feelings of suffering and pleasure arise from maturation, they are only metaphorically designated as "maturation."
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)? Answer:
The construction of marks is the characteristic of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Because of this conceptualization, one delineates the various images and categories of phenomena, giving rise to verbal expressions according to the meanings seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Regarding the meanings of seeing, hearing, cognizing, and knowing: that which is received by the eye is the meaning of seeing; that which is received by the ear is the meaning of hearing.
That which is naturally conceived and constructed as "it should be thus and thus" is the meaning of cognizing.
That which is internally experienced is the meaning of "knowing.
As for "all verbal expressions," this refers to the elucidation and discrimination of meanings.
Question:
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? Answer:
The characteristic of volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*) is the characteristic of formations.

By means of this activity, it causes the mind to engage in formation; that is to say, because it directs and employs the mind within the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate, and because it directs and employs the mind through various states such as suffering and pleasure.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of consciousness? Answer:
The characteristic of discernment (*vijñapti*) is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It is by means of this consciousness that one discerns various objects, such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
Question:
What is the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)? Answer:

It refers to the eye that has seen or currently sees visible forms, as well as the seeds accumulated therein within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the ālayavijñāna; this is the characteristic of the eye-element.
That which has previously seen forms refers to the capacity to maintain the object of experience for past consciousness, thereby manifesting the nature of the element (*dhātu*).
That which presently sees forms refers to the capacity to maintain the object of experience for present consciousness, thereby manifesting the nature of the element.
Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna* as the ripening (*vipāka*) that accumulates these seeds: this refers to the seed of the eye.
Alternatively, it is merely an accumulation for the purpose of projecting the future sense-faculty of the eye.
Or, it is already matured for the sake of producing the present eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
These two types are called the "eye-element" (*cakṣurdhātu*) because they are the causes for the arising of the eye.
Just as with the characteristics of the eye-element, so too are the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the form realm (rūpadhātu)? Answer:

All forms that have been seen or are currently being seen by the eye, as well as the predominance of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*) with respect to them, constitute the characteristic of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Regarding the predominance of the eye-faculty: it means that external objects arise through the predominant power of the physical sense organ (*rūpīndriya*).
As with the characteristics of the sphere of form (*rūpadhātu*), so it is with the characteristics of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Question:
What are the characteristics of the sphere of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
Answer:

It refers to the discernment that arises based on the eye and conditioned by forms, appearing as forms, as well as the ālayavijñāna which is the maturation of the accumulated seeds of this [discernment]; this is the characteristic of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
As it is with the element of eye-consciousness, so too are the characteristics of the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer:
It should be understood according to the elements (*dhātu*), as appropriate to each case.
That is to say, it should be explained according to the meaning that the eye shall see forms, as well as their seeds and so forth.
How is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) established?
It refers to all that is form: namely, the four great elements (mahābhūta) and that which is derived from the four great elements.

As for "derived," this means that the four great elements serve as the causes of its production, support, establishment, maintenance, and nourishment; thus, based on these five causes, it is said to be "derived."
The generative cause (*janakahetu*) is the originating cause (*utpādakahetu*), because derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) does not arise apart from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

The supporting cause (*niśrayahetu*) is the transformative cause (*pariṇāmakahetu*), because once the primary elements are relinquished, the derived matter lacks functional capacity, as it occupies a distinct location.

The "establishing cause" (pratiniyamahetu) is the concomitant cause (anuvartakahetu), because the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), which depends upon them, undergoes transformation in accordance with the great elements' own transformation.

The "supporting cause" (dhārakahetu) is the cause of persistence (sthitihetu); that is to say, it causes the various derived matters to arise in a continuous succession similar to themselves, thereby supporting them so that they do not cease.

The cause of nourishment (*puṣṭi-hetu*) is the cause of growth (*vṛddhi-hetu*), meaning that by means of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), those derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) are nourished and made to increase.
The four primary elements refer to the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
The earth element is the nature of solidity.
The water element is the nature of fluidity and moisture.
The fire element is the nature of heat.
The wind element is characterized by lightness and mobility.

Derived matter refers to the five sense organs, such as the eye; a portion of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible; and the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The eye faculty (cakṣur-indriya) refers to that which is derived from the four great elements, serves as the basis for visual consciousness, and has pure matter (rūpa-prasāda) as its essence.
The ear faculty (śrotra-indriya) refers to that which is derived from the four great elements, serves as the basis for auditory consciousness, and has pure matter as its essence.
The nose faculty is that which is derived from the four great elements, serves as the basis for nose-consciousness, and has pure matter as its essence.
The tongue faculty is that which is derived from the four great elements, serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness, and has pure matter as its essence.

The body faculty (*kāyendriya*) refers to that which is derived from the four great elements, serves as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), and has pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as its essence.

Visible form (*rūpa*) refers to the objects of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), which is derived from the four great elements; these are: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, even and uneven, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, the color of open space, manifesting color, and the color of the uniform expanse of space.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, beautiful, unbeautiful, and that which is contrary to both.

These twenty-five types of color, such as blue and so forth, are established by way of six causes: namely, by way of characteristic, by way of designation, by way of benefit and harm, by way of being the basis for action, by way of the characteristic of action, and by way of adornment.
In their respective order, they are four, ten, eight, one, one, and one.
"Distinct color" (prātibhāsika-rūpa) refers to that which can be apprehended in a location free from other obstructive contacts.
Space as a single color refers to the visible colors such as blue and so forth that are perceived above.

Sound is an object produced by the four great elements and apprehended by the auditory faculty; it may be agreeable, disagreeable, or neither; it may be caused by appropriated great elements, unappropriated great elements, or both; it may be conventionally established, derived, or conceptually constructed; and it may be included within noble speech or not included within noble speech.

These eleven kinds of sound are established by way of five causes: namely, by way of their characteristics, their benefit or harm, the differentiation of their causes, the differentiation of their explanations, and the differentiation of their expressions.
"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the object apprehended by the auditory faculty.
"Exposition of distinctions" (*viśeṣanirdeśa*) refers to the three [categories] beginning with "that which is commonly established in the world.
The remainder should be understood as appropriate to each case.
Sound dependent on derived primary elements refers to sounds such as speech.
Sound dependent on non-derived primary elements refers to sounds such as those from trees.
Sound dependent on both refers to sounds such as those from hands and drums.
That which is commonly established by the world refers to what is encompassed by conventional discourse.
That which is established through reasoning refers to what is taught by the noble ones.
That which is conceptually imputed refers to what is taught by non-Buddhists.
That which is subsumed under the categories of "noble" and "non-noble" speech refers to the eight kinds of verbal expression based on views and so forth.

As for odor (*gandha*), it is an object derived from the four great elements and apprehended by the olfactory faculty; it includes pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, neutral odors, innate odors, blended odors, and transformed odors.
It should be understood that this fragrance is established by way of three causes: namely, by way of its characteristic, by way of its benefit or harm, and by way of its differentiation.
As for innate fragrance, it includes *candana* (sandalwood) and so forth.
Blended fragrance refers to blended incense and the like.
Transformed fragrance refers to ripened fruits and the like.

Taste is an object produced by the four great elements that is apprehended by the gustatory faculty; it consists of bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland, whether agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral, and whether innate, blended, or transformed.
The establishment of this taste should be understood as explained for odor.

As for "a portion of the tangible," it refers to the objects apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) which is derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); namely: smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, softness, laxity, tension, cold, hunger, thirst, satiety, strength, weakness, oppression, itching, stickiness, illness, old age, death, fatigue, respiration, and vigor.

This portion of the tangible is established by eight causes: namely, by way of characteristic, by way of rubbing, by way of weighing, by way of contact, by way of grasping, by way of mixture, by way of the disharmony of the elements, and by way of the harmony of the elements.
It is cold because of the mixture of water and wind; it is viscous because of the mixture of earth and water.
Because the elements are in equilibrium, there is respiration, strength, and vigor; one who possesses vigor is fearless.
Satiety arises from two causes.
Due to the inequality of the elements (*dhātu*), there are other contacts such as hunger and so forth.

Regarding the forms subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there are briefly five kinds: namely, extremely condensed form (*paramāṇusaṃghātarūpa*), extremely remote form (*paricchedarūpa*), form derived from what is experienced (*anubhava-niṣyandarūpa*), form arisen from conceptual construction (*parikalpitarūpa*), and form produced by mastery (*vaśitvanirmitarūpa*).
Extremely condensed matter refers to the matter of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Extremely remote matter refers to this very same matter when it is separated from other obstructive contacts.
Matter derived from mental volition refers to non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Form arising from conceptual construction refers to the form of images.
Form produced by mastery refers to the forms that are the objects of the sphere of activity for liberation and meditative concentration.
How is the aggregate of feeling established?
That is to say, the six groups of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, up to and including feeling born of mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Furthermore, there are bodily feelings of pleasure, bodily feelings of pain, and bodily feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant;
there are mental feelings of pleasure, mental feelings of pain, and mental feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Furthermore, there is pleasant feeling with attachment, painful feeling with attachment, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling with attachment;
there is pleasant feeling without attachment, painful feeling without attachment, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without attachment.
Furthermore, there is pleasant feeling based on attachment, painful feeling based on attachment, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling based on attachment;
there is pleasant feeling based on renunciation, painful feeling based on renunciation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling based on renunciation.
Bodily feeling refers to feeling associated with the five consciousnesses.
Mental feeling refers to feeling associated with the mental consciousness.
Feeling accompanied by relish refers to feeling associated with craving for one's own existence (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*).
Feeling without relish refers to feeling that is dissociated from this craving.
Feeling based on indulgence refers to feeling associated with craving for the five excellent sensual pleasures.
Feeling based on renunciation refers to feeling that is dissociated from this craving.

This establishment is based on four causes: namely, by way of the basis (*āśraya*), by way of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), by way of the basis for the accumulation [of suffering] (*upacayāśraya*), and by way of affliction and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadāna*).
The establishment of bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*) is based on the accumulation of form; the establishment of mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*) is based on the accumulation of the formless.

Based on affliction (*saṃkleśa*), there is the establishment of "having relish" (*sāsvāda*) and so forth; based on purification (*vyavadāna*), there is the establishment of "being without relish" (*nirāsvāda*) and so forth.
That which is dissociated from this craving refers to that which is disjoined (*visaṃyoga*) and that which is conducive to disjunction (*visaṃyogānukūla*).
How is the aggregate of perception established?
It refers to the six groups of perception: perception born of eye-contact, up to perception born of mind-contact.

By means of these perceptions, one either discerns with signs, or discerns without signs; or discerns the small, the large, or the immeasurable; or discerns the sphere of nothingness, which is the absence of even the slightest existence.
The perception of signs refers to all perceptions other than those of improper speech, the concentration of signlessness, and the perception of the peak of existence.
The perception of signlessness refers to the perceptions excluded previously.
Limited perception refers to the perception capable of discerning the desire realm.
Vast perception refers to the perception capable of discerning the form realm.
Immeasurable perception refers to the perception capable of discerning the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-saṃjñā*) refers to being able to discern the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

The perception of improper discourse (*asamyag-vyavahāra-saṃjñā*) refers to the fact that because one has not yet learned language, although one gives rise to a perception regarding form (*rūpa*), one cannot discern that "this is called form"; therefore, it is termed the perception of signlessness (*animitta-saṃjñā*).

Regarding the perception of the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*): it is called the "signless perception" because it is the perception of nirvana, which is signless as it is free from all signs such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Regarding the perception of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra-samādhi*): it is called the "signless perception" because that perception is not clear or sharp, and thus cannot delineate various signs within its object.
"Small" refers to the inferiority of the desire realm.
"Great" refers to the superiority of the form realm.
"Immeasurable" refers to the boundlessness of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Therefore, based on those various perceptions (*saṃjñā*), they are also termed small, great, and immeasurable.
How is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) established?
It refers to the six groups of volition (*cetanā-kāya*): volition born of eye-contact, up to volition born of mind-contact.
Due to this volition (*cetanā*), it performs various wholesome deeds, it performs defilements (*saṃkleśa*), and it produces the differentiation of states.

Furthermore, this very volition—excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), together with the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—is collectively termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Although all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), with the exception of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), possess the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), volition (*cetanā*) is preeminent; as it serves as the leader for all formations, it is therefore mentioned specifically.
To clarify this meaning, it is said that "one performs wholesome dharmas through volition," and so forth.
"Wholesome" refers to what will be explained as faith and the like.
"Defilement" refers to what will be explained as the root afflictions such as greed, as well as the derivative afflictions and minor afflictions associated with greed and the others.

Regarding the distinction of states: this refers to the designation of "factors dissociated from mind" (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) applied to the various stages of formations (saṃskāra) issued from volition (cetanā).
Question:
What are the remaining mental factors (caitasika-dharma)?
Answer: They are:

attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), non-harming (*avihiṃsā*); greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*); the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*); lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), sleep (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Thus, regarding these fifty-five factors—whether universal, object-specific, wholesome, afflictive, secondary afflictions, or indeterminate—one should know that they correspond respectively to five, five, eleven, twelve, and fourteen.
Furthermore, these mental factors (caitasika-dharma) shall be analyzed extensively according to their characteristics and functions.
Volition (cetanā) has the nature of forming mental karma (manas-karman); its function is to direct the mind toward the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
"To have mental action as its essence, consisting of the mental formation within the mind" explains its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
"To employ the mind within the categories of the wholesome and so forth" explains its function (*karma*).
Because it initiates the mind toward virtuous and other such dharmas that are to be performed.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) has the nature of activating the mind, and its function is to sustain the mind upon its object of focus.

Regarding "holding the mind upon the object of focus": this means repeatedly directing the mind toward that very object; therefore, when the mind attains concentration, it is said to have attained *manasikāra* (attention).
Contact (*sparśa*) has as its essence the discernment of the transformation of the sense faculties based on the conjunction of the three; its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).

That is to say, when consciousness arises, the sense faculties that serve as its support undergo a transformative mode of activity (*ākāra*) in accordance with the arising of feelings such as suffering or pleasure; contact arises through the discernment of this transformative mode of activity.

Desire (*chanda*) has as its essence the aspiration for the performance of various activities regarding objects that are pleasing; its function is to serve as the basis for right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*).
Regarding "the aspiration for the performance of various activities": this refers to the desire to draw forth and accomplish all functions, such as seeing, hearing, and so forth.
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) has as its essence the confirmation and maintenance of a determined object according to how it has been determined; its function is to be unshakeable.
"Confirmation and maintenance according to how it has been determined" means that one resolves with the clear understanding: "This thing is necessarily thus, and not otherwise."
Due to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one cannot be led astray by any superior conditions.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) has as its essence the clear recollection and non-forgetting of familiar objects by the mind, and its function is the absence of distraction (*avikṣepa*).
"Familiarization with an object" refers to that which was previously experienced.
"Non-distraction in action" means that because mindfulness clearly recalls the object, it prevents the mind from becoming distracted.
Samādhi has the essential nature of causing the mind to be one-pointed with respect to the object under contemplation, and its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
"Causing the mind to be one-pointed" means that it prevents the mind from being distracted from a single objective sphere.
That which is the basis of wisdom is the mind, because when it abides in meditative concentration, it knows things as they truly are.
Wisdom has the discernment of phenomena regarding the objects of contemplation as its essence, and the severing of doubt as its function.
The severing of doubt means that through wisdom one discerns phenomena and thereby attains certainty.
Faith has the nature of conviction, purity, and aspiration regarding that which exists, possesses qualities, and possesses efficacy; its function is to serve as the basis for the desire to act.

That is to say: one gives rise to the practice of faith through patient acceptance toward that which truly exists as a substance; one gives rise to the practice of faith through pure conduct toward that which truly exists as a quality; and one gives rise to the practice of faith through aspiration toward that which truly exists as a capacity—thinking, "I have the power to attain and to accomplish."
*Hrī* (shame) has as its essence the feeling of self-reproach regarding various faults and evils, and its function is to serve as the basis for the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
*Apatrāpya* (embarrassment) has as its essence the feeling of shame before others regarding various faults and evils; its function is as described for *hrī*.
Non-attachment has as its essence non-clinging toward existence and the requisites for existence; its function is to serve as the basis for the non-engagement in unwholesome conduct.

Non-hatred has as its essence the absence of malice toward sentient beings, suffering, and the instruments of suffering; its function is to serve as the basis for the non-engagement in unwholesome conduct.

Non-delusion has as its essence the discernment derived from the wisdom of retribution, scripture, and realization; its function is to serve as the basis for the non-occurrence of unwholesome conduct.
Since shame and the other [virtuous mental factors] are easily understood, they will not be explained again.
Regarding the wisdoms of fruition, scripture, and realization: these refer respectively to the wisdoms produced by birth, hearing, reflection, and cultivation; this should be understood accordingly.
As for discernment (*viniścaya*), it refers to wisdom conjoined with diligence.

Diligence (*vīrya*) has as its essence the courageous mind that dons the armor of skillful means, being without inferiority, without retreat, and without satiety; its function is the fulfillment of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Possessing power, possessing diligence, possessing courage, firm and fierce, one does not abandon the yoke of the wholesome."
These various phrases—such as "donning the armor" and "courage of mind"—should be explained and assigned according to their respective order.
"Fulfilling the category of virtue" means being able to bring to completion the fundamental dhyāna entered at the outset.
"Accomplishing the wholesome category" means precisely cultivating and refining this [wholesome state] to its utmost excellence.

"Tranquility" (praśrabdhi) has as its essence the cessation of the coarseness (dausthulya) of body and mind and the resulting pliancy and harmony of body and mind; its function is the removal of all hindrances.
"Dispelling all obstacles" means that by the power of this [factor], the basis (āśraya) is transformed.

"Heedfulness" (apramāda) has as its essence the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas based on right effort, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, while guarding the mind against all tainted (sāsrava) phenomena; its function is to bring to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane merit.

That is to say, because one is able to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and prevent outflows by taking right effort and the others as a prerequisite, heedfulness is established as a provisional entity based upon these four dharmas.
Defiled phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) refer to the various outflows (*āsrava*) as well as their bases and objects.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has as its essence the state of mental evenness, the state of mental rectitude, and the state of mental effortless abiding, which rely upon right effort and the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and are contrary to dwelling in defilement; its function is to not provide a basis for the persistence of defilement.
Regarding "the equality of the mind" and so forth, this refers to distinguishing the varieties of equanimity (*upekṣā*) across its initial, middle, and final stages. Why is this?
Because equanimity is associated with the mind, and by being free from the state of inequality such as mental depression (*laya*) and so forth, one first realizes the equality of the mind.
Because the mind is equanimous and free from deliberate effort, continuing spontaneously, one subsequently realizes the state of mental rectitude;
because the mind is upright, one has no apprehension regarding the various defilements, and finally realizes the state of the mind abiding without effort.

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) has as its essence a portion of the wholesome root of non-aversion characterized by a mind of compassion and pity; its function is to refrain from injuring or afflicting others.
One should know that non-harming is not separate from non-aversion, and is therefore also a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
Craving has the nature of attachment to the three realms and the function of producing manifold suffering.
"Producing manifold suffering" means that by the power of craving, the five aggregates of clinging arise.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) has as its essence a mind of malice and resentment toward sentient beings, their suffering, and the instruments of suffering; its function is to serve as the basis for unpeaceful dwelling and for unwholesome conduct.
"Unpeaceful dwelling" means that because the mind harbors malice and resentment, one dwells frequently in suffering.
Pride has as its essence the loftiness of mind based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); its function is to serve as the basis for the arising of disrespect.
Disrespect refers to the cultivation of arrogance toward teachers, elders, and those possessed of virtue.
The arising of suffering refers to the production of future existence (*punarbhava*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) has the nature of non-knowledge regarding the three realms; its function is to serve as the basis for the arising of defilements through false certainties and doubts concerning all phenomena.
"False certainty" refers to inverted cognition.
"Doubt" refers to indecision.
"The arising of afflictions" refers to the manifestation of afflictions such as attachment.
That which serves as its basis refers to the arising of various afflictions due to ignorance.
Doubt has the nature of hesitation regarding the truths, and its function is to serve as a basis for the non-arising of wholesome qualities.
"Doubt regarding the truths" also includes doubt regarding reality, because it is subsumed under the Truths of Cessation and the Path as appropriate.
"The non-arising of wholesome factors" refers to the failure to engage in cultivation due to indecision.

The view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has as its essence the various forms of receptivity, desire, cognition, reflection, and vision that, in accordance with the five aggregates of clinging, perceive and grasp them as "I" and "mine"; its function is to serve as the basis for all types of speculative views.

The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consists in the acceptance, desire, cognition, examination, and view that, based on the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), perceives them as either eternal or annihilated; its function is to obstruct the middle way and liberation.
The practice of the middle way refers to the correct wisdom that contemplates dependent origination while remaining free from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to the acceptance, desire, cognition, investigation, and vision that, in relation to various views and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which serve as their basis, regard them as supreme, preeminent, superior, and excellent; its essential nature consists of these mental factors, and its function is to cling to what is an incorrect view as its basis.

The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) has as its essence the various forms of acceptance, desire, thought, examination, and view that, regarding various rules and observances—as well as the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) upon which those rules and observances depend—regard them as purification, liberation, and transcendence; its function is to serve as a basis for laboring in vain without result.
Regarding "observance of precepts and prohibitions" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): it is preceded by false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
It is "exertion without fruit" because, by means of this, one cannot attain liberation. Regarding "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*):

its essence consists of the denial of causes, the denial of results, the denial of functional efficacy, the subversion of real entities, or erroneous conceptualization; it comprises various forms of acceptance (*kṣānti*), desire (*chanda*), awakening (*buddhi*), reflection (*vitarka*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*). Its functions are: the severing of the roots of virtue; serving as the basis for the strengthening of the unwholesome roots; the arising of the unwholesome; and the non-arising of the wholesome.
Denying the cause refers to asserting that there is no giving, no affection, no sacrifice, no virtuous conduct, and no non-virtuous conduct.
Denying the result refers to asserting that there is no maturation (vipāka) produced by the karma of virtuous and non-virtuous actions.

Denying the function [of karma] means to deny this world and deny that world; to deny the existence of a mother and a father; and to deny sentient beings born by transformation. This is because one denies the function of traveling between different worlds, denies the function of maintaining the seeds [of existence], and denies the function of continuity.
The denial of real entities refers to the claim that there are no worldly arhats and so forth.
Erroneous discrimination refers to all other forms of conceptualization and inverted views.
The severance of the roots of goodness refers to [the loss of these roots] due to predominant false views, but not in every respect.
Question:
Among these five views, how many are views of superimposition (*samāropa-dṛṣṭi*)?
How many are views of denial (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer:

The four [perversions] are views of exaggeration (*samāropa-dṛṣṭi*), because they exaggerate both the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of the objects of knowledge, and because among all views they exaggerate them as being supreme and pure.

That is to say, the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the superimposition of the intrinsic nature of "self" and "mine" upon the objects of knowledge—the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the superimposition of the distinctions of "permanent" or "impermanent" regarding that self.
To superimpose the status of being supreme upon various wrong views is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To superimpose purity upon those very same views is the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
For the most part, these consist of the view of negation (*apavādadarśana*).
Regarding "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*): because false conceptualization does not necessarily entail diminution [of merit].
Question:
Among all the views concerning the past and future limits (*pūrvānta-aparānta*), how many of those views are subsumed within these five?
Answer:
Either two or all.
Question:
Regarding all views concerning matters that are undeclared (*avyākṛta*), how many of these five [categories of views] do they fall under?
Answer:
Either two, or all of them.
"Two" refers to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"All" refers to the five views together with their attendants (*parivāra*).
Question:
For what faults did the Bhagavān, upon observing them, disparage the conception of a self regarding the aggregates, elements, and bases by means of five aspects?
Answer:

Because he observed that those who embrace the view of a transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) have five kinds of faults, namely: the fault of having a different characteristic, the fault of impermanence, the fault of lack of sovereignty, the fault of being bodiless, and the fault of liberation without effort.

The fault of being of a different characteristic (*vilakṣaṇa-doṣa*) means that the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and so forth are not the nature of the self (*ātman*), because they possess characteristics distinct from the self.
The fault of impermanence (*anitya-doṣa*) means that within the aggregates of form and so forth, which are not the self, the self would consequently have to be impermanent.
Why is this so? It is because it is not the case that the supported is non-existent while the support is existent.
Regarding the fault of lack of sovereignty: one should not regard the self as possessing form and so forth, for the self would then be subject to a lack of sovereignty.
Why is this so? Because I lack sovereign control over form and the other aggregates.
Regarding the fault of being bodiless: it means that there is no self existing apart from form and the others in a separate location, for [otherwise] the self would be without a body.
Why is this? Because a self conceived apart from the body cannot be found.

As for the claim that one is liberated from faults without effort, even if such a conceptualization of a self-phase were to exist, it would be illogical; for if there were a formless self, it would follow that one would be liberated without effort.
Why is this? If the fetters of the body did not exist, the self would be liberated spontaneously.
Question:

Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, there are twenty modes of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): namely, reckoning form as the self; that "I have forms"; that "forms belong to me"; and that "I am within forms. The same applies to the remaining aggregates.

Thus, one reckons that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self; or that "I have consciousness," etc.; or that consciousness and the other aggregates belong to me; or that "I am within consciousness and the other aggregates.
Among these various views, how many are views of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)?
How many are views of "mine"?
Answer:
Five are views of "I," and fifteen are views of "mine."
That is to say: reckoning form as self, and reckoning feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self—these five constitute the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*);
the remaining fifteen constitute the view of "mine" (*mamakāradṛṣṭi*).
For what reason are the fifteen considered the view of "mine"?
Because it is associated with what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*), because it conforms to what belongs to the self, and because it is not separate from what belongs to the self.
"Associated with what belongs to the self" means: "I have form," up to "I have consciousness."
Why is this so? Because it is through association with "I" that one speaks of "that," for there is the notion of "that.
To follow along with what belongs to "mine" means to regard form as belonging to the self, up to and including consciousness as belonging to the self.
Why is this? Because if they are moved by that power of mastery—whether abandoned or employed—the world says, "That is mine.
To not be separated from what is "mine" means: "I am in form," and so on, up to "I am in consciousness."
Why is this so? Because they conceive of a real self as residing within the aggregates, following them throughout the entire body.
Question:
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), should it be said that it is determinate or indeterminate with respect to its object?
Answer:
It should be said that it does not attain certainty regarding its object, just as one falsely conceives the notion of a snake upon a rope.
Regarding those who lack certainty concerning phenomena: if one can ascertain the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form and so forth, one will certainly not give rise to false views of a self (*ātman*).
It is like a person who suddenly sees a rope and takes it to be a snake; failing to discern the characteristics of the rope, they give rise to the grasping of a snake.

Anger (*krodha*) has as its basis the perception of a present harm; it is a part of hatred (*dveṣa*), with mental fury as its essence, and its function is to serve as the basis for grasping weapons and venting indignation.
One should know that anger and the others are merely conventional designations, as they have no distinct nature apart from hatred and so forth.

As for resentment (*upanāha*): from this point onward, it is a part of hatred; its essence consists in harboring a grudge without relinquishing it, and its function is to serve as the basis for intolerance.
"From this point onward" means following after anger (*krodha*).
"Intolerance" (*akṣānti*) refers to being unable to endure harmful actions.

"Concealment" (*mrakṣa*)—which is a portion of delusion (*moha*)—has the nature of hiding one's committed transgressions when they are rightly pointed out by others; its function is to serve as a basis for remorse and lack of mental stability.
It is the natural law that one who conceals a committed offense will inevitably feel mental distress and remorse; by means of this, they cannot abide in peace.

*Nāha* (affliction) has resentment as its precursor and constitutes a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*). Its essential nature is a contortion of the mind. Its function is to serve as the basis for arrogant, violent, and coarse speech; its function is to give rise to non-merit (*apuṇya*); and its function is to cause one not to abide in peace.
Harsh and violent speech refers to words that manifest ferocity and distance, cutting to the very core of the heart.

Envy (*īrṣyā*) consists in being attached to gain and profit while being unable to endure the prosperity of others; it is a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*). Its essence is mental jealousy, and its function is to cause the mind to dwell in sorrow, distress, and lack of peace.

Avarice (*mātsarya*) has as its essence a stinginess of mind that is a portion of greed, characterized by attachment to gains and the requisites for life; its function is the failure to relinquish what one relies upon.
As for "failure to relinquish," because of this stinginess, one constantly accumulates even those items that are not currently being used.

Deceit (*māyā*) has as its essence the fraudulent manifestation of non-existent virtues out of attachment to gain and offerings, being a portion of greed and delusion; its function is to serve as the basis for wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

Guile (*śāṭhya*) has as its essence the artful employment of expedients to conceal actual faults and evils out of attachment to gain and offerings, being a portion of greed and delusion; its function is to obstruct correct instruction (*samyag-avavāda*).
To feign expedient means while concealing actual faults and evils means to rely on one pretext to evade another matter.
To obstruct correct instruction means that because one does not disclose one's transgressions as they truly are, one is unfit to receive instruction.

Pride (*māna*) has as its essence a portion of craving that causes the mind to be delighted, based either on signs such as youth, health, or longevity, or upon the attainment of any kind of tainted (*sāsrava*) prosperity or benefit; its function is to serve as the basis for all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The mark of longevity refers to first conceptualizing this mark through the perception of immortality, by which one gives rise to pride and negligence regarding one's lifespan.
"Any single defiled matter of prosperity and benefit" refers to matters such as noble lineage, physical beauty and strength, intelligence, wealth, and power.
"Delight" refers to a specific variety of afflicted joy.
"Harm" is a portion of hatred; its essence consists of a lack of affection, compassion, and pity, and its function is to injure and afflict sentient beings.

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is a derivative of greed, hatred, and delusion; its essence consists in not feeling personal shame regarding one's transgressions and evils, and its function is to serve as an associate to all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is a derivative of greed, hatred, and delusion; its essence consists in not feeling shame before others regarding various faults and evils, and its function is as described for lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Torpor (*styāna*) refers to a derivative of delusion; its essence consists in the mind’s lack of functional capacity, and its function is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Excitement (*auddhatya*) refers to a derivative of sensual desire; its essence is the lack of tranquility of mind due to recollecting signs of purity, and its function is to obstruct *śamatha*.
"Recollecting signs of purity" means that because one recalls past instances of playful laughter and the like that accord with sensual desire, the mind lacks tranquility.

Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) refers to a portion of delusion; its essence consists of the mind’s lack of acceptance toward all wholesome phenomena, the mind’s lack of purity, and the mind’s lack of aspiration; its function is to serve as the basis for laziness (*kausīdya*).
The basis of laziness (*kausīdya*) is due to a lack of faith, whereby there is no application of skillful means or the desire for practice.

Laziness is a derivative of delusion; its essence consists of attachment to sleep and reclining as a pleasure, characterized by a lack of mental exertion. Its function is to obstruct the cultivation of virtuous qualities through skillful means.

Heedlessness has as its essence the failure to cultivate wholesome dharmas by relying on laziness, greed, hatred, and delusion, and the lack of mental protection regarding tainted dharmas; its function is to serve as the basis for the increase of evil and the diminution of good.
Forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) has mindfulness associated with afflictions as its essence; its function is to serve as the basis for distraction.

Lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) has wisdom associated with afflictions as its essence; by means of this wisdom, one initiates improper conduct of body, speech, and mind, and its function is to serve as the basis for transgressing precepts.

One who acts with non-reflective awareness regarding body, speech, and mind refers to one who does not correctly observe matters such as coming and going; because they do not understand what should and should not be done, they frequently commit transgressions.
Distraction (*vikṣepa*) refers to that which belongs to the categories of greed, hatred, and delusion, having the nature of the mind’s outward wandering.

It is further of six kinds: natural distraction, external distraction, internal distraction, distraction of signs, distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and distraction of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Intrinsic distraction (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*) refers to the fact that the five groups of sensory consciousnesses lack the capacity for internal meditative concentration by their very nature.

External distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*) occurs when, during the actual practice of virtue, the mind wanders toward the five types of sensual pleasures; that is, while practicing the skillful means of hearing and other wholesome dharmas, one abandons those objects of focus and the mind wanders externally, dwelling amidst sensual desires.

Internal distraction refers to sinking, agitation, and attachment while correctly practicing virtue; that is, because the practitioner of meditative concentration gives rise to sinking, agitation, and attachment, they fall away from and lose calm concentration.

Regarding distraction by signs: one feigns the cultivation of wholesome qualities in order to gain the trust of others; that is, because one wishes to lead others to believe that one possesses virtue, one manifests these signs. Due to this cause and condition, the wholesome dharmas one has cultivated gradually decline and are lost.

Regarding coarse-dysfunctional distraction (*dausthulya-vikṣepa*): due to the force of the coarse dysfunction associated with the categories of clinging to "I" and "mine" (*ātma-ātmīya-grāha*) and the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), when practicing wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as the conceit of "I am," toward all sensations (*vedanā*) that have already arisen, thereby grasping at signs in a manner that is interspersed with such clinging.

This means that due to the coarse and heavy force of self-grasping and the like, one either grasps at pleasure and other sensations that have already arisen as "I," or grasps at them as "mine," or gives rise to the conceit of "I am"; because of this, the wholesome qualities one cultivates will never be pure.
"Appropriation" (upādāna) refers to the initial grasping and attachment.
"Interspersing" (vyavakiraṇa) refers to the subsequent state in which the mental continuum is interspersed by this [grasping].
"Grasping at signs" (nimittodgrahaṇa) refers to repeatedly grasping at various distinct characteristics within that very [continuum].

Distraction of mental attention (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*) refers to the scattering that occurs regarding other vehicles or other meditative concentrations, whether in terms of their basis or their entry.

That is to say, by relying on another vehicle or entering another concentration, one abandons what was previously practiced and gives rise to distraction. It should be understood that its function is to obstruct the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*). This is explained as distraction characterized by the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Sleep is that which, based on the conditions for sleep, belongs to the category of delusion; its essence is the contraction of the mind. It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; it may occur at the proper time or the improper time; and it may be appropriate or inappropriate.
Its function is to cause the neglect of one's duties and to serve as a basis for their loss.

As for the conditions for sleep: they consist of physical emaciation and fatigue, heaviness of the limbs, contemplating dark imagery, abandoning all activities, and having repeatedly practiced sleep at such times in the past.
This may be induced by the supernatural power of another’s incantations, or by such causes as the movement of a fan and the blowing of a cool breeze.
The phrase "a portion of delusion" (*moha-bhāga*) is used to distinguish it from meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and so forth serves to demonstrate that this sleep is not necessarily a portion of delusion.
"Proper time" refers to the middle watch of the night.
"Improper time" refers to the remaining portions of the day.
"It should be so" means that even if it is not the permitted time, it may be done due to illness or for the sake of physical adjustment.
That which should not be so is the remainder.
Regarding "transgressing and losing the basis for action," this refers to sleep as it pertains to the nature of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Bad conduct (kaukṛtya) is a derivative of delusion based on what one desires to do or does not desire to do, and what ought to be done or ought not to be done; its essence is mental regret. It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; it may occur at the proper time or the improper time; or it may be appropriate or inappropriate. Its function is to obstruct the stability of the mind.
Regarding "acting with pleasure," this refers to performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds preceded by a desire for them.
Regarding "acting without pleasure," this refers to being compelled to act as appropriate by the power of others or by the pressure of various afflictions.
The portion of delusion is subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
"Appropriate time" refers to the period until one has attained liberation;
"inappropriate time" refers to the period after one has already attained liberation.
"Appropriate" refers to what is fitting in a given situation;
"inappropriate" refers to what is not fitting.
"Investigation" (vitarka) has as its essence the coarse state of the mind, consisting of mental verbalization that seeks out [an object] based either on volition or on wisdom.
Regarding "based on volition or based on wisdom": in states of deliberation and non-deliberation, respectively, it consists of the mental verbalization of the aspect of seeking.
As for *vicāra* (sustained thought), its essence is the mental verbalization that investigates, based either on volition or on wisdom, causing the mind to become subtle.
Regarding "depending on volition and depending on wisdom": in states of deliberation and non-deliberation, respectively, these are the mental verbalizations with the aspect of investigation.
These two types have the function of being the basis for stability and instability.
Because the two types—vitarka and vicāra—are similar in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), they are distinguished by being established as coarse and subtle respectively.

Furthermore, all wholesome mental factors have the function of abandoning that which is to be countered by themselves, while the afflictions and secondary afflictions have the function of obstructing that which is capable of counteracting them.

Just as faith, shame, and so forth can sever lack of faith, lack of shame, and the like, so too do the afflictions such as greed obstruct their antidotes, such as non-greed; that is to say, they act as obstacles that prevent those antidotes from arising.

It should be understood that the secondary afflictions, such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, are able to obstruct loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables], and their respective antidotes are likewise.

Chapter One, Part Two: The Section on the Basis of Past Events, Chapter on the Three Dharmas. What are called the formations dissociated from mind?

These are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the maturation of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the commonality of group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the collection of names (*nāma-kāya*), the collection of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), transmigration (*pravṛtti*), determination (*pratiniyama*), association (*samyoga*), rapidity (*java*), succession (*anukrama*), time (*kāla*), direction (*deśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and integration (*sāmagrī*).

These formations dissociated from mind should be established through five categories of distinction: namely, by way of their basis, their intrinsic nature, their designation, their attention, and their level.

The two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) are complete with five doors; in the maturation (*vipāka*) of the non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), mental attention (*manasikāra*) is excluded, while the remaining [factors] consist only of the first three.

As for "acquisition" (*prāpti*), it is a conventional designation for the increase or decrease of wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral phenomena, established as their attainment or possession (*samanvāgama*).
The terms "wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena" indicate the basis;
"whether increasing or decreasing" indicates the essential nature. Why is this so?
Because there is an increase, one is said to possess superior faith and so forth; because there is a decrease, one is said to possess inferior faith and so forth.
The term "attainment" (prāpti) used in the expression "possessing attainment" indicates that it is a conventional designation (prajñapti).
In this manner, one should understand that the establishment [of other states] follows their respective applications.

As for the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): it refers to the conventional designation "attainment of non-ideation" applied to the cessation of the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors, occurring because one has already abandoned desire for the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the higher spheres, and takes the mental attention directed toward the ideation of renunciation as its precursor.
"One who has already abandoned desire for the Subhakṛtsna [heaven]" means one who has already abandoned craving for the third dhyāna.
"One who has not yet abandoned higher desire" means one who has not yet abandoned craving for the fourth dhyāna and above.
"Preceded by the mental application of the perception of renunciation" means that the mental application of the perception of liberation serves as the preliminary means (*pūrvopāya*).
"Not constantly active" means it is comprised within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

"Cessation" refers to the temporary cessation of those minds and mental factors that do not constantly manifest, which is induced by the concentrated mind; it is a specific state of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*), so it is called "cessation" because it is capable of causing cessation.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) refers to the provisional designation of the "attainment of cessation" for the cessation of all non-permanently active minds and mental factors, as well as a portion of the permanently active minds and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention that temporarily suspends perception, having already abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness and transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

The reason why it is not stated here that one has "not yet abandoned desire for the higher realms" is to show that even Arhats and others, having abandoned the desire of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), can also attain this meditative absorption.
"A portion of those who practice constantly" refers to that which is subsumed under the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*).

The maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) refers to the designation of "maturation of non-conception" applied to the cessation of non-constant mental states and mental factors among those born in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) refers to that which, within a commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*), is induced by prior karma and has a determinate duration; it is a provisional designation for "life-span.
The commonality of group refers to the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*) throughout a single lifetime.

Regarding the determination of duration: for a specific period of time—whether it be a hundred years, a thousand years, or otherwise—the homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) remains constantly established, due to the specific functional capacity induced by karma.

The "homogeneity of a group" (*nikāyasabhāga*) refers to the conventional designation of "homogeneity of a group" for sentient beings who, in such and such ways, are similar in their various types of individual existence (*ātman*).
Regarding "in various types," this refers to the distinctions between types such as humans, gods, and so forth.
Regarding "similarity in its own essence," this refers to the nature of being of a single class.
Regarding "arising" (*jāti*), it is the designation for the state of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that were previously non-existent and now exist.
Question:
External phenomena such as material forms (*rūpa*) also possess the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); why, then, is only the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) cited?
Answer:
This is for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) within the continuum of sentient beings. Why is this so?

Because the characteristics of the conditioned in external forms and the like are manifested by formation and disintegration, whereas the characteristics of the conditioned in internal formations (*saṃskāra*) are manifested by aging and so forth.
Aging refers to the state of transformation within the continuity of the formations belonging to a particular homogeneous class; it is designated as "aging" by way of conventional designation.

Duration refers to the state of non-disintegration within the continuity of the formations belonging to a particular homogeneous class; it is designated as "duration" by way of conventional designation.

Impermanence refers to the nature of transformation and disintegration within the continuity of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) belonging to a particular homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga); it is in this sense that "impermanence" is conventionally established.
This "transformation and disintegration of the continuity" refers to the time of casting off the life-force (āyuḥ).
It should be understood that herein, birth and so forth are established based on the state of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not based on the moment (*kṣaṇa*).
As for "name-group" (*nāmakāya*): it refers to the conventional designation of a name-group as an augmented expression regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
Discursive expression regarding intrinsic nature refers to the verbal expressions concerning things such as the eyes and ears of gods and humans.
A phrase-body (*padakāya*) refers to the provisional establishment of a phrase-body as discursive expression regarding the distinctions among phenomena.
Discriminative increase (viśeṣa-vardhana) refers to the teaching of such meanings as the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and the fact that all sentient beings must die.

A phoneme-group (vyañjana-kāya) refers to the conventional designation of "phoneme-group" applied to the various syllables (akṣara) that serve as the basis for those two [the name-group and the phrase-group].

The "syllables that are the basis for those two" refers to the syllables that serve as the basis for the expressions of both essential nature (*svabhāva*) and specific difference (*viśeṣa*), such as *a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth.
Furthermore, essential nature, specific difference, and these two types of expression collectively encompass everything.
All such things are expressed by these three; therefore, these three are established as the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
Here, the term "phoneme" (*vyañjana*) is used because it is capable of manifesting those two [names and phrases].
This is also called "manifestation" (*vyañjana*), because it can manifest the meaning.
Furthermore, this is called "name" (*nāman*), because there is no other transformation [of it]. Why is this so?

Just as the name "eye" is distinct [from the eye itself], this name may undergo changes through other synonymous terms such as "external," "illuminating," or "guiding," because these terms collectively manifest the same conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

However, apart from the specific distinctions of the characters *ya*, *yi*, and so forth, there are no further distinctions that can manifest these characters; therefore, they are called "syllables" (*akṣara*) because they do not undergo change into something else.
"Non-alteration" means not undergoing transformation.
"Ordinary beinghood" refers to the non-attainment of the noble dharmas; it is a conventional designation for ordinary beinghood.
"Cyclic existence" refers to the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect; it is a conventional designation for cyclic existence.
The reason why "evolution" (pravṛtti) is established only with respect to an uninterrupted continuity is that this term is not applied to a single moment or to a state of interruption.
"Specific difference" (anyathātva) refers to the conventional designation of specific difference with respect to the various distinctions between cause and effect.
