Regarding the various distinctions between cause and effect: this refers to the fact that desirable effects have virtuous conduct as their cause, while undesirable effects have non-virtuous conduct as their cause; such are the various mutual distinctions between causes and effects.
Regarding "conformity" (*samyoga*): it refers to the conventional designation of conformity based on the correspondence between cause and effect.

As for the correspondence between cause and effect: although they may belong to different categories, the fact that cause and effect accord with one another is also termed "correspondence," as in the case of how the practice of giving brings about the result of abundant wealth and so forth.
"Velocity" refers to the designation "velocity" applied to the rapid transition of cause and effect.
"Succession" refers to the designation "succession" applied to the sequential transition of cause and effect one by one.
Regarding the successive progression of cause and effect: this refers to their not arising simultaneously.
As for "time": it is a conventional designation established for the continuous progression of the succession of causes and effects.
Why is this? Because cause and effect continue to evolve in succession.
When these causes and effects have already arisen and already ceased, they are established as the past time.
If this has not yet arisen, it is established as the future time.
Having already arisen but not yet ceased, it is established as the present time.

As for "direction," it refers to the conventional designation of directions—namely east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—based on the distinctions between causes and effects.
Why is this? It is because cause and effect pervade the ten directions; thus, "directions" are used as a conventional designation.

One should know that herein only cause and effect subsumed under material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are discussed, for immaterial phenomena lack the functional capacity to be distributed across locations.
"Number" refers to the conventional designation of "number" applied to the individual distinctions among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
As for these individual distinctions: it would be illogical for there to be no distinction between one and numbers such as two or three.
"Conjunction" (*sāmagrī*) refers to the provisional designation "conjunction" applied to the gathering of causes, effects, and conditions.

As for the gathering of causes, effects, and conditions: for instance, in the case of the dharma of consciousness, its causal continuity necessarily depends upon the assembly of various conditions—namely, that the sense faculty is unimpaired, the object is present, and the attention capable of producing this consciousness is correctly aroused.
In this manner, all other [factors] should be understood according to reason.

Since such factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) are established solely based on differences in states (*avasthābheda*), one should know that they are all conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

That is to say: one type is established based on the distinctions of the states of increase and decrease regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth; three types are established based on the distinctions of the states of mind and mental factors; one type is established based on the distinctions of the state of abiding; one type is established based on the distinctions of the state of similarity; four types are established based on the distinctions of the state of characteristics; three types are established based on the distinctions of the state of verbal expression; one type is established based on the distinctions of the state of non-attainment; and the remaining types are established based on the distinctions of the state of cause and effect.
Regarding cause and effect: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are called "causes" because they are able to produce others, and "effects" because they arise from others.
How is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) established?
This refers to the distinctions between mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"Mind" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*—the storehouse consciousness containing all seeds perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). It is also called the "ripening consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*) and the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādānavijñāna*), because it is capable of accumulating all habitual tendencies.
"Habitual tendencies" (vāsanā) refers to the fact that by means of the active manifestation of the aggregates and so forth, their respective seeds are all increased and strengthened.
"The consciousness containing all seeds" (sarvabījaka-vijñāna) refers to the accumulation of the seeds from which all phenomena, such as the aggregates, are produced.
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is so called because it can contain and store the seeds of all phenomena, and because sentient beings grasp it as a self.
The *vipākavijñāna* (retribution consciousness) is so called because it is produced by prior karma.
The *ādānavijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) is so called because it repeatedly causes the continuity of birth and sustains the sense faculties and so forth, preventing them from perishing.
Furthermore, it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is able to accumulate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena.
How is it known that the ālayavijñāna exists?
If this consciousness did not exist, then [the phenomena of] appropriation, initial [cognition], clarity, seeds, karma, bodily sensation, the mindless attainments, and death would all be irrational.
The explanation of this verse is as stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*: "By means of eight aspects, it is proven that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists. That is to say:

because, apart from the ālayavijñāna, (1) the appropriation of the basis (*āśrayopādāna*) cannot be found; (2) the initial arising [of the body] cannot be found; (3) clear arising cannot be found; (4) the nature of seeds (*bījadharmatā*) cannot be found; (5) the nature of karmic activity (*karmakriyādharmatā*) cannot be found; (6) the nature of bodily sensation (*kāyikavedanādharmatā*) cannot be found; (7) dwelling in the mindless attainments (*acittakasamāpatti*) cannot be found; and (8) the consciousness at the time of death (*cyuti-vijñāna*) cannot be found."
How is it that the appropriation of the basis (āśrayopādāna) cannot be apprehended? It is due to five reasons.

First, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the projecting cause (ākṣepahetu) for the eyes and so forth, while the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) are produced by present conditions. As it is said: "The evolving consciousnesses arise through the power of the sense organs, objects, and attention," and so on at length; this is called the first reason.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness can be found to be either wholesome or unwholesome; this is the second reason.

Moreover, it is absolutely impossible for the six groups of consciousness to be subsumed under the category of uniform, resultant, and indeterminate (vipāka-avyākṛta) by nature; this is the third reason.

Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness each function based on their respective supports; when a particular consciousness arises in dependence upon its support, that consciousness alone should grasp its support, while it would be illogical for others to lack such grasping.
Even if one were to grant that they do grasp it, this would still be unreasonable because they are distinct from that consciousness. This is the fourth reason.
Furthermore, the basis [of consciousness] would incur the fault of being repeatedly appropriated. Why is this so?
Because that visual consciousness arises at one time and does not arise at another, and the same applies to the other consciousnesses; this is the fifth reason.
Why is it that its initial arising cannot be apprehended?
It is because if one were to raise this objection:
"If the ālayavijñāna exists, then two consciousnesses would arise simultaneously in a single sentient being."
One should tell him:
"You have falsely conceived the notion of a fault where there is no fault, for it is possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously. Why is this so?"

It is as if there were someone who, at one and the same time, desired to see, and so forth, up to desiring to cognize; it would be unreasonable for any single consciousness to arise first among them. Why is this?

At that time, there is no distinction in the mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the faculties and their objects appear without impairment; for what reason, then, do the consciousnesses not arise simultaneously?
Why is it that their clear manifestation cannot be apprehended?

That is to say, if one were to dogmatically maintain that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, then a clear and distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functioning in the same object as the visual and other sensory consciousnesses would be impossible to find. Why is this so?
When one recollects an object previously experienced, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises without clarity.

A mental consciousness directed toward a present object cannot possess such a lack of clarity; therefore, one must either believe that the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, or else admit that the sixth mental consciousness lacks the nature of clarity.
Why is it that the essential nature of the seeds cannot be apprehended?
It is because the six groups of evolving consciousnesses are each distinct from one another. Why is this so?

These six evolving consciousnesses arise from a wholesome state immediately after an unwholesome one, and conversely, a wholesome state arises immediately after an unwholesome one; they arise from either of these two immediately after a neutral state. A middling realm arises immediately after a lower realm, a sublime realm arises immediately after a middling realm, and even a lower realm arises immediately after a sublime realm. An outflow-free state arises immediately after an outflowing state, and an outflowing state arises immediately after an outflow-free state. A supramundane state arises immediately after a mundane state, and a mundane state arises immediately after a supramundane state. It is not logically tenable that a consciousness possessing such characteristics should constitute the essence of the seed.

Furthermore, since the continuity of the mind is interrupted for long periods and flows on uninterrupted over a great duration, it is illogical that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) could maintain the seeds.
Why is their functional activity (*karmakriyā*) thus unattainable?
This means that if the various consciousnesses did not arise simultaneously, it would be illogical for their functional activities to proceed together. Why is this so?
Briefly stated, there are four types of cognitive activity of consciousness: namely, discerning the external environment, discerning the physical basis, discerning the self, and discerning objects.

These four kinds of consciousness perform their respective functions of discernment, each being perceptible as manifesting simultaneously at every single moment; it is not the case that such diverse functional activities exist within a single consciousness at one and the same moment. Therefore, there must necessarily be the simultaneous arising of multiple consciousnesses.
How is it that the essential nature of bodily sensation cannot be apprehended?

It is as follows: suppose there is someone who, whether reflecting in accordance with reality, reflecting contrary to reality, not reflecting at all, or engaging in investigation—whether the mind is in meditative concentration or not—gives rise to many and manifold bodily sensations.
If the ālayavijñāna did not exist, such bodily sensations would be impossible to obtain;
since they are indeed presently obtained, the ālayavijñāna must certainly exist.
Why is it that consciousness cannot be found when one abides in the mindless attainments?
As the Blessed One said:
"When one enters the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, it should be known that at that time, consciousness does not depart from the body."

If the ālayavijñāna did not exist, then at that time consciousness would have to depart from the body; if consciousness were to depart from the body, one would necessarily lose life. It cannot be said that [the location of] consciousness is fixed.
Why, then, is it impossible to perceive the consciousness at the moment of death?

This means that at the time of death, as consciousness gradually abandons the physical body that serves as its basis, a sensation of cold arises either from the top or the bottom; yet, it is not the case that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) ceases to function at any point during this process.
Therefore, we know that only the ālayavijñāna is capable of maintaining the body and conforming to its various parts.
If this consciousness were abandoned, the sensation of coldness could be perceived while the body would lack tactile awareness; such is not the case with the manovijñāna.
Therefore, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the consciousness at the moment of death could not be established.

As for the *manas*, it takes the ālayavijñāna as its object at all times; its nature is that of cogitation, and it is always associated with four afflictions, namely: self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, this manas operates throughout all states—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—with the sole exceptions of when the Noble Path is manifest, when one is in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), or when one is in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi).

Furthermore, the six consciousnesses take the immediately preceding ceased consciousness as their *manas*; it should be understood that herein, the *manas* is made manifest by way of its object (*ālambana*), its etymological definition (*nirukti*), its association (*samprayoga*), and its moment of arising (*utpatti-kāla*).
Why is there no afflicted manas when the Noble Path is manifest?

Because the wisdom of ultimate reality and the active manifestation of the view of self are utterly incompatible. After emerging from the Noble Path, it arises again from the ālayavijñāna, because it has not been permanently severed during the stage of training (śaikṣa).

Furthermore, because the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is far more tranquil than the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), this afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) cannot manifest therein.
As for the "manas that has just ceased," it is so called because it is immediately perceived [by the subsequent consciousness].
The meaning of "uninterrupted awakening" (anantara-bodha) is the "meaningful" (artha); it should be understood that here this is explained according to its manifest characteristics.
"Consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
Visual consciousness has the nature of discerning forms by depending on the eye.
Auditory consciousness has the nature of discerning sounds by depending on the ear.
Olfactory consciousness has the nature of discerning odors by depending on the nose.
Tongue-consciousness has the nature of discerning flavors based upon the tongue as its condition.
Body-consciousness has the nature of discerning tangibles based upon the body as its condition.
Mental-consciousness has the nature of discerning mental objects based upon the mind as its condition.
It should be understood that herein consciousness is established by way of its basis (*āśraya*), its object (*ālambana*), and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
How are the elements (*dhātu*) established?

It is said that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of ten elements: the five sense-faculties such as the eye, the five objects such as visible form, and a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations are a portion of the dharma-dhātu;
the aggregate of consciousness is the seven consciousness-elements, namely, the six consciousness-elements of the eye and so forth, as well as the mind-element.
For what reason are the elements (dhātus) and bases (āyatanas) established without distinct characteristics?

Since the individual characteristics of the eye and so forth have already been explained within the establishment of the aggregates (skandha), the establishment of the elements (dhātu) is derived from the aggregates, and the establishment of the sense bases (āyatana) is derived from the elements.
Which dharmas of the *dhātu* are not subsumed within the *skandhas*?
Within the *dharmadhātu*, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are not subsumed by the *skandhas*.

These unconditioned dharmas are further of eight kinds: namely, the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome dharmas, the suchness of unwholesome dharmas, the suchness of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, space (*ākāśa*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
Thus, among the eight unconditioned phenomena established in this way, one should know that they are differentiated according to their bases;
the three types of *tathatā* (suchness) are provisionally established through analysis, not by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The suchness of wholesome phenomena refers to the nature of selflessness, emptiness, signlessness, the reality limit, and the ultimate dharmadhātu.
For what reason is suchness called "suchness"?
Because its intrinsic nature is without change— that is,
because the true nature of selflessness never undergoes alteration at any time— it is said to be "unchanging.
One should know that this is precisely the nature of selflessness, for it is free from the two kinds of self.
For what reason is this further called "emptiness"?
Because it is not traversed by any defilements. Why is that?
By virtue of this condition, all phenomena of affliction are rendered entirely empty and quiescent.
Although at times it is said that there are afflictions, one should know that these are merely defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
What is meant by "adventitious defilement"?

It refers to the fact that because the seeds of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) have not yet been uprooted, the mind of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) evolves in two modes of activity;
it does not refer to the mind of the true nature (*dharmatā-citta*), for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharmatā of all phenomena is primordially pure.
For what reason is this further called "signless"?
Because all signs are quiescent.
"Signs" refers to form, sensation, and so forth, up to awakening.
All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are quiescent within the nature of *tathatā*; therefore, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Why, then, is it further called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
Because it is the object of non-erroneous cognition.
"Reality" (bhūta) means being free from inversion.
Because this state is ultimate, it is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi); for beyond the nature of selflessness, there is nothing further to be sought.
Why, then, is this also called the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha)?
Because it is the sphere of activity of the most excellent noble wisdom.
For what reason, then, is this called the *dharmadhātu*?
Because it is the characteristic upon which all the sublime teachings (*saddharma*) of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas depend.
Just as it is with the suchness of wholesome phenomena, one should know that the suchness of unwholesome phenomena and the suchness of indeterminate phenomena are likewise.
As for space, it refers to the nature of formlessness, because it accommodates all conditioned activities.

That which has no form-nature (*arūpatva*) refers to that which is merely opposed to form (*rūpa*), being a phenomenon without intrinsic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that serves as the objective domain of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); this is called space (*ākāśa*).

Regarding the phrase "objective domain of the mental consciousness," because it is subsumed within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the expression "merely opposed to form" is used to distinguish it from feeling (*vedanā*) and other [aggregates] that are common [to all], as well as true suchness (*tathatā*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), impermanence (*anityatā*), and so forth.
Although rabbit horns and the like are also devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they do not contradict other phenomena because they are absolutely non-existent.

Furthermore, rabbit horns and the like do not contradict only form (*rūpa*), as they are common to other phenomena such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. Therefore, the expression "non-existence characterized by contradiction with form" is stated specifically to distinguish it from non-material phenomena such as sensation.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of sensation and the other aggregates possesses the characteristic of existence (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*) and not the characteristic of non-existence.
As for analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is a cessation that is not dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), because it does not permanently destroy the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) refers to cessation that is dissociation (*visamyoga*), because it permanently destroys the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The unshakable (*āniñjya*) refers to the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) consisting in the cessation of suffering and pleasure, for one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of universal purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the higher realms.

The cessation of perception and feeling refers to the unconditioned state resulting from the cessation of all non-permanent mental states and mental factors, as well as a portion of the permanent mental states and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention that brings about the stilling of perceptions, once one has become detached from the desire for the sphere of nothingness.
It should be understood that within this there are two kinds of phenomena to be abandoned: namely, the various afflictions and the feeling upon which they depend.
Feeling is of two kinds: namely, the mutable and the immutable.

In their respective order—suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—one should know that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is established through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Through the abandonment of the two types of sensation, immovability (*āniñjya*) and the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*) are established, respectively.
The abandonment of afflictions refers to the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained by removing the coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) of this category.
The abandonment of feeling refers to the transformation of the basis attained by removing the meditative hindrance that opposes its antidote.

Therefore, when one attains the second dhyāna, although the cessation of suffering is realized, it is not established as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the sensations of change have not yet been completely abandoned.

Furthermore, the five kinds of form, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and these eight unconditioned phenomena mentioned here—these sixteen together are collectively termed the dharma-dhātu.
How are the bases (āyatana) established?
It is said that the ten material elements (rūpa-dhātu) are the ten material bases; the seven consciousness elements (vijñāna-dhātu) are the mind base (mana-āyatana);

and the dharma-element (dharma-dhātu) is the dharma-base (dharma-āyatana). By this principle, all [phenomena] are subsumed within the three categories of aggregates, elements, and bases: namely, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), the dharma-element, and the mind base.

The ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) subsumes itself; and the sphere of mind (*mano-āyatana*) subsumes the seven consciousness elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Therefore, these three factors subsume all phenomena.
Having thus established the aggregates, elements, and bases, we shall now further analyze them based on this principle.
Question:
Since the eyes, ears, and noses each exist in two varieties, why are twenty-one elements not established?
Answer:
Although there are two [aspects], their realms are not distinct. Why is this so?

Their characteristics are similar because both possess the characteristic of the eye; their functions are similar because both perform the function of the eye-consciousness with respect to the object of the eye.
In this same way, the ear and nose should be understood according to reason.
To ensure the physical majesty of the body, two types [of faculties] arise for each. Why is this?
Because it is through such a distribution of one realm across two locations that the body attains its majestic form, and not by any other means.
Question:
Does visual consciousness arise based on each individual eye,
or does it also depend on both?
Answer:
It can also be based on both, because it apprehends them with clarity. Why is this so?

If both eyes are opened together, the perception of forms is clear and distinct, unlike when only one is opened; it is like lighting two lamps in a single room, where they together emit a single light that illuminates everything with extreme clarity.
Just as a single ray of light revolves around two lamps, one should know that the principle herein is likewise.
Question:
When various objects simultaneously appear before each individual sense-door, regarding these many objects, do multiple consciousnesses arise sequentially?
Do they arise simultaneously?
Answer:
Only a single consciousness arises at one time with various modes of activity.
If edible food comes into contact with the tongue faculty, one should know that the body-consciousness and the tongue-consciousness arise simultaneously and constantly.
Furthermore, because sound is intermittent, it does not proceed from one place to another in a continuous succession to reach a different location.

However, it is like a lamp placed in its own location, which can simultaneously emit light everywhere according to its power; the principle that sound is emitted instantaneously and pervades all places is likewise so.
Question:
Why is it that when sound is obstructed by something nearby, it is heard indistinctly?
Answer:
Because sound is subject to resistance (*sapratigha*), it arises within subtle gaps and minute openings of obstructions; therefore, it is not distinct.
Question:
Among the six consciousnesses, how many possess discrimination?
Answer:
Only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) possesses discrimination, by virtue of the three types of discrimination.

As for the three types of discrimination, they are: intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), recollective discrimination (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), and conceptualizing discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).
Intrinsic discrimination refers to the discrimination that operates upon the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) currently being experienced.
Recollection-based conceptualization refers to the conceptualization that follows by recollecting various conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) previously experienced.
Inferential conceptualization refers to the conceptualization that constructs and deliberates upon objects not currently perceived in the past, future, or present.

Furthermore, there are seven kinds of discrimination: namely, spontaneous discrimination regarding the object of focus, discrimination with signs, discrimination without signs, discrimination through seeking, discrimination through investigation, afflicted discrimination, and non-afflicted discrimination.

First, "conceptualization" refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), which lack conceptual differentiation regarding the characteristics of their objects because they operate spontaneously within their own respective domains.

"Conceptualization with images" refers to the two types of conceptualization—namely, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*)—because they grasp the various images of past and present objects.
Discrimination of the signless refers to the discrimination that seeks after objects in the future.
All remaining types of discrimination take conceptualization (abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa) as their intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because it functions through volitional deliberation;
at times it seeks, at times it investigates, and at times it engages in various conceptualizations, whether defiled or undefiled.
Question:
If consciousness is so named because it discerns form and other objects, why is it called "eye-consciousness" and so forth, rather than "form-consciousness" and so forth?
Answer:
The principle established by the fivefold explanation applies to the eye and so forth, but not to form and so forth. Why is this?
Because consciousness within the eye is called "eye-consciousness," since consciousness arises depending on the locus of the eye.
Furthermore, it is because consciousness arises by virtue of the existence of the eye. Why is this so?
Because if the faculty of the eye exists, visual consciousness necessarily arises; thus, one who is not blind can even see in the dark.
Visual consciousness does not necessarily arise simply because form exists, for those who are blind cannot see.
Furthermore, it is called "eye-consciousness" because it is the consciousness produced by the eye.
Because the consciousness also undergoes transformation due to the transformation of the eye; for while the visible form remains unchanged, the consciousness undergoes change.
This is like when the disease kāmalā impairs the visual faculty, causing one to perceive all colors such as blue as yellow.
Furthermore, it is called "eye-consciousness" because it belongs to the eye; this is because the seeds of consciousness follow along with the eye and thereby arise.
Moreover, it is called "eye-consciousness" because it assists the eye; this is because it brings about benefit or harm to it.

Why is this so? It is because the consciousness, conjoined with the sense faculties, experiences objects that cause benefit or harm to those faculties; it is not the case for the external objects themselves.
Furthermore, it is called "eye-consciousness" because it is the consciousness of the eye, and both are subsumed within the category of sentient beings.
Form is not like this, because it is not determinate.
As it is with eye-consciousness, so it is with the other consciousnesses.
Question:
Is it by means of the eye that forms are seen,
or is it by means of consciousness and so forth?
Answer:
It is not that the eye sees forms, nor is it consciousness and so forth; because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity, "seeing" is conventionally established based on their conjunction.

Furthermore, by virtue of six characteristics, the eye is preeminent among the factors in the seeing of forms, whereas consciousness and the others are not; therefore, it is said that the eye can see all forms.
What are the six?
First, by way of the cause of production, because the eye can produce them.
Second, by way of the locus, because seeing depends upon the eye.
Third, by way of immutability, because the eye is always of a single nature.
Fourth, by way of sovereign transformation, because it arises moment by moment without depending on the convergence of conditions.
Fifth, by way of majesty, because it serves as the adornment for the body that is its basis.
Sixth, by way of authoritative scripture (*āgama*), as it is said in the Sūtra:
"The eye is able to see forms.
Such sixfold characteristics as described cannot be found within consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other [factors].

Regarding the movement and transformation of consciousness, one should know that it arises through various types of differentiation. For what reason are the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena established within the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*, but not within the *skandhas*?
Because they do not possess the meaning of a "heap" (*skandha*).

Why is this so? Because the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are designated as "aggregates" (*skandha*) when they are briefly summarized as a collection of diverse distinctions, such as those of past and future.

The meaning of "accumulation" is the meaning of "aggregate. Since permanent phenomena do not possess this characteristic of accumulation, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not included within the aggregates.
For what reason are these very same phenomena explained through the distinct categories of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
It is because one wishes to cause the sentient beings to be converted to develop skillfulness regarding both the extensive and concise presentations.

Why is this so? Within the framework of the aggregates (*skandha*), form and consciousness are explained briefly; within the frameworks of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), seventeen are explained extensively as appropriate.

Furthermore, within the framework of the aggregates, feeling and the others are explained extensively; within the frameworks of the elements and bases, they are explained briefly as a single category: the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, within the gateway of the aggregates (*skandha*), only the establishment of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is taught; within the gateway of the elements (*dhātu*), there is an extensive exposition on the establishment of the grasper (*grāhaka*), the grasped (*grāhya*), and the nature of grasping (*upādāna*); and within the gateway of the bases (*āyatana*), only the establishment of the grasper and the grasped is taught, because this [gateway] reveals exclusively the gateway for the arising of grasping.
Having already explained the meaning of the ancillary discussion, I shall now interpret the main text.
Question:
As it is said in the Sūtras regarding the eye and the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*).
If it is the eye, is it also the eye-element?
And if it is the eye-element, is it also the eye?
Answer:
There may be that which is an eye but not the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), namely, the final eye of an Arhat.

There may be that which is the eye-element but not an eye, namely, when one is within the eggshell, during the *kalala* stage, the *arbuda* stage, or the *peśī* stage; or while in the mother’s womb, if the eye has not yet been obtained, or if it was obtained but subsequently lost.

If one is born among the beings of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there may be eyes that are causes for [future] eyes, or there may be eyes that are also the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu), namely in other states;
or there may be neither eyes nor the eye-element, namely when one has already entered the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu).

And as it is with the eye and the eye-element, so too should one understand, as appropriate, the ear, nose, tongue, and body, along with their respective elements— the ear-element and so forth— regarding the birth of the various noble ones in the formless realm.

Regarding the "final eye of an arhat," this refers to the final moment at the time of entering nirvāṇa; at that time, the eye is not the "eye-element" (cakṣurdhātu), because it is no longer a cause for any further eye.

Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) who possess the cause for eyes: this refers to those who, falling away from that state, are destined to be born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); because the *ālayavijñāna* maintains the seeds of the eyes, they will certainly produce eyes upon rebirth.
Because those born among that assembly of noble ones do not regress, there is no eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).

Regarding the presence of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) but the absence of the body (*kāya*): this refers exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), for they possess only the cause of the body.
It is not the case that [the mind] exists within the eggshell and so forth, because it must possess a body; if the body is destroyed, the life-span also ceases.
Question:
If there is a mind, is it also the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
If there is a mental element (manodhātu), is it also the mind (manas)?
Answer:
There may be that which is mind but not the mental element; namely, the final mind of an Arhat.

There may be that which is the mind-element (*manodhātu*) but not the mind (*manas*), namely, the causal basis of the mind belonging to one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Or there may be that which is both the mind and the mind-element, namely, in all other states.
There may be cases where there is neither mind (*manas*) nor the mind-element (*manodhātu*), namely, when one has already entered the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

There are instances where only the mind-element exists but not the mind; the reason for not including those who have entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is that they still possess the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).
Question:
If one is born and raised in that realm, does one use the eyes of that realm to see the forms of that realm?
Answer:
There are cases where one uses the eye of that very stage to see the forms of that same stage, or those of another stage.

That is to say: one born and growing in the desire realm may use an eye of the desire realm to see forms of the desire realm; or use an eye of the form realm to see forms of the form realm; or use an eye of a higher stage to see forms of a lower stage.
Just as the eye is directed toward forms, so too is the ear directed toward sounds.
Just as one is born and grows in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so too is one born and grows in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"Born" refers to the moment of first receiving birth.
"Vṛddhi" (growth) refers to subsequent increase.

If one is born and grows in the desire realm, one then uses the nose, tongue, and body associated with the desire realm to smell, taste, and feel the odors, flavors, and tangibles associated with the desire realm.

If one is born and grows in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one perceives the touch of one's own level with a body composed of form. Since the intrinsic nature of that realm is definitively devoid of odor and taste—because its inhabitants are free from craving for edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)—it follows by this principle that the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue do not exist there either.
If one is born and raised in the desire realm, one uses a mind characterized by desire to comprehend the dharmas of the three realms as well as untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
Just as it is for one born and raised in the desire realm, so it is for one born and raised in the form realm.

If one is born and grows in the formless realm, one cognizes the dharmas of one's own level and untainted dharmas by means of a mind consisting of formless formations; or, by means of an untainted mind, one cognizes the dharmas of the three realms and untainted dharmas.

Regarding the statement that "the mind of one practicing in the formless realm cognizes the dharmas of its own stage and untainted (anāsrava) dharmas," this refers to the noble disciples; whereas ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who are outsiders cognize only the dharmas of their own stage.
If one dwells in this dharma, there may be those who, by the power of prior hearing and cultivation (*śruta-vāsanā*), also take the higher stages as objects in order to give rise to them.
Question:
For what reason are the aggregates (*skandha*) arranged in such a sequence?
Answer: Because consciousness abides therein; that is to say, by means of the four stations of consciousness and consciousness itself.

Furthermore, because the former serves as the basis for the latter: it experiences in accordance with the characteristics of form; it cognizes in accordance with what has been experienced; it volitionally constructs in accordance with what has been cognized; and it discriminates in various places in accordance with what has been volitionally constructed.
"Experiencing according to its phenomenal characteristics" means that pleasant feelings and so forth arise due to the dual power of the faculties and their objects in accordance with those feelings.
"Cognizing according to what has been experienced" means grasping the various characteristics in accordance with what was experienced.
To act according to what has been cognized means that one performs various karmas in accordance with what has been conceived.

To discern each respective place according to what has been acted upon means that consciousness transforms within various objects and different realms of rebirth in accordance with the karma performed.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of defilement and purification; that is to say, if one relies on a particular basis from which defilement and purification arise;
or if, through the acts of experiencing, grasping signs, and formative construction, there is defilement and purification;
or [it refers to] that which is defiled and that which is purified.
It is for this reason that the order of the aggregates is taught.
If [the order] is based on the locus where defilement and purification arise, it refers to the body endowed with sense faculties (*sendriya-kāya*).
If it is based on experience, it refers to feelings that are either defiled or undefiled, and so forth.
In their respective order, there is defilement and purification.
If one acts by grasping at signs, then—due to functioning either in accordance with or contrary to reality—there is, respectively, defilement and purification.

Regarding that which is defiled and that which is purified: it means that the mind possesses *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness), and [the purification occurs] because the state of being free from *dausthulya* arises.
For what reason are the elements (*dhātu*) arranged in this specific order?
Because it evolves according to the distinctions of worldly affairs, how does it evolve through the distinctions of worldly affairs?

It is said that among people in the world, they first see one another; having seen one another, they exchange greetings; having exchanged greetings, they then receive bathing, ointments, and flower garlands; next, they receive various kinds of excellent food and drink; next, they receive various kinds of bedding and female attendants; and only thereafter does the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) engage in discrimination in various places.
The external elements are established according to the sequence of the internal elements, and the consciousness elements are established following that same sequence.
As it is with the sequence of the elements (*dhātu*), so it is with the bases (*āyatana*).
Question:
What is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha)?
Answer:

Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, in brief, is called the single aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), in the sense of being a collection, just like a heap of wealth.
In this manner, it should be understood up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*):
based upon eleven kinds of bases for craving, distinctions such as "past" and so forth are established with respect to phenomena such as form (*rūpa*).

The eleven kinds of craving are: craving for attachment, craving for hope, craving for clinging, craving for an internal self, craving for objects, craving for sensual desires, craving for meditative concentration, craving for the suffering of unwholesome conduct, craving for the pleasure of wholesome conduct, craving for the distant, and craving for the near.
Based on such objects of craving, the various distinctions of the past and so forth are established in their respective order.

Furthermore, there are other distinctions: namely, the distinction between what has arisen and what has not yet arisen; the distinction between the grasper and the grasped; the distinction between the extroverted and the introverted; the distinction between the defiled and the undefiled; and the distinction between the proximate and the remote. Accordingly, the distinctions of the past and so forth are established among all phenomena, such as form and the rest, as appropriate.
That which has already arisen refers to the past and the present;
that which has not yet arisen refers to the future.
The "external gate" refers to the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).
The "internal gate" refers to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-bhūmi*).
The remaining phrases are easily understood and need not be further analyzed.
Furthermore, because their characteristic of suffering is vast, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*), like a great heap of timber.
Because, based upon form and so forth, there arises the vast suffering of birth and so on.
As the Sūtra says:
"In this way, this entire great mass of suffering accumulates."
Furthermore, they are called *skandhas* (aggregates) because they bear the burden of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), just as one bears a load on the shoulders.

To "bear the burden of defilement" means that various defiled phenomena, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*), depend upon [the aggregates] such as form (*rūpa*). For example, in the world, a certain part of the body is able to bear a load; this very part is called the "shoulder" and is also called a "skandha."
Form and the other [aggregates] are likewise; because they can bear the burden of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
Question:
What is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*)?
Answer:
It has the meaning of the seeds of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
That is to say, based on the seeds of all phenomena within the *ālayavijñāna*, they are designated as "elements" (*dhātu*), because "element" carries the meaning of "cause."
Furthermore, the meaning of "dhātu" (element) is that which maintains its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Moreover, the meaning of "dhātu" is that which maintains the nature of cause and effect.

That which maintains the nature of cause and effect refers, within the eighteen *dhātus*, to the various elements of the faculties and their objects, as well as the six consciousness-elements, respectively.
Furthermore, the meaning of *dhātu* (element) is the sense of maintaining the distinctions among all phenomena.
Regarding the maintenance of the distinctions among all phenomena,
various sūtras state that the elements such as earth (*pṛthivī*), as well as the remaining elements, are all subsumed within the eighteen *dhātus* as appropriate.
Question:
What is the meaning of "basis" (āyatana)?
Answer:
The meaning of being a gateway for the growth of consciousness is the meaning of "base" (*āyatana*).
It should be understood that the meaning of being a seed, which encompasses the differentiation of all phenomena, is also the meaning of "base.
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said:
Form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a floating bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion.
Question:
For what reason is form like a mass of foam, and so on, up to consciousness being like a magical illusion?
Answer:
Because it is without self, because it is devoid of purity, because its flavor is slight, and because it is not solid.
That which is the meaning of being non-existent, remote from falsehood, and lacking solidity—these are the meanings of the phrases spoken in this sutra.
Furthermore, in order to counteract the four inversions of self, purity, pleasure, and permanence, the various phrases such as "non-self" and so forth are taught in their respective order.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Two;
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Three.
The Commentary by Sthiramati Bodhisattva, compiled by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter One, Part Three: The Section on the Exposition of the Fundamentals, "The Chapter on the Three Dharmas. Furthermore, what is the extensive analysis of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
The summary verse says:
"Substantial existence and so forth, the knowable and so forth; Form and so forth, the outflows and so forth, the arisen and so forth;
The past and so forth, the various conditions and so forth— What, how many kinds, and for what purpose?"
Question:
Among the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana), what is substantially existent?
How many are substantially existent?
For what purpose is that which exists substantially investigated?
Answer:
That which does not depend on designations and is distinct from other sense-bases and objects is the meaning of "existing substantially."
All things are substantially existent.
One examines substantial existence in order to abandon the attachment to a substantially existent self.
These three questions are established for the purpose of severing the two types of delusion regarding characteristics and entities, as well as the adherence to the view of reification (*samāropa*).
"What is it that truly exists?"—this explains the characteristics of true existence in order to eliminate delusion regarding characteristics.
"All truly exists"—this is for the purpose of eliminating delusion regarding phenomena.
"Abandoning attachment to a real self"—this is for the purpose of eliminating the grasping of superimposition (*samāropa*).
In this manner, other instances should be understood accordingly.
"Not depending on verbal designations for the faculties and objects" means that one apprehends their own respective referents without conceptualizing verbal designations such as "form" or "feeling."

"Not depending on this or other faculties and objects" means that one cognizes one's own object of cognition without depending on these other meanings; it is not like the case of things such as a jar, where the cognition of a "jar" must arise by depending on names, conventions, and qualities such as color and fragrance.
What is provisional existence?
How many things are provisionally existent?
For what purpose is provisional existence investigated?
This means that, in dependence upon names and conventions, these other faculties and objects are of the nature of being conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
All things are conventionally existent;
one investigates conventional existence in order to abandon the attachment to a truly existent self.
What is conventional existence?
How many things are conventionally existent?
For what purpose is conventional existence investigated?
This means that the objects of the defiled are conventionally existent.
All things are conventionally existent;
one investigates the conventional in order to abandon attachment to a self characterized by defilement.
That which has defilement as its object is so called because it can give rise to all forms of defilement.
That which has the characteristic of defilement is the self, because one clings to the self as the cause of defilement.
What is ultimate existence?
How many things are ultimately existent?
For what purpose is ultimate existence investigated?
This means that the objects of purification are ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*).
All things are ultimately existent;
however, one examines ultimate existence in order to abandon the attachment to the characteristic of a pure self.
Regarding the object of purification (*viśuddhyālambana*): it is that which serves as the basis for attaining purification, because it is the objective domain of supreme wisdom.
That "all things exist as ultimate reality" (*paramārthasat*) is because all phenomena are not separate from *tathatā*.
The selflessness of all phenomena is called suchness (*tathatā*), because that selflessness truly exists.
What is the object of knowledge?
How many are the objects of knowledge?
For what purpose does one examine the objects of knowledge?
It is because there are five kinds of objects of knowledge:
form, mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned.

"Matter" refers to the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*), comprising the ten material elements (*dhātu*), the ten material bases (*āyatana*), and all forms included within the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
"Mind" refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), comprising the seven consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*).

Mental concomitants (caitasika-dharma) refer to the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), and a portion of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana).
Mental non-concomitants (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra) refer to the dissociated portion of the aggregate of formations and a portion of the dharma-element and the dharma-base.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Whether it be the basis upon which defilement and purification occur; that which is defiled or purified; that which causes defilement or purification; the state thereof; or the nature of its purity—it is by virtue of depending on these that all such things are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
The "locus" refers to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
The "objects of defilement and purification" refers to mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).
The "agents of defilement and purification" refers to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) such as greed and faith, respectively.
"States" (avasthā) refers to the designation of dharmas dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) based upon the states of form (rūpa), mind (citta), and mental factors (caitta).
"Pure nature" (viśuddhi-svabhāva) refers to pure unconditioned dharmas (anāsrava-asamskṛta-dharma).
It is not all [of them] as might be expected. Why is this?
Because only the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are of a pure nature.

Furthermore, "the phenomena that are objects of knowledge" refers to those which are the domain of the wisdom of faith and understanding; the domain of the wisdom of reasoning; the domain of the wisdom of non-distraction; the domain of the wisdom of internal realization; the domain of the wisdom of other-nature; the domain of lower wisdom; the domain of higher wisdom; the domain of the wisdom of revulsion; the domain of the wisdom of non-arising; the domain of the wisdom of non-birth; the domain of the wisdom of wisdom; the domain of ultimate wisdom; and the domain of the wisdom of great significance.
It should be understood that within this context, the meaning of the knowable is revealed through the objects of thirteen kinds of knowledge.

These thirteen kinds of knowledge are: knowledge born of hearing, knowledge born of reflection, mundane knowledge born of cultivation, ultimate knowledge, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, and Mahāyāna knowledge.
These various knowledges correspond to their respective order as the knowledge of conviction and so forth.
The "knowledge of others' minds" is called the "knowledge of other-nature" because it takes the mind of another as its object.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is called "lower knowledge" because it arises first with respect to the truths. The subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is called "higher knowledge" because it arises after the knowledge of phenomena.

It is called the "knowledge of revulsion" (*vidūṣaṇajñāna*) because it serves to produce revulsion; the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) because it serves to prevent [defilements] from arising; the "knowledge of non-origination" (*anutpādajñāna*) because it takes non-origination as its object; the "knowledge of knowledge" (*jñānajñāna*) because it takes knowledge as its object; the "ultimate knowledge" (*niṣṭhājñāna*) because it takes the ultimate as its object; and the "knowledge of great significance" (*mahārthajñāna*) because it takes great significance as its object.
Benefiting oneself and benefiting others is called the "great purpose.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is a knower or a seer, one investigates the objects of knowledge.
What is it that is cognized?
How many are the objects of cognition?
For what purpose are they investigated as objects of cognition?

It should be understood that their meaning as objects of cognition consists of: being non-conceptual, being conceptual, being the cause, being the transformation, being the characteristic, being that which is produced by the characteristic, being the antidote and the counteracted, and subtle differentiation.
That which is non-conceptual refers to the five bodies of sensory consciousness.
That which is conceptual refers to the body of mental consciousness.
The cause refers to the ālayavijñāna.
"Transformation" refers to the remaining consciousnesses.
"Aspects" refer to the sense faculties and their objects.
"That which is produced from aspects" refers to the various consciousnesses produced by the sense faculties and their objects.

Regarding "the remedial and the remediable," this refers to states such as having greed versus being free from greed, having hatred versus being free from hatred, and having delusion versus being free from delusion.
Regarding "subtle distinctions," this refers to the distinctions among the seven types of discernment that are difficult to recognize.

Regarding the seven kinds of discernment that are difficult to recognize: first is the discernment of the unknowable vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which is so because its mode of activity is non-conceptual at all times.

Second is the discernment of various modes of activity; this refers to how a single phenomenon or a single action possesses various characteristics, and because it is difficult to establish [these], it is subtle.

Third is simultaneous discernment, which refers to the simultaneous arising of various consciousnesses at one and the same time; how then do they each individually discern their own respective objects?
This objection is difficult to establish, and for this reason, [the nature of consciousness] is subtle.
One should know that this term "subtle" applies universally.

It refers to the rapid transformation and discernment between the four types of remedies and their respective objects to be remedied; that is, how can one who is bound by all fetters possess a mind of desire and so forth, yet in an instant transform it to give rise to a mind free from desire and so forth?

Regarding the discernment of the five habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): this refers to the perfuming of the mind by the manifestation of various karmas. How is it that these habitual tendencies are neither distinct from the mind nor identical to the mind, and furthermore, how do they evolve sequentially at the time of producing their results?

Sixth is the discernment of continuity: how is it that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of immeasurable kinds of karma that project one's own body, which reside within consciousness, give rise to a momentary awakening at the point when life is about to end—distinct from other [karmic states]—so that the habitual tendencies of other karmas may transfer to another realm of existence and cause rebirth to continue?

The seventh is the discernment of liberation, which refers to the mind of an Arhat realizing the first nature of phenomena (dharmatā) free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca). Having transcended all types of contaminated formations (sāsrava-saṃskāra) previously accumulated throughout saṃsāra, how does this mind continue to flow in its modes of activity?
Because this objection cannot be established, it is subtle.
Thus, one should know that all things are objects of cognition.
One examines the object of cognition in order to abandon attachment to such things as a "seer" and so forth.
The mention of "the seer" and so forth should be understood as indicating the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the toucher, and the cognizer.
What is it that is thoroughly penetrated?
What is that which is thoroughly penetrated?
For what purpose is that which is thoroughly penetrated investigated?

It is said: because of transformation, because of following what is heard, because of entering into practice, because of coming, because of going, and because of renunciation—these are the meanings of that which is thoroughly penetrated.

Regarding "that which is thoroughly penetrated," this refers to the objective spheres of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Because they are manifested through the various modes of operation of the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi*), these penetrated spheres are termed "transformation."
Because one thoroughly understands the various sounds of different realms through the supernormal power of the divine ear, it is called "following what is heard.
Because one thoroughly understands various mental activities such as the presence of desire through the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, it is called "entering into conduct."
Because one thoroughly knows through the supernormal power of recollecting past lives the successive events of past existences, it is called "coming.
Because one thoroughly understands through the supernormal power of the divine eye the matters of future births and destinations, it is called "going."

Because one thoroughly understands the means for liberation from the three realms through the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), it is called "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
All such things are what is to be thoroughly penetrated, because the [remaining] three supernormal knowledges subsequently take all objects as their universal cognitive range.
In order to abandon attachment to a self characterized by personal majesty, one investigates that which is thoroughly realized:
What is possessed of form?
How many things are possessed of form?

For what purpose is there the contemplation of that which possesses form (*rūpin*)? It is because of the following meanings: by way of the intrinsic nature of form; by way of dependence on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); by way of the accumulation of delight; by way of having a location; by way of pervading space; by way of being describable as a location; by way of being the range of activity for locations; by way of being the common range of activity for both [internal and external]; by way of connection; by way of persistence; by way of manifestation; by way of transformation and decay; by way of demonstration; by way of accumulation and establishment; by way of the external door; by way of the internal door; by way of long duration; by way of limitation; by way of temporariness; and by way of presentation—these are the meanings of "possessing form."
Regarding the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*): it means that form itself is taken as its own nature; therefore, it is called "possessing form" (*rūpin*).
It is not called "possessing form" because it is conjoined with other forms; for this reason, the intrinsic nature of form is explained first.
Regarding "depending on the primary elements" (*mahābhūta*), this indicates that they are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*) because they are conjoined with other forms.

All derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) are called "possessing form" because they are conjoined with the forms of the primary elements; all forms of the primary elements are called "possessing form" because they are mutually conjoined with one another.

Regarding "accumulation through delight" (*nandisamudaya*): it refers to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that have delight as their cause of accumulation; thus they are called "accumulation through delight.
This is not like present delight and craving, which are called "accumulation through delight" because they have prior contact, sensation, and so forth as their cause of accumulation.
That which possesses a location has spatial dimensions.
That which occupies space has its physical magnitude pervading the ten directions.
That which can be described as having a location can be said to be "here" or "there."
"Functioning according to location" means that it takes as its object the nature of the specific location where it resides.
"Functioning with a common object" means that it takes as its object that which is commonly perceived by two sentient beings.
It is not like formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*), because others cannot apprehend what one has personally experienced.

As for "being connected" (*saṃyukta*), it means that visual consciousness and the others are also called "bound to form" (*rūpabaddha*), because they are connected to the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
"Following along" refers to ordinary beings born in the formless realm, because they are followed by the seeds of all forms.
"Manifesting" refers to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), because they are able to manifest the objects of perception.

"Subject to transformation and decay" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Because they are affected by contact with hands and the like, or afflicted by sensations and the like, they undergo transformation and decay as appropriate; for "transformation and decay" is the very meaning of "form" (*rūpa*).
"Manifestation" refers to the fact that various verbal expressions manifest meanings.
"Accumulated establishment" refers to the fact that matter consisting of atoms or more possesses subtle parts that can be established.
The "external gate" refers to the forms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because they are produced by craving for the exquisite objects of desire.
The "internal gate" refers to the forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because they are produced by craving for the meditative mind.
By this principle, those various forms are called the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Regarding "long-lasting": it means that the forms of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot be established, because they have finite limits at both the prior and subsequent ends of time.
"Having a limit" refers to the form of those in training (*śaikṣa*), because they have already established a limit to birth and death.
"Temporary" refers to the form of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because they possess only the single body of the present existence.
"Manifestation" refers to the various forms manifested by the Tathāgatas and others; these are merely manifestations and not real.
All of them are possessed of form, or [are so] as appropriate to each case.
"All are with form" refers to the form of transformation and decay, and so forth.
"According to what is appropriate" refers to the other six categories, such as external forms and the rest.
It should be understood that the distinctions among these forms are the same as those for feeling and the other aggregates.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that possesses form, one examines that which possesses form.
What is that which lacks form?
How many things lack form?
For what purpose is the formless (ārūpya) examined?
The meaning of "formless" is that which is contrary to having form (rūpa).
All [factors] are formless, or [they are so] as the case may require.
In order to abandon attachment to a formless self, one examines the formless.
That "all are formless" means they are associated with the characteristics of the formless.
How can there be anything visible?
What is "with visibility"?
For what purpose is it examined as being with visibility?
It means that which is the objective domain of the eye is the sense of "being with visibility."

The remaining distinctions are as explained for "possessing form" (*rūpin*); that is, just as it was previously stated that from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form up to its manifestation it is called "possessing form," so too from the intrinsic nature of being visible (*sanidarśana*) up to its manifestation it is called "visible."
All are with visibility, or as the case may require.
Regarding "all are with visibility," this refers to those that are associated with visibility and so forth. Why is this so?
Because all formless phenomena are associated with visible form, they are also termed "visible.
One examines what is visible in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is the object of the eye.
What is non-visibility?
How many are non-visible?
For what purpose is non-visibility investigated?
That which is contrary to being visible is the meaning of being invisible.
All things are invisible, or [invisible] as the case may require.
One examines invisibility in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is not an object of the eye.
What is the resistant?
How many are resistant?
For what purpose is the resistant investigated?
That is to say, all that is visible is also resistant.
Furthermore, it is called "resistant" for three reasons: by way of its nature, by way of accumulation, and by way of being unrefined.

Regarding "category" (*jāti*): it refers to all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) acting as mutual obstructions (*pratighāta*) for one another and being mutually obstructed by one another. To act as an obstruction to coming and going is the meaning of "having resistance" (*sapratigha*).

One should simply say they act as mutual obstructions; however, the reason for further stating that they are mutually obstructed is to establish that light and other such forms are also "having resistance," because they are exclusively objects of obstruction and lack the nature of being an active obstruction, as is their inherent nature.
"Kind" (*jāti*) has the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
"Accumulated" refers to that which is above the level of the atom (*paramāṇu*), because a single atom lacks resistance.

"Unrefined" refers to matter that does not function through mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*); for matter transformed by the power of mastery over meditative absorption is without resistance, as is the case with the gods of the Heaven of Equal Mind (*samacitta*).

Furthermore, the sense of "having resistance" (sapratigha) refers to the basis for harm; that is, whatever serves as a basis or an object capable of giving rise to hatred is called "having resistance.

Precisely because they possess this sense of having resistance, all [phenomena] are "having resistance," or rather, they are so designated according to their respective natures, which refers to the remaining meanings.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is not omnipresent, one examines that which is resistant.
What is non-resistant?
How many things are non-resistant?
For what purpose is non-resistance (*apratigha*) investigated?
It means that the opposite of resistance (*sapratigha*) is the meaning of non-resistance.
All [phenomena] are non-resistant, or as the case may require.
In order to abandon attachment to a pervasive self, one examines what is non-obstructive (*apratigha*).
What is with-outflows (*sāsrava*)?
How many are with-outflows?
For what purpose are they examined as being with outflows (*sāsrava*)?

It means that they are "with outflows" by virtue of being the intrinsic nature of outflows, being associated with outflows, being bound by outflows, being pursued by outflows, being conducive to outflows, and being of the same category as outflows. This is the meaning of being "with outflows."
Regarding the nature of the outflows (*āsrava-svabhāva*): because they possess the nature of being outflows by virtue of their own essential nature, they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

Regarding the association with the outflows (*āsrava-saṃprayukta*): because the mental states and mental factors that coexist with the outflows, as well as the eyes and so forth, are associated with the outflows and serve as the basis for the outflows, they are respectively called "with outflows."
"Bound by outflows" refers to wholesome dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*), because they bring about future existence through the power of the outflows.
"Followed by outflows" refers to the dharmas of other stages, because they are also pursued by the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the various outflows belonging to those other stages.

Regarding "conducive to outflows" (*āsrava-anuloma*): it refers to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). Although they are accompanied by the latencies of the afflictions (*kleśa-dausthulya*), they are nonetheless established as being of an outflow-free nature (*anāsrava-svabhāva*), because they turn away from all existence (*bhava*) and accord with their antidotes.
Regarding the category of "with outflows" (*sāsrava*): this refers to the contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat, as they are produced by afflictions (*kleśa*) from previous lives.

The five appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), fifteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of three elements and two bases are with outflows. This is because, excluding the aforementioned portion of the three elements and two bases that constitute the retinue of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which are not with outflows, the remainder are indeed with outflows.
One examines that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) in order to abandon attachment to a self conjoined with outflows.
What is without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
How many are without outflows?
For what purpose is the untainted (*anāsrava*) investigated?
The meaning of "untainted" is that which is contrary to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
All five aggregates of non-appropriation (*anupādānaskandha*), as well as a portion of three realms and two bases (*āyatana*), are untainted.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), one contemplates what is without outflows.
What is "with conflict" (*saraṇa*)?
How many things are with conflict?
For what purpose is there the contemplation of that which is with contention (*saraṇa*)?
It means that by relying on such greed, hatred, and delusion, one grasps swords and staves and initiates all manner of strife, litigation, and conflict.
The grasping of swords, staves, and so forth is the cause of contention; greed and the like are the intrinsic nature of contention.
Thus, by virtue of being its intrinsic nature, its association, its bondage, its accompaniment, its conformity, and its category, it possesses the meaning of "being contentious."
To whatever extent there are outflows (*āsrava*), to that same extent there are disputes (*saraṇa*), because they share the same underlying referent.
One examines "that which is with dispute" (*saraṇa*) in order to abandon the attachment to a self associated with dispute.
What is the absence of contention?
How many things constitute the absence of contention?
For what purpose is the absence of contention investigated?
That which is contrary to the characteristic of contention is the meaning of non-contention (*araṇā*).
To the extent that there are outflows (*āsrava*), to that same extent there is non-contention.
One investigates non-contention in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from contention.
What is that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)? How many things are associated with outflows?
For what purpose is that which is associated with outflows investigated?
That is to say, based on such greed, hatred, and delusion, one becomes defiled by and attached to a future personal existence.

Because it is its intrinsic nature, because it is associated with it, because it is bound by it, because it follows after it, because it conforms to it, and because it is of its same category—this is the meaning of being "defiled."
Regarding "attachment to future existence": greed, hatred, and delusion are the causes for attachment to future existence; therefore, they are called "defilements" (*saṃkleśa*).
How is it that hatred is a cause for attachment to future existence?
This means that because one feels aversion and envy toward all pure dharmas and is stained by attachment to future existence (*punarbhava*), there is conflict (*raṇa*) to such an extent;
likewise, there is defilement (*saṃkleśa*) to the same extent.
In order to abandon attachment to a self associated with defilement (*saṃkliṣṭa*), one examines that which is defiled.
What is undefiled (*asaṃkliṣṭa*)?
How many are undefiled?
For what purpose is non-defilement (asaṃkliṣṭa) investigated?
It means that being the opposite of defilement is the meaning of non-defilement.
To the extent that there is a measure of non-contention (araṇā), so too is there a measure of non-defilement.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from defilement, one contemplates non-defilement.
What is reliance on indulgence?
How many are reliance on indulgence?
For what purpose is there the contemplation of reliance on indulgence?
It means that if one relies on such greed, hatred, and delusion, one becomes stained by attachment to the five objects of desire.

Because it is their intrinsic nature, because of their association, because of being bound by them, because of their persistence, because of their conformity, and because of their category, this is the meaning of reliance on indulgence.
What kind of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) gives rise to defiled attachment?
It is the malice and envy toward renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
In this way, up to the extent that there is defilement, so too is there indulgence (*gardha*) upon which it depends.
In order to abandon attachment to the self as being conjoined with indulgence, one examines that which relies on indulgence.
What is that which relies on renunciation?
How many are those that rely on renunciation?
For what purpose is there the contemplation of reliance on renunciation?
It means that reliance on renunciation is the sense of being contrary to indulgence (*gardha*).
To whatever extent there is freedom from defilement (*asaṃkleśa*), to that same extent there is renunciation.
