In order to abandon attachment to and clinging toward a self that is free from indulgence, one investigates renunciation.
What is conditioned? How many things are conditioned?
For what purpose is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) investigated?
It should be understood that the meaning of "conditioned" refers to those phenomena for which arising, cessation, duration, and change can be discerned.
All things are conditioned, with the sole exception of one portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).
One examines conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) in order to abandon attachment to a self that is impermanent.
What is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
How many are unconditioned?
For what purpose is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) investigated?
It means that the opposite of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the meaning of the unconditioned.
A portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) is unconditioned.
In order to abandon attachment to a permanent self, one contemplates the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question: Should the five aggregates without grasping (*anupādāna-skandha*) be called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned?
Answer:
One should not say that it is either conditioned or unconditioned. Why is this?
Because it is not produced by any karma or afflictions, it should not be called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
because it accords with desire whether it is limited by time or not limited by time, it should not be called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why is this so? Because the appropriated aggregates can be taken up according to one's desire, whether they are manifest or unmanifest;
the unconditioned is not like this, because it is eternally abiding.
Question:
As the Bhagavat has taught, all phenomena are of two kinds, namely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why, then, is it now said that this phenomenon is neither conditioned nor unconditioned?
Answer:
This, too, does not depart from these two kinds. Why is that?
If by this meaning it is called "conditioned," it is not by this same meaning that it is called "unconditioned.
If by this meaning it is called "unconditioned," it is not by this same meaning that it is called "conditioned."
Based on this principle, only two types are taught.
Why is this? Because they are designated as "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) in the sense of appearing or not appearing according to one's desire.
Because it is not produced by any karma or afflictions, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, this too is not apart from these two kinds.
What is the mundane?
What is the mundane?
For what purpose is the mundane investigated?
That which is comprised within the three realms, as well as that which appears as resembling those [realms] subsequently attained through supramundane wisdom—this is the meaning of "mundane."
"Appearing as that" means appearing as the characteristics subsumed within the three realms.
As for the appearances manifesting as suchness and so forth, these are supramundane, because they have never been attained before.

Thus, a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*), fifteen of the elements (*dhātu*), ten of the bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, and a portion of three elements and two bases constitute the mundane (*loka*).

Regarding the "portion," this refers to excluding those factors subsumed under correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), those that appear as if they were supramundane following such knowledge, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is the basis for the world, one examines the world.
What is supramundane?
How many things are supramundane?
For what purpose is the supramundane observed?

It is because it serves as the antidote to the three realms, being non-erroneous, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and non-conceptual; this is the meaning of the non-conceptual supramundane.
That which can counteract the three realms refers to the various noble paths (*āryamārga*).
These are further divided into two types:

first, those attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which counteract the inversions such as [the notion of] permanence; because they are free from inverted conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they are called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*).

That which is attained by the two types of bodhisattvas and others is called "non-conceptual" because it counteracts the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena such as form and because it is free from conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, it is called non-conceptual because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not the basis for any conceptualization.
Furthermore, that which is acquired after emerging from the supramundane is also called "supramundane," because it relies upon the supramundane.
Thus, a portion of these aggregates (*skandha*), as well as a portion of two bases (*āyatana*) and three realms (*dhātu*), are supramundane.
In order to abandon attachment to a solitary self, one examines that which transcends the world.
What is "already arisen"?
How many are "already arisen"?
For what purpose is that which has already arisen observed?
It means that the past and the present constitute the sense of "already arisen.
All [conditioned phenomena] in part are already arisen.
One investigates that which has already arisen (*jāta*) in order to abandon attachment to a non-eternal self.

Furthermore, there are twenty-four kinds of what has already arisen: namely, initial arising; continuous arising; nourished arising; dependent arising; transformed arising; matured arising; regressive arising; progressive arising; pure arising; impure arising; functioning arising; arising with seeds; arising without seeds; arising as a manifestation of mastery over images; successive arising; momentary destruction arising; arising through separation and meeting; arising from different states; arising from birth and death; arising from formation and disintegration; arising at the prior time; arising at the time of death; arising at the intermediate time; and arising at the time of continuity.
"Arising at the very beginning" refers to the moment of initial rebirth.
"Arising through continuity" refers to the period following rebirth.
"Arising through nourishment" refers to the four types of nourishment caused by sleep, dreams, food and drink, and the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That which has arisen based on a support refers to the internal sense faculties.
That which has arisen through transformation refers to the modification of the sense faculties that can conform to the arising of pleasant feelings and so forth.
"Already arisen through maturation" refers to the stage of old age and decay.
"Already arisen through decline" refers to abandoning a birth in a happy realm and being born in an evil realm.
"Already arisen through excellence" refers to that which is the opposite of the latter.
Regarding those who have already attained purity: this refers to those who, through playfulness, forgetfulness, mental distraction, or resentment, are characterized by negligence.

Because the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*), the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), and the various gods of the Form and Formless Realms (*rūpa-arūpya-dhātu*) are largely negligent, they exercise mastery over the objects of their enjoyment and the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) in which they dwell, according to their respective capacities.
"Already arisen but not yet purified" refers to those remaining [skandhas].
"Already arisen and in operation" refers to the state of coming and going.
"Already arisen with seeds" refers to all except for the final skandha of an Arhat.
That which has arisen without seeds refers to the final aggregate (*skandha*).

That which has arisen as a manifestation through mastery over images refers, respectively, to matter that is concordant with the objects of knowledge, matter produced from liberation, and the matter of the Tathāgatas and so forth.
"Arising through successive succession" refers to the continuity of preceding and succeeding births.
"Arising after momentary destruction" refers to the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in each individual moment.

"Arising through conjunction and separation" refers to the states of encountering or parting from what is pleasant or unpleasant, as well as the mind’s states of being with or free from craving for existence.
"Already arisen in different states" refers to the stages such as the kalala and so forth.
"Already arisen in birth and death" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
"Already arisen in formation and destruction" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
That which has already arisen at the prior time refers to the existence of the prior time (pūrvakālabhava).
That which has already arisen at the time of death refers to the existence at death (maraṇabhava).
That which has already arisen at the intermediate time refers to the intermediate existence (antarābhava).
Regarding "that which has already arisen in the continuum," this refers to the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
What is not yet arisen? How many are not yet arisen?
For what purpose is that which is "not yet arisen" investigated?
It refers to future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); this is the meaning of "not yet arisen.
A portion of all phenomena constitutes "not yet arisen."
In order to abandon attachment to a permanent self, one contemplates that which is "not yet arisen.
Furthermore, being the opposite of "already arisen" is the meaning of "not yet arisen.
How, then, can it be an apprehender?
What is the grasper?
For what purpose is the grasper investigated?
It refers to the material sense faculties, as well as the mind and mental factors; these constitute the meaning of "grasper."

The three aggregates in their entirety, a portion of the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations, the characteristic of being a faculty, and the characteristic of association—respectively, these twelve elements (*dhātu*) and six bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, along with a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), specifically that which is associated and constitutes its own essence, are the grasper (*grāhaka*).
In order to abandon attachment to a self that experiences objects, one examines the grasper (*grāhaka*).
This "self that experiences" is the conceit that "I am able to obtain desirable and undesirable objects.

Furthermore, there are four types of graspers: the grasper of the non-attained, the grasper of the attained, the grasper of distinct present objects in their specific characteristics, and the grasper of all objects at all times in both their specific and general characteristics.
"Non-reaching apprehenders" refers to the faculties of the eye, ear, and mind.
"Reaching apprehenders" refers to the remaining faculties.
"Apprehenders of their own-characteristics, present, and distinct objects" refers to those produced by the five physical faculties.
That which can apprehend all self-characteristics and common characteristics at all times and across all objects refers to that which is produced by the sixth faculty.
Furthermore, because consciousness and so forth arise through conjunction, the nature of being an apprehender is provisionally established.

Why is this so? It is because the consciousnesses and other phenomena produced through the conjunction of various conditions are conventionally designated as "graspers," but not according to ultimate reality, for all dharmas are devoid of functional activity.
What is the grasped?
How many are the grasped?
For what purpose is the grasped investigated?
This means that all subjects (grāhaka) are also objects (grāhya), because the sense organs such as the eye are objects apprehended by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Alternatively, there are objects that are not subjects, namely, those objects which are the exclusive domain of the act of grasping itself.

The term "only" (*kevala*) has the sense of "exclusively. This statement is intended to distinguish [the object] from the mental factors (*caitta*), all of which are also objects of apprehension (*grāhya*).
One examines the apprehended object in order to abandon attachment to a self that resides within the objective sphere.
What is the external door?
How many are the external doors?
For what purpose is the external door investigated?

This means that phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are, by definition, "external" (*bahirmukha*), with the exception of the wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) based on the Buddha's teachings, as well as the mind, mental factors, and associated dharmas subsumed under the practice in accordance with those teachings (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
Question:

For what reason are the wisdoms born of hearing and reflection, as well as the mind, mental factors, and so forth subsumed under "practice in accordance with the Dharma," not considered "external gates"?
Answer:
Because the *niṣyanda-dharma* (outflowing phenomena) serves as the cause, through its power one takes *nirvāṇa* and so forth as an object.
By "outflowing phenomena" is meant the teachings of the various Buddhas that belong to the category of direct realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkāra*).

The four elements of nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness, as well as the two bases of odor and flavor—entirely and partially included within the desire realm—are the external doors (*bāhyamukha*).
One examines the external doors in order to abandon attachment to a self that is not free from desire.
What is the internal door?
How many are the internal doors?
For what purpose does one contemplate the internal door?
That which is the opposite of the external orientation is the meaning of the internal orientation (*antarmukha*).
With the exception of the four elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, and a portion of the remainder, these constitute the internal orientation.
One examines the internal orientation in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from desire.
What is defilement? How many are defiled?
For what purpose is defilement investigated?
This refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena; such is the meaning of being defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Regarding "obscured-unspecified," this refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth associated with the universal mental faculty (*sarvatraga-manas*), as well as the various afflictions bound to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
A portion of the aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). The ten elements are:
the seven consciousness-elements, the form-element, the sound-element, and the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*).
The four bases are: the form-base, the sound-base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
In order to abandon the attachment to a self conjoined with afflictions, one examines what is defiled.
What is undefiled? How many are undefiled?
For what purpose is non-defilement investigated?
It refers to wholesome (*kuśala*) and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena; this is the meaning of non-defilement.
The eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the remaining elements and bases, are non-defiled.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from afflictions, one examines what is non-defiled.
What is the past? How many things are the past?
For what purpose is the past investigated? It is because its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) have already arisen and ceased;

because cause and effect have already been experienced; because the functional activity of defilement and purity has already subsided; because the grasping of causes has already perished; because the fruit and its specific characteristics both exist and do not exist; because it is characterized by recollection and conceptualization; because attachment to it is the characteristic of defilement; and because relinquishing it is the characteristic of purity—this is the meaning of the past.
"Those whose causes and effects have already been experienced" refers to those that have already arisen and have already ceased, respectively.

"Those whose functions of defilement and purification have already passed away" refers to the absence of the functional capacity to defile or purify the mind, as in the case of present craving and so forth, or faith and so forth.
Regarding "the cause that has already been subsumed having perished": this is because it ceases only after the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been deposited.

Regarding "the fruit and its own-characteristic being both existent and non-existent": this means that at the present time, the habitual tendencies thus projected exist, whereas the substantial entity (*vastu*) that projects them does not exist.
The characteristic of recollective conceptualization refers to the fact that there is only the appearance of that object of cognition (*ālambana*).
All [conditioned phenomena] are, in one respect, past, because they exclude the future, the present, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration, one examines the past.
What is the future? How many things are of the future?
For what purpose is the future investigated? It is because its causes have not yet arisen;

because its own-characteristic has not yet been attained; because cause and effect have not yet been experienced; because the natures of affliction and purification have not yet manifested; because the own-characteristics of cause and effect exist and do not exist; because there is a longing for the characteristics of affliction; and because there is no longing for the characteristics of purification—this is the meaning of the future.
"Having causes but not yet arisen" is stated to exclude unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), for although they have not yet arisen, they lack causes.
"Not having attained their own-characteristic" means that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has not yet come into being.
Regarding "causes and results not yet experienced," this means that their seeds have not yet performed their function and their nature has not yet arisen.
A certain portion of all [phenomena] is future.
One examines the future in order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration.
What is the present? How many things are the present?
For what purpose is the present investigated?

It is because its own-characteristic has already arisen but not yet ceased; because the experience of cause and effect has not yet been fully undergone; because defilement and purity are manifest before one; because it can reveal the characteristics of the past and future; and because its activity is manifest—these are the meanings of the present.
Regarding "the experience of cause and effect, whether already experienced or not yet experienced," this means that because the cause has already ceased while the fruit still exists.
Regarding "that which can manifest the characteristics of the past and future," this means that the present world is that which can designate the characteristics of the past and future worlds.
Why is this so? Because the past and future are conventionally designated based upon the present.
The future is conventionally designated with reference to the state yet to be attained, and the past is conventionally designated with reference to the state already attained.
Regarding "the manifestation of activity": this refers to phenomena such as the eye serving as the actual basis for consciousness and so forth.
A portion of all [phenomena] is the present.
One examines the present in order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration.
Question:
For what reason are the past, future, and present described as "named things" (*nāmadheya-vastu*), whereas *nirvāṇa* and so forth are not?
Answer:
Because that which is personally realized within cannot be expressed, and because only the past, future, and present serve as the basis for verbal expression.
Why is this so? By means of speaking of things such as the past, three types of verbal objects (*vāgvastu*) within the sūtras are thereby revealed.

This means that [the establishment of time] is based on the three periods—past, future, and present—and not on nirvāṇa and so forth, because the latter is personally realized within and is free from verbal expression, making it impossible to describe.
Furthermore, only the past, future, and present serve as the basis for the verbal expressions of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing.
What is wholesome?
How many are wholesome?
For what purpose is the wholesome investigated?

The meaning of "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is defined by way of: intrinsic nature, association, persistence, origination, ultimate truth, birth-attainment, application, manifest offering, benefit, inclusion, antidote, tranquility, and outflow.
A portion of the five aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is wholesome.
As for the ten elements, they refer to the seven consciousness elements, the element of form, the element of sound, and the element of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
As for the four bases, they refer to the base of form, the base of sound, the base of mind, and the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is conjoined with phenomena, one examines what is wholesome.
That which is wholesome by nature refers to the eleven mental factors, such as faith and so forth.
That which is wholesome through association refers to those phenomena that are associated with them.
"Virtue by conformity" refers to the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those very dharmas.
"Virtue by origination" refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by them.
"Virtue in the ultimate sense" refers to *tathatā* (suchness).

Virtue acquired at birth refers to those very same wholesome dharmas which, due to having been practiced in previous lives, result in such a retribution; by virtue of this intrinsic nature, one spontaneously and effortlessly abides in delight therein without the need for deliberation.
"In that very place" refers to the locus of faith and so forth.
"By this intrinsic nature and not by means of reflection" means it is effortless (*anābhoga*) and does not depend on the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and the like.

Spontaneous abiding in happiness does not refer solely to sensual pleasure; it also includes that which is acquired at birth, as well as that which arises spontaneously in conjunction with faith and other [wholesome factors].

Skillfulness in means refers to relying upon and associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, attending to it correctly, and practicing the cultivation of pure wholesome dharmas in accordance with the Dharma.
"Cultivating pure goodness" refers to all wholesome dharmas arising from hearing and so forth within the True Dharma.

"Presently making offerings to goodness" refers to visualizing the Tathāgata, constructing shrines, or painting sacred images; or visualizing the True Dharma, transcribing and editing the Dharma-treasury, and performing acts of worship.
Benefiting others through goodness means benefiting all sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Gathering [beings] through goodness means, by means of meritorious actions consisting of giving and meritorious actions consisting of ethical discipline, gathering those who seek the maturation of heavenly bliss, gathering those who seek birth in wealthy and noble families, and gathering those who seek that which accords with the pure dharmas.
The phrase "attracting the maturation of heavenly bliss and birth into a wealthy and noble family" reveals the causes for attaining nobility.
The phrase "attracting that which accords with the pure dharmas" reveals the cause for attaining nirvana.

Regarding the wholesome factors of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*), these are: the counteraction of revulsion and destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of suppression (*viṣkambhaṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of dissociation (*visamyoga-pratipakṣa*), the counteraction of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*), and the counteraction of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*).
These various antidotes shall be explained in detail later.

Regarding "the excellence of tranquility": this refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred, the permanent abandonment of delusion, and the permanent abandonment of all afflictions; whether it be the cessation of perception and feeling, the nirvana-realm with remainder, the nirvana-realm without remainder, or the nirvana-realm of non-abiding—all such as these are termed the dharmas of the excellence of tranquility.

Regarding the "outflowing wholesome" (*niṣyanda-kuśala*): this refers to one who has already attained tranquility; by the predominant power of this [attainment], they give rise to superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which are common or uncommon to both mundane and supramundane realms.
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Three;
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Four.
Compiled by Bodhisattva Sthiramati.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
In the *Mūlavastu*, Chapter One: The Section on the Three Dharmas, Part Four. What is the unwholesome?
How many are unwholesome?
For what reasons is the unwholesome (akuśala) examined?

It is by way of intrinsic nature, association, persistence, origination, ultimate truth, birth-attainment, application, manifest worship, harm, attraction, opposition, and obstruction—these are the meanings of the unwholesome.
A portion of the five aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
One examines the unwholesome in order to abandon attachment to a self that is conjoined with what is non-dharmic.

That which is unwholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*) refers to all remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) capable of inciting misconduct, excluding those associated with the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) and the afflictions of the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, what is this?

Those [mental factors] bound to the desire realm that do not arise spontaneously are unwholesome; those that arise spontaneously and can incite unwholesome conduct are also unwholesome; the remainder are obscured-neutral.
Unwholesome by association refers to those phenomena that are associated with these very afflictions and secondary afflictions.
Unwholesome by persistence refers to their respective latencies (*vāsanā*).
Unwholesome by way of undertaking refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by that [unwholesome mind].
Unwholesome in the ultimate sense refers to all cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Innate unwholesomeness refers to obtaining such a maturation (*vipāka*) due to habitual practice of the unwholesome, whereby one spontaneously and effortlessly dwells in the unwholesome by virtue of that very nature.

Skillful means that are unwholesome refers to relying upon and associating with unwholesome persons, thereby hearing incorrect teachings and engaging in improper mental attention, which leads to the performance of unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.

Regarding "making offerings in person to those who are unwholesome": this refers to having first formed a mental image of and taken refuge in a particular class of celestial beings, and then—motivated either by an intent to kill or by wrong views—establishing shrines and engaging in acts of offering, thereby causing immeasurable multitudes to extensively plant roots of non-merit.
"Establishing shrines preceded by the intent to kill" refers to establishing shrines at places where cattle, sheep, and so forth are slaughtered as sacrifices to celestial deities.
"Establishing shrines preceded by wrong views" refers to establishing shrines at places where one seeks merit or makes vows through such practices as self-starvation and other forms of suffering.
Destructive unwholesomeness refers to the various forms of misconduct of body, speech, and mind committed in all circumstances.

Appropriating unwholesomeness refers to the fact that after performing various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, one brings about and appropriates undesirable results of maturation (*vipāka*)—either projecting (*ākṣepa*) or completing (*paripūri*) them—in both the miserable realms (*apāya*) and the happy realms (*sugati*). In the miserable realms, one fully experiences both the projected and completed results of maturation; in the happy realms, one experiences only the completed results, meaning that having been born there, one undergoes the suffering of poverty through the power of those evil deeds.
That which is unwholesome by way of being countered refers to those factors that are the objects countered by their respective remedies.
That which is unwholesome by way of being an obstacle refers to those factors that can obstruct the various categories of wholesome qualities, such as frequenting crowds and assemblies.
What is the indeterminate?
How many are indeterminate?
For what purpose is the indeterminate investigated?

That is to say, the meaning of "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) is established by way of intrinsic nature, association, persistence, origination, ultimate truth, birth-attainment, application, manifest offering, benefit, enjoyment, attraction, antidote, tranquility, and outflow.
The eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), elements, and bases, are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the eight elements: these refer to the five material sense-faculties and the elements of odor, taste, and tangibility; the same applies to the eight bases.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is distinct from both the dharma and the non-dharma, one examines the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding those that are indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*): these are the eight material elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), the factors associated with the mind (*manas-saṃprayukta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).

Regarding "associated with the indeterminate": this refers to the mind and mental factors—comprised within the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*)—of one who possesses a mind that is neither defiled nor pure.
A "mind that is neither defiled nor pure" indicates a state of mind that is contrary to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
"Being embraced by the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes" clarifies their mode of activity (*ākāra*), because they proceed by way of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).

"Following along with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)" refers to the very latencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-vāsanā*), because the mind is perfumed by the sets of names and so forth; from these latencies, subsequent conceptual proliferations arise.
That which is originated by the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by those minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are so categorized.

"Categorized by this" means the minds and mental factors belonging to one who harbors a mind that is neither defiled nor pure, and which are encompassed by the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.
The indeterminate by way of ultimate truth refers to space and non-analytical cessation.
The indeterminate acquired through birth refers to the retribution of all unwholesome and contaminated wholesome dharmas.

Regarding "indeterminate by way of expedient means" (*upāya-avyākṛta*): this refers to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) belonging to a mind that is neither defiled nor wholesome.

The phrase "a mind that is neither defiled nor wholesome" indicates that the modes of deportment and so forth produced by such a mind are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), whereas all other [mental states], as appropriate, are either wholesome or unwholesome.

Regarding "indeterminate acts of present offering," this refers to a case where someone, with a single-minded devotion and taking refuge in a particular class of celestial beings, establishes a shrine and performs acts of worship while remaining free from the intent to kill and from wrong views; such that for immeasurable multitudes, neither merit nor demerit arises in connection with that place.

Regarding "beneficial neutral [action]," it refers, for example, to when someone practices giving toward their own servants, wife, children, and so forth, with a mind that is neither defiled nor pure.
Regarding "indeterminate through enjoyment," this refers to when someone enjoys material requisites with a mind that lacks discernment and is free from defilement.
A mind lacking discernment is distinguished from what is wholesome in nature, while a mind free from defilement is distinguished from what is unwholesome in nature.

Regarding "drawing forth and grasping the indeterminate": this refers to a case where, because one has practiced a craft or art (*śilpasthāna*) in the present life, one draws forth and grasps a body of such a nature in a future life; by means of this body, one quickly reaches mastery in practicing that craft or art.
Indeterminate [states] as antidotes refers to cases such as when someone, in order to cure a disease and attain well-being, takes medicine with a mind of careful discernment.
Indeterminate [states] as tranquility refers to the various afflictions of the form and formless realms, which are suppressed and concealed by *śamatha*.
Regarding "outflow-unspecified" (*naiḥṣyandika-avyākṛta*): this refers to the category of factors co-arising with the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*), which is proven to be an outflow;

thus, it is called "outflow-unspecified. The factors associated with and co-existent with the transformative mind are termed the "co-arising category. These minds and mental factors are of an unspecified nature because they initiate transformations for the sake of sport; however, one should know that if they are for the purpose of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, they are wholesome (*kuśala*).
Furthermore, there is the manifestation of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena;

what does this mean? It refers to the manifestations made by the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the ultimate consummation, for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings. One should know that within these manifestations, not a single phenomenon can be found that is truly existent.

Regarding "that which is manifested," this refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by virtue of the power of those beings to be converted, manifest various things such as the wholesome and the unwholesome.

As for the manifestation of the unwholesome, it refers to creating illusory forms such as thieves and so forth, and manifesting acts such as severing their heads and feet, in order to terrify other sentient beings and bring them under control.
What is that which is bound to the desire realm?
How many things are bound to the desire realm?
For what purpose is that which is bound to the desire realm investigated?

This means that all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas belonging to one who has not yet abandoned desire constitute the sense of being "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

The phrase "not yet having abandoned desire" indicates that one has still not abandoned even a small portion of the desires of the desire realm; this is the sense of not yet having attained *samādhi*.
If it were otherwise, that which is not a dharma of the *anāgamya* concentration would also have to be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Why is this?

Because, having already attained *samādhi*, one takes delight in cessation; and because a portion of the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) to be countered has been severed, one may also be said to possess "partial detachment from desire" (*ekadeśavairāgya*).

The external forms and so forth, because they are produced by the predominant power of karma of those who have not yet abandoned desire, are also called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

When the Sūtra states that all sentient beings are produced by the predominant power of common karma, it is to show that even those born in the form and formless realms have not yet abandoned desire, as the seeds of such karma continue to follow them.
The four elements, two bases in their entirety, and a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The four elements are: the element of odor, the element of flavor, the element of nose-consciousness, and the element of tongue-consciousness.
The two bases refer to the bases of odor and taste.
"The remainder of one part" refers to excluding those factors bound to the form and formless realms, as well as untainted (anāsrava) factors.
One examines the factors bound to the desire realm in order to abandon attachment to a self that is predominant in desire.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form?
How many things are bound to the realm of form?
For what purpose is that which is bound to the realm of form investigated?

This refers to all wholesome and indeterminate dharmas belonging to one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); this is the meaning of being bound to the realm of form.
Excluding the four elements and two bases previously mentioned, a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases constitutes that which is bound to the realm of form.
"One part" refers to excluding those factors associated with the desire realm and the formless realm, as well as untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*).
One examines those associated with the form realm in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is free from the desires of the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
How many are bound to the formless realm?
For what purpose is that which is bound to the formless realm investigated?

This refers to all wholesome and indeterminate dharmas belonging to one who has already abandoned desire for the form realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm; this is the meaning of being "bound to the formless realm.
A portion of the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates constitutes that which is bound to the formless realm.
The three elements (dhātu) refer to the mind element (manodhātu), the mental-object element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).
The two bases (āyatana) refer to the mind base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dharmāyatana).
The four aggregates (skandha) refer to sensation and the others.
There are also forms produced by samādhi, but they are not mentioned here because they are few in number.
"A portion" refers to excluding those factors associated with the desire realm, the form realm, and the untainted (anāsrava) factors.
One examines those associated with the formless realm in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is free from desire for the form realm.
Furthermore, there are five types of detachment: partial detachment, complete detachment, penetrating detachment, suppressive detachment, and detachment through permanent eradication.

Regarding partial and complete detachment: this refers to detachment from a specific stage (*bhūmi*). If one has severed up to the eighth grade of afflictions (*kleśa*) within that stage, it is partial detachment;
if the ninth grade has already been severed, it is complete detachment.

Alternatively, this may be explained in terms of detachment from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*): if one is at the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), it is partial detachment; if one is at the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*), it is complete detachment.
"Thoroughly penetrating detachment" refers to detachment through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Detachment through suppression" refers to detachment from desire by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
"Detachment through permanent destruction" refers to detachment from desire by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of detachment: detachment by nature (*svabhāva-vairāgya*), detachment through impairment (*upaghāta-vairāgya*), detachment through maintenance (*dhṛti-vairāgya*), detachment through superiority (*adhipati-vairāgya*), detachment through delusion (*moha-vairāgya*), detachment through antidotes (*pratipakṣa-vairāgya*), detachment through thorough knowledge (*parijñā-vairāgya*), detachment through permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa-vairāgya*), detachment with something superior (*sottara-vairāgya*), and unsurpassed detachment (*anuttara-vairāgya*).
One should know that these ten kinds of detachment from desire (vairāgya) carry the sense of being contrary [to desire], rather than the sense of necessarily severing it.
Detachment by way of its own nature is called "natural detachment" (svabhāva-vairāgya).
Up to the point that detachment through permanent abandonment is called "detachment by permanent abandonment.
One should understand that the meanings of these various phrases are to be distinguished according to their types.
As for detachment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vairāgya*), it refers to the state of aversion toward painful feelings and those phenomena conducive to painful feelings.
The "renunciation through affliction" refers to the state of aversion arising in one who indulges in sensual desires after having experienced their feverish distress.
The "sustenance of renunciation" refers to the state of aversion toward exquisite delicacies that arises after one has eaten to satiety.

"Superior detachment" refers to the state of aversion toward inferior states once one has attained superior ones; it is like a person in the world who, having already attained a superior position such as that of a lord of a city, develops a sense of aversion toward inferior positions such as that of a village headman.

Those who are foolishly detached from desire refers to those ordinary worldlings who develop aversion toward the realm of nirvāṇa because they do not comprehend its nature of tranquility, and because they are firmly attached to the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Detachment through antidote refers to the abandonment of all afflictions by means of the mundane and supramundane paths.

Thoroughly knowing detachment refers to the state of aversion toward the phenomena of the three realms that arises in one who has already attained the path of seeing; this occurs because, having fully understood the nature of suffering in conditioned existence, one feels aversion toward all contaminated things.

Permanent abandonment of desire refers to the state of having permanently severed the afflictions of each respective stage (*bhūmi*) and thereby developed a nature of revulsion and turning away from them.
Superior abandonment of desire refers to the abandonment of desire possessed by all worldly beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Supreme detachment refers to the detachment possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
What is the state of training (*śaikṣa*)?
How many are those in the state of training?
For what purpose is one who is in training (*śaikṣa*) examined?
It means that all wholesome dharmas belonging to one who seeks liberation constitute the meaning of "one in training.
From the stage of accumulating the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) onwards, one is called a seeker of liberation.
It should be understood that the stage of seeking to realize liberation is called the stage of accumulating the provisions (*sambhāra*).
Ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) constitute those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*).

Regarding the ten elements, these refer to the seven consciousness-elements, the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), and the element of mental objects (*dharma-dhātu*).
Regarding the four bases, they are the bases of form, sound, mind, and phenomena.
One examines those in training (*śaikṣa*) in order to abandon attachment to a self that seeks liberation.
What is one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
How many are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
For what purpose are those beyond training investigated?
It refers to all wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) belonging to one who has attained ultimate perfection in all the bases of training (*śikṣāpada*); this is the meaning of "beyond training."
Because Arhats and others have already attained the ultimate perfection in the trainings of higher ethics, mind, and wisdom, they are called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and a portion of the aggregates (skandha) constitute that which is beyond training.
In order to abandon attachment to the self as one already liberated, one examines the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
How many are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training?
For what purpose is that which is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee investigated?

It refers to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas belonging to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); the defiled and indeterminate dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*); and the indeterminate dharmas as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is the meaning of "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee."

Regarding "all ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*): this refers to those excluding those seeking liberation, because the latter seek to train in the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*) and are therefore called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).

As for the defiled and neutral states of those in training: as appropriate, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) are defiled, while the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is neutral.

The eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases, are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
One examines what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner in order to abandon attachment to a self that is not liberated.
What is abandoned by insight?
How many are abandoned by insight?
For what purpose is that which is abandoned by insight investigated?

That is to say, the defiled views and doubts arising from conceptual discrimination; the bases of views and the bases of doubt; the afflictions and secondary afflictions consisting of wrong conduct toward those views and so forth; the bodily, vocal, and mental actions instigated by those views and so forth; and all the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the evil destinies—these are the objects to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Among these, "defiled views and doubt arising from conceptual discrimination" refers to the five views and so forth that arise preceded by hearing incorrect teachings and the like.
The phrase "arising from conceptual discrimination" is used to distinguish them from the innate *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (view of extremes).
Question:
What are the characteristics of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
Is it innate (*sahaja*)?
Answer: It refers to the view of annihilationism.
One who has already trained in clear realization gives rise to such fear:
Now, where does this "I" reside?
That which is the locus of views refers to the factors associated with and co-existent with those views, as well as their seeds.
The same applies to the locus of doubt.

Regarding the afflictions and secondary afflictions arising from wrong conduct based on views and so forth: this refers to all portions of greed and other such afflictions that arise by depending on the gateway of views and so forth, and by taking views and so forth as their objects; these are to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
"One part" refers to the exclusion of that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is complete in its views, one examines what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
What is abandoned through cultivation?
How many are to be abandoned by cultivation?
For what purpose is that which is to be abandoned by cultivation investigated?

It refers to those contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that are contrary to what is to be abandoned by seeing; having attained the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), these are the objects to be abandoned by cultivation. This is the meaning of "to be abandoned by cultivation."

Those things that are the opposite of what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) refer to all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), excluding the defiled views and so forth arising from conceptual construction.

The term "contaminated phenomena" also includes the wholesome states conducive to the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśala*), because they are accompanied by the latent predispositions (*dausthulya*).
All [phenomena] are, in one part, abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
"In one part" means excluding those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
One examines what is abandoned through cultivation in order to relinquish attachment to a self that is perfected through cultivation.
What is that which is not to be abandoned?
How many are those that are not to be abandoned?
For what purpose is that which is not to be abandoned investigated?
This refers to all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, with the exception of the wholesome states conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which are not subject to abandonment.
Untainted phenomena refer to the supramundane noble path (*āryamārga*), the subsequently attained [knowledge], and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
A portion of the ten elements (dhātu), four bases (āyatana), and the aggregates (skandha) is not to be abandoned (aprahātavya).
Question:
What kind of form (rūpa) and sound (śabda) are not to be abandoned?
Answer:
Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the nature of wholesome bodily and vocal karma is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
It is investigated as being not to be abandoned for the purpose of relinquishing attachment to a perfected self (*ātman*).
What is dependent origination?
How many things are dependently originated?
For what purpose is dependent origination investigated?

The meaning of dependent origination is explained by way of: its characteristics; the analysis of its members; the summary inclusion of its members; the establishment of the conditions for its members; the establishment of the functions of its members; the inclusion of its members within the categories of affliction; its meaning; its profundity; its distinctions; and its direct and reverse order. This is the meaning of dependent origination.

Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): because they arise from conditions without volitional effort, because they arise from conditions that are impermanent, and because they arise from conditions of functional efficacy, these are the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
On account of these characteristics, the Blessed One said:
"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises," namely, ignorance as the condition for formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, as explained at length.
The phrase "because this exists, that exists" clarifies the meaning of dependent origination as being without agency (*nirīha*).

It indicates that a resultant phenomenon exists solely by virtue of the existence of its conditions; it is not the case that the conditions possess a real, functional activity capable of producing the resultant phenomenon.
The phrase "because this arises, that arises" clarifies the meaning of dependent origination through impermanence;
for it is not the case that a produced phenomenon can be established by means of a cause that is itself unarisen.
The phrase "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) clarifies the meaning of dependent origination as a functional efficacy.
Although all phenomena are devoid of agency and impermanent, it is not the case that every result arises simply because any single phenomenon serves as its condition.
Why is this so? It is because of the distinct functional capacities of all phenomena (*dharma*).
For example, through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise; and so on, until through the power of birth (*jāti*), aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) come to be.
Regarding the analysis of the members: this refers to analyzing dependent origination into twelve divisions, due to the distinctions among the twelve members of dependent origination.
What are these twelve?
These are ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age and death.

To summarize these factors: the twelve factors previously analyzed—ignorance and so forth—are now further condensed into four, namely: the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), the projected factors (*ākṣipta-aṅga*), the producing factors (*abhinirvartaka-aṅga*), and the produced factors (*abhinirvṛtta-aṅga*).
It is solely by means of these four factors that all phenomena arising from causes and conditions are briefly and exhaustively subsumed:
namely, at the time of the cause, there is the projector and the projected; and at the time of the result, there is the producer and the produced.
The projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*) refer to ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because they give rise to future birth, they involve the prior lack of knowledge regarding the objects of the [Four] Truths, whereby various karmic actions are performed and their latencies (*vāsanā*) are infused into the mind.
The "projected factors" refer to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
This is because, through the power of the mental latencies (*vāsanā*), they enable the seeds for the sequential arising of future name-and-form and so forth to increase.
The "generative factors" refer to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).

Due to the power of craving for desire and so forth, which has not yet been permanently severed, one first gives rise to a longing for the distinctions between virtuous and non-virtuous conduct within the realm of desire and so forth, thereby initiating covetous desire.

Because there is consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*), at the moment of death, it accords with craving and brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) due to the presence of the manifesting power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of one or another karma.
The "limbs of arising" refer to birth, aging, and death.

Because the manifest presence of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of such karmic distinctions exists, the maturation (*vipāka*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth arises—just as previously projected—within the specific homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of a particular realm of existence (*gati*) or a single birth.
The mention of birth, aging, and death is intended to reveal that they depend upon the three characteristics of the conditioned.
The reason aging and death are established as a single member is to demonstrate that death occurs even when separated from aging.
In the case of birth from a womb, the factors such as the six sense bases do not arise apart from name-and-form and so forth; therefore, these are established as distinct links.

As for the establishment of the conditions for the links, they are established by way of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), by way of projection (*ākṣepa*), by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and by way of coexistence (*sahabhū*). Thus are the conditions for the links established.

The conditions for the members [of dependent origination] are established according to their respective characteristics based on the four types of conditions. For example, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*): because it is a predisposition from a previous life, it functions as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); this is because the various karmas produced by that perfumed continuity are capable of creating future existence (*punarbhava*), and at that time, the manifesting ignorance is able to induce them.
It acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
because it induces the continuous arising of the flow of various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through their differentiation, and because one contemplates it.

It acts as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because it takes as its objective sphere the state of delusion (*moha*) based on improper mental application (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) such as conceiving [it] as supreme, and because it co-exists with that [delusion].
It serves as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because by its dominant power it causes the associated volition (*cetanā*) to engage with objects erroneously and perform its activity.
All such cases should be understood exhaustively according to their respective applications.
Regarding the establishment of the functions of the links: the link of ignorance has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding existence; second, it acts as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding those sentient beings who are deluded about existence (*bhava*), it means that because they are obscured by that [delusion], they do not know the past, present, and future as they truly are.
Due to this cause and condition, they give rise to such doubts as:
"Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist? and so forth.
Regarding its being a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*): it is because, through their power, they cause karma leading to renewed existence (*punarbhava*) to increase.
Volitional formations have two kinds of functions:
first, they differentiate sentient beings into various categories within the realms of existence; second, they serve as a condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "causing sentient beings to differentiate among their destinies": it is because the power of karma causes sentient beings to proceed toward various distinct realms of existence.

Regarding the phrase "acting as a condition for consciousness": it is because the power of habitual tendencies enables the seeds for the arising of future name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth to increase.
Consciousness has two functions:
first, it maintains the karmic bonds of all sentient beings; second, it serves as a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding its maintenance of the karmic bonds of sentient beings, this is because it arises and ceases simultaneously with the latencies (*vāsanā*) projected by formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding its acting as a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): because name-and-form attains growth through the entry of consciousness (*vijñāna*) into the mother’s womb.
Name-and-form has two functions:
first, it sustains the individual existence (*ātman*) of sentient beings; second, it acts as a condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Regarding the "appropriation of the sentient being's own body," this is because once it has arisen, it is included within the specific category of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of sentient beings.

Regarding its being "the condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)," this is because the subsequent members, such as the six sense bases, arise based upon the preceding members, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The six sense bases have two functions:
first, they encompass the complete physical bodies of sentient beings; second, they serve as the condition for contact (*sparśa*).
Regarding the encompassing of the complete physical bodies of sentient beings, it is because once they have been born, their remaining faculties are without deficiency.
Contact has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to circulate among the objects they enjoy; second, it serves as a condition for sensation (*vedanā*).
Regarding its role in causing sentient beings to circulate among objects: based on this as a gateway, they experience the three types of objects—those conducive to pleasant sensation and so forth.
Feeling has two kinds of functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to flow through the cycle of existence within the fruits of their enjoyment; second, it acts as a condition for craving.

Regarding its function of causing sentient beings to flow through the cycle of existence within the fruits of enjoyment: this is because, depending upon feeling, they experience the various desirable and other types of karmic maturation.
Regarding that which has craving as its condition: it serves as the gateway for the arising of various forms of craving, such as the longing for union with this [object] and so forth.
Craving has two functions:
first, it leads sentient beings to wander through birth and death; second, it acts as the condition for grasping (*upādāna*).
That which draws sentient beings into the cycle of birth and death does so because, through its power, the flow of birth and death continues without interruption.
That which acts as a condition for grasping (*upādāna*) does so by way of the seeking of sensual gratification, as craving turns toward desire and the like.
Grasping has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to produce consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*) for the sake of future existence; second, it acts as a condition for becoming (*bhava*).

Regarding its function of producing consciousness accompanied by grasping for the sake of future existence: it ensures that the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) become determinative so that the continuity of future existence—differentiated according to destinies such as the hells—is uninterrupted.
Regarding its acting as a condition for existence (*bhava*): by the power of this [condition], the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) undergo transformation.
Existence has two functions:
first, it brings about the manifestation of future existence for sentient beings; second, it acts as a condition for birth (*jāti*).
That which causes future existence to manifest is so called because it can project [one] into another realm of rebirth without interval;
that which acts as a condition for birth is so called because, through its power, another homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) comes into operation.
Birth has two types of functions:
first, it causes the successive arising of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling for all sentient beings; second, it serves as the condition for aging and death.
Regarding its ability to cause name-and-form and the others to arise in succession, this is because it can project the distinctions between subsequent stages.
Regarding its being the condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): because this birth exists, the transformation and disintegration of that continuity all come to be.
Aging and death have two functions:

first, they repeatedly cause the temporal state of sentient beings to change, thereby destroying their youth and vigor; second, they repeatedly cause the lifespan of sentient beings to change, thereby destroying their life-force.
Regarding the inclusion within the defilements of the branches: ignorance, craving, and grasping are included within the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*);
formative forces (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are included within the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*);
and the remaining [branches] are included within the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
Question:
For what reason is the link of consciousness (vijñāna) included within the defilement of karma?
Answer:
Because it is manifested by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), its meaning is as follows:

the meaning of being without an agent; the meaning of having causes; the meaning of being devoid of a sentient being (*sattva*); the meaning of dependent origination (*paratantra*); the meaning of being without functional activity; the meaning of impermanence; the meaning of momentariness; the meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect; the meaning of the correspondence between cause and effect; the meaning of the differentiation of cause and effect; and the meaning of the determination of cause and effect—these are the meanings of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This means that because it is free from a creator such as Īśvara and so forth, it has the sense of being "without a creator.
Because it takes ignorance and so forth as its causes, it has the sense of "having a cause.
Because there is no inherent self, it has the sense of being "devoid of a sentient being."
Because it arises dependent upon a multitude of conditions, it has the meaning of being "other-dependent" (paratantra).
Because the activity of those conditions is empty, it has the meaning of being "without activity.
Because it is not permanent, it has the meaning of being "impermanent" (anitya).
Because there is no momentary abiding once the time of arising has passed, this is the meaning of "momentariness" (*kṣaṇika*).
Because the time of the cause’s momentary destruction and the fruit’s momentary arising are equal, this is the meaning of the "uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect."
Because [effects] do not arise from every [cause] in every way, this is the meaning of the correspondence between cause and effect.

Because [effects] arise from causes that are not of a single or uniform type, resulting in effects that are not of a single or uniform type, this is the meaning of the distinction between cause and effect.
Because the fruit is not received within other continuums, this is the meaning of the determination of cause and effect.

As for its profundity: it is profound because of the profundity of the cause, the profundity of characteristics, the profundity of arising, the profundity of abiding, and the profundity of transformation; such is the meaning of profundity.
That is to say, by means of these very meanings—such as the absence of an agent—it reveals five kinds of profundity in the dharma of dependent origination.
The profundity of the cause is revealed through two types of meaning, because it serves as an antidote to the theories of an unequal cause and the theory of no cause.
The profundity of its characteristics is revealed through one sense, because it has the characteristic of selflessness (*anātman*).
The profundity of its arising is revealed through two senses: although resultant phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions, they are not produced by those conditions.
The profundity of abiding is revealed by two meanings: because although there is no actual establishment, it appears as if there were abiding.
The profundity of transformation is revealed by four meanings: because the causal flow of transformation is difficult to comprehend.

Furthermore, although all dependently originated phenomena perish moment by moment, their persistence can be observed; although there are no active causal conditions, functional causal conditions can be observed; although they are devoid of sentient beings, sentient beings can be observed; and although there is no agent, the non-destruction of karmic fruits can be observed. Therefore, they are profound.
Regarding the fact that the fruits of karma are indestructible: although there is no internal agent, there is the performance of actions and the experiencing of their retributive fruits.

Furthermore, all phenomena do not arise from themselves, do not arise from another, do not arise from both, nor do they arise without causes from neither self- nor other-action; therefore, they are profoundly deep.
"Not arising from self" means that all phenomena are not created by themselves, because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) prior to their arising.
"Not arising from another" means that those various conditions (*pratyaya*) are not the agents [of creation].
"Not arising from both together" means precisely because of these two types of causes.
"Not arising without a cause of its own making or the making of another" means that conditions possess efficacy toward the arising of the fruit.
Furthermore, there is a distinction: because it arises in dependence upon various conditions, it is not self-created.
Although there are various conditions, it does not arise without a seed; therefore, it is not created by another.
Since neither of those possesses an active function, they do not act in concert.
Since both the seed and the various conditions possess efficacy, it does not arise without a cause.
Therefore, it is said as follows:

Because it arises from its own seeds, it does not come from another; because it depends on various conditions, it is not self-made; because it lacks independent agency, it is not co-arisen; and because it possesses functional efficacy, it is not causeless.

If the principle of dependent origination is already profoundly deep when it dispels the dualistic extremes of "neither self nor other," how much more so when all four positions are entirely forgotten; therefore, dependent origination is the ultimate in profundity.

As for "differentiation," it refers to the meaning of differentiation as follows: differentiation of the arising of consciousness; differentiation of internal death and birth; differentiation of external growth of grain; differentiation of formation and destruction; differentiation of sustenance by food; differentiation of the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant destinies; differentiation of purification; and differentiation of majestic power. This is the meaning of differentiation.
The differentiation of the arising of consciousness refers to such cases as the arising of visual consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms.

The differentiation of internal death and birth is spoken of in reference to the world of sentient beings; it means that with ignorance and so forth as conditions, volitional formations and so forth are produced.

Regarding the differentiation of the production of external grains: it refers to the seed being the condition for the sprout, the sprout being the condition for the stalk, and so on, such that branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arise in succession.

Regarding the differentiation of formation and destruction: it refers to the arising of the great earth and so forth, conditioned by the predominant power of the collective karma of all sentient beings.
The distinction of sustenance (*āhāra*) refers to the fact that the four types of sustenance serve as conditions for the continuity and maintenance of sentient beings within the three realms.

The distinction of differentiation between desirable and undesirable destinies (*gati*) refers to the fact that wholesome and unwholesome conduct serve as conditions for proceeding to good and evil rebirths.

Regarding the distinction of purification: it refers to the arising of the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) by taking as a condition the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya); in this manner, through the stages of the path of vision (darśanamārga) and so forth, one gradually attains the fruit of arhatship and so on.

Alternatively, with the external hearing of sounds from others and internal appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) as conditions, right view arises, leading in succession to the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
As for the distinction of majestic power (*prabhāva*), it refers to the arising of supreme qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by taking internal realization as a condition.
Based on these distinctions, one should explain the dependent origination of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in detail accordingly.

Regarding "conformity and reversal" (*anuloma-pratiloma*): this refers to the conformity and reversal of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and the conformity and reversal of purification (*vyavadāna*); this is what is called the conformity and reversal of dependent origination.

Regarding the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) in direct and reverse order: they may be explained according to the sequence of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*), namely, "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," and so forth, which is the explanation in direct order;
or they may be explained according to the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*), namely, the suffering of old age and death, and the origin of old age and death.
The extinction of old age and death, the path leading to the extinction of old age and death, and so forth, are explained in reverse order.
Regarding the sequence of purification in both forward and reverse order: it means that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so forth; this is explained in forward order.
"Due to the absence of what is there no aging and death?
Due to the cessation of what does aging and death cease?
Thus it is explained in reverse order.
One should contemplate the meaning of dependent origination in this way:
all things are dependently originated, with the sole exception of those unconditioned phenomena that constitute a portion of the dharma-element and the dharma-sphere.
One contemplates dependent origination in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is either causeless or possesses an uneven cause.
What is the condition?
How many are conditions?
For what purpose is the investigation of conditions undertaken?
The meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to being a cause, an immediately preceding condition, an object-condition, and a dominant condition;
thus, all things are conditions.
One examines conditions in order to abandon the attachment to a self as the cause of phenomena.

Regarding "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya): this refers to the ālayavijñāna and its wholesome habitual tendencies serving as causal conditions for all contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, respectively.
The ālayavijñāna is further of two kinds: namely, the matured (*vipāka*) and the cultivated (*prāyogika*).
The matured is the causal condition for all dharmas acquired at birth.
The cultivated is the causal condition for all skillful means (*upāya*) dharmas as well as for other future ālayavijñānas.
Furthermore, the *ālayavijñāna* of preparatory application refers to the accumulation of perfumation by the manifesting *pravṛttivijñānas* and so forth within this present life.

"Virtuous habitual tendencies" refers to the habitual tendencies of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); because these habitual tendencies arise with the supramundane realization of the outflow-like dharma as their condition, they are able to serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for supramundane dharmas.
Furthermore, its characteristics as causal conditions consist of: intrinsic nature, differentiation, accompaniment, concomitant activity, augmentation, obstruction, and appropriation.

It should be understood that within this context, the meaning of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is revealed through six types of causal characteristics, beginning with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Specifically, the two phrases concerning intrinsic nature and its differentiation establish the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); the remaining phrases, in their respective order, establish the co-existent, associated, homogeneous, pervasive, and ripening causes (*sahabhū-, saṃprayukta-, sabhāga-, sarvatraga-, and vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it refers to the intrinsic nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because the efficient cause is established based upon this intrinsic nature.

One should know that all causes are subsumed within the efficient cause; however, in order to clarify their specific distinctions, other causes such as the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-hetu*) and so forth are separately established.
Regarding the distinctions, there are briefly twenty types of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*):

first, the efficient cause of arising, which refers to the conjunction of conditions in relation to consciousness; for it is by virtue of this conjunction that what was previously non-existent comes into being.

Second is the efficient cause as sustenance (*anupālana-kāraṇa*), which refers to food in relation to sentient beings who have already been born or are seeking birth; for by its power, once born, their continuity remains uninterrupted.
Third is the efficient cause as support (*dhṛti-kāraṇa*), which refers to the great earth in relation to sentient beings; for it carries them so that they do not fall.
Fourth is the productive cause as illumination, which refers to a lamp in relation to various forms, because it removes the obstruction of darkness.
Fifth is the productive cause as transformation, which refers to fire in relation to fuel, because it causes that continuity to undergo change.

Sixth is the efficient cause as separation (*vibhāga-kāraka*), which refers to, for example, a sickle in relation to that which is to be cut, because it causes a connected object to become divided into two parts.

Seventh is the efficient cause as transformation (*pariṇāma-kāraka*), which refers to, for example, craftsmanship and knowledge in relation to objects such as gold and silver, because they transform their original parts into different characteristics.
Eighth is the causal efficacy of conviction (*adhimukti*), such as smoke in relation to fire, because it is through this that one infers what is not directly perceived.
