Ninth is the causal efficacy of manifestation (*vyañjana*), such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in relation to the object to be established (*sādhya-artha*), because it is through this that one attains correct certainty (*niścaya*).
Tenth is the "capable cause of attainment" (*prāpti-kāraka*), which refers to the Noble Path in relation to Nirvāṇa, because by means of this, one realizes that [Nirvāṇa].

Eleventh is the "capable cause of conventional designation" (*vyavahāra-kāraka*), which refers to names, concepts, and views; for it is through these that one grasps signs according to names and, being attached to them, gives rise to subsequent verbal designations.

Twelfth is the efficient cause as dependence (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*); that is, because one depends upon this, a desire for that arises. For example, depending on hunger and thirst, one seeks food and drink; thus, it is the cause for the arising of that desire.

Thirteenth is the inducement of the productive cause, which refers to a remote condition; for example, ignorance in relation to old age and death, because through these various stages, it successively induces future existence.

Fourteenth is the productive cause (*janaka-kāraka*), which refers to proximate conditions; for example, ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*), because it gives rise to future existence immediately thereafter.

Fifteenth is the sustaining cause (*parigrahaka-kāraka*), which refers to all other conditions; for example, the field, water, and fertilizer in relation to the production of grain. Although [the grain] is produced from its own seed, these factors augment its power.

16. The productive cause (*āvāhaka-kāraka*) refers to a concordant condition (*anukūla-pratyaya*); for example, a minister serving a king so as to please him, because it produces [the result] by way of being concordant.

17. The determinative cause (*pratiniyama-kāraka*) refers to a specific condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*); for example, the conditions for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) in relation to the results of the five destinies, because their distinct natures (*svabhāva*) summon their respective, individual results.

The eighteenth is the "cooperative cause" (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), which refers to the harmonious conditions. For example, when the sense organs are unimpaired, the objects are present, and attention (*manasikāra*) correctly arises, these depend upon one another to produce the resulting consciousness; for each performs its own function only by waiting for other causal factors.
19. Contradictory efficient cause (*viruddha-kāraka*), namely the obstructing condition (*vibandha-pratyaya*); for example, hail in relation to grain, because it is capable of damaging it. 20.
Non-contradictory efficient cause (*aviruddha-kāraka*), namely non-obstruction; for example, grain being free from obstacles, which is the opposite of the former.

Regarding this differentiation of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the mention of only the conjunction of consciousness and so forth is intended merely as a summary; it serves as a single point upon which the wise may rely to infer the remainder through analogical reasoning.

Regarding "companions" (sahāya): this refers to those phenomena that arise together and are necessarily complete without deficiency, such as the four great elements and the derived matter corresponding to them; however, it is not the case that every aggregate must invariably possess the four great elements and the derived matter such as visible form.
If, in a given instance, there is such a quantity [of factors], they must arise together and are mutually inseparable.
"Equal application" (samaprayoga) means that these factors possess a common application and a common object, such that none are lacking, just as it is with the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).

Regarding the aforementioned discussion on associates, it was established that among the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) were explicitly mentioned;

this was merely a brief indication of the general outline, for since the nature of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is determined by their mutual inseparability, they are likewise included within the category of associates.

If that were so, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) should not be established separately, because all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are already subsumed under the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Nevertheless, there is a difference in meaning: while all phenomena are co-existent, proceed together, share the same object, and are mutually inseparable, it is on account of this "proceeding together" (*samprayoga*) that the associated cause is established; it does not consist merely of the sense of being "co-existent," as is the case with minds and mental factors.

"Augmentation" refers to the fact that by cultivating wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas in the past limit, one is able to cause wholesome and other such dharmas in the future limit to increase progressively and arise in successive stages.
"Cultivation in the prior limit" refers to the meaning of that which was previously repeatedly practiced and manifested.

"Successive arising of ever-increasing excellence in the posterior limit" means that because those [practices] nourish the various seeds, they arise in future lives as that same kind, but with increasing excellence.
Because such dharmas can serve as causes for similar growth, they are established as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

As for "obstruction," it means that according to the various afflictions one repeatedly practices, all delusions continue to grow and become firm, thereby causing the continuum to remain far removed from *nirvāṇa*.
This universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) does not merely cause similar afflictions to increase. Why is this?

If one habitually practices afflictions such as attachment, it causes all afflictions such as aversion to continue increasing and become firm; because these deep and heavy fetters obstruct the attainment of liberation, the universal cause is thus established.

"Appropriation" (parigraha) refers to unwholesome and wholesome contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) because they are able to appropriate a personal basis (*ātma-bhāva*); this is precisely the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

Because these [phenomena] can project and appropriate a future retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) comprised of a personal basis that is entirely dissimilar [to its cause]—namely, non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—the retributive cause is established based on the meaning of appropriation.
The term "wholesome with outflows" (*kuśala-sāsrava*) is used to distinguish [this category] from that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*);
because it opposes birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it cannot produce a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Chapter One: The Section on Fundamental Matters, Part Five: The Three Dharmas. Regarding the "immediately antecedent condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*): it is so called because there is no interval between [the preceding and succeeding moments], and because it serves as the immediately antecedent condition for the arising of mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) belonging to both the same category and different categories; this is the meaning of the immediately antecedent condition.

Regarding "without interval" (*anantara*) in the sense of "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*): it does not necessarily mean being without interval within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Even if moments are separated, as long as there is no intervening mind of a different nature in between, it is also termed "without interval."
If it were not so, the mind entering a mindless absorption would not be an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in relation to the mind emerging from that absorption;

yet it is indeed such a condition. Therefore, within a single continuum, because there is no intervening mind between the preceding mind and the subsequent mind, they stand in the relation of equal-and-immediate condition.
Just as it is with the mind in relation to the mind, one should know that the same applies to mental factors (*cittadharma*).

Regarding the arising of homogeneous and heterogeneous minds and mental factors as equivalent and immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*): this means that wholesome minds and mental factors, in relation to wholesome [factors] of their own class, and to unwholesome or neutral [factors] of other classes, serve as the equivalent and immediate condition for the minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter.

In this way, it is also the case for unwholesome and neutral minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in relation to those of their own or different categories, as well as for the minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter.

Furthermore, the minds and mental factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter in the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states.

In this manner, one should understand that for each respective mind and mental factor of the form realm and so forth, when they arise immediately after [a preceding state], they do so in relation to the form realm and so forth, as well as the desire realm and so forth, according to what is appropriate.
Question:
Does every kind of mind arise immediately after every kind of mind?
Or is there a specific, fixed determination for each?
Answer: Yes.

If one were to explain in detail and at length here how such a mind arises immediately after such a mind, it would give rise to immeasurable discourse; therefore, one should merely establish the general characteristics of the arising of the mind in brief.
It is said that the arising of various mental states occurs by means of ten powers:

first, the power of habitual practice; second, the power of aspiration; third, the power of skillful means; fourth, the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); fifth, the power of induction; sixth, the power of the cause; seventh, the power of the object; eighth, the power of recollection; ninth, the power of attention (*manasikāra*); and tenth, the power of continuity.
The power of habitual cultivation is further of three kinds: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
If one has not yet fully mastered the characteristics of entering, abiding in, and emerging from the various meditative concentrations, it is the inferior grade.
Although they have already attained realization, because they have not yet become well-accustomed to it, this is the medium grade.
Because they have both realized it and subsequently become well-accustomed to it, this is the superior grade.
If one possesses the power of inferior-grade cultivation, they are only able to enter the various dhyānas and formless attainments in sequential order.
If one possesses a middling degree of the power of cultivation, they are also able to enter by means of transcendence, though they can only skillfully transcend a single interval (*ekāntarika*).

If one possesses a superior degree of the power of cultivation, they may, according to their desire, either skip all [intervals] or enter the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in either forward or reverse order.

Regarding the power of aspiration: it refers to one who has already attained the second dhyāna; having entered the first dhyāna, if they wish to emerge from it with a mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, or wish to emerge with a wholesome mind of the desire realm or an unobscured-neutral mind, they are able to manifest such a mind and emerge from meditative absorption.
Thus it is explained in detail; one should understand all other stages accordingly. Regarding the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*):

for a beginner, a mind of the form realm arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm; a wholesome mind of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration arises immediately after [a wholesome mind of] the desire realm; a wholesome mind of the first fundamental dhyāna arises immediately after the wholesome mind of the *anāgamya*; and so on in detail, until the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), which should all be understood accordingly.

The power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-bala*) refers to having entered a pure *samāpatti*, whereby at times one again gives rise to a pure attainment, and at other times gives rise to an afflicted one.

The power of induction (*ākṣepa-bala*) refers to arising from meditative concentration until the mind of the dhyāna-stage manifests; this continues as it alternates and proceeds with moments of non-concentrated mind, until finally, due to the manifestation of afflictions contrary to that state, one immediately regresses and loses it.
This mind associated with contradictory afflictions can only manifest through the four powers, beginning with the power of the cause (*hetubala*).
As for the power of the cause, it means that because one has previously habituated oneself to that which is capable of causing regression from the obstructions, one must necessarily regress.

The power of the object (*viṣayabala*) refers to the fact that because objects manifest with the predominance of pure characteristics (*śubhanimitta*), they are able to give rise to afflictions such as desire in accordance with them.
The power of recollection (*anusmaraṇabala*) refers to the production of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) through the recollective discrimination of past objects.
The power of attention (*manasikāra*) refers to the mental engagement through investigation that contemplates various pure and sublime appearances.

The power of continuity consists of nine types of death-minds associated with self-love (*ātmasneha*), which cause the continuity of rebirth in the desire, form, and formless realms within the three worlds, respectively.

That is to say, for one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, the continuity of rebirth is linked by the death-consciousness associated with craving for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-tṛṣṇā*) in the desire realm.
If one is reborn in the form or formless realms, the continuity of rebirth is linked by the death-consciousness associated with craving for self-existence in the form or formless realms.

In this way, for those who pass away from the realm of form or the formless realm—whether they are reborn in that very same realm or in another—there are six types of consciousness; these should all be understood according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, this self-love is exclusively innate; it does not discern its objective referent and is subsumed under the category of obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta). Nevertheless, it is capable of differentiating the distinct states of one's own personal identity.
By the force of this [craving], the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is continuously linked for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

It is the same for noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned desire: at the time of death, until they reach the stage of unclear perception (*asaṃprakhyāna-saṃjñā*), they are able to give rise to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of this craving; however, they are able to discern it, as it is suppressed by the power of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

For a noble one who has already abandoned desire, because the power of the antidote is strong, although this craving has not yet been permanently severed, it no longer manifests; nevertheless, by the force of its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it causes [the being] to arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a continuity.
The first moment of the continuum is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*).

From that point onward, it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, as the case may be; however, this excludes the mind at death in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because the mind at death in the intermediate state is always defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Just as the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) is so, the moment of consciousness that links to the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is likewise exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, it should be understood that for those Bodhisattvas who take rebirth through the power of their vows, all moments of mind at the time of death and so forth are invariably wholesome (*kuśala*).

Having already explained the meaning of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) as it arises from the discussion of causes, the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is defined as follows:

it is the meaning of an object-condition because there is an object-condition that has limits, an object-condition that has no limits, an object-condition with non-differentiated aspects (*ākāra*), an object-condition with differentiated aspects, an object-condition that has a real entity (*vastu*), an object-condition that has no real entity, an object-condition that is a real entity, an object-condition that is a conceptual construction, an object-condition that is perverted, an object-condition that is non-perverted, an object-condition that is obstructed, and an object-condition that is unobstructed. This is the meaning of the object-condition.
The object of focus with delimited boundaries refers to the objective spheres of the five groups of consciousness, because each of the five groups of consciousness has its own distinct sphere.
The object of focus without delimited boundaries refers to the objective sphere of the mental consciousness, because the mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its objective sphere.

Regarding "having no distinct mode of activity, object, or focal point": this refers to the objective sphere of the mental consciousness that conceptualizes names and notions for sentient beings; it is because such a consciousness cannot apply names to its objects.
"Having a different mode of activity as its objective referent" means that which is contrary to this.
"Having a real entity as its objective referent" refers to objective referents other than views, pride, and the mental factors associated with them.
The object of focus that is a non-entity (*avastu*) refers to those previously excluded objects of focus, because they arise in relation to oneself.

The object of focus that is an entity (*vastu*) refers to all other objects of focus, excluding those that take uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*) as their object, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) across different realms or stages, those that lack certainty regarding entities, and future objects of focus.

"Objects of perception that involve conceptual differentiation" refers to those objects of perception previously excluded, because they take as their object only what has been conceptually differentiated by themselves.
"Objects of perception involving inversion" refers to objects of perception characterized by modes such as permanence and so forth.
"Objects of non-erroneous observation" refers to the objective spheres characterized by such aspects as impermanence.
"Obstructed objects of observation" refers to the objective spheres perceived by those who have not yet abandoned the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding "unimpeded objects of focus" (*anāvaraṇālambana*): this refers to the objective spheres perceived by those who have already abandoned the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, if one wishes to definitively determine the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), one should establish the characteristics of the object through its marks (*lakṣaṇa*), its distinctions (*prabheda*), its formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*), its thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*), and its abandonment (*prahāṇa*). As for the characteristic of the object: if an object is the cause for the arising of mind and mental factors that manifest as resembling it, and once they have arisen, [the mind] is still able to grasp and clearly realize that object through internal self-cognition (*pratyātma-adhigama*), that is the characteristic of the object.
There are twenty-nine types of distinctions:

first, those with non-existent objects of cognition, namely, inverted minds and mental factors, as well as those that take as their objects of cognition past and future phenomena, dreams, reflections, illusions, and the like.
Second, those with an object (sālambana), namely other objects of perception;
third, those with an object that is itself without an object (anālambanālambana), namely matter (rūpa), mental non-associated formations (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
fourth, those with an object that has an object (sālambanālambana), namely mind and mental factors (cittacaitta).
Fifth is the object of right nature, which refers to wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*).
Sixth is the object of wrong nature, which refers to defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*).
Seventh is the object of neither right nor wrong nature, which refers to unobscured-neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*).
8. Object of focus that is rational (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), namely wholesome mind and mental factors;
9. Object of focus that is irrational (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), namely defiled mind and mental factors;
10. Object of focus that is neither rational nor irrational, namely those mind and mental factors other than these.

Eleventh is the similar object-condition (*sabhāga-ālambana*), which refers to such cases as wholesome states taking wholesome states as their object, states of one's own level taking states of that same level as their object, contaminated states taking contaminated states as their object, and uncontaminated states taking uncontaminated states as their object.

The twelve types of heterogeneous objects of cognition refer to such cases as: wholesome [states] taking unwholesome [states] as their object; states of one stage taking states of another stage as their object; and tainted or untainted states taking untainted or tainted states as their objects, and so forth.
Thirteen are objects of a different nature (*visabhāga-ālambana*), namely, the objects of mind and mental factors accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Fourteen are objects of a single nature (*sabhāga-ālambana*), namely, the objects of mind and mental factors without vitarka and without vicāra.

Fifteenth is the object of the powerful [state], which refers to the objects of the mind and mental factors associated with the attainment of non-perception and its preparatory stages, as well as the objects of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.

In this context, the first two phrases are called "majestic power" (*vaśitā*) because they can eliminate conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); the remaining [phrases] are called "majestic power" because their nature is vast.
The sixteen abbreviated and subtle objects of focus refer to the objective spheres of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Seventeenth is the extremely subtle object of focus (*ālambana*), namely the object of focus of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); beyond this, there is no further state of extreme subtlety.

Eighteenth is the object of focus of the afflictions (*kleśa*), namely that these very [afflictions] possess an object of focus; as it is said in the Sūtra regarding the object of focus of cessation (*nirodha*).
Nineteenth, the object of focus consisting of phenomena refers to the collections of names, phrases, and syllables of the sacred teachings.
Twentieth, the object of focus consisting of meaning refers to the meaning of these phenomena.
Twenty-first, the limited object of focus refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
Twenty-second is the vast object of focus, which refers to the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-third is the object of focus characterized by signs, which refers to the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Twenty-fourth is the signless object of focus, which refers to nirvāṇa and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Twenty-fifth is the object of focus of reality (*tattvālambana*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*) and the truths (*satya*) that are the objects of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).

Twenty-sixth is the object of focus for abiding (*vyavasthānālambana*), which refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) that serve as the means for that meditative concentration.
Twenty-seventh is the object of mastery (*vaśitā-ālambana*), which refers to the objects of all virtues from the liberations (*vimokṣa*) up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Twenty-eighth is the object of the momentary (*muhūrta-ālambana*), which refers to the object of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as it pertains only to this single lifetime.
Twenty-nine is the "concomitant objective support" (anuvartaka-ālambana), which refers to the objective sphere of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is called "established" because the substance of the objective sphere is not real, being merely an establishment.

One knows that the nature of the object of cognition is not real by virtue of four reasons: because there are contradictory perceptions; because no object of cognition can be apprehended apart from the cognition itself; because there would be no need for effort to avoid error; and because [the object] shifts according to the three types of knowledge.
By this principle, the nature of the grasper is also not real.
As for the three knowledges, they are: sovereign knowledge (*vaśitājñāna*), investigative knowledge (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*).
To clarify these four reasons, a verse is spoken: "Among ghosts,
animals, humans, and gods, each according to what is appropriate for them,
because their minds differ regarding the same object, it is held that the referent is not real."
Regarding past events and the like, within dreams and the two kinds of reflections,
although the objects of perception are not real, the appearance of the object is nonetheless established.
If the nature of an object were established as a real entity, non-conceptual wisdom would not exist.
If this [transformation] did not exist, it would be unreasonable for the fruit of Buddhahood to be realized.
Through the power of their vows and understanding, bodhisattvas who have attained mastery cause the earth and so forth to manifest as they wish;
those who have attained meditative concentration do likewise.
For one who has achieved discernment, who possesses wisdom and has attained meditative concentration,
when contemplating all phenomena, they appear exactly according to their true meaning.
When non-conceptual wisdom functions, no objects whatsoever appear.
One should know that there are no objects; because of this, consciousness also does not exist.
"Thorough knowledge" refers to knowing, as it truly is, the distinctions of characteristics and the establishment of objective spheres.
"Abandonment" refers to the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained by Śrāvakas and others, as well as by those of the Mahāyāna.

Although the transformation of the basis attained by the Śrāvakayāna and so forth achieves liberation regarding the objects of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one does not attain mastery over them.
The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained through the Mahāyāna possesses two kinds [of conditions].
Having already explained the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the meaning is now determined according to the text.

As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), its meaning consists of: dominance as support, dominance as inducement, dominance as coexistence, dominance as objective field, dominance as production, dominance as maintenance, dominance as the enjoyment of results, dominance as mundane purification and detachment from desire, and dominance as supramundane purification and detachment from desire. This is the meaning of the dominant condition.

Regarding the predominance of support (*dhṛty-adhipati*), this refers to cases such as the wind-circle supporting the water-circle; the receptacle world supporting the sentient world; the primary elements supporting derived matter; and the sense faculties supporting their respective consciousnesses, and so forth.

Regarding that which induces predominance: this refers to the collective karma of all sentient beings with respect to the receptacle world, as well as contaminated karma with respect to its ripened fruit, and so forth.

Regarding those with simultaneous predominance (*sahabhū-adhipati*): this refers to the mind with respect to mental factors (*caitasika*), attention (*manasikāra*) with respect to the mind, contact (*sparśa*) with respect to feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth.
This subsequent predominance is established based on the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

The predominance of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-adhipati*) refers to the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, because by their predominant power, visible forms and so forth arise.
The predominance of production (*janman-adhipati*) refers to the male and female faculties, because by their predominant power, one enters the womb.
The dominant factor for maintenance refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because by its dominant power the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) is maintained.

The dominant factors for the enjoyment of results refer to the faculties of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity, because based upon these one is able to experience desirable and undesirable maturation (*vipāka*).

The predominance of mundane purity and detachment refers to the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, because by means of these, one subdues all afflictions (*kleśa*).

The predominance of supramundane purity and detachment refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known," which have been established, because by means of these, one eradicates all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) forever.
What are the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*)?
How many are homogeneous and partially homogeneous?
For what purpose are the homogeneous and partially homogeneous investigated?

This means that because those similar faculties arise in a continuum toward their respective objects without being separated from consciousness, and because they arise as a self-similar continuum apart from consciousness, this constitutes the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).

Initially, these are "homogeneous" (sabhāga), because the sense faculties and their corresponding consciousnesses are similar to one another, arising in a continuous succession with respect to their respective objects.
Because the sense faculties evolve in a manner similar to the consciousnesses, they are designated as "homogeneous."
The second is the "homogeneous" (sabhāga), because the sense faculties arise in a continuous succession that is similar to their own kind, even when separated from consciousness.
Since the faculties do not conjoin with consciousness, the meaning of the arising of a faculty-series that is similar to its own nature alone is termed "homogeneous."

A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—namely, the five material elements and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) such as the eye—and so forth, are both *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous).
One examines *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga* in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is either associated with or dissociated from consciousness.
What is appropriation?
How many are appropriated?
For what purpose is appropriation investigated?
This means that because it is the physical basis for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*), it has the sense of being "appropriated" (*upātta*).
If sensation arises in dependence upon this physical form, it is called "appropriated.
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the five elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) possessing form, and a portion of four others, constitute what is appropriated.
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) refers to that which is comprised by the sense faculties and their respective bases.
The five elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) possessing form in their entirety refer to the eye and so forth.
A portion of four [elements] refers to those forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are not separated from the sense faculties.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that exercises mastery over the body, one examines the appropriated [bases].
What are the faculties?
How many are the faculties?
For what purpose are the faculties (*indriya*) examined? It is because they possess supremacy (*ādhipatya*) in:

(1) the apprehension of objects; (2) the non-interruption of the lineage; (3) the maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); (4) the experience of the fruits of pure and impure karma; (5) worldly detachment from desire; and (6) supramundane detachment from desire. This is the meaning of "faculty."

The predominance regarding the apprehension of objects refers to the six [faculties], such as the eye, because by their predominant power, the mind and mental factors operate toward objects such as visible forms.

The predominance regarding the non-interruption of the lineage refers to the male and female faculties, because by their predominant power, the succession of descendants such as sons and grandsons flows on without ceasing.
The rest is as explained under the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

The entire aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one portion of the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and six elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety, and one portion of the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) are faculties (*indriya*).
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) refers to the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, male, and female.
A portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) refers to the faculties of life-force, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The twelve elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety refer to the six sense faculties (*indriya*) and the six consciousness elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
The six bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety refer to the six internal bases.

A portion of the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*) and the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) refers to the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the faculties of pleasure and so forth, and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
The faculties are examined in order to abandon attachment to a superior self.
What is the nature of suffering as suffering?
How many are of the nature of suffering as suffering?
For what purpose is the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) investigated?

It means that because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of painful feeling is itself suffering, and because the specific characteristics of those phenomena that accord with painful feeling are also suffering, this is the meaning of the nature of suffering as suffering.

Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*): it refers to painful feeling itself; because it takes the essence of suffering as its own characteristic, it is called the nature of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).

Regarding the specific characteristic of those phenomena that are concordant with painful feeling: it refers to the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*) that can produce this feeling; because they are concordant with painful feeling, they are called the nature of suffering-as-suffering.
One portion of all things is the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
One examines the nature of the suffering of suffering in order to abandon the attachment to a self that possesses suffering.
What is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?
How many are of the nature of suffering through change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)?
For what purpose is the nature of suffering through change investigated? It means:

because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of pleasant feeling is subject to change; because the specific characteristic of those phenomena that accord with pleasant feeling is subject to change; and because the mind of attachment toward them is subject to change—this is the meaning of the nature of suffering through change.

In this context, pleasant feelings and those phenomena conducive to pleasant feelings can give rise to distress when they undergo transformation; therefore, this transformation constitutes the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
Furthermore, because of craving, the mind undergoes transformation, which is also the suffering of change.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Entering into a mind that undergoes transformation;
all [conditioned phenomena], in one respect, are of the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)."
In order to abandon the attachment to a self that possesses pleasure, one contemplates the nature of suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
What is the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)? How many things possess the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations?
For what reason is conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*) observed as suffering (*duḥkhatā*)?

It is because the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is such; because the intrinsic nature of those phenomena conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is such; because it is gripped by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of both [painful and pleasant feelings]; and because it is not free from the insecurity (*anāśvāsa*) that follows upon the two kinds of impermanence (*anityatā*). This is the meaning of the suffering of conditioned existence.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refers to the feeling associated with the ālayavijñāna.
Phenomena conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refer to all conditioned formations that accord with this feeling.

"Those two being grasped by heavy burdens (*dausthulya*)" means that they are accompanied by the heavy burdens of the two sufferings: the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

"Not being free from the instability accompanied by the two kinds of impermanence" means that because one is not liberated from these two sufferings, one at times falls into a state of suffering and at times falls into a state of pleasure; it is not the case that one is always in a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Therefore, the meaning of being unstable due to the accompaniment of impermanence is the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Excluding one portion of the aggregates within the three realms and two bases, all else are of the nature of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The "three realms" refer to the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The two bases refer to the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
"A portion" refers to excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) aspect.
One examines the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is neither painful nor pleasant.
What is that which possesses maturation (*savipāka*)? How many possess maturation?
For what purpose is that which possesses maturation investigated?
This refers to unwholesome states and wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), which possess maturation (*savipāka*).

Because unwholesome states and wholesome states associated with outflows can produce the future *ālayavijñāna* and its associated maturations, these two types are termed "possessing maturation" on account of those maturations.
A portion of ten elements, four bases, and all aggregates is possessed of maturation (*savipāka*).
Regarding the ten elements: these refer to the seven consciousness-elements, as well as the elements of form, sound, and phenomena.
Regarding the four bases: these refer to the bases of form, sound, mind, and phenomena.
"One part" refers to excluding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
One examines "having maturation" (*savipāka*) in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is capable of abandoning or continuing the aggregates.
Furthermore, "maturation" refers exclusively to the ālayavijñāna and its associated mental factors; all others are merely "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) and are not themselves maturation.

The "remainder" refers to the eyes, ears, and so forth, as well as suffering, pleasure, and so forth; these are the remainder of the ālayavijñāna. They are designated solely as "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) because they arise from maturation.
What is nutriment?
How many are nutriments?
For what purpose is nutriment investigated?

That is to say, because there is transformation and decay, there is one who undergoes transformation and decay; because there is an objective sphere, there is one who possesses an objective sphere; because there is longing, there is one who longs; because there is grasping, there is one who grasps—this is the meaning of "nutriment."
The first is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because it nourishes the sense faculties and the primary elements at the time of its transformation and decay.
The second is contact as nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*), because by depending on contact with desirable objects, it benefits the basis [of existence].
The third is the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*), because by the power of directing the mind toward and longing for desirable objects, it sustains and benefits the physical basis.
The fourth is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), because by the sustaining power of the *ālayavijñāna*, the body remains alive.
Why is this so? Because if one were separated from this consciousness, the body upon which it depends would rot and decay.
Three aggregates, eleven elements, and a portion of five bases constitute nutriment.
One examines food in order to abandon attachment to a self that subsists by means of food.
Furthermore, there are briefly four ways in which these four types of sustenance are established by way of their distinctions:
first, the sustenance that subsists upon an impure basis, namely ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because they are bound by all fetters.

Second, the sustenance that dwells in both pure and impure bases refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form and formless realms, because they still possess remaining fetters.
Third, the sustenance that dwells in purely clean bases refers to Arhats and others, because they are liberated from all fetters.

Fourth is dwelling through the manifestation of eating; this refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have already realized great majesty and power, because they dwell solely by manifesting the power of eating.
How is it that there is something superior?
What is "surpassable" (*sottara*)?
For what purpose is it examined as being surpassable?
It means that because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and a portion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are surpassable, this is the meaning of "surpassable."

Excluding one portion of the dharma-element and the dharma-base, all [other phenomena] are with superior; this is because among all phenomena, nirvana and the pure suchness possess the most excellent characteristics.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that clings to inferior things, one examines that which is "surpassable.
What is "unsurpassable"?
How many are unsurpassable?
For what reason is the "unsurpassed" (anuttara) examined?
It means that because it is a portion of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it has the sense of being unsurpassed.
A portion of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), as previously described, is unsurpassed.
One examines the unsurpassed in order to abandon attachment to a self that is the most excellent entity.
By means of the principles of differentiation explained here, other immeasurable modes may be examined by analogy.

Furthermore, there are briefly three types of distinctions among the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases: namely, the distinction of the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa), the distinction of the characteristics of the object of conceptualization (vikalpita-lakṣaṇa), and the distinction of the characteristics of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa).
Regarding the distinctions of the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to that which is imagined within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

[The imagined entities are] the self (*ātman*), sentient being (*sattva*), life-principle (*jīva*), living being (*jantu*), nourisher (*poṣa*), person (*pudgala*), mind-born (*manuja*), and youth (*mānava*), and so forth. Within the aggregates and so forth, there is no such intrinsic nature as a self; these are merely imagined characteristics.

The differentiation of the characteristics of the imagined (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-prabheda) refers to the very phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, because it is within these that false conceptualizations such as "self" and "sentient being" arise.

Regarding the distinctions of the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*): this refers to the non-existence of a self (*ātman*) and the existence of selflessness (*anātman*) within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases themselves. Because it is free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence, suchness (*tathatā*) takes the non-existence of a self and the existence of selflessness within the aggregates and so forth as its characteristic.

It should be understood that herein, based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and primarily based on the principle of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), three characteristics are taught.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of distinctions: namely, the distinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-prabheda*), the distinction of conceptualization (*vikalpa-prabheda*), the distinction of the basis (*āśraya-prabheda*), and the distinction of continuity (*saṃtati-prabheda*).
The distinction of characteristics refers to the distinct individual characteristics of each of the aggregates, elements, and bases, such as form, sensation, and so forth.

The distinction of differentiation refers to the infinite varieties within those very aggregates, elements, and bases, such as being substantially existent or nominally existent, conventionally existent or ultimately existent, having form or being formless, and being visible or invisible.
The analysis is as previously explained.

Regarding the distinction of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*): it should be understood that as far as there are distinctions among the bases of sentient beings, so too are the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; this is because the various phenomena such as the aggregates within each individual internal body are diverse.

Regarding the differentiation of the continuum (*saṃtati-prabheda*): it refers to the occurrence of the aggregates, elements, and bases in each and every moment; for within a single body, the nature of each and every phenomenon, such as the aggregates, undergoes transformation from moment to moment.
Question:
What is it that is to be understood through skill in the distinctions of characteristics?
Answer:
Having understood the faults and afflictions of self-grasping,
[he asks]:
"Regarding skill in the distinctions of conceptualization, what is it that is to be understood?"
Answer:
It is the thorough understanding of the conceptualization of aggregates and their disadvantages.
Question:
What is understood through skillfulness regarding the distinctions of the basis?
Answer:
One understands the faults and disadvantages of attaining [results] without having practiced and losing them despite having practiced.
Question:
What is it that is understood through skill in the distinctions of the continuum?
Answer:
One understands and dwells having realized the faults of conceptualization.

Furthermore, there are six types of distinctions regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases: namely, the distinction of the external door, the distinction of the internal door, the distinction of long duration, the distinction of limited duration, the distinction of momentary duration, and the distinction of manifestation.
Regarding the distinction of the external gate: this refers primarily to the distinctions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The term "primarily" is used to exclude the wisdoms born of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) that have outflowing phenomena (*niṣyandadharma*) as their cause.
The distinction of internal doors refers to all stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
The distinction of duration refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The distinction of limits refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) with the exception of the final aggregates, elements, and bases at the moment of their last instant.
Regarding the distinction of temporal duration: this refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of the final moment of all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the distinction of manifestation: this refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases manifested by the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained ultimate perfection.

2. Chapter on Compendium (*Saṃgrahavastu*). In the second chapter, the Compendium, within the *Mūlavastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, furthermore, if one were to briefly explain compendia, there are eleven kinds: namely, compendium by characteristic (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*), compendium by realm (*dhātusaṃgraha*), compendium by category (*jātisaṃgraha*), compendium by state (*avasthāsaṃgraha*), compendium by accompaniment (*sahāyasaṃgraha*), compendium by direction (*digsaṃgraha*), compendium by time (*kālasaṃgraha*), compendium by partiality (*ekadeśasaṃgraha*), compendium by totality (*sakalasaṃgraha*), compendium by mutual inclusion (*anyonyasaṃgraha*), and compendium by ultimate meaning (*paramārthasaṃgraha*).

Regarding mutual inclusion: this means that each of the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) includes itself by its very nature.
For example, the aggregate of form includes the aggregate of form; and so on, as explained at length, up to the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) including the base of mental phenomena.

Regarding inclusion within the realms (*dhātu*): this means that the *ālayavijñāna*, which contains all the seeds of the aggregates, elements, and bases, is able to include those realms, because those seeds exist within it.

Regarding inclusion by category: although the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) differ, they are mutually inclusive because they share the same essential meaning—namely, the meaning of "aggregate," the meaning of "element," and the meaning of "base.

As for the meaning of "aggregate" and so forth: form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and the others all possess the sense of being a collection (*caya*). Although their individual characteristics differ, they are all mutually inclusive when compared with one another, as they belong to the same class.

Regarding the meaning of *dhātu* (elements) and so forth: it means that the eye, ear, and so on all possess the sense of being able to maintain and experience; therefore, they are mutually inclusive in all their aspects. Regarding the meaning of *āyatana* (bases) and so forth:
it means that the eye, ear, and so on all possess the sense of being gateways for growth and production; because they correspond [to this function], they are mutually inclusive in all their aspects.

Regarding inclusion by state (*avasthā-saṃgraha*): this means that the aggregates, elements, and bases in a state of pleasure are included within their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); the same applies to states of suffering and states of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, because these states are equivalent.

Just as form, sensation, and so forth, although they are of the same category of aggregates (*skandha*), yet differ in their states such as suffering and pleasure— wherein a state of pleasure includes only states of pleasure and not states of suffering and so forth—
likewise, a state of suffering and a state of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure each include only their own respective states.
As it is with the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding inclusion by association (*sahāya-saṃgraha*): this means that because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the other aggregates are mutual associates, they include their respective companions.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases.

Just as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and its accompanying factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) together comprise the five aggregates, so too each individual factor among sensation and the rest, along with its own accompaniments, comprises all five aggregates.
As it is with the aggregates, so it is with the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*); because they act as mutual companions, each one comprises all elements and bases.

Regarding inclusion by direction: this means that the aggregates, elements, and bases of the eastern direction mutually include one another; the same applies to the aggregates, elements, and bases of the other directions. Regarding inclusion by time:
this means that the aggregates, elements, and bases of the past mutually include one another; the same applies to the aggregates, elements, and bases of the future and the present.

Regarding "inclusion by a single part": this refers to those phenomena included within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) that are included only as a single part and not the remainder.

For example, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) includes only a single part of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the aggregates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) include only a single part of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the elements of desire (*kāma*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) include only a single part of the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*); and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth include only a single part of the base of mind (*manas-āyatana*) and the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*). Such are the cases.

Regarding inclusion by way of the complete set (*sakalāṅga-parigraha*): this refers to those phenomena that are included within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), and which are capable of including the full set.

For example, the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*) includes the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) includes the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); and the station of non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva-sthāna*) includes ten bases (*daśāyatana*), excluding smell and taste.
By this principle, [the aggregate of form] encompasses all phenomena included within the other aggregates, elements, and bases in their entirety.
Regarding mutual inclusion: how many elements and how many bases are subsumed within the aggregate of form?
One part of ten.
How many elements (dhātus) and how many bases (āyatanas) are subsumed under the aggregate of feeling? One part.
As it is with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception and formations.
How many elements and how many bases are subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness?
Seven elements and one base.
How many aggregates (*skandha*) and how many bases (*āyatana*) are subsumed under the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
It comprises a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and one entire base.
As it is with the eye-element, so it is with the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the mind-element (manodhātu)?
One aggregate and one base.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the phenomena-element (dharmadhātu)?
The three aggregates in their entirety, a portion of the aggregate of form, and one base in its entirety are subsumed under the eye-consciousness element.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the consciousness aggregate?
A portion of the consciousness aggregate and a portion of the mind base.
As it is with the eye-consciousness element, so it is with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements.
How many aggregates and how many elements are included in the eye base?
A portion of the aggregate of form and one entire element.
As it is with the sense base of the eye, so it is with the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
How many aggregates and how many elements are subsumed within the sense base of the mind?
One aggregate and seven elements.
How many aggregates (*skandha*) and how many elements (*dhātu*) are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
It includes three aggregates in their entirety, a portion of one [aggregate], and one element in its entirety.
Thus, all other phenomena are designated by the names of aggregates, elements, and spheres, as well as by other names that are not aggregates, elements, or spheres.

One should understand that, as previously elucidated, such categories as substantial existence (*dravyasat*), nominal existence (*prajñaptisat*), conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*), ultimate existence (*paramārthasat*), the knowable, the cognizable, and the realizable; and those with form (*rūpin*) or without form (*arūpin*); visible (*sanidarśana*) or invisible (*anidarśana*)—are each, as appropriate, fully subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding "according to what is appropriate": for example, each aggregate (*skandha*) subsumes all elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*); each element subsumes all aggregates and bases; and each base subsumes all aggregates and elements. One should understand this through such detailed explanations as they apply.

Regarding inclusion by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this refers to being included within the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
Such modes of inclusion are established in accordance with what is commonly recognized by the world.
Furthermore, there are six types of principles for inclusion by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):

First, regarding inclusion by locus: as it is said in the world that Jambudvīpa includes humans and the forest retreat (āraṇya) includes deer, one should know that here, the inclusion of the eye-consciousness and so forth within the eye-faculty and so forth is likewise.

Second is inclusion by support (*ādhāra-parigraha*): just as it is said in the world that ropes and the like support bundles of firewood and so forth, one should know that herein the body-faculty likewise supports the eye-faculty and the other faculties.

Third is inclusion by common purpose (*eka-kārya-parigraha*): just as it is said in the world that a multitude of people with a common task support and rely upon one another through mutual trust, one should know that herein the associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that operate with a single object likewise support one another.

Regarding the inclusion by way of appropriation: just as it is said in the world that a master can appropriate his own servants and so forth, one should know that the appropriation of one's own body by the *ālayavijñāna* is likewise.

Regarding the inclusion by way of non-diffusion: just as it is said in the world that a vessel contains water, one should know that herein, all samādhis likewise contain the other minds and mental factors.

Regarding the sixfold "comprehensive inclusion" (*saṃgraha-saṃkṣepa*), just as it is said in the world that the ocean encompasses all streams, one should know that herein the aggregates of form, feeling, and so forth likewise encompass the eye, ear, and so forth.
All eleven types of inclusion mentioned previously are explained based on this comprehensive inclusion.
Question:
What benefit is obtained through skillfulness in gathering?
Answer:
One attains the benefit of brief synthesis regarding the focal object; as one briefly gathers the mind toward various respective objects, so too do the roots of virtue increase and become preeminent.

Chapter 3: The Chapter on Association (*Saṃprayoga*) from the *Mūlavastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*. Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are six kinds of association: namely, inseparable association (*avinirbhāga-saṃprayoga*), combined association (*saṃsarga-saṃprayoga*), accumulated association (*samudāya-saṃprayoga*), coexistent association (*sahabhū-saṃprayoga*), functional association (*kāritra-saṃprayoga*), and concurrent association (*ekārtha-pravṛtti-saṃprayoga*).

Regarding "association through non-separation": this refers to all material forms (*rūpa*) that possess spatial dimensions being mutually inseparable from the location of the atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is because these various forms, being subsumed within atoms, occupy the same locus and are thus inseparable.

Regarding "conjunction through combination": this refers to all material forms with spatial dimensions that are larger than atoms, which mutually combine with one another, such as the mutual combination of the atoms of earth and water within turbid water.
Association by aggregation (*saṃghāta-saṃprayukta*) refers to the mutual gathering of spatially differentiated matter, such as two lumps of clay striking one another to form a mass.
Association by coexistence (*sahabhū-saṃprayukta*) refers to the simultaneous evolution of the aggregates, elements, and bases within a single body, sharing the same arising, abiding, and cessation.

Regarding "correspondence through activity" (*kṛtya-samprayoga*): this refers to mutual inclusion regarding a single task to be performed, such as two bhikṣus corresponding with one another in accordance with a single task they are undertaking.
“Concomitance by association” (samprayoga-sahagata) refers to the mutual concomitance of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) with respect to a single object.

This concomitance by association has further meanings: it is association with what is of another nature (*parabhāva*), not with what is of one's own nature (*svabhāva*). For example, a mind does not associate with another mind, nor does feeling (*vedanā*) associate with another feeling, and so forth.
Furthermore, association is not inconsistent with non-association, as in the cases where greed is not associated with hatred, or the wholesome is not associated with the unwholesome, and so forth.
Moreover, association occurs at the same time and not at different times, as in the case where the present is not associated with the past or the future.

Furthermore, those that correspond to the same sphere and level do not correspond to different spheres or levels; for example, the desire realm does not correspond to the form or formless realms, and the first dhyāna does not correspond to the second dhyāna, and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the universal association of concomitants, namely feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, and consciousness; because these six factors are invariably associated in all states, for if even one of them is absent, the others are likewise absent.

Furthermore, there is the association with defiled universal concomitants (kliṣṭa-sarvatraga-sahabhū-samprayoga), namely, the four types of afflictions within the defiled mind (kliṣṭamanas); because these four factors are constantly associated [with it] at all times.

Furthermore, there are those that do not function in association at all times; that is to say, depending upon the mind, at one time wholesome factors such as faith arise, while at another time afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed arise.

Furthermore, there is association by way of state and common activity, namely, the various associated dharmas with pleasant feeling, and the various associated dharmas with painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, there is uninterrupted concomitance of similar activity, which refers to the state of being with mind (*sacittaka*).
Additionally, there is interrupted concomitance of similar activity, which refers to that which is separated by a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, there is external-door concomitance, which refers for the most part to the mind and mental factors associated with the desire realm.
There is also internal-door concomitance, which refers to all the mind and mental factors belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*).

Furthermore, there is that which has been practiced and is associated with practice, namely: all minds and mental factors belonging to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as well as a portion of the minds and mental factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The term "one part" refers to the inclusion of all exclusively mundane wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, as appropriate.

Furthermore, it includes those with which one has not previously practiced association, namely: supramundane minds and mental factors, as well as the supramundane subsequently attained minds and mental factors occurring at the initial and final stages.

The expression "at the initial and final moments" is used to indicate that from the first moment onward—and indeed from the second moment onward—the supramundane mind and mental factors are of a nature never previously cultivated.
Question:
What benefit is gained by being skillful regarding association (*saṃprayoga*)?
Answer:
One is able to thoroughly understand that the various phenomena of affliction and purity, such as sensation and perception, are associated or dissociated solely in dependence upon the mind.

Through this understanding, one is able to abandon the attachment to a self that conceives of itself as the one who feels, perceives, intends, and remembers, whether in states of affliction or purity; furthermore, one is skillfully able to swiftly enter into the realization of non-self.

Chapter Four: On Attainment (*Prāpti*) In the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, within the "Basic Section" (*Mūlavastu*), Chapter Four: On Attainment. Furthermore, the characteristics of attainment have already been explained as follows: regarding wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, the conventional designations "acquisition" and "attainment" are established based on their increase or decrease.
This differentiation is threefold: namely, accomplishment through seeds, accomplishment through mastery, and accomplishment through active manifestation. Regarding accomplishment through seeds:

it refers to when one is born in the desire realm, the afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the desire, form, and formless realms are accomplished by virtue of the accomplishment of their seeds.

Regarding those born with innate wholesome states (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) in the desire realm who are possessed of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the three realms: this is said in reference to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet abandoned desire.

If one has already abandoned desire or is born in a higher stage, then with respect to whichever stage of desire has been abandoned, the afflictions and secondary afflictions of that very stage are both possessed and not possessed, according to the sequence: because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been permanently destroyed, yet they have been impaired by the path of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
Regarding innate wholesome states (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*), one achieves them according to the specific realm in which one is born.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one is said to "achieve" the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by virtue of possessing their seeds; yet, this is also termed "non-achievement."
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the form and formless realms are accomplished by virtue of the accomplishment of their seeds.

Furthermore, regarding innate wholesome states, if one is born in the formless realm, the afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the desire and form realms are accomplished by virtue of the accomplishment of their seeds, yet they are also said to be non-accomplished.
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the formless realm are established by virtue of the possession of their seeds.

Furthermore, regarding innate wholesome states, if one has already attained the path that serves as the antidote for the three realms, then according to whichever specific category of antidote has arisen, the possession of the seeds of that corresponding category becomes non-possession.
As various types of antidotes have not yet arisen, so various types [of afflictions] are established by virtue of being accomplished through their seeds.
One who has obtained the path that is the antidote to the three realms refers to one who has already attained the supramundane noble path (*āryamārga*).

"Whichever types of counteragents have arisen accordingly" refers to the fact that the counteragents for the superior grades of afflictions and so forth, which are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), have already arisen.
"The seeds of such and such types are attained as accomplished or not accomplished" means that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been permanently destroyed.

Mastery-accomplishment refers to those wholesome dharmas of skillful means, as well as mundane and supramundane qualities such as meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis, along with a portion of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, which are accomplished by virtue of mastery-accomplishment.

Regarding the wholesome dharmas of skillful means: these refer to the wisdom born of hearing and so forth; for although their seeds existed previously, they could never arise as manifest phenomena unless they were cultivated and increased through repeated practice in this present life.
A portion of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena refers to those such as the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) and the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika-citta*).

Regarding "accomplishment through manifestation" (*samudācāra-samanvāgama*): it refers to the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), which—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—are accomplished by virtue of their being manifested in the present.
If one has already severed the roots of goodness, all wholesome dharmas are said to be "accomplished" by virtue of the presence of their seeds, yet they are also called "unaccomplished.
As for those who lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*, such as the *icchantikas*, they ultimately accomplish only defiled dharmas.

Because they lack the cause for the attainment of liberation, they are also called *ātyantika* (those who are ultimately [incapable], as the cause for their attainment of liberation will never be accomplished.
Question:
What is designated as the cause for the attainment of liberation?
Answer:

If, regarding true suchness (*tathatā*), one has previously accumulated the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) of afflictions, and then encounters favorable conditions that serve as antidotes, one is able to permanently destroy this state of susceptibility; this is called the cause for attaining liberation.
If it is contrary to this, it is called "having no cause for liberation.
Question:
What benefit is gained by achieving skill in these accomplishments?
Answer:
One is able to thoroughly understand the increase and decrease of all phenomena.
Because of this knowledge of increase and decrease, one abandons the notion of certainty regarding the rise and fall of the world, and is even able to sever both craving and aversion.

Section Two: The Section on Ascertainment (Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī). Chapter One: On the Truths (Satya-vastu). Part One of the First. Furthermore, to state it briefly, there are four kinds of ascertainment: namely, ascertainment of the truths (satya-viniścaya), ascertainment of phenomena (dharma-viniścaya), ascertainment of attainment (prāpti-viniścaya), and ascertainment of discussion (saṃkathya-viniścaya).
The discernment of the truths further consists of four types, namely, those taught in reliance upon the Four Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
It refers to the birth of sentient beings and the locus upon which that birth depends—namely, the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world, respectively.
Whether it be birth itself or the place of birth, both are designated as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As for the "birth of sentient beings," this refers to the birth of all sentient beings within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods.
These are known as Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, Jambudvīpa in the south, and Uttarakuru in the north.

The heavens are as follows: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; as well as the Heaven of Infinite Space, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
The locus upon which sentient beings depend is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). This refers to the water-circle resting upon the wind-circle, and the earth-circle resting upon the water-circle.
Upon this earth-circle exist Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, the four great continents, the eight intermediate islands, the inner ocean, and the outer ocean.
The four outer terraces of Mount Sumeru are the distinct abodes of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Beyond the Cakravāḍa mountains, there are the celestial palaces in the sky, which are the distinct abodes of the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, as well as the various heavens of the Form Realm, and the distinct abodes of the Asuras.

And there are the various distinct locations where the *naraka*s (hells) reside, namely: the hot hells, the cold hells, and the solitary hells, as well as certain distinct locations where animals and hungry ghosts (*preta*) reside.
The area illuminated by the pervasive radiance of one sun and one moon for as long as a day and a month is called a single world-system (*loka-dhātu*).

Within such a thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand suns, a thousand moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, a thousand sets of four great continents, a thousand assemblies of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmakāyika heavens; this aggregate is collectively termed a small thousandfold world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
One thousand small chiliocosms are collectively termed a second-order dichiliocosm.
One thousand dichiliocosms are collectively termed a third-order trichiliocosm.
This entire trichiliocosm is encompassed on all sides by the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains.
Furthermore, this trichiliocosm undergoes destruction and formation simultaneously; it is like rain falling from the sky in unbroken, uninterrupted succession, with drops as thick as axle-trees.

In this way, throughout the immeasurable worlds of the eastern direction—uninterrupted and without interval—some are about to be destroyed, some are about to be formed, some are currently being destroyed, some remain after having been destroyed, some are currently being formed, and some remain after having been formed.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in all the ten directions.

Thus, whether it be the world of sentient beings or the receptacle world, because they are produced by the power of karma and afflictions and arise through the predominance of karma and afflictions, they are collectively termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Regarding the phrases "produced by the power of karma and afflictions" and "arisen through the predominance of karma and afflictions," these two clauses respectively demonstrate that both the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) are of the nature of suffering.

Furthermore, there are pure worlds that are not subsumed under the Truth of Suffering; for they are not produced by the power of karma and afflictions, nor are they arisen through the predominance of karma and afflictions, but are rather induced by the predominance of pure roots of goodness resulting from great vows.

The place thus produced is inconceivable; it is realized only by a Buddha, and is not even within the meditative range of those who have attained dhyāna, let alone those who merely engage in discursive thought.
