Furthermore, all ten afflictions give rise to various forms of wrong conduct by being deluded about suffering and its origin, as they serve as the causal basis and support for those [afflictions].

Why is this so? Because both the truths of suffering and its origin are the causes and conditions for the ten types of afflictions, and they also serve as their basis; therefore, all delusions regarding these causes, conditions, and bases give rise to various forms of wrong conduct.
Furthermore, all ten afflictions give rise to various wrong practices by being deluded regarding cessation and the path, because they are able to produce fear toward them.

Why is this so? Because through the power of the afflictions, one takes pleasure in and clings to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), giving rise to the perception of a precipice toward pure phenomena and thereby generating great terror.
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists give rise to all manner of false and inverted discriminations regarding the truths of cessation and the path.
Therefore, all ten delusions give rise to various erroneous practices based on confusion regarding cessation and the path.
What are the realms?
With the exception of hatred (*dveṣa*), all others are bound to all three realms.
Hatred is bound only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it arises by taking as its object a disagreeable or harmful state.
Furthermore, greed in the desire realm is associated with pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
As it is in the desire realm, so it is in the first and second dhyānas.
In the third dhyāna, it is associated with pleasure and equanimity; above that, it is associated with equanimity alone.
Greed in the desire realm that is associated with pleasure occurs in the five groups of sensory consciousness;
that which is associated with joy occurs in the mental consciousness;
and that which is associated with equanimity occurs in all instances.
The reason why [the mind] at the final moment of the continuum is not associated with sorrow or suffering is that it proceeds by way of an exultant mode of activity (*abhipramodana-carita*).
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is associated with suffering, sorrow, and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
That which is associated with suffering exists in the five bodies of sensory consciousness;
that which is associated with grief exists in the sixth consciousness.
The reason it is not associated with joy or pleasure is that it proceeds by way of a mode of operation characterized by dejection.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is called "afflicted conduct" (*daurmanasya-carita*) because it oppresses one's own mental continuum.
That which is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) exists in all places.

As previously stated, pride (*māna*) is associated with joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity in the desire realm; in the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with pleasure (*sukha*), joy, and equanimity; in the third dhyāna, it is associated with pleasure and equanimity; and above that, it is associated with equanimity alone.
Pride is not associated with pleasure in the desire realm because the five sensory consciousnesses are absent there.
If that is so, how is it associated with pleasure in the first and second dhyānas?
There is no fault, because it is associated with the pleasure of the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
How can there be pleasure of the mental level in that [state]?
Because it is taught that joy and pleasure exist in that stage.
As the Sūtra says:
"What is joy (*prīti*)?

It refers to the mental gladness, mental elation, mental satisfaction, mental composure, and mental tranquility experienced by one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*), based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and which is comprised within feeling (*vedanā*)."

"Depending on the evolving consciousnesses" means depending on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because other consciousnesses do not exist during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
What is meant by "bliss"?

It refers to the experience of joy and well-being, comprised within the category of feeling (*vedanā*), which is experienced by one who has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and relies upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their support.

The intended meaning of this sūtra is that when the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) arises in dependence upon the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with such a collection of mind and mental factors; through its mode of joyful exultation (*prīti*), it causes this entire collection to become uplifted and delighted, and furthermore, it causes the very substance of the *ālayavijñāna*, which serves as their basis, to be peaceful, blissful, and at ease.

Because this pleasant feeling performs two functions, although its essence is one, it is established as two types—either joy (*prīti*) or pleasure (*sukha*); therefore, it is said to be associated with these.
Pride is associated with pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

As it is with pride, so it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*), joy, and equanimity in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), it is associated with whichever feelings are present there.
How is it that wrong view in the desire realm is associated with both sorrow and joy?
It is because those who have previously performed wholesome or unwholesome deeds experience either delight or dejection upon seeing that these actions bear no fruit.
The reason it is not associated with suffering or pleasure is that all views belong to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).

Doubt is associated with mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), it is associated with whatever feelings are present there.
The reason why the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not associated with joy (*prīti*) is that as long as the unsettled mind has not ceased, joy does not arise.

Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), for those who doubt or who have attained higher dhyānas, joy and bliss (*sukha*) may still function in accordance [with their state] because they are sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, in those cases as well, they are associated with joy and bliss.
Ignorance is of two kinds: namely, associated and unshared.
Because associated ignorance is associated with all afflictions, it can be associated with whatever feeling is present in a given instance.

Non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the higher realms, it may be associated with whatever feelings are present.
Whether it is associated with joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*), or not, the principle should be explained in the same manner as for doubt (*vicikitsā*).
For what reason are all afflictions associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Because all afflictions subside and cease only when they fall into a state of neutrality. Why is this so?

As the afflictions arise and continue in succession, they gradually become attenuated; when their power is about to be exhausted and they fall into a neutral state, they necessarily correspond with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) within that state.
Furthermore, craving in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) resides in the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya).
As it is with craving, so it is with hatred (dveṣa) and ignorance (avidyā).
In the form realm (rūpadhātu), craving resides in four groups of consciousness, because that realm lacks the consciousnesses of smell and taste.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they exist solely within the mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāya*).
As it is with craving, so it is with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Pride, views, and doubt exist in all realms solely within the mental consciousness, because they function through the gates of weighing and so forth.
Furthermore, greed, hatred, and pride function with respect to only a portion of objects within the desire realm;
as it is in the desire realm, so it is in the form and formless realms.
Pride functions with respect to only a portion of objects because it arises as an inflation of the mind toward only a specific portion [of those objects].
The remaining afflictions operate by universally taking all objects as their cognitive range across all locations.
What are these groups?

They are the two groups of afflictions: the group to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) and the group to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).
In the desire realm, ten afflictions are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
As it is for those abandoned through the vision of suffering, so it is for those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
If one gives rise to wrong conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti*) regarding these [truths], they are abandoned through the vision of that [specific truth].
Question:
If one takes this as an object, does one then become deluded regarding it and give rise to wrong conduct?
Answer:
It is not necessarily so; for while they take the untainted as their object, the afflictions only increase in accordance with tainted entities.

If a certain place is the causal condition and the basis for those [afflictions], and one gives rise to erroneous conduct toward it due to delusion, that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

As it is with those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with those abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, according to their respective applications.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are nine afflictions (*kleśa*) each for those abandoned through the vision of the four truths, excluding hatred (*dveṣa*).
As it is with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), so it is with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, the total number of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is one hundred and twelve.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are six afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): namely, innate self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as craving (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
What is called the innate view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the manifestation of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) based upon this [view], even though the noble disciple has already generated the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
As the Sūtra says:

"Venerable Daśaka, you should know that regarding the five aggregates of clinging, I do not perceive a self or what belongs to a self; nevertheless, within these five aggregates of clinging, there exists the conceit 'I am,' the desire for 'I am,' and the underlying tendency toward 'I am,' which have not yet been permanently severed, fully understood, extinguished, or vomited out."
It is like a wet nurse who has a garment stained with grease; although she washes it thoroughly with water and earth to remove all impurities, if it has not yet been perfumed, the stench persists.
Furthermore, it is only after being fumigated with various kinds of fragrant substances that the foul odor is finally eliminated.

Likewise, although the noble disciples of the Buddha have permanently severed the defilement of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*), if they have not yet perfumed their mental continuum through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), the non-conceptualizing view of a self regarding phenomena—which is induced by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless, ingrained false attachment—continues to operate.
Furthermore, through the continuous succession of the perfuming of the path, that [view] is permanently extinguished.
As for the innate view of extreme adherence (*sahaja-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), it is comprised within the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Because of this view, the mind retreats from the realm of nirvāṇa and gives rise to great terror, thinking: "Where has my self gone now?"

Regarding the afflictions such as greed that are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): this refers to those excluding those subsumed under the category of the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are five [afflictions] abandoned through the path of cultivation, with the exception of hatred (*dveṣa*).
As it is in the realm of form, so it is likewise in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, there are sixteen afflictions in total that are abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
What is meant by "abandonment"?
It refers to abandonment through such specific distinctions, abandonment by means of this mental attention (*manasikāra*), and abandonment attained from this [source].
Regarding such distinctions in abandonment, they consist of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), distancing (*vivarjana*), and obtaining the antidote (*pratipakṣalābha*).

"Thorough knowledge" refers to the thorough knowledge of the causal basis (*nidāna*), the thorough knowledge of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), and the thorough knowledge of the disadvantages (*ādīnava*).

Regarding "universal knowledge of the causal conditions": this refers to knowing that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions have not yet been permanently severed, and so forth, as previously explained.
Regarding "universal knowledge of the intrinsic nature": this refers to knowing that once these afflictions have arisen, they utterly disturb and agitate the nature of the mind.

Regarding the thorough knowledge of faults: it means knowing that these afflictions can lead to self-harm, can lead to harming others, and can lead to harming both; that they can produce faults in the present life, can produce faults in future lives, and can produce faults in both the present and future lives; and that they cause sentient beings to experience the physical and mental suffering born of these faults.
Regarding "distancing": although those [afflictions] may arise temporarily, one does not adhere to them firmly.

By means of the three types of thorough knowledge—thorough knowledge of the causal basis, the object, and so forth—one does not firmly adhere to any afflictions that have already arisen, but rather employs skillful means to distance oneself from them.
"Attaining the antidote" means causing that which has not yet arisen not to arise, and causing that which has already arisen to be abandoned.
One attains the path of the antidote in order to cultivate and refine the path so that unarisen and already arisen afflictions do not arise and are permanently severed.
Question:
What kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) is able to sever [the afflictions]?
Answer:
The attention that takes the general as its object contemplates all phenomena as being devoid of self-nature and is able to sever the afflictions.
"Attention that takes the general as its object" refers to the attention that operates by synthesizing and taking the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object.
Question:

If it is only the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object in their totality—perceiving them as selfless—that can sever the afflictions, why is the practice of [contemplating] impermanence and so forth demonstrated?
Answer:
One does not cultivate those practices for the sake of severing afflictions, but rather for the sake of cultivating the practice of non-self.
By relying on the practice of impermanence, one attains the practice of suffering; by relying on the practice of suffering, one attains the practice of non-self.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is non-self.
Therefore, this practice of non-self is established as supreme.
There are three kinds of unsurpassed [attainments]: namely, the unsurpassed in wisdom, the unsurpassed in practice, and the unsurpassed in liberation.
Regarding the unsurpassed in wisdom, this refers to the wisdom of non-self; having attained this wisdom, there is nothing further to be sought.
The unsurpassed practice refers to the practice of swift progress through delight, for it is the foremost among all practices.
Unsurpassed liberation refers to the unshakable liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), for it is the most excellent among all liberations.
These three unsurpassed [attainments] are explained according to their sequence as relying upon the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
Question:
From what are they obtained through abandonment?
Answer:

It is not from the past, because that has already ceased; it is not from the future, because that has not yet arisen; it is not from the present, because the path and [the afflictions] do not coexist. Rather, it is through the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the various afflictions that they are abandoned.
In order to sever such and such categories of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), such and such categories of remedies (*pratipakṣa*) are produced.
When these categories of remedies arise, those very categories of coarse heaviness are extinguished.
It is equal and impartial, just as when light arises in the world, darkness is extinguished.
Because one is dissociated from this category [of afflictions], future afflictions are caused to abide in the state of non-arising; this is called "abandonment."
Furthermore, what is the karma produced by the predominance of the afflictions?
It refers to either karma of volition (*cetanā*) or karma after having willed (*cetayitvā*); these are collectively termed the characteristics of karma.

Moreover, there are five kinds of karma: namely, the karma of appropriation (*upādāna-karma*), the karma of function (*kāritra-karma*), the karma of application (*prayoga-karma*), the karma of transformation (*pariṇāma-karma*), and the karma of realization (*prāpti-karma*).
The action of appropriation refers to the eyes and so forth being able to see forms and so forth.
The action of function refers to earth and so forth being able to support and so forth.

Alternatively, it refers to the activity performed by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, such as the fact that all material form (*rūpa*) possesses resistance and susceptibility to transformation, and so on.
Action consisting of application refers to bodily actions and so forth that arise preceded by mental resolve.
Action consisting of transformation refers to goldsmiths and others fashioning ornaments and the like.
Regarding the "activity of realization" (*sākṣātkriyā-karman*), this refers to the realization of nirvāṇa and so forth by means of the noble path and other such factors.

Within the present context, the intended meaning primarily distinguishes the activity of application (*prayoga-karman*), though it also incidentally includes both the activities of realization and function (*kāritra*).
What is the karma of volition?
It refers to meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma.
What is the karma subsequent to volition?
These are bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
Furthermore, these three types of action—bodily, vocal, and mental—are either wholesome or unwholesome.

The unwholesome ones are the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*), namely: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.

The "wholesome" refers to the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), namely: abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from frivolous speech, as well as non-greed, non-hatred, and right view.

In this context, the reason only the paths of action are used to manifest bodily and other types of karma is that this is taught in accordance with the Sūtras by way of emphasizing the predominant factor; for their preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and so forth are also subsumed within bodily and other types of karma.
Among the ten paths of action, the first three consist of four, and the latter three consist of three; these follow their respective order as the characteristics of bodily, vocal, and mental karma.

Furthermore, the characteristics of killing and the other [paths of action] should be analyzed by way of five aspects: namely, by way of the object (*vastu*), the intention (*āśaya*), the means (*upāya*), the affliction (*kleśa*), and the completion (*niṣṭhā*) of killing and so forth.
The "object" refers to sentient beings and non-sentient things; depending on these as appropriate, one initiates acts such as killing.
The "intention" refers to the intention of perceiving the object as such, as well as the intention to perform this particular course of action.
Skillful means refers to this activity, whether initiated by oneself or another, through body, speech, or mind.
Afflictions refer to greed, hatred, and delusion, either collectively or individually as appropriate.
Regarding "completion": through various means, the path of action (*karmapatha*) is fulfilled in such and such a manner, either at that very moment or at a later time.
Within this context, the act of killing refers to those who are sentient beings.
The intention (*āśaya*) refers to this perception and the intent to cause harm.
The means (*upāya*) refers to such things as swords or clubs used for the purpose of harming.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) refer to greed and so forth.
"Completion" refers to the fact that those sentient beings, by means of their preparatory effort, die either immediately or at a later time.
Regarding [the offenses of] taking what is not given and so forth, both the objective basis (*vastu*) and completion should be analyzed in detail; the rest should be understood according to reason.
The act of taking what is not given refers to that which is possessed by another, whether it be animate or inanimate.
Its completion refers to taking it as one's own property.
Sexual misconduct refers to engaging with women who are not appropriate partners;
or, even if they are appropriate, doing so in an improper manner, at an inappropriate place, at an inappropriate time, or in excessive measure.
It also includes all improper acts with men and eunuchs.
"Ultimate" refers to mutual sexual union.
Regarding the matter of false speech: it consists of claiming to have seen, heard, sensed, or known what one has not seen, heard, sensed, or known.
The intention refers to the thought of distinction, desiring to speak with distinction.
The culmination refers to the assembly at that time and the understanding by the person addressed.
The objective basis for divisive speech refers to sentient beings, whether they are in harmony or not in harmony.
The intention refers to the mental state of wishing for separation and discord regarding those very persons.
The culmination refers to the victim’s comprehension of what has been said.
The objective basis of harsh speech refers to sentient beings who are capable of being harmed.
"Completion" refers to the utterance of harsh words.
Regarding the matter of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*), it refers to that which leads to or encompasses what is unbeneficial.
"Completion" refers to the actual utterance of such speech.
The object of covetousness refers to the wealth and resources possessed by others.
The intention refers to the arising of the perception [of them as one's own] and the desire for them.
The preparatory effort refers to the deliberation and calculation of wishing to possess them for oneself.
"Ultimate" means to resolutely grasp [the object] as one's own.
"The matter of malice" refers to sentient beings who are capable of causing harm.
"Ultimate" here refers to the definitive infliction of injury and so forth.
The object of wrong view refers to the sense that something truly exists.
The intention refers to giving rise to the perception that what truly exists does not exist, as well as the desire for that [perception].
The culmination refers to definitive denial.
As the Sūtra says:
"One intentionally creates karma.
What is meant by "intentionally creating karma"?

Briefly, there are five kinds: karma intentionally performed because of being commanded by others; karma intentionally performed because of being entreated by others; karma intentionally performed due to a lack of understanding; karma intentionally performed due to fundamental attachment; and karma intentionally performed due to inverted discrimination.

Regarding "karma intentionally performed because of another's instruction": it is, for example, when one who does not desire or delight [in the act] nonetheless initiates intentional unwholesome karma due to being instructed by the powerful force of another.

Regarding intentional karma performed due to being exhorted by another: it is, for example, when someone, though not desiring or finding pleasure in it, because of another's exhortation or guidance, regards it as beneficial and initiates intentional action toward unwholesome karma.

Regarding intentional action performed without clear understanding: it is like someone who, failing to discern virtues and faults and being devoid of any firm attachment, acts according to their whims and initiates unwholesome actions through intentionality.

Regarding intentional action performed through fundamental attachment: it is, for example, when one whose mind is shrouded by unwholesome roots such as greed and hatred, with intense attachment, initiates intentional unwholesome action.

Regarding "volitional karma created through inverted discrimination": it is like someone who, relying on the view of an uneven cause and taking delight in false teachings, initiates volitional unwholesome karma in order to seek desirable future maturation.

Among these five, regarding karma created through volition based on fundamental attachment and karma created through volition based on inverted discrimination: if these two types are performed or increased, they will not fail to undergo their maturation.
Why is this so? Because the first three types of intentional karma, though performed, do not increase; being light, they do not necessarily result in maturation (*vipāka*).
The latter two types of intentional karma, whether performed or increased, are heavy and therefore necessarily result in maturation.
"Producer" refers to that which initiates and brings into operation various karmas.
"Augmenter" refers to that which causes habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) to increase, thereby nourishing the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) within the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
As the Sūtra says regarding "karma that is definitely experienced": what is meant by "definite"?
It refers to the determination of the action performed, the determination of the maturation to be experienced, and the determination of the temporal state.

Regarding the determination of action: by the power of past karma, one has brought about a continuous stream of determinate maturation (*vipāka*), such that within this present life, one must necessarily perform this particular action.
Why must this action be performed?
Because the time limit has been determined, one will never exceed that limit but must necessarily perform this karma.

Even the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot create an obstruction to prevent its performance; for the fruit continues to evolve in accordance with the determining power of the cause.
Regarding the determination of the maturation (*vipāka*), it is as previously explained concerning karma created through intentional reflection (*saṃcetanīya-karman*).
Regarding the determination of the state (*avasthā*), this refers to karma determined by its state, such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth.
Just as by this karma one must experience ripening in the present life, by this karma one must experience ripening upon rebirth, and by this karma one must experience subsequent ripening.

Furthermore, regarding the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the ten unwholesome courses of action: within the three miserable realms, according to whether they were committed as inferior, middling, or superior, one experiences the maturation of rebirth among animals, hungry ghosts, or hell-beings.
Regarding the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*): each [action] brings about the deterioration of one's own person and possessions within the human realm according to its specific characteristics.

That is to say, after passing away from the miserable realms and being reborn among humans, due to [the commission of] killing, stealing, and so forth, one experiences the deterioration of one's own person and possessions according to their respective characteristics—namely, a short lifespan, constant poverty, and so on—as appropriate to each case.
As for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), each [unwholesome action] brings about the corresponding decline of external things according to its specific characteristic.
That is to say, killing and the other [non-virtues], each according to its own characteristic, bring about the decline of external things such as the harvests.
That which is called the external lack of luster in one's possessions is the sovereign result (*adhipatiphala*) of killing, and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Because of the cultivation and repeated cultivation of all ten unwholesome paths of action, one is born in the hells, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost; these are their ripened results (*vipākaphala*)."

If one is born into the same class of beings as these people, due to killing, one now obtains a short lifespan; due to taking what is not given, one lacks wealth and resources; due to sexual misconduct, one’s spouse is unchaste; due to false speech, one is frequently slandered; due to divisive speech, one’s friends and kin fall apart; due to harsh speech, one constantly hears unpleasant sounds; due to frivolous speech, one’s words lack authority; due to covetousness, greed becomes increasingly intense; due to malice, hatred becomes increasingly intense; and due to wrong view, delusion becomes increasingly intense. Because delusion is predominant in those with wrong views, this is their outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Due to the excessive cultivation of the karma of killing, all external things lack luster; due to taking what is not given, one frequently encounters frost and hail; due to sexual misconduct, there is much dust and grime; due to false speech, there is much foul stench; due to divisive speech, the terrain is uneven, precipitous, and obstructed; due to harsh speech, the ground is saline, barren, stony, and foul; due to frivolous speech, the seasons become irregular; due to covetousness, fruits and crops are meager; due to malice, the taste of fruits is bitter and acrid; and due to wrong view, the taste of fruits is bitter and acrid or they are entirely without fruit—these are their dominant results (*adhipati-phala*).

Furthermore, regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the ten paths of wholesome action: it refers to receiving the ripening of human or celestial existence within the realms of humans and gods.

Regarding the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*): it refers to obtaining, within those very same places, the flourishing of one's own body and various requisites, each according to its respective characteristic.
Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*): it refers to the attainment of external phenomena flourishing in accordance with their respective characteristics within those very same realms.

Just as the three distinctions of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and so forth are established for unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*), so too should the three distinctions of fruit for wholesome courses of action associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) be established accordingly for humans and gods.

Furthermore, when wholesome and unwholesome karma brings about the maturation of rebirth within the happy and miserable realms, there are two types of distinction: namely, projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) and completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*).
The karma that attracts refers to that by which one is able to draw forth the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
The karma that completes refers to that by which, once born, one experiences desirable or undesirable fruits.

Furthermore, there are some karmas by which a single body is drawn forth through the power of one karma; that is to say, because the power of one karma nurtures the seeds of maturation for a single lifetime.
There are also some karmas by which many bodies are drawn forth through the power of one karma; that is to say, because the power of one karma nurtures the seeds of maturation for many lifetimes.
There are some karmas that, through the power of many karmic forces, draw forth a single body; this is because many moments of karma repeatedly nourish the seeds of maturation for a single lifetime.

There are some karmas that, through the power of multiple karmic forces, result in the acquisition of many bodies; this is because the karmas of multiple moments mutually support one another and successively nourish the seeds for the maturation of many births.
Question:
If a single sentient being accomplishes many karmas, how does he experience their ripened fruits (vipāka-phala) in succession?
Answer:

Within that body, that which is heaviest ripens first; or that which is present at the time of death; or that which was previously habitually practiced; or that which was performed first—these karmic maturations ripen first.
As the Sūtra says:
"There are three kinds of karma, namely: meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma.
Meritorious karma refers to wholesome karma bound to the desire realm."
Non-meritorious karma refers to unwholesome karma.
Immovable karma refers to wholesome karma bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
Question:
Why are wholesome karmas bound to the realms of form and formlessness called "immovable"?
Answer:

Just as wholesome and unwholesome karmas that are fully developed in other destinies within the desire realm may, upon encountering conditions, shift to produce maturation in a different destiny; such is not the case for those bound to the realms of form and formlessness. Therefore, they are called immovable.
Karma bound to the form and formless realms does not possess such a quality, because the realm and level of its experienced maturation (*vipāka*) are fixed.
Therefore, it is called "immovable" (*āneñjya*) in the sense that its maturation cannot be shifted.
Furthermore, because it is comprised within the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), it is said to be "immovable.
Question:
As stated in the Sūtras, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
If there are meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable [karmas],
how is it that meritorious and immovable formations arise conditioned by ignorance?
Answer:
There are two kinds of delusion: first, delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*); second, delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*).

Due to delusion regarding maturation, one initiates non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*); due to delusion regarding the true meaning, one initiates meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya- and āniñjya-saṃskāra*).

Those who engage in non-meritorious conduct due to delusion regarding maturation do so because such conduct is invariably defiled in nature; when conjoined with ignorance, it necessarily precludes the acceptance of the correct view regarding the characteristics of maturation.

Regarding those who, out of delusion concerning the true meaning, initiate merit-based and immovable practices: "true meaning" refers to the Four Noble Truths; delusion with respect to them is termed "delusion concerning the true meaning."
Although one who has not yet seen the Truths may give rise to a virtuous mind, because they are still bound by those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are also called deluded.

By the power of those tendencies, they fail to know the suffering of the three realms as it truly is, and are thus able to initiate meritorious and immovable formations that serve as the cause for future existence (*punarbhava*).
One who has already seen the truths is incapable of initiating this karma, because they lack delusion regarding the nature of reality.
Therefore, it is said that such karma arises from these [afflictions].
Furthermore, regarding the path of action of killing, greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the preliminary means, while hatred brings it to completion.
As it is with the path of action of killing, so it is with harsh speech and malice.
When killing has greed as its preliminary means, it is for the sake of [obtaining] skin, meat, and so forth.
When it has hatred as its preliminary means, it is for the sake of eliminating enemies and the like.
Delusion serves as the preliminary means because it leads to activities such as sacrificial rites;
hatred constitutes the final consummation because one who lacks compassion will certainly not kill other sentient beings.
Harsh speech and the others should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the karmic path of taking what is not given, it has greed, hatred, and delusion as its preliminary means (*upāya*), and it is brought to completion by greed.
As with taking what is not given, so it is with sexual misconduct and covetousness.
Question:
How do desire and so forth employ desire and so forth as their means?
Answer:

It was previously stated that the nature of the karmic path of covetousness consists in definitively grasping another's resources as one's own. If, regarding those very same resources, one first gives rise to a different form of greed and initiates the preparatory effort of seeking them with the desire to possess them for oneself, this is established as the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of covetousness.
If anger arises first, one should ensure that no other [afflictions] follow; this is the expedient for anger.
If delusion arises first—meaning one takes another's property as one's own and perceives no fault in doing so—this is the expedient for delusion.
The remaining [paths of action] should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the path of action of false speech, with greed, hatred, or delusion as the preliminary means, it is brought to completion through any one of these three.
As it is with false speech, so it is with divisive speech and frivolous speech.
Regarding the path of action of wrong view, greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the preliminary means, while it is brought to completion by delusion alone.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
there is collective karma and non-collective karma; there is powerful karma and weak karma.
What is collective karma?
If karma can cause the various distinctions within the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), why is it called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) karma?
If karma can cause the various distinctions within the sentient world (*sattvaloka*), [why is it called shared karma?]

Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to act as mutual predominant conditions for one another; by the power of this karma, it is said that sentient beings stand in relation to each other as predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*), because they possess mutual predominant influence. This is also termed "collective karma" (*sādhāraṇakarma*).
By virtue of this power, sentient beings act as reciprocal causes for the transformation of one another’s minds and mental factors.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In this way, sentient beings see one another and so forth, yet they do not experience [one another], nor is such [experience] easily obtainable."
What is karma of powerful force?

It refers to unwholesome karma intentionally committed by a person (*pudgala*) who possesses strong power of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bala*). Because it is suppressed by the power of counteraction, karma that was destined to be experienced in the hells (*naraka*) is transformed into karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), and karma that should have been experienced in the present life is transformed so that it is not experienced at all.
The reason this karma is called "powerful" is that its counteractive force is strong.

This counteractive karma is superior in power compared to the karma it opposes, as it causes the transformation and cessation of the various painful karmic maturations (*vipāka*) produced by that opposed karma.
Furthermore, all wholesome karma intentionally performed is called "powerful" because its power of counteraction is stronger than that of unwholesome karma.
Based on this karma, the Blessed One said:

"My noble disciples can thoroughly perfume their minds with immeasurable and vast karma; thus, whatever measurable karma they may perform, that karma cannot lead them away, cannot cause them to remain [in saṃsāra], and cannot cause them to be included among its ranks."
Furthermore, for a person whose power of counteractive measures is weak, any unwholesome karma intentionally committed is termed "powerful" in comparison to all wholesome karma.
Moreover, karma intentionally committed that is certain to ripen, which one neither abandons nor understands, is called powerful karma.

The meaning intended here is that all wholesome and unwholesome karmas are without distinction; those whose maturation is determined and which cannot be severed by the power of the noble paths are all termed "powerful karma."
Furthermore, all unwholesome karma bound to the desire realm is inherently powerful, because it is accompanied by numerous primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Moreover, that which has been previously habituated is called "powerful karma," because it has repeatedly perfumed the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*).
Furthermore, karma performed during a state of strength is called "powerful karma," because it is produced by intense attachment and pure faith during one's prime of life.
Additionally, karma performed by those who are incurable is called "powerful karma," because the karma of those who lack the nature for nirvāṇa cannot be overcome by the power of remedies.
Furthermore, powerful karma is generated by way of the field, namely, karma such as harming one's mother and so forth.
Moreover, powerful karma is generated by way of mental application, namely, making great vows for unsurpassed enlightenment and so forth.
The karma produced by this is of such fierce power that it is called "powerful karma.

Furthermore, powerful karma is generated through nine causes: namely, by reason of the field, the object, the physical basis, the support, the attention, the intention, the accompaniment, repeated cultivation, and being practiced in common with many sentient beings; it is through these nine causes that powerful karma is generated.
The "field" refers to one who possesses great merit and is worthy of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
The "object" refers to the material things given, which are numerous and exquisite.
The "essential nature" refers to such qualities as where ethical discipline (*śīla*) excels giving, and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) excels ethical discipline.
The basis refers to the performance of various meritorious deeds by one who has already abandoned desire.
The mental attention refers to the mental attention accompanied by intense and pure faith.
The aspiration refers to the aspiration consisting of the longing for nirvāṇa.
"Accompaniment" refers to the mutual inclusion [of this practice] with other meritorious deeds through further extensive cultivation.
"Cultivating extensively" means practicing repeatedly or reflecting upon it repeatedly.
That which is practiced in common with many sentient beings refers to performing an action oneself, instructing others to do it, or rejoicing in its performance.
That which is contrary to this is karma of inferior power.
As the Blessed One said:
If it is said that such and such a man or person, according to such and such karma—whether performed or accumulated—will in turn experience such and such a maturation.
If this were the case, one would not be able to cultivate the pure holy life, nor could one know the right way to exhaust all suffering and bring an end to it.

If someone were to say that various men and individuals, according to such and such karma conducive to experience—which they have performed or increased—will in turn receive such and such a corresponding maturation of experience; [then this would be so].
If such a thing were possible, one should cultivate the pure holy life (brahmacarya), and it would also be possible to know the complete exhaustion of all suffering and bring an end to suffering.
What is the underlying intent (abhiprāya) of this statement in the Sūtra?

In this context, the Buddha’s intention was to refute such false doctrines as the claim that karma associated with pleasure can produce a maturation associated with pleasure, karma associated with suffering can produce a maturation associated with suffering, and karma associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure can produce a maturation associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; therefore, he made this statement.
If it is said that such and such a man, a person (pudgala), having performed or accumulated such and such karma, will in turn experience such and such a maturation (vipāka).
If this were the case, one should not cultivate the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*), nor could one know the complete exhaustion of all suffering and bring an end to suffering.
Why should one not cultivate the pure holy life?

For those whose afflictions are extremely fierce and intense, they must exert themselves and spur themselves on by means of wisdom, maintaining the prohibitive precepts even while accompanied by sorrow and suffering.

If maintaining the prohibitive precepts were to result in being accompanied by sorrow and suffering again at the time one undergoes their ripening in the future, then such maintenance would be devoid of benefit.

Furthermore, if one violates the prohibitions by engaging with the wives of others and so forth while accompanied by joy and pleasure, yet continues to associate with that same joy and pleasure when experiencing their karmic maturation in the future, then one's diligent efforts to abstain from such acts have been in vain.
Therefore it is said:
if such a thing were to exist, one should not cultivate the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
For what reason, moreover, could one not know the right way to exhaust all suffering and bring an end to suffering?

Since practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in such a manner results in the maturation of suffering, the Blessed One preached this sutra to refute the false teachings of those non-Buddhist outsiders who claim that actions associated with pleasure result in the maturation of pleasure, actions associated with suffering result in the maturation of suffering, and actions associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure result in the maturation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; for it is certain that the maturation cause and its maturation fruit are similar to one another.

Furthermore, this correct teaching is authorized as follows: actions associated with pleasure that are conducive to pleasant feeling result in the ripening of pleasant experience; those conducive to painful feeling result in the ripening of painful experience; and those conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling result in the ripening of neither-painful-nor-pleasant experience.

Karma associated with suffering that is conducive to pleasant feeling results in the ripening of pleasant experience; that which is conducive to painful feeling results in the ripening of painful experience; and that which is conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling results in the ripening of neither-painful-nor-pleasant experience.

Karma associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is conducive to pleasant feeling results in the ripening of pleasant feeling; that which is conducive to painful feeling results in the ripening of painful feeling; and that which is conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling results in the ripening of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Karma associated with pleasure is of two kinds: namely, wholesome and unwholesome.

According to their respective natures, they accord with future experiences of painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations, and are further able to bring about the maturation (vipāka) of pleasure and so forth.

In this way, karmic actions associated with suffering and those associated with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure each have two types that accord with pleasure and so forth, resulting in the maturation of pleasure and so forth, as appropriate.
Such is the intended meaning (*saṃdhi*) of this sūtra.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, Fascicle Seven;
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, Fascicle Eight.
