Chapter One: The Section on Determination, Part Four: The Chapter on Truths. What is the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?

To state it in brief, it refers to the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) samādhi and its corresponding wisdom (*prajñā*), along with their associated factors, which arise immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because its essential characteristic consists of non-conceptual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,

and because its characteristic is the wisdom of the absolute equality between the object of cognition and the cognizing subject, by means of which one penetrates the suchness (*tathatā*) that is the absence of intrinsic nature in both the grasped and the grasper.
Furthermore, it takes as its characteristic the dharma-knowledge that universally negates both the provisional person and the provisional phenomena of individual beings.
How does it take as its characteristic the dharma-knowledge that negates the provisional person of individual beings?
Because this wisdom does not conceptualize the characteristic of a self within one's own continuum,
"non-conceptualization" has the meaning of "elimination.
How is it that the wisdom of phenomena, which takes as its object the various conventional designations of phenomena, acts as the means of elimination?
Because this wisdom does not conceptually differentiate the characteristics of phenomena such as form within one's own continuum,
how is it that the wisdom whose characteristic is the object of the two types of conventional designation completely dispels them?

Because this wisdom is undifferentiated in all respects, it does not conceptualize the characteristics of self or phenomena. Furthermore, if one were to explain the distinctions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) separately, they are as follows: immediately following the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), there are the sixteen types:

the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*); the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origin (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding origin (*samudaye dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding origin (*samudaye ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding origin (*samudaye ’nvayajñāna*); the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhe ’nvayajñāna*); and the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*). These constitute the sixteen aspects.

Among the noble truths, the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti* and *anvayajñānakṣānti*), as well as the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*), constitute the specific characteristics of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Suffering" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
"Phenomena of suffering" refers to the teachings that arise based upon the predominance of the truth of suffering.
Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of the superior dharmas that observes the truths within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

Knowledge-endurance (*jñāna-kṣānti*) refers to the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) through direct realization regarding each individual truth of suffering, by virtue of the prior power of observation; by means of this wisdom, one permanently abandons all afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The meaning explained here is as follows: within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), by the predominant power of wisdom comprised of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) which observes the sūtras and other teachings arising from the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as its basis, one directly realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of that suffering within one’s own continuum. Thereby, the essence of supramundane wisdom—right view—is produced. By means of this wisdom, one permanently abandons all twenty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering. Therefore, it is called the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*).

The knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) refers to that by which, immediately following the receptivity (*kṣānti*), one realizes liberation from the afflictions previously abandoned. Why is this so?

First, by means of patience (*kṣānti*), one permanently abandons all afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya-kleśa*), causing the basis (*āśraya*) to be transformed. Immediately following this, through the arising of such knowledge (*jñāna*), one realizes the transformation of the basis; this is called the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*).

The patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) refers to the arising of uncontaminated wisdom immediately following the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*),

which internally realizes for itself that the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge of suffering are each distinct, and that all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category.

Why is this? Because the first two kinds—whether they be patience (*kṣānti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*)—are the source of all subsequent noble dharmas, both those of training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); it is from them that these latter arise.
Therefore, untainted wisdom arises as a distinct internal realization;

taking this as its object, it declares that all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category. For this reason, it is called the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti).

Regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*): it refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises immediately after this [subsequent acceptance of suffering], which definitively confirms and validates the subsequent acceptance of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-kṣānti*). Why is this so?

Because the untainted knowledge arises immediately following the subsequent acceptance of suffering, and by means of internal realization (*pratyātma-saṃvedana*), it confirms and validates that subsequent acceptance of suffering; therefore, it is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering.

In this manner, regarding the other truths, one should understand that all the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) function accordingly: within this stage, one awakens to the grasped (*grāhya*) by means of the dharma-patiences and dharma-knowledges, and awakens to the grasper (*grāhaka*) by means of the subsequent patiences (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*).

Why is this so? The supramundane path has two objects, namely *tathatā* (suchness) and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). The path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge takes *tathatā* as its object, while the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge takes correct cognition as its object; it is because these various patiences and knowledges understand [their respective objects] in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, within this stage of all patience and knowledge, one is said to be "abiding in the contemplation of the signless" (*animitta-vihāra*). As the Bhagavān spoke of the person abiding in the sixth signless dwelling, it is precisely those who currently abide in this stage of patience and knowledge; for within this stage, no signs whatsoever can be apprehended.

Furthermore, there are six types of abiding in the signless (*animitta*): namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the signless (*animitta*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
These sixteen moments of mind are called the path of seeing.

Why is this so? Because these sixteen moments of mind, subsumed under such patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as they perceive each of the previously unseen objects of the Four Noble Truths through four moments respectively.

Furthermore, regarding the "moment of mind" (*cittakṣaṇa*): it is designated as a single moment when the cognition of an object of knowledge reaches its completion; it does not refer solely to the time when that which was previously non-existent arises for the first time.
Why is this? Because the production of the knowing wisdom that reaches its culmination regarding the objects of knowledge is designated as a single *kṣaṇa*.
As it is said that "suffering should be fully known" constitutes a single mental *kṣaṇa*, so too it is with "origination should be permanently abandoned," and so forth.
Furthermore, as previously stated regarding the distinctions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), these are all provisional designations and not ultimately real.
Why is this? Because within the supramundane state, each is individually realized internally, transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Furthermore, the entire Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) should be thoroughly understood through four aspects: namely, by way of establishment, by way of reflection, by way of realization, and by way of fulfillment.

Regarding "establishment" (*vyavasthāpana*): it refers to when Śrāvakas and others, having attained the ultimate according to their own realization, desire to cause others to understand as well; thus, by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they establish the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) through immeasurable sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*). This refers to such statements as: "Within the various truths, there are such-and-such types of patience (*kṣānti*) and such-and-such types of knowledge (*jñāna*)," and so forth.

"Contemplation" refers to the correct cultivation of the means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*), wherein one repeatedly practices contemplation using mundane knowledge according to how things are established.

"Realization" refers to having thus practiced repeatedly, personally and internally realizing the initial path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is the supramundane state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
"Perfection" refers to the subsequent completion of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in this stage, culminating in the attainment of the ultimate state.

Once that ultimate state has been attained, one further establishes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) through the application of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
These four characteristics constitute the wheel of the true path, which revolves repeatedly and successively, turning in mutual dependence without interruption.

As the Sūtra says, "Dust is distanced and defilement is left behind, and the eye of the True Dharma arises regarding all phenomena"—this is spoken with reference to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

The receptivities to the dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) can distance one from dust, and the knowledges of the dharmas (*dharmanirvedha*) can free one from defilement, because they have as their intrinsic nature the sublime noble eye of wisdom regarding the truths for the first time.
Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) can distance one from dust, because all dharma-patience eternally severs the dust of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) can remove defilement, because all dharma-knowledge arises based on having already severed the stains of the obstacles.

Furthermore, regarding these two stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), the path attains purity through universal comprehension and permanent abandonment, respectively; it is in reliance upon this that one speaks of being "distant from dust and free from defilement."

Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, thoroughly penetrated the Dharma, and reached the ultimate firmness of the Dharma; having transcended all hope and doubt, not relying on other conditions, unable to be led astray by others regarding the Teacher’s instruction, and having attained fearlessness among all dharmas"—this also refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because it is taught that for those beings to be converted, there is the immediate realization of the Noble Truths;
"one who sees the Dharma" refers to the various patiences regarding the dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), because through them one penetrates the true Dharma.
"Attaining the Dharma" refers to the various knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the dharmas, because they are able to realize the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"Thoroughly penetrating the Dharma" refers to the various types of receptivities (*kṣānti*);
this is because these two categories thoroughly penetrate all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).

"Those who have reached the ultimate firmness of the Dharma" refers to those possessing the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*), because they have attained finality regarding all that is to be known.

"Those who have transcended all expectations" means that, through the supramundane path of the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges, they have realized the noble fruit long desired; thus, they have no further hope or anxiety regarding what they themselves have realized.

One who has transcended all doubts and hesitations has no uncertainty regarding the realization of others within this stage, because they know that others, too, are capable of realizing this supreme state.
"Not depending on other conditions" means that although there is no guidance from others regarding the path being cultivated, one possesses natural skillfulness.

"That which others cannot lead away from the Great Teacher’s instruction" means that having attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Buddha’s holy teaching, one cannot be diverted or led astray by false paths even when transitioning into future births.

Regarding the attainment of fearlessness among all phenomena: it is because, within the context of answering questions concerning the realized teachings, one who possesses evil desires and overweening pride never has even the slightest trace of a timid or inferior mind.
What is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

It refers to all mundane paths and supramundane paths, weak, medium, and superior paths, as well as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) that exist upon the path of seeing; all these are termed the path of cultivation.

Why is this so? Because the noble disciples of the Buddhas have already attained the direct realization of the Truths; from that point onward, they repeatedly practice the worldly path and other means as a skillful method to sever the remaining fetters—this is called the Path of Cultivation.

The mundane path refers to the mundane first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, and fourth dhyāna, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, dhyāna and the formless attainments (ārūpya) should be analyzed extensively by way of four aspects: namely, by way of defilement (saṃkleśa), purity (śukla), establishment (vyavasthāna), and purification (viśuddhi).
Regarding "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*), it refers to the four indeterminate roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*):
first, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); second, views (*dṛṣṭi*); third, pride (*māna*); and fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because the mind is defiled by these four afflictions, all obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states within the various doors of defiled meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) in the form and formless realms continue to arise without interruption, along with the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Why is this so? Because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one is defiled by the afflictions of the higher dhyānas, due to greedily relishing the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) in pure concentration.
Because of views (*dṛṣṭi*), one is defiled by the afflictions of the higher dhyānas, because one relies upon those dhyānas to give rise to speculative views concerning the past and so forth.

Due to pride (*māna*), one is defiled by the defilement of pride regarding the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), because one gives rise to arrogance based on having realized superior concentration.

Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one is defiled by the defilement of doubt regarding the higher meditative absorptions; those seeking liberation, because they have not yet penetrated the true principle, constantly give rise to doubt concerning what has been realized in its excellence, wondering: "Is this liberation, or is it not liberation?"
In this way, these afflictions constantly defile the mind, causing the two types of delusions—those of the form and formless realms, both great and small—to flow on in succession.
"Pure and white" refers to the pure dhyānas and the formless attainments; they are called pure and white because their nature is wholesome.
Although this belongs to the mundane realm, it is also termed "pure" because it is free from the stains of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*).

Regarding its establishment, there are four kinds of establishment: namely, establishment by way of factors (*aṅga*), establishment by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), establishment by way of categories (*prakāra*), and establishment by way of names and concepts (*saṃjñā*).
In the dhyānas, there is a fourfold establishment;
in the formless attainments (ārūpyas), there are only three types, excluding the establishment of factors (aṅga).
As for the establishment of factors, it means that the first dhyāna has five factors.
What are the five? First, applied thought (vitarka);
second, sustained thought (vicāra); third, joy (prīti); fourth, bliss (sukha); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
The second dhyāna has four factors.
What are the four?
First, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
The third dhyāna has five factors.
What are the five? First, equanimity;
second, mindfulness; third, correct awareness; fourth, bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors.
What are the four?
First, purity of equanimity; second, purity of mindfulness; third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
Question:
The dharmas are immeasurable; why, then, are only vitarka and so forth established as branches?
Answer:
Because they are the branches of counteraction, the branches of benefit, and the branches of essential nature that serve as the basis for those two.
Because these three factors are complete and require nothing further, in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are the two factors of counteraction;
they are able to sever the vitarka and vicāra of the desire realm, such as sensual desire, ill-will, and harmfulness.

The two factors of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are the factors of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*), because once the objects to be countered have been remedied by the factors of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one attains the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the essential nature factor (*svabhāva-aṅga*) upon which those two depend, because applied thought and the others function in reliance upon the power of concentration (*samādhi*).
In the second dhyāna, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is the factor of counteraction (*pratipakṣāṅga*), because it serves as the antidote to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are the factors of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*).
One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the factor of essential nature (*svabhāvāṅga*) which serves as the basis for those two; its meaning is as previously explained.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are the factors of antidote, because these three can counteract joy (*prīti*).
Bliss (*sukha*) is the factor of benefit.
One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the factor of essential nature, which serves as the basis for those two; the meaning is as previously explained.
In the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness are the factors of counteraction, because these two can counteract pleasure.
The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is the factor of benefit.
One-pointedness of mind is the essential factor that serves as the basis for those two;
no factors are established among the formless [attainments] because of the single flavor of śamatha.
What is the establishment of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?
It refers to entering the first dhyāna by means of seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
What are the seven types of mental attention? They are:

mental attention that discerns characteristics, mental attention of resolute conviction, mental attention of withdrawal, mental attention of delight in gathering, mental attention of investigation, mental attention of the culmination of application, and mental attention of the fruit of the culmination of application.
This detailed analysis is as found in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, in the section on the "Subsequent Yoga.
How does one enter the first dhyāna by means of the seven types of mental attention?

It is by means of mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration that one perceives the defects and so forth within the desire realm, thereby comprehending its coarse characteristics.
Because these characteristics do not exist within the first dhyāna, it is called the "characteristic of tranquility.
This is termed the *manaskāra* of "discerning the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*).

Such mental attention is still interspersed with hearing and reflection; from this point upward, one transcends hearing and reflection and focuses exclusively on the characteristic of cultivation, taking the characteristics of coarseness and tranquility as its object. One cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, repeatedly contemplating the nature and characteristics of coarseness and tranquility exactly as they were investigated. This is termed the *manaskāra* of "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika*).

By practicing this, the attention that arises together with the path of initial abandonment is called "attention of detachment" (*prāvivekyamanasikāra*), because it is able to abandon the superior grades of afflictions and because it is able to distance oneself from the corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

This practitioner further delights in higher abandonment and the merits of higher abandonment; having already touched a small measure of the joy and happiness of seclusion, in order to eliminate lethargy and drowsiness, they occasionally cultivate pure and sublime mental attention (*manasikāra*) to gladden the mind—this is called the mental attention of "embracing joy" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*).

Because such a practitioner is sustained by the collection of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) through skillful means (*upāya*), the afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and stains (*mala*) bound to the desire realm no longer manifest. Consequently, in order to examine thoroughly whether these afflictions have been abandoned or not, one further applies the mind to observe the signs of purity (*śubhanimitta*) that accord with their arising; this is called "attention consisting of observation" (*mīmāṃsāmanasikāra*).

In this way, the practitioner repeatedly observes and cultivates the path of antidotes in order to achieve temporary dissociation from all afflictions of the desire realm. Because this mental engagement associated with the path of antidotes constitutes the final preparatory stage for the first dhyāna, it is called the "mental engagement of the culmination of preparation."

Immediately following this, one realizes the fundamental initial dhyāna accompanied by mental attention; this is called the "mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the means. Furthermore, through the mental attention of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), one generates a mind of aspiration in order to correctly understand what is to be abandoned and what is to be attained;

for the sake of abandoning and for the sake of attaining, one applies the correct means toward the sought-after object through the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*). Through the mental attention of detachment (*viveka manaskāra*), one abandons the superior-grade afflictions; through the mental attention of delight in cultivation (*ratisaṃgrāhaka manaskāra*), one abandons the middle-grade afflictions; through the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā manaskāra*), one settles the mind in what has been realized and remains free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*); through the mental attention of the culmination of the means (*prayoganiṣṭha manaskāra*), one abandons the inferior-grade afflictions; and through the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the means (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala manaskāra*), one experiences the fruit of the cultivation of those aforementioned mental attentions.

Just as one cultivates the seven modes of attention for the purpose of realizing entry into the first dhyāna, so too should it be understood accordingly up to the realization of entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, regarding the coarse characteristic (*audārikatva*), it refers to all lower stages from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness. Briefly, there are two types of such coarse characteristics:
first, abiding in heavy suffering because one dwells in a state lacking tranquility;
second, having minimal vital formations because one's lifespan is short.

The characteristic of tranquility refers to all higher stages, from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because they are the opposite of the characteristic of coarseness.
Regarding the establishment of categories: in the first dhyāna concentration, one cultivates three grades—namely, weak, medium, and superior.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is for the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments; their cultivation likewise consists of these three grades.
Due to the cultivation of the first dhyāna in its weak, medium, and superior grades, three types of karmic fruition arise within that first dhyāna.
Just as it is with the first dhyāna, so it is for the other dhyānas: both their cultivation and the resulting fruits each consist of three grades.

Regarding the three grades of cultivation within the various dhyānas that produce three kinds of fruits, these refer to the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā heavens, as explained extensively above.
Because there are no distinct locations within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), no differentiation among the fruits of birth is established. Why is this so?
Because in the formless realm there are no stable abodes such as palaces or dwellings, no differentiation among the fruits of birth is established.
However, because the formless absorptions are cultivated in three grades, when their maturation arises, there are higher and lower levels, as well as inferior and superior qualities.
That the maturation arises with higher and lower levels is due to differences in lifespan and other such factors.
Regarding "inferiority and superiority," this refers to the distinctions between the defiled and the undefiled, as well as between the predominant and the minor.
Regarding "establishment by name and concept," this refers to the distinctions among the samādhis within the four dhyānas, which have immeasurable names and are incalculable and inconceivable.

Why is this? Within the concentrations subsumed under the first dhyāna, there are the samādhis entered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained ultimate great majesty; even the names of those samādhis are not understood by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, so how could they know their number, let alone enter them through realization?
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the number of samādhis exceeds one hundred;
likewise, in other Mahāyāna sūtras, the number of samādhis is said to be immeasurable.
As it is with the meditative concentrations included within the first dhyāna, so it is with those included within the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
All that has been explained thus far is based upon the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
"Purified" refers to the ultimate concentration within the first dhyāna, up to the ultimate concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called purified dhyāna.

Regarding the "attainment of the limit of the formless" (*ārūpyakoṭi-samādhi*): it is because one cultivates the meditative concentration of capability (*karmanya-samādhi*) to its ultimate limit in order to induce superior qualities, such as the attainment of mastery (*vaśitā*).

The supramundane path refers to the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, which are comprised within the categories of dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge during the path of cultivation.
The characteristics of these eight knowledges have already been explained in detail within the context of the path of seeing.

As well as the samādhis associated with them, these are either subsumed under the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) or subsumed under the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is exclusively mundane, because indistinct perception (*asaṃprakhyāna-saṃjñā*) is constantly active therein.
Because unclear perceptions constantly manifest before one, it serves as the basis for the non-extremely-clear functioning of the Noble Path; therefore, it is invariably comprised within the mundane.
By this principle, because that perception is weak and inferior and cannot sharply grasp the characteristics of the object of focus, it is called "signless" (animitta).
Furthermore, how is it known that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) lacks the noble path?
As the Blessed One has taught:
"Only up to the attainment of the sphere of perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*) can one truly illuminate and penetrate [reality] as it is.
The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is supramundane; because it is realized subsequent to the Noble Path, it must be induced within the human realm.
Regarding "inducing" (*āvāhaka*), it has the meaning of initial arising.
It can manifest either in the human realm or in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because that which has already arisen previously manifests once again.
"Or in the human realm" means in this very life.
"Or in the form realm" means being reborn there in a future life.
How could a noble disciple who has already attained the formless attainments and is detached from the desire for the form realm ever again be born in the form realm?

It is not necessary to be permanently free from desire for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) in order to enter the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); therefore, four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated here.
If one has already become free from desire for the form realm, is it the case that all such persons are able to enter the peaceful liberations (*śāntavimokṣa*) of the formless realm?
If one is able to enter the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm, has one already abandoned all desire for the realm of form?
Answer:

Regarding this first case, it refers to one who, relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), has already abandoned desire for the realm of form, yet is unable to attain entry into the meditative absorption of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm.

The second case refers to those noble ones who have already attained the fourth dhyāna; not seeking rebirth in the formless realm and having developed aversion toward it, the activity of the fourth dhyāna constantly manifests before them.

By relying on the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) after having abandoned and severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one can gradually enter the meditative concentration of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the third case, it refers to this same practitioner who diligently seeks freedom from desire; by relying on the path of severing the fetters, they can gradually enter the meditative concentration of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those characteristics mentioned above.
Question:
For what reason does the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) not arise as a manifest presence within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer:

For those born in the formless realm, this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for the most part does not manifest before them; this is because those who abide in the maturation (*vipāka*) of the liberation of tranquility do not generally initiate the application of effort toward this attainment of cessation.

Why is this? Because the noble disciples, desiring to abide in the dwelling of tranquility, bring forth this meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) within the human realm and other such states.

Those who have already been born into the formless realm abide naturally and effortlessly in the maturation of the foremost tranquil liberation; they no longer exert skillful effort to seek this meditative attainment of cessation so as to bring it into manifestation.
The "mild path" refers to the mild-mild, mild-medium, and mild-superior paths.

By means of these paths, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—namely, the superior-superior, superior-medium, and superior-inferior grades—within each stage (bhūmi) bound to the three realms.
The middle path refers to the middle-weak, middle-middle, and middle-strong grades of the path.
By means of this path, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—middle-middle, middle, and middle-weak—belonging to each respective stage within the triple world.
The "superior path" refers to the three grades of the superior path: the superior-soft, the superior-middle, and the superior-superior.
By means of this path, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—namely, the soft-superior, the soft-middle, and the soft-soft—belonging to each stage within the three realms.

These paths—mild, medium, and superior—are each further divided into three sub-levels (mild and so forth), establishing nine grades, in order to demonstrate that the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation are severed gradually.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions can the path of the lowest-of-the-low grade sever the afflictions of the highest-of-the-high grade?

Because these afflictions manifest as coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) within the bodies of those who utterly lack shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), being extremely fierce and violent; they are thus easy to perceive and easy to discern. Therefore, these superior-grade afflictions are like coarse impurities that can be removed by even a slight counteractive measure.

If the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions manifests in a subtle and hidden manner within the continuum of one who possesses the contrary [qualities], it is difficult to perceive and difficult to discern; it can only be eliminated by a powerful antidote, just as subtle and hidden stains are removed only by a potent cleanser.

By this principle, it should be understood that the remaining establishments of the opposites between the remedial factors (*pratipakṣa*) and the objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*) are likewise established through mutual inversion.
As for the path of application (*prayogamārga*), it refers to that path by which one is able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Why is this so? Because when one correctly cultivates this path, one is able to gradually abandon a portion of the grossness (*dauṣṭhulya*) arising from various categories of superior afflictions and the like, thereby gradually attaining the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); this is called the path of expedient means within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to that path by which, immediately and permanently, afflictions are severed so that nothing remains. Why is this?
Because by means of this path, one is able to immediately and permanently eliminate the categories of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) produced by these afflictions, leaving none remaining.

Furthermore, the transformation of the basis from its coarse and heavy state to one free from such coarseness and heaviness is called the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
As for the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it refers to the path by which one realizes the liberation obtained through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is this so? Because by means of this path, one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) obtained through the permanent abandonment of afflictions.

As for the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), it refers to all the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths employed as skillful means to abandon further grades of afflictions; this is called the path of superior progress.

Why is this so? Because the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that serve as the means for abandoning the remaining afflictions of this category are superior to this category; therefore, they are called the path of special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Furthermore, abandoning the means for severing afflictions, or diligently contemplating all phenomena through skillful means, or diligently abiding in all phenomena through skillful means, or progressing in the cultivation of other *samāpattis* and all such paths, is called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Furthermore, the phrase "again" (or "moreover") is used to clarify other meanings.

The path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) refers to: abandoning the various skillful means of the path that sever afflictions and instead correctly contemplating the Dharma of the sūtras and so forth; or dwelling in and observing the Dharma previously contemplated and realized; or entering into other superior meditative attainments (*samādhi*). All such instances are termed the path of superior progress.
Furthermore, that which is for the purpose of eliciting superior qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*), or for abiding in all existing paths, is called the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*). Why is this so?

If it is for the purpose of eliciting superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or once they have arisen, to abide in their manifestation—paths such as these are called the path of advancement.

Thus, having already explained in detail the distinctions among the characteristics of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), we shall now, following the momentum of this discussion, further analyze the distinctions in the cultivation of the various paths.
What is cultivation?

Briefly stated, there are four kinds: namely, cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*), and cultivation by counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation by acquisition refers to the cultivation of unarisen wholesome dharmas so that they may arise.
Cultivation by practice refers to the cultivation of already arisen wholesome dharmas so that they remain firm, are not forgotten, and further increase and expand.
The cultivation of removal refers to cultivating the already arisen unwholesome and unvirtuous states so that they are permanently abandoned.
The cultivation of antidote refers to cultivating the as-yet-unarisen unwholesome and unvirtuous states so that they do not arise.
These four types of distinctions in cultivation are explained according to their respective applications based on the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Cultivation for the sake of attainment is called "cultivation for attainment" (*pratilambhabhāvanā*), because by the power of this cultivation, one attains wholesome dharmas not previously attained.

Cultivation through habituation is called "cultivation by habituation" (*āsevana-bhāvanā*), because by the power of this cultivation, one repeatedly practices until all wholesome dharmas are attained.

Cultivation for the sake of removal is called "cultivation of removal" (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*), because by the power of this cultivation, one removes unwholesome dharmas that are currently manifesting.
Cultivating the antidote is called "cultivation as an antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), because it causes future unwholesome dharmas to become dharmas that do not arise.

Furthermore, when a dharma arises, it can establish its own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); this is called "attainment cultivation" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), because from this, the same category [of dharmas] increases and continues to arise in succession.
Furthermore, the cultivation of this very path as it manifests before one is called "cultivation through practice" (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*), because this very path is being practiced while present.

Moreover, when this very path manifests, it is able to abandon its own obstructions; this is called "cultivation through removal" (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*), because by means of this, the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) that are its specific counter-factors are extinguished.

Furthermore, when this very path abandons its own obstacles and causes them to abide in the state of non-arising in the future, it is called "cultivation as an antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*); for, having attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it establishes those obstacles in the future so that they abide in the state of non-arising.

Furthermore, it is called "cultivation as an antidote" (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) because it possesses four types of antidotes: namely, the antidote of revulsion and destruction (vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa), the antidote of abandonment (prahāṇa-pratipakṣa), the antidote of maintenance (dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa), and the antidote of distancing (dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa).

The antidote of repulsion consists in seeing many defects in all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), namely, by means of such modes as being like a disease or an abscess, one repulses the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
The antidote of abandonment refers to the path of preparation and the uninterrupted path, because they are able to abandon all afflictions.
The antidote of maintenance refers to the path of liberation, because it sustains the attainment of that abandonment.
The "counteractive of distancing" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) refers to the subsequent paths, because by means of them, the previously abandoned afflictions become further removed.
These four types of distinctions in counteractives are the meaning of the distinctions in the cultivation of the aforementioned counteractives.

Furthermore, there are eleven types of distinctions in the path: namely, the path of investigating phenomena; the path of diligent application; the path of cultivating meditative concentration; the path of the means for clear realization; the path of approaching clear realization; the path of clear realization; the path of pure renunciation; the path distinguished by faculties; the path of purifying the three trainings; the path of generating all virtues; and the path that universally encompasses all paths.

It should be understood that herein, based on the distinctions of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth, eleven types of paths are established in their respective order: namely, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the four kinds of right practice (*samyakpratipatti*), the four tracks of the Dharma (*dharmapada*), calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

The path of observing phenomena refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, because by means of these, one first observes all phenomena—body, sensation, mind, and dharmas—through such modes as impurity and so forth.

The path of diligent application refers to the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), because after having thoroughly examined all phenomena, one exerts diligent energy in order to abandon all hindrances.
Cultivating the path of concentration refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Having thus purified all hindrances, one further cultivates *samādhi* through the gates of desire, effort, mind, and investigation, so as to bring about a state of pliancy and fitness.
The path of expedient means for clear realization refers to the five faculties, such as faith and so forth.

Having thus cultivated and refined samādhi, one diligently practices the superior conditions of *ūṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit) as expedient means, desiring to realize the untainted noble path.
The path that approaches direct realization (*abhisamaya*) refers to the five powers, such as faith and the rest.

Having thus obtained the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), one cultivates the practice of subduing obstacles such as lack of faith in order to penetrate the principles of the truths (*satya*) without interval, because these constitute the proximate means for "patience" (*kṣānti*) and the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The path of clear realization refers to the seven factors of enlightenment, because by means of these, one initially realizes the truth individually and within oneself.

The path of purification and deliverance refers to the noble eightfold path, because from this point onward, one cultivates the path of deliverance in order to bring about the permanent purification of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
By this principle, the factors of enlightenment follow such a sequence.
Regarding the path according to the distinctions of the faculties, this refers to the four right practices (*samyak-pratipatti*).
This is due to the distinctions between the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stages (*maula*), as well as the distinctions between sharp and dull faculties.

The practitioner of painful right practice relies on the preparatory stages (*anāgamya*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), because, respectively, their calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are deficient.
The practitioner of pleasant right practice relies on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), because both paths proceed simultaneously.
The two types of slow penetration refer to those with dull faculties relying on suffering or pleasure.
The two types of quick penetration refer to those with sharp faculties relying on suffering or pleasure.

The path for purifying the three trainings refers to the four bases of dharma (*dharmapada*), because by means of these one purifies the three trainings, such as higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) and so forth.
Non-attachment and non-hatred can purify and cultivate the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), because one never violates the precepts through the gateway of sensual desire or ill will.
Right mindfulness can purify and cultivate the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), because by not forgetting the object of focus, it sustains the mind and brings it to concentration.
Right concentration can purify and cultivate the training in higher wisdom, because through the mind attaining concentration, one is able to realize knowledge in accordance with reality.
That which gives rise to the path of all virtues refers to śamatha and vipaśyanā, for by means of these, one is able to accomplish all virtues.

That which encompasses all paths refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), because by means of these, one can encompass all paths—those of the beginning, the middle, and the ultimate.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) encompasses the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*) subsumes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) subsumes the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
