5. In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, Chapter One on the Truths, Part Five: Furthermore, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are without distinction; they are all established by means of five gates, namely: by way of their object (*ālambana*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their companions (*sahāya*), their cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).
Just as the first application of mindfulness has five gates, so it is with the remaining factors of enlightenment.
As for the objects of focus of the four applications of mindfulness, they are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four matters: namely, the matter of what I depend upon, the matter of what I enjoy, the matter of my own self-substance, and the matter of my defilement and purification.
For what reason are only these established as the objective referents (*ālambana*)?

Due to inverted cognition, foolish ordinary beings for the most part conceive of a self; depending upon the body endowed with sense faculties, they experience pleasure, pain, and so forth, apprehending the grasping of objects as their characteristic, becoming defiled by craving and the like, and purified by faith and the like.
Therefore, in order to first correctly observe the true characteristics of phenomena, these four types of things are established as the objects of focus (*ālambana*).
As for the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Because the Buddha’s sūtras contain expressions such as "contemplating the body and so forth," as well as the term "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they follow this respective order.
The "auxiliaries of the foundations of mindfulness" refers to the mental states and mental factors associated with them.
"Those" refers to those two dharmas: mindfulness and wisdom.
"Cultivating the foundations of mindfulness" means practicing the contemplation of the body and so forth with respect to the internal body and so forth.
As it is with the internal, so it is with the external and with both the internal and external.
The "internal body" refers to all internal bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) within this body.

It is called "internal" because it is comprised of the internal bases—the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—within one's own person, and because it is included among the category of sentient beings.
The "external body" refers to all external objects consisting of the external sense-spheres (*bāhyāni rūpāyatanāni*).

It is called "external" because it is comprised within the external sense-spheres—such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and because it does not belong to the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).
The "internal-external body" refers to all external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) that serve as the support for the faculties associated with the internal bases.

Because the external bases such as visible forms—which reside as the support for the faculties associated with the five bases (the eye, etc. within one's own body—are included among the category of sentient beings and are subsumed under the external bases, they are called "internal-external."
Furthermore, regarding all internal bases of form within the bodies of others, they are designated as "internal" and "external" based on their status as bases and based on the body [they belong to].
How does one cultivate the contemplation of the body in relation to the body?

This means that by observing the equality between the body as a conceptual image and the body as the actual object, one observes the body within the objective field of the body due to their similarity; therefore, it is called "contemplating the body as the body."
By means of the gateway of investigating and discerning the reflected image-body, one thoroughly and precisely observes the essential body.
"Internal feeling" refers to feeling produced based on the internal body.
Because they take the sense bases such as the eye as their objects and arise in dependence upon one's own body, they are called "internal.
As for "external feeling," this refers to feelings that arise in dependence on an external body;
because they take objects such as visible forms as their objects and arise in dependence upon another's body, they are called "external."
Internal-external feeling refers to feeling produced based on the internal and external body.
It is called "internal-external" because it takes the internal sense bases within one's own body as its object, and because it takes the internal sense bases within another's body as its object.
As it is with feeling, so it is with mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).

Just as one cultivates the contemplation of the body in relation to the body, so too does one cultivate the contemplation of feelings and so forth in relation to feelings and so forth, as appropriate.
Furthermore, "cultivation" refers to desire, diligence, exertion, perseverance, vigor, non-cessation, right mindfulness, right awareness, and heedfulness, due to the distinctions in cultivation.
"Cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of non-attention (*amanasikāra*).
"Diligent cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of laziness (*kausīdya*).
"Exerting cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
"Vigorous cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of mental inferiority (*cittadaurbalya*).
Inferiority of mind refers to a state of timidity arising from self-contempt regarding the superior qualities to be realized.
Vigorous cultivation refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of negligence and fatigue.
"Laxity and fatigue" refers to the affliction produced by environments such as mosquitoes and gadflies.
"Failure to practice without ceasing" refers to the secondary affliction of contentment arising from having attained only a small measure of wholesome qualities.
Because one gives rise to the joy of contentment upon obtaining even a small amount of virtue, one ceases further advancement toward superior categories of virtue.
"Cultivating right mindfulness" refers to the application of mindfulness as an antidote to the secondary affliction of forgetting the sublime instructions.
Cultivation through correct awareness refers to the remedy for the secondary affliction of remorse regarding transgressions.

Remorse regarding transgressions refers to acting without correct awareness in matters such as coming and going, whereby one first violates a training rule and subsequently gives rise to regret and distress.
The cultivation of heedfulness refers to the counteractive measure against the secondary affliction of abandoning the yoke of all wholesome qualities.

To abandon the yoke of wholesome qualities means that, due to the fault of heedlessness, one fails to bring to completion the application of diligence toward the superior categories of wholesome factors that have been undertaken for cultivation.

Regarding the fruits of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): they consist of the abandonment of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*), the entry into the Four Noble Truths, and the dissociation from the body and so forth; these are called the fruits of cultivation.

As for the abandonment of the four perversions: the four foundations of mindfulness, in their respective order, are able to abandon the four types of perversion—purity, pleasure, permanence, and self—by virtue of cultivating the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), by thoroughly knowing that all sensations (*vedanā*) are suffering (*duḥkha*), by penetrating the distinctions of the bases and conditions of consciousness and how they undergo moment-to-moment transformation, and by observing that in defilement and purity there are only phenomena (*dharma*) and no agent.
Furthermore, these four types of mindfulness, as they enter into the Four Noble Truths in their respective order, are also called the fruits of cultivation.

Through the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of Suffering; for all physical bodies possess the characteristic of suffering through conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), as they are manifested by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Therefore, when cultivating meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*), this [factor] is able to act as an antidote, because this pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) arises with specific distinctions within the body.

Through the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because feelings such as pleasure are the basis for the convergence of craving and other afflictions.

By means of the application of mindfulness to the mind, one enters into the truth of cessation; observing that consciousness, being devoid of a self, shall ultimately be non-existent, one fears the gate of annihilation and thus gives rise to a dread of nirvana, which is forever abandoned.
One enters the Truth of the Path by means of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), in order to abandon the factors to be countered and to cultivate the remedial factors.

Furthermore, these four [foundations of mindfulness] can, in their respective order, realize the fruits of dissociation from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; for by practicing them, one is gradually able to distance oneself from the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the body and so forth.

Regarding the objects of the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*): they are the dharmas that have already arisen and those not yet arisen, as well as the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
The first right endeavor takes as its object the discordant dharmas that have already arisen, because one generates the desire to abandon those evil and unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen.

The second right abandonment takes as its object the unarisen factors to be countered; the third right abandonment takes as its object the unarisen remedial factors; and the fourth right abandonment takes as its object the remedial factors already arisen.
As stated in the sūtras, this should be explained in detail through extensive correlation.
The essential nature of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) is vigor (*vīrya*).
The companions of the right abandonments are the mental states and mental factors (*cittacaittadharma*) associated with them.
Regarding the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), as stated in the Sūtra: "One generates desire, exerts oneself, initiates right effort, and applies and sustains the mind.
Herein, these phrases reveal the practice of right effort (*vīrya*) and its basis.
The basis is desire (*chanda*), because one initiates diligence preceded by a longing for it.
Right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) refers to exertion and so forth.

Among the mental attentions (*manasikāra*) regarding the signs of calming (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), when one attends to the signs of calming and so forth, disregards the focal object (*ālambana*), and practices exclusively the antidote, at that time it is called exertion.
One exerts right effort in order to diminish lethargy and restlessness.
Why is this? When the secondary affliction of lethargy arises, one trains the mind by means of mental orientations (*manasikāra*) such as those that are pure and sublime, in order to diminish it.
When the secondary affliction of restlessness arises, one restrains and sustains the mind by means of internal realization and the method of brief withdrawal;
at that time, it is called "initiating right effort."
This is precisely to clarify the skillful means for diminishing laxity and excitement; therefore, it is followed by the statement: "exerting the mind" and "upholding the mind.

Regarding the fruit of the cultivation of right abandonment: it refers to the complete relinquishing of all that is to be countered, and the attainment or increase of the antidotes; this is called the fruit of cultivation.
The first two right abandonments exhaustively relinquish all that is to be countered; as appropriate, they abandon all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen and those yet to arise.
The third right abandonment attains the antidote, because it gives rise to all wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen.
The fourth right abandonment increases the antidote, because it causes wholesome dharmas that have already arisen to increase and expand.

The objective referent (*ālambana*) of the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) refers to the tasks accomplished by one who has perfected meditative concentration (*samādhi*). What, then, is this?
It is the various miraculous transformations and such activities initiated through the power of perfected samādhi; these constitute the objective referent.
The essential nature of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The accompaniments of the bases of supernormal power refer to desire, effort, mind, and investigation, as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with them.
Desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) refers to the realization of one-pointedness of mind through earnest application.
Earnest application refers to attaining concentration through the means of intense aspiration and intense reverence.
Diligent samādhi refers to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind through uninterrupted application.
Diligence means constant exertion without even a moment’s interval.
Regarding "mental samādhi": this refers to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind through the prior cultivation of concentration power. Why is this so?

Because by repeatedly cultivating the power of concentration in previous lives, the potential of its seeds is increased; through the force of these seeds, the mind spontaneously undergoes a transformation that accords with samādhi, whereby one swiftly realizes one-pointedness of mind.
The samādhi of observation refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through internal discernment based on hearing the teachings of others.
Furthermore, the samādhi of desire refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the arising of desire.
The samādhi of exertion refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the arousal of right effort by means of strenuous application.
The samādhi of the mind refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the stabilization of the mind.
Regarding the samādhi of observation: it refers to touching one-pointedness of mind by means of uplifting the mind.

To clarify its nature as the cause for generating the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the passage from the *Samyakprahāṇa-sūtra* beginning with "arousing desire, exerting effort," and so forth, is cited; these involve holding the mind and uplifting the mind, which constitutes this sequential order.

The samādhi of mental application (*citta-samādhi*) is the attainment of concentration through the stabilization of the mind; because by inwardly pacifying, withdrawing, and gathering the mind, one quickly realizes concentration.

The samādhi of observation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*) is the attainment of concentration through the exertion of the mind; because by relying on the gateway of observation to exert and train the mind, one quickly attains concentration.
The cultivation of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) refers to the frequent practice of the eight types of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
What are these eight? They are:
desire (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), right awareness (*samprajanya*), volition (*cetanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
These eight types are briefly subsumed into four: namely, application, appropriation, continuity, and antidote.
Application consists of aspiration, diligence, and faith.
Desire is the basis for diligence, and faith is the cause of desire.

Why is this so? Because through the seeking of desire, one exerts diligent effort in order to attain this objective; such seeking of desire does not exist apart from faithful acceptance, as they share the same essential nature.
"Appropriation" refers to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), because by means of this pliancy, the body and mind are benefited and sustained.
"Continuity" refers to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right situational awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*), because by not forgetting the object of focus, the mind is settled in a single state.
If laxity arises, one understands it as it truly is; thus, according to their respective order, the remedies are volition (*vitarka*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This is because once the two powers of application—exerting the mind and maintaining the mind—have arisen, one can distance oneself from lethargy and agitation, and furthermore, because these can induce the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth, which are free from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Furthermore, there are two kinds of cultivation through desire, diligence, mind, and investigation: namely, cultivation that is both free from the accumulation and dispersion of causes and conditions, and cultivation that is neither inferior nor distracted; these two are based upon cultivation that is concordant [with the goal]. Herein, it is shown that desire and the others have the dual meaning of cultivation as being able to distance oneself from both accumulation and dispersion, as well as from causes and conditions.
The cause of gathering is the state of sinking produced through the gateway of laziness due to being devoid of *vipaśyanā*.
The cause of scattering is the state of elation produced through the gateway of restlessness due to being devoid of the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
"Aggregation" refers to being constricted within by way of the gateway of lethargy and drowsiness.
"Dissipation" refers to being scattered outwardly by way of the gateway of conforming to signs of purity and excellence.
Cultivation in accordance with non-inferiority refers to observing all phenomena by relying on the observation of their characteristics.
Cultivation in accordance with non-distraction refers to observing matters such as hair and body hairs by relying on the perception of impurity.
The cultivation that accords with the basis of those two refers to the cultivation of the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*).
Relying on this sequence, the Blessed One said:

"My desire and inclination are neither inferior nor arrogant; they are not gathered within nor dispersed without. Possessing perceptions of before and after, as well as of above and below, my mind is opened and free from entanglements, accompanied by light."
Cultivating one's own mind, one should ensure that one’s mind is free from all obscurations and veils.

Regarding the fruit of cultivating the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*): because one has already thoroughly cultivated and refined meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to penetrate and manifest whatever dharmas one wishes to realize or master, in accordance with one's will.

Furthermore, within various distinct phenomena, one attains mastery over their functional efficacy; thus, according to one's aspirations, one can accomplish diverse feats such as supernormal powers and can further induce superior qualities.
The objects of the five faculties are the four noble truths,
because they are comprised within the means of the clear realization of the truths and are practiced as such.
The essential nature of the five faculties consists of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The companions of the five faculties refer to the associated mental states, such as the mind and its concomitants.
The cultivation of the five faculties refers to the cultivation of the faculty of faith through the practice of receptivity toward the [Four] Truths.
Once conviction has arisen regarding the truths through the faculty of energy, one initiates the practice of the application of energy for the sake of awakening.
Once energy has been aroused regarding the truths through the faculty of mindfulness, one initiates the practice of the application of non-forgetfulness.
Once the faculty of concentration has established mindfulness upon the truths, one cultivates the practice of mental one-pointedness.
Once the mind has attained concentration upon the truths through the faculty of wisdom, one cultivates the practice of discernment.

Regarding the fruit of cultivating the five faculties: it means being able to swiftly bring about the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), because through this predominant power one can soon give rise to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, it means being able to cultivate and refine "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), and induce "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), thereby entering the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in this very life.
As it is with the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), so it is with the five powers (*pañcabala*).
The distinction is that because these can diminish the obstacles that are their respective adversaries and cannot be overcome, they are called "powers."

This means that the objects of focus and other attributes of the five powers (*pañcabala*) are similar to those of the faculties (*indriya*), yet there is a distinction in their results. Why is this so?
As it is said regarding the result: because they are able to diminish obstacles such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), they are superior to the former.

Although they are similar to the five faculties in terms of their objects, intrinsic nature, and so forth, they are established as distinct powers because there is a difference in the sense that they cannot be overcome.
The objective referent (*ālambana*) of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) is the suchness (*yathābhūtatā*) of the four noble truths.
Suchness is so called because it is the object of ultimate purity (*paramārtha-viśuddhi*).
The essential nature of the factors of enlightenment consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
These seven factors constitute the essential nature of the factors of enlightenment.
Mindfulness is the factor of support, for by means of binding the mind to the object, it ensures that all wholesome dharmas are not forgotten.
The investigation of dharmas is the factor of its own essence, because it is the awakening to their specific characteristics.
Vigor is the factor of departure, because by its power one is able to reach the destination.
Joy is the factor of benefit, because by its power the body becomes pliant and well-adjusted.

Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are the factors of non-defilement; for it is by virtue of this non-defilement, by depending upon this non-defilement, and because their very essence is non-defiled.
Respectively, one is undefiled by means of *śamatha*, because this can eliminate the fault of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
one is undefiled by means of *samādhi*, because by relying on meditative concentration, one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has non-affliction as its essence, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in the state of being undefiled by permanently eliminating greed and sorrow.
As for the accompanying factors (*sahāya*) of the awakening factor, these refer to the associated mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharmas*).

Regarding the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment: it means that, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, and relying on cessation, one cultivates the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment by turning toward relinquishment.
As it is with the awakening factor of mindfulness, so it is for each up to the awakening factor of equanimity.
These four sets of propositions demonstrate, in their respective order, the cultivation of the awakening factors by taking the objects of the Four Noble Truths as their domain.

Why is this so? If one takes the essence of suffering as the object of perception when it becomes afflictive suffering, one necessarily seeks to distance oneself from that objective realm of suffering; therefore, it is called "relying on seclusion."

When one takes the origin of suffering, characterized by craving, as the object of the truth of the origin of suffering, because one necessarily seeks detachment from this objective sphere, it is called "relying on detachment.
When one takes the cessation of suffering as the object of the truth of the cessation of suffering, because one necessarily seeks its realization, it is called "relying on cessation."
"Relinquishment" refers to the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, because by its power one relinquishes suffering.
Therefore, when taking this as an object, one necessarily seeks to cultivate it with respect to that objective; thus, it is called "dedication toward relinquishment."

Regarding the fruit of cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*): it is the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the seven factors of enlightenment constitute the very essence of the path of seeing.
Regarding the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*): it is precisely the suchness (*yathābhūtatā*) of these same Four Noble Truths at a subsequent time.
Because its objective referent (*ālambana*) subsequent to the path of seeing consists of the reality (*yathābhūtatā*) of the truths previously perceived, it takes that as its essence.

As for the essential nature of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga-svabhāva*), it refers to right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these eight dharmas are called the essential nature of the factors of the path.
Right view is the factor of discernment, because it involves the analytical investigation of reality as previously realized.
Right intention is the factor of instructing others, because it establishes speech through the skillful means of articulating that which has been realized.

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the factors that cause others to have faith; in their respective order, they cause others to gain certain conviction that those who have realized the truth possess the purity of view, ethical discipline, and right livelihood.

Why is this? Because, by means of right speech, one is well able to engage in questioning, answering, debate, and discernment in accordance with what one has personally realized; through this, one understands that views are purified.
By means of right action, one’s conduct in coming, going, advancing, and halting is fully perfected; through this, one understands that there is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).

By means of right livelihood, one seeks clothing, bowls, and requisites in accordance with the Dharma as permitted by the Buddha; through this, one understands that there is purity of livelihood (*ājīva-viśuddhi*).
Right effort is the factor for purifying the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because by means of it, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are permanently severed.

Right mindfulness is the factor for purifying the obstacle of secondary afflictions (*upakleśāvaraṇa*), because by means of it, one does not forget the signs of right tranquility (*śamatha*) and arousal (*pragraha*), and thus never admits secondary afflictions such as lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).

Right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the factor that purifies the obstacles to the most excellent qualities, because it brings forth immeasurable superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The accompanying factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga-parivāra*) refer to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) associated with it.

Regarding the cultivation of the factors of the path, it is as explained for the factors of enlightenment: that is, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, and relying on cessation, one cultivates right view with a mind directed toward relinquishment; this is explained in detail, and so forth.
The meaning of these various phrases should be understood in accordance with the principles previously explained.

Regarding the fruit of cultivating the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), it refers to the analytical instruction of others, so as to cause them to believe in the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the purification of the secondary afflictive obscurations (*upakleśāvaraṇa*), and the purification of the obscurations to supreme qualities (*viśeṣaguṇāvaraṇa*).

The four modes of right practice (*samyak-pratipad*) are: the practice with difficulty and slow progress, the practice with difficulty and quick progress, the practice with ease and slow progress, and the practice with ease and quick progress.

The first refers to those of dull faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas; the second refers to those of sharp faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas; the third refers to those of dull faculties who have already attained the fundamental dhyānas; and the fourth refers to those of sharp faculties who have already attained the fundamental dhyānas.

Regarding "the practice of suffering": this refers to the bases of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), because, respectively, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are weak therein.
"Correct practice of joy" refers to the transformation of the dual path based on dhyāna.
"Slow penetration" refers to those of dull faculties relying on the two stages of suffering and pleasure.
"Swift penetration" refers to those of sharp faculties relying on the two stages of suffering and pleasure.
The four tracks of the Dharma are non-attachment, non-hatred, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Non-attachment and non-hatred enable the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) to be purified, because one does not transgress the precepts through the gateway of greed or anger.
Right mindfulness can purify the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), because it prevents forgetfulness regarding the object of focus and maintains the mind in concentration.
Right concentration can purify the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*), because one whose mind is concentrated is able to know things as they truly are.

Śamatha refers to the gathering of the mind within so that it abides, abides evenly, abides securely, abides closely, becomes disciplined, becomes tranquil, becomes most thoroughly tranquil, becomes one-pointed, and is held in equipoise.
These nine modes of practice cause the mind to abide; this is *śamatha*.
That which causes it to abide does so by withdrawing from external objects of focus, internally abandoning distraction, and initially binding the mind.

"Abiding in equipoise" (samasthāpana) means that after first binding the coarse and restless mind, one immediately binds the mindfulness to the object of focus in a continuous stream, gradually becoming subtle and concise.
"Stable abiding" (avasthāpana) means that at times, when mindfulness is lost and the mind wanders outward, one immediately withdraws and gathers it back.
"Abiding closely" means that from the very beginning, in order to prevent the mind from scattering toward external objects, one draws near to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

"Being disciplined and compliant" means that from the outset, by perceiving the faults within the causes of distraction—namely, phenomena such as forms—and through the power of this superior influence, one subdues the mind so that it does not flow outward in dispersion.

"Tranquility" refers to the profound perception of the faults within the afflictions of mental agitation, distraction, and unwholesome thoughts, thereby subduing the mind so that it does not flow outward in dispersion.

Regarding "extremely tranquil": even if at times mindfulness is lost and distraction occurs, such that vitarka and other mental factors suddenly manifest, one immediately subdues them so that they do not arise again.
"One-pointed focus" refers to dwelling continuously in superior samādhi through diligent application that is uninterrupted and flawless.

"Equanimous maintenance" refers to the continuous flow of the concentrated mind, free from distraction, because it has been well-cultivated and thus operates without effort, being detached from deliberate application.

Vipaśyanā refers to the discernment of phenomena, their most thorough discernment, universal investigation, and comprehensive examination; it is for the purpose of counteracting the fetters of coarse heaviness, for the purpose of subduing all perversions, and to cause the non-perverted mind to dwell in perfect stability.

Among these, the various phrases are taught in reliance upon the objects of focus for correct practice, or the objects of focus for skillfulness, or the objects of focus for the purification of afflictions.
The discernment of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is due to their extent (*yāvad-bhāvikatā*).
The ultimate discernment is due to their mode of existence (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*).
Thorough investigation (*parivitarka*) consists of establishing the characteristics of phenomena through wisdom (*prajñā*) accompanied by conceptual mental attention (*savikalpa-manasikāra*).
"Thoroughly examining" means investigating with complete detail.
Furthermore, four types of paths are established based on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
There may be a certain class of persons who have already attained *śamatha* but not *vipaśyanā*; such individuals cultivate *vipaśyanā* by relying upon their *śamatha*.
There may be a certain class of persons who have attained vipaśyanā but not śamatha; such persons rely on vipaśyanā to further cultivate śamatha.
There may be another class who have attained neither śamatha nor vipaśyanā; such persons should single-mindedly subdue dullness and agitation, practicing both paths simultaneously.

There may be a certain class of individuals who have already attained both śamatha and vipaśyanā; for such individuals, these two paths—śamatha and vipaśyanā—operate in union, in equilibrium, and as a pair.
In this context, four types of paths are explained based on śamatha and vipaśyanā.

First, because one has already attained śamatha, one sits in quietude and stabilizes the mind, up to maintaining it in equanimity; yet, because one has not yet attained vipaśyanā, one returns once more to sitting in quietude and, relying upon samādhi, discriminates among all phenomena, up to examining them thoroughly and precisely.
The second is the opposite of this.
The third has not yet attained either; thus, one practices both simultaneously.
How does one practice?
That is to say, having heard the Dharma, one advances toward the cultivation of correct contemplation by means of upholding it; based on this, one first cultivates calm abiding (śamatha).
Once these two have been attained, they proceed in conjunction with one another.
The three faculties are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" refers to all the faculties present during the path of preparation and within the fifteen mental moments of the path of seeing.

In this context, it is shown that the faculties belonging to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) subsumed within the aids to penetration (nirvedha-bhāgīya), as well as those existing during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), constitute the essence of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).

Regarding the "faculties" (indriya), these refer to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā-ādi), due to the distinctions in their bases such as the *anāgamya* stage and so forth.
As appropriate, there is one of the following: the faculty of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), grief (*daurmanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) refers to that which is comprised by grief and dejection when, following the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), one aspires to and seeks to realize higher liberation.

These ten faculties are called the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) because, while previously not knowing the truth, they are cultivated and transformed with the desire to come to know it.

Regarding the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*): from the sixteenth moment of the mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards, all faculties present within the various paths of those in training (*śaikṣa*) constitute the essence of the faculty of having known.

Why is this so? Because from the sixteenth moment of the mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), within this path of the learner (*śaikṣamārga*), there is no object among those that ought to be known which has not already been known; therefore, it is called the faculty of "that which has been known" (*ājñātendriya*).
The faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) refers to all the faculties present in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Regarding these "faculties," they are the nine faculties previously mentioned, excluding the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*); in the context of the path of no-more-learning, these are designated as the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge.
"Those who possess full knowledge" refers to arhats and others; the faculties possessed by them are called the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), because that which is to be learned no longer exists.

Furthermore, regarding the analysis of the meaning of cultivation based on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): when one practices the path of cultivation while relying on the stage of the first *dhyāna*, one also cultivates all the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because one attains mastery over them.

Just as one cultivates the wholesome roots of the desire realm by relying on the stage of the first dhyāna, so too, when practicing the path of cultivation while relying on any of the higher stages, one is able to cultivate all the wholesome roots belonging to the lower realms and lower stages, because one has attained mastery over them.

It should be understood that the meaning explained here is as follows: when one relies upon a higher stage and practices the path in its presence, although the wholesome roots belonging to lower realms and lower stages do not manifest, they are nonetheless all cultivated.
Why is this? Because one attains mastery therein.
Mastery refers to the mastery over the increasingly superior manifestation [of the dharmas].

The ultimate path refers to that which, by relying on the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), has forever stilled all heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*), forever severed all acquisitions of bondage (*bandhana-prāpti*), and forever realized the acquisition of disjunction from all bonds (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

From this point on, through the uninterrupted transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one realizes the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*): the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
What are these ten? They are:
the right view of one beyond training, up to the right concentration of one beyond training; the right liberation of one beyond training; and the right knowledge of one beyond training.

Such dharmas as these are called the ultimate path. What is meant by "all heavy burdens" (*dausthulya*)? Briefly stated, there are twenty-four kinds: namely, the heavy burden of all-pervasive conceptual proliferation; the heavy burden of experience; the heavy burden of afflictions;

the heavy burden of karma; the heavy burden of maturation; the heavy burden of the obstacle of afflictions; the heavy burden of the obstacle of karma; the heavy burden of the obstacle of maturation; the heavy burden of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the heavy burden of discursive thought; the heavy burden of food and drink; the heavy burden of sexual union; the heavy burden of dreams; the heavy burden of illness; the heavy burden of old age; the heavy burden of death; the heavy burden of fatigue; the heavy burden of solidity; the heavy burden of the coarse; the heavy burden of the medium; the heavy burden of the subtle; the heavy burden of the obstacle of afflictions; the heavy burden of the obstacle to meditative concentration; and the heavy burden of the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These twenty-four kinds briefly encompass all *dausthulya* (dysfunctions).

Regarding the *dausthulya* of pervasive conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of clinging to phenomena such as the eye and so forth; having persisted since beginningless time, they adhere to the *ālayavijñāna* in an uninterrupted succession. This very thing is termed the "habitual tendency of conceptual proliferation."
From these latencies (*vāsanā*), the various phenomena such as the eye-faculties, as well as the grasping at names and expressions, arise repeatedly.
"Experiencing the heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers to the latencies of all contaminated feelings (*vedanā*).
The heaviness of afflictions refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions.
The heaviness of karma refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma.
The heaviness of maturation refers to the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*) resulting from maturation.
The heavy burden of the afflictive hindrances refers to the nature of intense and long-lasting afflictions.
The heavy burden of the karmic hindrances refers to the nature of karmic obstructions such as the immediate [sins] that can obstruct the Path.

The heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the maturation-obstruction (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*) refers to the acquisition of a self-nature (*ātma-bhāva*) in the hells and so forth, which is contrary to the direct realization of the truths (*satya-abhisamaya*).
The heaviness of the "coverings" (*nīvaraṇa*) refers to the nature of intense craving and so forth, which acts as an obstacle to the application of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*).
Coarseness of discursive thought refers to the nature of discursive thoughts such as those that obstruct the aspiration for the joy of renunciation.
Coarseness of food and drink refers to the lack of functional fitness regarding the practice of moderation in eating, whether one eats excessively or too little.
Grossness of sexual union refers to the nature of physical and mental exhaustion resulting from the mutual intercourse of two bodies.
Grossness of dreams refers to the nature of physical dullness and debility produced by sleep.
The heaviness of illness refers to the state of insecurity produced by the mutual conflict of the elements (*dhātu*).
The heaviness of old age refers to the state of non-compliance arising from the decay and transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The coarseness of death refers to the state in which the faculties are disordered at the time of passing away.
The coarseness of fatigue refers to the state in which the limbs and body are suddenly exhausted due to such acts as traveling long distances.

The "solid heavy residues" (*dausthulya*) refer to the nature of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and heavy residues belonging to those who lack the dharma of *nirvāṇa*, according to their respective categories.
The "coarse, medium, and subtle heavy residues" refer to the heavy residues of the desire, form, and formless realms, respectively.
The heaviness of the afflictive hindrances refers to that which is to be remedied by the enlightenment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The heaviness of the hindrances to meditative concentration refers to that which is to be remedied by the qualities arising from the nine successive attainments.
The "coarseness of the cognitive obstructions" refers to that which is to be remedied by the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Because all such coarseness has been eternally stilled according to their respective natures, it is called the "ultimate path" (*niṣṭhāmārga*).

As it is said: for one who practices in this way, there is the perfection of liberation of mind and the perfection of liberation through wisdom; the bodily heaviness is forever stilled, due to having achieved mindfulness as the cause.

In the initial gateway, one is well-disciplined, well-guarded, well-restrained, well-covered, and thoroughly cultivated; that is to say, regarding forms cognizable by the eye, and so on, up to mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, it is likewise.
The acquisition of bondage refers to the conventional designation of the nature of bondage upon the accumulation of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
The acquisition of dissociation refers to the conventional designation of the nature of dissociation upon the dispersal of coarse heaviness.
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) refers to the samādhi present at the stage of the final path of abandoning fetters within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This, in brief, is of two types: that subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and that subsumed under the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
That which is comprised within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to that from which point onward one is no longer obstructed by any hindrances and is able to destroy all hindrances.

That which is comprised within the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to that from which the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arise immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, this samādhi is uninterrupted, firm, of a single flavor, and all-pervasive.
Why is this vajra-like concentration called "uninterrupted"? It is because its continuous flow is not interrupted or deficient by worldly activities.
"Solid" means it cannot be destroyed by any obstacle and can destroy all obstacles, because it is extremely firm and fierce.
"Of a single flavor" means its nature is non-conceptual, because it is purely of one flavor.
"Pervasive" means that it takes as its object the *tathatā* (suchness) of the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharma*).
To clarify this meaning, the Blessed One said:

"It is like a great mountain of solid rock—without fissures, without gaps, without holes, a single seamless mass, perfectly complete—which cannot be moved or shaken by violent winds from the ten directions."

Regarding the immediate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*), this refers to the three types of transformation of the basis possessed by one who has already realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
What are these three? They are:
the transformation of the basis of the mind, the transformation of the basis of the path, and the transformation of the basis of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).

The transformation of the basis of the mind (*citta-āśraya-parāvṛtti*) refers to having attained the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) and realizing that the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure by its very essence; because it is forever free from all adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it is called "transformation of the basis," which is precisely the meaning of the transformation of the basis of *tathatā*.

Regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the path: it means that when the former mundane path undergoes clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is transformed into the supramundane; this is designated as "in training" (*śaikṣa*) because there remains further work to be done.

When all that is to be remedied has been permanently eliminated and one is forever free from the desires of the three realms, the essence of this path reaches ultimate perfection and is established as the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Regarding the transformation of the basis as the elimination of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*): because the *ālayavijñāna* is forever freed from all afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called the transformation of the basis.
Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) refers to the knowledge obtained through the exhaustion of causes, or that which takes exhaustion as its object. Why is this so?
Because this knowledge arises due to the exhaustion [of defilements], it is called "knowledge of exhaustion."
Alternatively, it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) because it takes exhaustion as its object.

The intended meaning of this is that, within this state, because the origin of suffering has been permanently severed such that nothing remains, the knowledge thus attained is termed "knowledge of exhaustion."
Alternatively, it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" because it takes the exhaustion of causes as its object.
As for "knowledge of non-arising," it refers to the knowledge obtained through the abandonment of results, or that which takes the non-arising of results as its object.
Why is this so? Because there is non-arising, the wisdom attained is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Alternatively, because it takes non-arising as its object, it is called the knowledge of non-arising.

The meaning of this statement is as follows: because one possesses the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) whereby all future fruits of suffering will ultimately never arise, one attains this knowledge; thus, even though it takes other truths as its object, it is still called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*).
Alternatively, it is called the knowledge of non-arising because it takes the non-arising of the Truth of Suffering as its object.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) are explained in reliance upon the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Why is this? Right speech, right action, and right livelihood of one beyond training constitute the aggregate of morality (śīla-skandha) of one beyond training.
Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-skandha) of one beyond training.
The right view, right intention, and right effort of one beyond training constitute the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training.
Right liberation of one beyond training constitutes the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training.
The right knowledge of one beyond training is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Furthermore, the Truth of the Path has four aspects: namely, the aspect of the path, the aspect of correctness, the aspect of practice, and the aspect of deliverance.
Why is it called the "characteristic of the path"?
Because by means of this, one seeks the true meaning. Why is that?
Because this noble path is the route by which all noble ones realize the true meaning, it is therefore called the "Path" (mārga).
Why is it called "Suchness" (tathatā)?
Because it is able to counteract all afflictions.
Why is this so? Because all afflictions are contrary to reason, and the Path is able to eliminate them; for this reason, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Why is it called the "aspect of practice" (ākāra)?
It is because it is well able to accomplish the mind, ensuring that it does not become inverted. Why is this so?
Because the mind fails to awaken to the true principle and gives rise to inversions such as permanence regarding phenomena that are impermanent and so forth.
One is well able to cultivate and rectify this inverted mind, causing it to leave behind inverted perceptions and realize the true meaning; therefore, it is called "practice" (*caryā*).
Why is it called "manifesting the marks of emergence"?
Because one proceeds toward the track of true permanence.
Why is this so? Because by means of this noble path one is able to proceed toward liberation and the ultimate state of permanence; therefore, it is called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Question:
Within the various truths, there are sixteen modes of practice, all of which pertain to both the mundane and the supramundane.
What is the distinction between these mundane and supramundane modes?
Answer:

This is due to the distinction between the natures of non-entrance and entrance into the objects of knowledge; the distinction between the natures of being obstructed and unobstructed; and the distinction between the natures of conceptualization and non-conceptualization.

Why is this so? Within the various truths, there are sixteen aspects such as impermanence and suffering. Because worldly beings engage with the objects of knowledge without penetrating the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), because they are accompanied by latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), and because they give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) through the gateway of conventional designations, they respectively fail to enter [the truth] skillfully, encounter obstacles, and possess discrimination.
Supramundane practice is the opposite of this: it is characterized by skillful entry, absence of obstruction, and non-conceptuality.
By this principle, there is a mutual distinction between mundane and supramundane practices.
How is it that supramundane practice is non-conceptual, yet skillfully enters the sphere of the knowable?

When those various practices manifest before one, although one directly realizes and perceives the meaning of impermanence, one does not perceive this as "the meaning of impermanence" by way of the gate of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) involving names and expressions.
Just as the contemplation of impermanence functions with respect to the meaning of impermanence, so too do the other contemplations function with respect to their respective meanings, as appropriate.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Ten; *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Eleven.

2. Chapter on Dharmas (Dharmaviniścaya), Part One of the Second Section of the Viniscayasamgrahani. What is the determination of dharmas (dharmaviniścaya)?
"Dharma" refers to the twelvefold collection of the noble teachings.

What are the twelve? First, the sūtras; second, the verses (geya); third, the prophecies (vyākaraṇa); fourth, the stanzas (gāthā); fifth, the spontaneous utterances (udāna); sixth, the causal origins (nidāna); seventh, the parables (avadāna); eighth, the past events (itivṛttaka); ninth, the birth stories (jātaka); tenth, the extensive discourses (vaipulya); eleventh, the marvelous accounts (adbhutadharma); and twelfth, the treatises (upadeśa).
The *sūtra* refers to a concise exposition of the meanings that ought to be explained, composed in prose.
Question:
For what reason does the Tathāgata not extensively expound the meanings that ought to be explained?

Answer: The Tathāgata, observing ten kinds of benefits, briefly teaches all dharmas; that is to say: they are easy to establish, easy to proclaim, and easy to uphold; one shows reverence for the Dharma; the provisions for enlightenment are swiftly brought to fulfillment; one is able to quickly penetrate the true nature of all dharmas; one attains verified pure faith in the Buddhas; one attains verified pure faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha; one realizes and touches the supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life; one delights the minds of the wise through discussion and definitive discernment; and one gains entry into the ranks of the intelligent and the sagacious.
What is meant by "easy to establish"?

It refers to the fact that while various preachers of the Dharma may establish and reveal the meanings to be taught through immeasurable gateways, here they are presented with concise words so as to be easily established.
What is meant by "easily expounded"?
It refers to the ability to extensively reveal great meaning through few words and phrases,
as in the detailed exposition beginning with "able to cause the mind to abide and to abide thoroughly."
"Easy to receive and uphold" means that it enables those who hear it to easily receive and uphold it, and because they revere the Dharma.

"The provisions for awakening are swiftly brought to fulfillment" means that by understanding that the Buddha-dharmas are realized through profound wisdom, one develops deep reverence and love for this very Dharma; through the gateway of such reverence and love, the provisions of faith and so forth are swiftly fulfilled.

Regarding the phrase "one who can swiftly penetrate the true nature of all phenomena": it is precisely through the power of the skillful means of revering the Dharma that one's wisdom becomes increasingly sharp and keen, enabling one to gradually penetrate the true nature of all phenomena.

Those who have attained verified faith (*avetyaprasāda*) in the Three Jewels do so because, through realizing the sublime establishment of the Noble Teaching, they give rise to pure faith toward the Teacher and others.

Those who have touched and realized the supreme dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) do so because, having applied intense application and correct reflection upon the profound intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the Tathāgatas, they attain the superior joy of realization.
"Discourse that resolves and determines matters and delights the hearts of the wise" means that it is well able to elucidate profound and hidden meanings.
"Attaining inclusion among the ranks of the brilliant and sagacious" means that its vast and beautiful reputation spreads throughout the ten directions.
One should know that the latter two types are combined as a single benefit.
Regarding "Verses" (geya): this refers to those passages within the various sūtras that are restated in verse, either in the middle or at the end.
Furthermore, because sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha) require further explanation through verse, they are called "Verses."

"Vyākaraṇa" (prediction) refers to those instances where, upon the passing away of noble disciples and others into the past, their virtues and faults as well as the distinctions regarding their places of rebirth are predicted.
Furthermore, sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are also called vyākaraṇa, because they reveal and elucidate profound and secret intentions.
Verses (*geya*) refer to those discourses taught in verse, consisting of two, three, four, five, or six lines.
Spontaneous utterances (*udāna*) refer to those discourses where the Tathāgata, being pleased, speaks of his own accord, such as the *gāthā* which says:
"If one applies courageous diligence toward such a Dharma, and meditates with tranquil reflection, at that time one is called a brahmin."
"Origination" (*nidāna*) refers to speaking in response to a request,
because such a teaching arises in dependence upon a particular person (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, the formal establishment of a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to a specific cause and condition is also termed "origination."
This refers to [teachings] based on such causes and conditions and based on such matters, as explained at length.
As for "illustrative examples" (*nidarśana*), it refers to those discourses containing analogies; these various parables are taught so that the primary meaning may be made clear.
*Itivṛttaka* refers to the proclamation of events concerning the previous lives of the noble disciples and others.
*Jātaka* refers to the proclamation of events concerning the fundamental practices of the bodhisattvas.
Vaipulya refers to discourses associated with the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
It is called Vaipulya, and it is also called Vistara-bhañjana (Extensive Destruction) and Anuttara (Peerless).
For what reason is it named Vaipulya?
Because it is the basis for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
For what purpose is it called "Extensive Refutation"?
Because it is able to extensively destroy all obstacles.
For what reason is it called "Incomparable"?
Because there are no phenomena that can serve as its counterpart.
These terms, such as "Vaipulya" and so forth, are all distinct names for the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
It is called the Mahāyāna because it is endowed with seven kinds of greatness (*mahattva*).
What are these seven kinds of greatness?

First is the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*), because the bodhisattva path takes as its object the vast teachings of immeasurable sūtras, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and so forth.
Second is the greatness of the practice (*pratipatti-mahattva*), because one correctly practices all the vast deeds for the benefit of oneself and others.
Third is the greatness of the three types of knowledge, because of the thorough realization of the great selflessness of persons and phenomena.

Fourth is the greatness of diligence, because of the arduous cultivation of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of difficult practices through skillful means over three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Fifth is the greatness of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), because of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Sixth is the greatness of realization (*prāpti*), because of realizing the immeasurable and innumerable great qualities of the Tathāgata, such as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
The greatness of the sevenfold karma consists in manifesting all acts such as the attainment of enlightenment until the very end of saṃsāra, thereby establishing the vast undertakings of the Buddhas.

Regarding the marvelous teachings: it refers to those instances where the most extremely rare, extraordinary, and wondrous dharmas of the śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas are proclaimed.

"Discourse" refers to that which provides non-erroneous explanations of all profound and hidden characteristics of phenomena, because it discourses upon the profound meanings of the sūtras and other texts through the non-erroneous characteristics of all phenomena.
Thus, these twelve divisions of the noble teaching, such as the sūtras and so forth, are subsumed within the Three Piṭakas.
What are the three?
First, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
This, in turn, is twofold:
first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The five categories—sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, and udāna—are subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
These four—nidāna (origins), avadāna (parables), itivṛttaka (past events), and jātaka (birth stories)—are subsumed within the Vinaya Piṭaka and its associated literature among the two Piṭakas.

Regarding these, the nidāna, which proclaims the establishment of the various rules of training (śikṣāpada) through their causal origins, is subsumed under the authentic Vinaya Piṭaka; the other three, beginning with the avadāna, are subsumed as its associated literature.
These two—Vaipulya and Adbhutadharma—are subsumed within the Sūtra Piṭaka of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Regarding Vaipulya:
its words and meanings are vast and extensive; it is correctly subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The *dhāraṇī-piṭaka*, characterized by inconceivable distinctions, vast majesty, and supreme correspondence, is therefore also subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The *upadeśa* category is subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka among the two piṭakas of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
Question:
For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the Three Piṭakas?
Answer:
The Sūtra Piṭaka is established as an antidote to the secondary affliction of doubt;
for it proclaims the discourses (sūtras), verses (geya), and so forth, in order to sever the doubts that sentient beings to be converted may harbor regarding various phenomena.
The Vinaya Piṭaka is established as an antidote to the secondary afflictions associated with the enjoyment of the two extremes.
These two extremes refer to the extreme of indulgence in sensual pleasures and the extreme of self-mortification.

Regarding the remedy for enjoyment: it is established to prohibit the enjoyment of hoarded goods and the like, while permitting the enjoyment of hundreds of thousands of robes and other items that accord with the Dharma.

Furthermore, the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established in order to remedy the secondary affliction of attachment to one's own views; for it extensively explains throughout its various sections the specific characteristics of all phenomena according to their true nature.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established in order to reveal the three types of training (*śikṣā*). Why is this?
Because sentient beings who are to be converted must understand the three trainings by relying on this Piṭaka, as it extensively expounds the three kinds of training to be practiced.
In order to establish the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā) and the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā), the Vinaya Piṭaka was established;
for it is by depending upon this Piṭaka that these two trainings can be accomplished.

Why is this? It is because one must rely upon the noble teachings of the training path—the extensive explanation of the prātimokṣa discipline—in order to be able to cultivate and purify ethical conduct (śīla).
Based on pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one gives rise to freedom from regret and so forth;

because the mind gradually cultivates and trains until it attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established in order to bring about the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
The training in higher wisdom can only be established by relying upon this treasury. Why is this?
Because within this treasury, the skillful means for discerning all phenomena are extensively revealed.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established in order to reveal the meaning of the True Dharma, for the words and meanings of this Piṭaka are easy to understand.

The Vinaya Piṭaka is established to manifest the basis for the realization and establishment of the meaning of the Dharma, for by relying on this Piṭaka one is able to cultivate the two types of training for realization.
The Vinaya is the basis for realizing the meaning of the Dharma and the foundation for its practice;
"foundation" here carries the sense of a support.
The Abhidharma Piṭaka was established so that those who possess wisdom may dwell in the enjoyment of the Dharma through discussion and definitive discernment.

Relying upon this treasury, those who possess wisdom engage in mutual questioning and answering, debate and deliberation, and dwell in the joy of receiving the Dharma; for within this treasury, the true nature of phenomena—their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and so forth—is revealed through immeasurable gateways.
Thus, the Tripiṭaka comprises eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandha), which were constantly received and maintained by the Venerable Ānanda according to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Question:
What is the measure of each individual aggregate of Dharma?
Answer:
The measure of the *dharmaskandha* is the number of ten hundreds.
"Ten hundreds" means the number one thousand.
If that is so, why not simply state that there are one thousand of them?
It is in order to reveal the reason for establishing one thousand *dharma-skandhas* for each individual category. Why is this so?

First, by incrementing the unit count, the number ten is formed; by further incrementing the number ten, the number hundred is formed. Numbers such as the thousand are established based on the numbers ten and hundred: ten hundreds are called a thousand (*sahasra*); a hundred thousands are called a hundred-thousand (*lakṣa*); and a hundred hundred-thousands are called a *koṭi*.

In this manner, for all subsequent numerical categories, one must invariably employ either the number ten or the number hundred as the basis. Therefore, within this context, only these two numbers—ten and hundred—are taken collectively to establish each individual aggregate of dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
By this calculation, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandha) total eight koṭis and forty lakṣas.
Question:
To whom does the domain of the phenomena subsumed within these three baskets (piṭaka) belong?
Answer:
It is the objective sphere traversed by all minds and mental factors produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
"Traversed" (so-xing) has the meaning of "object-condition" (ālambana).

Furthermore, based on these characteristics of the object of focus (*ālambana*), the meanings of "having an object" (*sālambana*) and so forth are established for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All minds and mental factors have an object, have a mode of activity (*ākāra*), have a basis (*āśraya*), and are associated (*samprayukta*)."
What is the object of focus for that [cognition] regarding these phenomena?
It refers to the sūtras and so forth.
This indicates that the objects of focus are the teachings comprised of the collections of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya), such as the sūtras.
What kind of activity does it perform?
It refers to the meaning associated with the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.

This indicates that the verbal teachings arising from the meanings of the aggregates and so forth constitute this mode of activity (*ākāra*), which is performed by those minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
What is its basis?
It is the communication of others, recollection, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
This indicates that when correctly teaching the Dharma, one relies upon the communication of others, as it is said: "because [it arises] from the vocal sounds of others."
Subsequently, recollection serves as the basis, because one repeatedly practices in accordance with what has been heard.

Furthermore, at a later stage, habitual tendencies serve as the basis; due to the powerful force of these tendencies from subsequent repeated practice, [the object] appears as if it were present even though recollection has ceased.
What is association (*samprayoga*)?
It refers to being mutual auxiliaries, whereby there is an equal comprehension regarding the object of focus and the mental activity.

This is because the mind and mental factors act as mutual auxiliaries, and through the meaning of association such as the aggregates (*skandha*), they equally comprehend the objects of focus, such as the discourses (*sūtra*).
What are the distinctions among the objects of focus regarding phenomena?

Briefly stated, there are four kinds: the pervasive object of focus, the object of focus for counteracting conduct, the object of focus for skillfulness, and the object of focus for purifying afflictions.

The pervasive objects of focus (vyāpyālambana) are further of four kinds: namely, the object of focus consisting of the conceptual image (savikalpa-pratibimba), the object of focus consisting of the non-conceptual image (nirvikalpa-pratibimba), the object of focus consisting of the limit of phenomena (vastuparyanta), and the object of focus consisting of the accomplishment of what was to be done (kāryapariniṣpatti).

The object of focus consisting of a conceptual image refers to the objects of focus for all śamatha and vipaśyanā that arise through the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Mental attention of resolute conviction is exclusively mundane mental attention.
The object of focus consisting of non-conceptual images refers to the objects of focus for both calm abiding and insight that arise from genuine mental attention (*bhūta-manasikāra*).
Genuine mental attention consists exclusively of supramundane mental attention and the mental attention subsequently attained therefrom.
The object of focus regarding the limits of phenomena refers to the "exhaustive nature" and the "nature as it is" of all phenomena.
The exhaustive nature refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

To reveal that the essential nature and entities of all knowable phenomena have only such a measure and limit, the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) are established.
As for "the nature as it is" (*yathāvadbhāva*), it refers to the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths and suchness (*tathatā*).

Because one understands the objects of knowledge through such various conceptual gateways as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," "all conditioned phenomena are suffering," "all dharmas are selfless," "nirvāṇa is tranquility," and "emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness," it is called the nature of things as they truly are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*).

Alternatively, one may comprehend the objects of knowledge through the gateway of the truths; that is, one should understand, as appropriate, that the aforementioned aggregates, elements, and bases are suffering, and so forth, up to the path.

Alternatively, one may comprehend the objects of knowledge through the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*): that is, each of the truths is understood by way of its four aspects, and all phenomena, being without differentiation, are understood through the aspect of suchness (*tathatā*).
Alternatively, one may comprehend the objects of knowledge through the *udāna* gate of all phenomena, namely: "all conditioned formations are impermanent," up to "nirvāṇa is quiescent.
Or, one may comprehend the objects of knowledge through the gates of liberation, namely: emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, and so forth.
The object of focus for the accomplishment of what is to be done refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
For one who has already attained the transformation of the basis, there is no manifestation of objects of focus characterized by inversion.
Such a transformation of the basis is inconceivable.

It was previously stated that within the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*), there are sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) and three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); these two categories mutually encompass one another.
Question:
How many aspects are subsumed under emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Answer:
Two, namely, the practice of emptiness and the practice of selflessness.
Question:
How many modes of practice are subsumed under wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
Answer:

Six—namely, the mode of impermanence (*anitya*), the mode of suffering (*duḥkha*), the mode of cause (*hetu*), the mode of origination (*samudaya*), the mode of birth (*jāti*), and the mode of condition (*pratyaya*). This is because, by means of these, one has no aspiration or seeking toward the three realms.
Question:
How many modes of practice (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the signless (*animitta*)?
Answer:
The eight refer to the eight aspects of the Path of Cessation (*nirodha-mārga*), because by means of them one cannot engage with various [conceptual] signs (*nimitta*).

Regarding the objects of focus for the practice of remedies (*pratipakṣa-pratipatti-ālambana*), there are briefly five types: those whose conduct is dominated by greed take impurity (*aśubhā*) as their object; those dominated by hatred take the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as their object; those dominated by delusion take the nature of conditions and the realm of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as their object; those dominated by pride take the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu-prabheda*) as their object; and those dominated by discursive thought take mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) as their object.
For what reason do those whose temperament is dominated by craving and so forth take impurity and other such objects as their spheres of cultivation?
It is because, through this, they are able to pacify and eliminate excessive craving and the like.

Skillfulness regarding the objects of focus consists briefly of five types: namely, skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense bases, skillfulness regarding dependent origination, and skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible.
How should one contemplate skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible?
One should contemplate it as one does skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Question:
What is the difference between skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*) and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*)?
Answer:
If one causes all phenomena to flow and moisten all phenomena, thereby ensuring they arise free from causelessness and uneven causes, this is skill in dependent origination.

This means that [ignorance] and other such factors moisten the formations (*saṃskāra*) and other phenomena; these phenomena do not arise without a cause, nor do they arise from an unequal cause such as Īśvara. Insight that contemplates in this manner is called skillfulness in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).
Skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*) consists in the arising [of effects] through the appropriate grasping of causes and conditions;
that is to say, although only dharmas serve as causes, it is only by virtue of grasping a corresponding cause that a corresponding effect can arise.
Just as wholesome conduct results in desirable maturation and unwholesome conduct results in undesirable maturation, so it should be understood by analogy.
Such insight through observation is called skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
The objects for purifying afflictions are the coarseness of the lower stages, the tranquility of the higher stages, suchness, and the four noble truths.

Regarding the coarseness of the lower stages and the tranquility of the higher stages, this is explained according to the mundane path, because by means of these one subdues the various enveloping fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Regarding "True Suchness and the Four Noble Truths," this is spoken in reference to the supramundane path.
