True Suchness is mentioned briefly, while the Four Noble Truths are mentioned extensively, because by means of these, all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are permanently destroyed.

Furthermore, having already discussed the examination of dharmas such as the sūtras, one should now explain the principles of all dharmas, for it is by relying on these principles that one is able to examine those dharmas.
Question:
If one wishes to correctly exert effort and carefully examine all phenomena, by how many kinds of principles can one correctly examine them?
Answer:

By means of four types of reasoning: namely, the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), the reasoning of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*), the reasoning of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*), and the reasoning of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).

The reasoning of dependence refers to the fact that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they necessarily depend upon a collection of conditions. For example, when a sprout arises, it depends on conditions such as the seed, the season, water, and the field; likewise, when the various consciousnesses arise, they depend on conditions such as the sense faculties, the objects, and mental attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth.

The principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇayukti*) refers to the distinct functions of phenomena with different characteristics. For example, the sense organs such as the eye serve as the basis (*āśraya*) for consciousnesses such as visual consciousness; objects such as form serve as the objective referent (*ālambana*) for visual consciousness and the like; and the various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, perform the function of discerning form and so forth.
It is also comparable to goldsmiths and silversmiths who are skilled in the craftsmanship of creating objects such as gold and silver. Such is the analogy.

The principle of proof (*upapattisādhana-yukti*) refers to the proclamation of statements that do not contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish a meaning that is yet to be established.
The meaning to be established refers to the meaning to be established as comprised within the specific characteristics of its own nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).

"Words that do not contradict the various means of valid cognition" refers to statements such as the formulation of a thesis (*pakṣa*) that are not inconsistent with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition].

"The principle of the nature of things" (*dharmatā-yukti*) refers to the established nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and their inherent nature (*dharmatā*) as they have existed since beginningless time within all phenomena, whether characterized by specific or general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Just as fire can burn and water can rot, so too do all such phenomena achieve their nature through the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Though the eye is perfectly clear, it is empty, lacks permanence, and so forth, up to being without self."
Why is this so? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, having correctly and diligently observed the four principles regarding all phenomena, how does one initiate investigation (*vitarka*)?
That is to say, one gives rise to four kinds of investigation:

first, investigation of names; second, investigation of things; third, investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature; and fourth, investigation of the provisional designation of distinctions.
Investigation of names refers to the analytical search for the self-characteristics of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes of all phenomena, finding that none are established as real.
Because these sets of names and so forth exist only as designations, one observes that their self-characteristics are all unestablished as real.

Investigation of phenomena (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*) means to investigate how the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—are not established as real.

Since the entities (*vastu*) proclaimed by the aggregates and so forth are like the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so on, they are all not established as real; therefore, one contemplates that their characteristics are not established as real.
"Seeking" (*vitarka*) means investigation.

"Seeking the designation of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*) refers to seeking within the correspondence between the designator and the designated among all phenomena, [and finding that] intrinsic nature is merely the causal basis for conventional verbal designation.
Regarding the correspondence between the signifier and the signified: this means that these two serve as the mutual causes for comprehension. Why is this so?
For one who is skilled in linguistic conventions, upon merely hearing the signifier, comprehension of the signified arises through the gateway of recollection.
Alternatively, one may apprehend only the signified object, and through the gateway of recollection, come to achieve comprehension of the signifier.

Within such a conventionally established correspondence, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the eye and so forth are merely nominal designations, because these names arise solely with respect to the causes for conventional expressions, such as the physical mass of flesh.
If one investigates in this manner, it is called the investigation into the provisional designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*).

As for the investigation into the provisional designation of distinctions (*viśeṣa-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*), it refers to seeking out the distinctions within the correspondence between the designators and the designated among all phenomena, [finding that they are] merely the causal basis for the provisional designation of names and conventions.

Why is this so? Because within the correspondence between the signifier and the signified, when one investigates distinctions such as permanence or impermanence, having a superior or being unsurpassed, possessing form or being formless, or being visible or invisible, these are merely the causal nature of conventionally established names and expressions.
Observing in this manner is called the investigation of conventional designations regarding distinctions.
Furthermore, having applied oneself with right effort to the investigation of phenomena, one will necessarily attain knowledge of things as they truly are.
How does one give rise to knowledge in accordance with reality?
It refers to the arising of four types of knowledge in accordance with reality:

first, the knowledge in accordance with reality induced by the investigation of names; second, the knowledge in accordance with reality induced by the investigation of things; third, the knowledge in accordance with reality induced by the investigation of the provisional establishment of intrinsic nature; and fourth, the knowledge in accordance with reality induced by the investigation of the provisional establishment of distinctions.
Knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of names, refers to the knowledge that names are unapprehendable as they truly are.
Knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of things, refers to the knowledge that the characteristics of things are likewise unapprehendable as they truly are.

The knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation into the provisional designation of intrinsic nature, refers to the knowledge that realizes that a truly existent intrinsic nature cannot be found.

The knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation into the provisional designation of specific differences, refers to the knowledge that realizes that truly existent specific differences cannot be found.
Regarding these four types of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), as previously investigated, one understands that name and so forth are all truly unapprehendable.
Furthermore, for one who practices samādhi in accordance with the Dharma, how should the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmi*) be understood?
This stage briefly consists of five aspects: namely, retention (*dhṛti*), receptivity (*kṣānti*), the mirror (*ādarśa*), clarity (*prabhāsvara*), and reliance (*niśraya*).

Regarding "retention": it refers to having already accumulated the provisions for awakening (*bodhisambhāra*) and, during the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, possessing extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) concerning the noble truths (*āryasatya*). Because one establishes the objects of focus for calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) according to what has been extensively learned, it is called "retention."

Furthermore, one who has already accumulated the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) listens to and receives teachings such as the *sūtras* in order to seek the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*); therefore, this is called "much learning" (*bahuśruta*).

"Application" (*adhivāsana*) refers to appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward these objects; by means of this mental attention, based on what has been much learned, one correctly contemplates it, thereby maintaining the mind with respect to the characteristics of the meanings heard.

"Mirror" refers to the samādhi with signs (*sanimitta*) that takes this object as its condition. This samādhi takes extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) as its object; because it is conjoined with the sign of meditative concentration, it is called "with signs. This is because this samādhi still bears the image (*pratibimba*) of the objective entity (*jñeya-vastu*), which is of the same nature (*sabhāga*).
Furthermore, this samādhi can minutely examine the objective reality of the objects of knowledge; therefore, it is likened to a mirror.

"Clarity" refers to the non-apprehending wisdom regarding both the grasper and the grasped, because through this wisdom, the clear realization (abhisamaya) subsumed within the path of seeing (darśanamārga) proceeds.
How does a bodhisattva, relying on the stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*), train in skillful means and realize non-apprehension?

It is as follows: having well accumulated the two provisions of merit and wisdom; having already passed the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*); having heard the teachings of the sūtras that accord with and penetrate suchness (*tathatā*); and having given rise to samādhi through correct mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), the bodhisattva relies upon the mind in meditative concentration to contemplate the cognitive image (*pratibimba*) known within that concentration. Observing that this image is not different from the concentrated mind, he relies upon this image to abandon the perception of external objects, contemplating only the self-perceived image within the concentration.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind, he causes the mind to abide within and realizes that objects of perception of every kind are entirely non-existent.
Since the apprehended object does not exist, all that apprehends it is likewise not real; therefore, one next realizes that the apprehending subject is non-existent.
Subsequently, one further abandons within the internal mind the two kinds of self-nature that were previously grasped, thereby realizing non-apprehension.
Based on this principle, the Buddha, the Blessed One, has excellently proclaimed:

"When a bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, they observe that the reflected image is nothing but mind; once the conceptualization of external objects is eliminated, they scrutinize that it is merely one's own mental representation."

One knows the internal mind that dwells therein; one knows that the apprehended object does not exist, and subsequently, the apprehending subject is also absent; finally, one touches upon non-apprehension.
"The basis" refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because one abandons all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and attains the pure transformation of the basis.

It should be understood that within this context, the *yogabhūmi* is explained by means of two aspects: cause and fruit. The four factors beginning with "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) explain the cause of this stage, while the final factor explains its fruit.
Furthermore, what is skill in phenomena (*dharma-kauśalya*) among all phenomena?
What is skill in meaning (*artha-kauśalya*)?
What is skill in phrasing (*vyañjana-kauśalya*)?
What is skillfulness in terminology?
What is skillfulness regarding the intentional meaning of the past and the future?
These five questions correspond to the various phrases taught in the sūtras.
As the Venerable Ānanda told Śāriputra:
"Elder, you should know that if bhikṣus are accomplished in five qualities, they will be able to quickly receive, receive much, receive well, and not lose what has been received."
In this sutra, by means of these five dharmas, the four categories of meaning—such as "quick reception" and so forth—are established as appropriate.
What is skillfulness regarding the dharmas (*dharmakauśalya*)?

It is because of being well-learned (*bahuśruta*); through skillfulness regarding the dharmas, one is able to quickly receive [the teachings], for those who possess great learning are for the most part able to quickly grasp the distinctions between words and phrases.
What is skillfulness regarding the meaning?
It refers to being skilled in knowing the characteristics within the Abhidharma and Vinaya; thus, through skillfulness regarding the meaning, one is able to receive much [teaching].

If one thoroughly understands the characteristics of the Abhidharma and so forth, one will then be able to collect a vast amount of textual material regarding the phenomena explained in terms of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
What is skill in phrasing?
It is the thorough knowledge of the etymological explanations of words and phrases.
What is skill in terminology?
This means being able to skillfully understand conventional expressions such as "self" and "mine," and because one does not deeply cling to them, one speaks in accordance with them.
If one attains proficiency in both the words and their meaning, one will then be able to excellently comprehend what is taught.
Because they skillfully understand the interpretation of words and phrases, they are adept at understanding conventional expressions such as "self" and "mine.
Because they do not deeply cling to them but speak in accordance with reality, they are able to correctly receive and comprehend both the literal text and its meaning.
What is skillfulness regarding the intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) of the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and the future limit (*aparānta*)?
It refers to being able to skillfully know the experience in the past limit and the renunciation in the future limit.

If one is skillful regarding the intentional meaning of the past and future limits, one will be able to receive [the teachings] and not lose them; by relying on the dharmas received in the past limit, one will subsequently be able to realize renunciation.
By thoroughly understanding the Tathāgata’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), one is able to realize the solid core of the noble teaching.
How does one abide in the Dharma among all phenomena?

If one does not attain the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), but merely exerts oneself in the application of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī*), this cannot be called abiding in the Dharma.

If one does not obtain both hearing and reflection, but merely exerts oneself in the skillful means of cultivating meditative wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), one still cannot be said to abide in the Dharma.
Only when one abides through the skillful means of both [hearing and reflection] can one be called one who abides in the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says:
"Venerable One, you should know that if bhikṣus abide in the Dharma in this manner, they may be called bhikṣus who abide in the Dharma.
In this Sūtra, the Blessed One reveals that only those who are able to abide by fully relying upon hearing, reflection, and cultivation are called those who abide in the Dharma.
One does not attain the designation "abiding in the Dharma" merely by practicing through the cultivation of a single expedient means;
rather, if one only upholds, recites, and explains the Dharma to others, this is called the wisdom born of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*).

As it is said: if, in a certain case, one extensively investigates the text, recites and proclaims it, and repeatedly reflects upon it, yet cultivates only the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) without cultivating the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and abandons yoga and so forth, such a person cannot be established as one who "dwells in the Dharma."
If one practices the skillful means of samādhi without being content, this is called the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

As it is said: "If there is one who does not attain [the wisdoms of] hearing and reflection, but only cultivates the wisdom of cultivation, they likewise cannot be established as one who abides in the Dharma."
Therefore, the Blessed One, with reference to the bhikṣu Dharmasthita, spoke these words:
"If a bhikṣu has reached the ultimate mastery of the Dharma—namely, the sūtras, the geyas, and so forth, as explained at length."
Furthermore, it is later stated that one does not abandon yoga; such points should be understood according to reason.
If one possesses the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and relies upon the two types of abiding, this is called "abiding in the Dharma and not abandoning yoga."
"Those such as these" refers to being insatiable regarding the means for cultivating *samādhi*, which demonstrates the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
"Means for cultivating *samādhi*" refers to the means that are both uninterrupted and earnest, as well as the means that are non-erroneous (*aviparīta*).
This demonstrates two kinds of skillful means:
first, that subsumed under uninterrupted and earnest application, as it says "not abandoning yoga";
second, that subsumed under non-erroneous application, as it says "not abandoning mental attention."
"Being insatiable" means not giving rise to attachment while practicing the superior methods of *śamatha*, as it is said that one does not abandon internal *śamatha*.
This indicates that because one does not give rise to attachment and because one practices the superior methods of *śamatha*, it is termed "not abandoning."
Furthermore, for what reason is the Vaipulya portion within the twelvefold holy teaching called the Bodhisattva-pāramitā-piṭaka?

It is because within this portion all the pāramitās are extensively explained by way of their number, their characteristics, their sequence, their etymological definitions, their cultivation, their classifications, their subsumption, their opposites, their qualities, and their mutual determination.
Question:
Where is this taught?
Answer:
As it is said in the sutras, the Mahāyāna is the treasury of the bodhisattva’s pāramitās.
How are the number, characteristics, and sequence of these pāramitās proclaimed, and how are they further analyzed in relation to one another?
There are two kinds of enumeration:
first, enumerative calculation; second, definitive enumeration.
Enumerative calculation refers to the six pāramitās.
Regarding the determination of the number: it means that the number of pāramitās is exactly six, neither more nor less.
Why is this? Because, in brief, the path of all bodhisattvas consists of two types:
First, the path of higher rebirth; second, the path of definitive excellence.
These are subsumed under three [categories] each, respectively. Why is this so?
There are three types of higher rebirth:
first, great material wealth; second, a great physical form; and third, a great retinue.
The perfection of generosity brings about the fruit of great material wealth.

The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) results in the fruit of a great physical form, because by maintaining pure ethics one is born in the higher realms and attains a body of noble status.
The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) results in the fruit of a great retinue, because all sentient beings who are capable of practicing patience will come to rely upon and follow them.
The definitive supreme path is of three kinds:

first, the skillful means for subduing all afflictions and cultivating wholesome qualities; second, the skillful means for maturing sentient beings; and third, the skillful means for maturing the Buddha-dharmas.
If any one of these three is lacking, the Bodhisattva’s path of definitive excellence will certainly not be accomplished.

Regarding the skillful means for maturing sentient beings, this refers to the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), because by relying upon it, one manifests supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to mature sentient beings.
Furthermore, because the pāramitās are the skillful means for the nirvāṇa of non-abiding, their number is exactly six. Why is this so?
It is because bodhisattvas, in order to overturn abiding in [passive] nirvāṇa, gather superior rebirths within saṃsāra.
In order to overturn abiding in saṃsāra, one remains untainted within saṃsāra itself.

Therefore, the first three are the means for attaining higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*), while the latter three are the means for non-defilement (*anāsrava*); these should be understood as previously explained, according to their respective applications.

Regarding the skillful means of non-defilement: through diligence, one cultivates the remedies; through meditative concentration, one suppresses the afflictions; and through wisdom, one permanently eradicates all latent tendencies of the afflictions.
Furthermore, because they are intended to benefit all sentient beings and to counteract all afflictions, there are only six perfections (*pāramitā*). Why is this so?
By means of giving, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gathers material resources and thereby benefits all sentient beings through skillful means;

by means of ethical discipline, he does not cause injury, oppression, or affliction, thereby benefiting all sentient beings through skillful means, because he does not, respectively, destroy the wealth, body, or mind of others.

By means of patience (*kṣānti*), one is able to endure injury, harm, oppression, and disturbance, employing skillful means to gather and benefit all sentient beings, because of the ability to tolerate others' encroachment upon one's own wealth and so forth.
By means of these three types, one is well able to gather and benefit all sentient beings.
Through diligence, although one has not yet permanently subdued all afflictions, one cultivates their antidotes based upon wholesome qualities.
Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one permanently suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*);
through wisdom (*prajñā*), one permanently eradicates the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
By means of these three, one is well able to counteract all afflictions.
Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the characteristics of the perfections (*pāramitā*) of the bodhisattvas.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*)?

It is when bodhisattvas, dwelling in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas, relying upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and guided by compassion, relinquish all actions of body, speech, and mind at all times.

Thus, the characteristics of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) are revealed by way of lineage (gotra), aspiration (praṇidhāna), intention (āśaya), activity (karma), and essential nature (svabhāva).
As for lineage, it refers to the dharma-nature (dharmatā) of the bodhisattva.
Aspiration refers to the bodhicitta.
Intention refers to the mind guided by compassion.
Activity refers to the relinquishing of all that one possesses.
As for its essential nature, it refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*)?

It refers to all actions of body, speech, and mind belonging to a bodhisattva who, abiding in the bodhisattva’s true nature (*dharmatā*), relies upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and with a mind guided by compassion, undertakes and maintains all the bodhisattva precepts.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)?

It refers to all physical, verbal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva who, abiding in the *dharmatā* of a bodhisattva, relying upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and guided by compassion, is able to endure and accept the suffering caused by enemies.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*)?

It refers to all actions of body, speech, and mind belonging to bodhisattvas who, dwelling in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas, rely upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and with compassion guiding their minds, give rise to all supreme and wholesome qualities.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*)?

It refers to when bodhisattvas, abiding in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas, relying upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and with a mind guided by compassion, give rise to the sovereign application of all types of physical, verbal, and mental karma; at that time, their entire mind remains constantly settled in stability.
What is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?

It refers to when bodhisattvas, dwelling in the *dharmatā* of bodhisattvas, relying upon the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and with a mind guided by compassion, exercise mastery over all types of physical, verbal, and mental actions, thereby discerning all phenomena.

Furthermore, if the practice of giving relies upon the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), is capable of inducing the nature of omniscience, encompasses the nature of omniscience, and is able to perform all the tasks of omniscience, this is called the characteristic of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
These four phrases, in their respective order, manifest the characteristics of the pāramitās by way of their arousal, their habitual tendencies, their essential nature, and their outflow.
As for "initiation," it means that based upon the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), whatever acts of giving are performed are all dedicated toward the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*).
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) refer to that which can bring about the nature of omniscience.
This is because the continuity of the practice of giving, having been cultivated, is able to bring about the nature of *sarvajña* (omniscience) in a future life.
As for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it refers to the appropriation of the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This is because at that time, when the practice of giving has reached ultimate perfection, one is able to accomplish the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
Regarding "outflow" (*niṣyanda*): it means being capable of performing all the activities of omniscience.

This is because, from this point onward, by means of the gateway of the outflow consisting in the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and so forth, one initiates all the activities of a *sarvajña* (omniscient one).
The characteristics of the perfection of giving, up to and including the characteristics of the perfection of wisdom, should all be explained in this same manner.
As for the sequence, it means that each preceding perfection serves as the basis for each subsequent one.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, through their cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), have practiced the relinquishing of both internal and external things; thus, they disregard body and life, renounce great treasuries of jewels, and uphold the prohibitive precepts.
Because he guards the precepts, he never retaliates when others revile or abuse him.

Through such means, he is able to endure; by being able to endure hardships such as cold and heat, even when encountering these conditions, he does not cease his application but exerts diligent effort.
Through the application of diligence, one realizes the ultimate fruit and brings meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to fulfillment.
Once concentration is fulfilled, by means of knowing reality as it is through a mind of pure meditative absorption, one realizes the ultimate supramundane great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).
Furthermore, each preceding perfection is supported by each subsequent one;
that is to say, ethical discipline supports generosity, and so on, up to wisdom supporting meditative concentration.
Through the possession of ethical discipline (*śīla*), generosity becomes purified.
Why is this? Because by practicing generosity, one gathers and benefits sentient beings; because by possessing ethical discipline (*śīla*), one does not cause them harm.

Therefore, since a bodhisattva is well able to bestow pure instruments of happiness upon those who receive gifts by remaining free from harm, giving becomes purified through the power of ethical discipline.
In this way, through the power of patience, ethical discipline becomes pure. Why is this?
Because one is able to endure the harm inflicted by others and never violates the precepts one has undertaken to train in.
Through diligence, patience becomes purified.

Why is this? Because by the power of valor, one does not consider it difficult to remain for a long time within birth and death (saṃsāra), and is thus able to endure the sufferings of sentient beings' hostility and the like.
Through meditative concentration, diligence becomes pure. Why is this?
Because, accompanied by joy and bliss, one is able to diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas without rest.
Through the possession of wisdom, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) becomes pure. Why is this?
If one repeatedly contemplates all phenomena through immeasurable gateways, one can realize internal tranquility and increase meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, a verse states:
"There is no meditative concentration that does not depend upon wisdom.
Moreover, the sequential order of the perfections is established according to their coarseness or subtlety.
Why is this so? Among all the practices, generosity is the coarsest; therefore, it is established first.
Among the practices such as patience, ethical discipline is again the coarsest; therefore, it is established next.

This continues up to wisdom (*prajñā*). Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is considered coarse, whereas wisdom is the most subtle; therefore, it is established last. Regarding the etymological explanation:

as for why the practice of giving (*dāna*) performed by Bodhisattvas is called the "Perfection of Giving" (*dānapāramitā*), it is because it is a great giving, free from faults, and free from defilements; thus, it is named the Perfection of Giving.
"Great giving" refers to the complete relinquishing of all internal and external things and the practice of giving over a long period of time.
"Free from faults" refers to being far removed from such faults as seeking in an uneven or improper manner.
"Free from defilement" means having forever severed all stinginess, which is the quality to be remedied.
As it is said in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa Sūtra* regarding the inexhaustibility of giving:
"What is meant by being free from defilement?"
Because they have forever severed that which is to be abandoned, along with its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
These three phrases reveal the three kinds of supremacy of the *pāramitās*.
What are these three?
First, the excellence of the intrinsic nature and its accumulation; second, the excellence of the means; third, the excellence of the fruit.
"Accumulation" refers to practicing giving over a long period of time.
Just as there are three kinds of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), so it is for each up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Regarding the "abandonment of faults" in the case of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the others, this refers to being free from the superimposition of a self (*ātma-adhyāropa*) and so forth, as explained at length in the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, they are called *pāramitās* because they are endowed with twelve kinds of excellence (*vaiśeṣya*). What are these twelve excellences?
First is the excellence of vastness, because they do not seek any worldly happiness and because they are supreme.
Second, it is supreme in its duration, because it has been accumulated through practice over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Third, it is supreme in its purpose, because it is for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Fourth is the excellence of inexhaustibility, because through dedication toward great enlightenment, it is ultimately inexhaustible.

Fifth is the excellence of uninterruptedness, because by attaining the superior resolve of equality between self and others, it causes all sentient beings to swiftly fulfill the perfections such as generosity.

Sixth is the supremacy of being free from obstacles, because by merely rejoicing in the acts of giving and so forth performed by others, one causes the perfections (*pāramitā*) to be swiftly fulfilled.

Seventh is the supremacy of great mastery, because by attaining various *samādhis* such as the "Space-Treasury" (*ākāśagarbha*), one causes the perfections of giving and so forth to be swiftly fulfilled.
Eighth is the supremacy of appropriation, because it is appropriated by non-conceptual wisdom.
Ninth is the supremacy of initiation, which refers to the perfections such as generosity practiced during the stage of supreme patience within the level of conduct through aspiration.
Tenth is the excellence of attainment, which refers to the perfections such as generosity attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Eleventh is the excellence of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), which refers to the perfections such as generosity practiced in the remaining eight stages.

The supremacy of the twelve perfections refers to the perfections such as generosity belonging to the tenth stage and the stage of a Tathāgata; these are so designated because they are perfected by Bodhisattvas and perfected by Buddhas, respectively.

Furthermore, they are called *pāramitās* because they are the deeds of the most excellent and because they are the destination of the most excellent; for they are what all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perform and reach.
Furthermore, they are called *pāramitās* because they reach the further shore of all that is to be known, as they abide in the Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, they are called *pāramitās* because they rescue both oneself and others from the most extreme calamities, enabling oneself and others to cross over the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
The common [etymology] has already been explained; the uncommon one shall now be stated.
Because it enables the donor to abandon future poverty and suffering, and enables the recipient to abandon present distress and affliction, it is called "giving" (*dāna*).

It is called "precept" (śīla) because it can cause the sense faculties to be eternally tranquil, because it can lead one toward pure and auspicious rebirths, and because it serves as a basis for coolness.

This is because, in their respective order, they are able to lead to the guarding of the sense-faculties; they are the cause for proceeding toward pure and auspicious rebirths; and they serve as the basis for the gradual progression from freedom from remorse up to nirvāṇa.

It is called patience (*kṣānti*) because it is far removed from the ashes of all anger and heat, because it is far removed from the mind that harbors resentment and seeks to harm, and because it manifests constant peace and security for those who cause injury.
"Malicious intent" refers to the arising of a mind seeking retribution.
"Not relinquishing" means not abandoning this mind.
One who can destroy such malicious intent is called a "harm-doer."
Because it manifests this fearlessness, it is called "manifesting" (*vidarśana*); because it brings about constant peace and security for those who cause harm, it is so named.
Because it is associated with the activity of increasing damage [to the afflictions], it is called "diligence" (*vīrya*).
Those associated with the function of harming refer to the first two right abandonments, because they are able to harm unwholesome dharmas.
Those associated with the function of growth refer to the latter two right abandonments, because they are able to grow all wholesome dharmas.
It is called *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) because it can hold, can pacify, can still, can discipline, and can also induce [virtuous qualities].
"Can hold" means binding the mind to the object.
"Capable of pacifying" means to still all forms of distraction.
"Capable of settling" means to cause the mind to become tranquil.
"Capable of taming" means to subdue the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
That which can induce [realization] refers to the ability to induce sovereign activity.

It is called *prajñā* (wisdom) because it is the wisdom induced by others, because it is internally realized wisdom, because it is wisdom of specific distinctions, because it is wisdom that attains tranquility, and because it is the wisdom of supreme virtue.
Knowledge derived from others refers to the wisdom arising from the speech and sounds of others, as well as the wisdom associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
Knowledge realized within oneself refers to supramundane wisdom (*lokottaraprajñā*).
Knowledge of categories refers to the wisdom attained subsequent to supramundane realization.
Knowledge of attaining tranquility refers to the wisdom that counteracts afflictions during the path of cultivation.
Knowledge of supreme excellence refers to the wisdom capable of bringing forth superior qualities.
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Ten; Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Eleven;
Composed by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati as a Commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. (Fascicle Twelve)
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, Chapter Two: "Dharma," Part Two: What is cultivation?

Briefly, there are five kinds: namely, cultivation based on reliance and sustenance (*niśraya-dhāraṇa*), cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*), cultivation based on intention (*āśaya*), cultivation based on skillful means (*upāya*), and cultivation based on mastery (*vaśitā*).
There are four kinds of cultivation based on reliance and sustenance:
first, cultivation based on causes, which refers to the practice of correct conduct in the *pāramitās* by means of the power of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second is cultivation based on maturation (*vipāka*), which refers to the correct practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) through the superior power of one's own physical body.
Third is cultivation based on aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), which refers to the correct practice of the perfections through the power of one's original vows.
The cultivation based on the power of discernment consists of practicing the correct application of the *pāramitās* through the power of wisdom.
There are also four types of cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*):

first, cultivation based on mental attention of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), which refers to generating superior resolute belief toward all the scriptural teachings associated with the *pāramitās*.

Second is cultivation based on the mental attention of relishing (*āsvādana-manasikāra*), which means perceiving the superior merits of the already attained *pāramitās* and giving rise to deep relish for them.

Third is cultivation based on the mental attention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*), which means generating profound sympathetic joy toward the acts of generosity and so forth performed by all sentient beings in all worlds.

Fourth is the cultivation of mental attention based on joyful aspiration (*abhirati-manasikāra*), which means generating a deep yearning and aspiration for the superior perfections (*pāramitā*) of both oneself and others in the future.

Furthermore, there are six kinds of cultivation based on intentional aspiration (*āśaya-bhāvanā*): namely, by means of the aspiration of tirelessness, the aspiration of vastness, the aspiration of joy, the aspiration of gratitude and virtue, the aspiration of non-attachment, and the aspiration of excellence, one cultivates the various perfections.

In this context, the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) means that for even a single sentient being and for a single moment, a bodhisattva might give as an offering the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise give as an offering his own body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, continuing such giving for as many great eons (*mahākalpa*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

Just as one gives to a single sentient being, so too does one give to the entire realm of sentient beings; when giving in this manner, one causes them all to swiftly attain maturity in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When practicing such differentiated giving, the bodhisattva’s intention is characterized by insatiability.
This kind of intention is called the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the perfection of generosity.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of giving, it proceeds in continuous succession without a single moment of decline or interruption, until they finally sit upon the seat of enlightenment.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, they give rise to great joy toward those sentient beings who are the recipients of that generosity; even though these sentient beings experience joy because they are the objects of such generosity, it cannot compare to the joy of the bodhisattvas.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, they regard all sentient beings embraced by that generosity as having rendered great kindness to themselves, rather than seeing themselves as having rendered kindness to them, because [those beings] have assisted their own attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the benefits of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, although they generate great merit through extensive giving toward immeasurable sentient beings, they do not hope for gratitude or for future karmic rewards.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s unstained intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, they bestow upon all sentient beings the fruits of the vast accumulation of generosity thus practiced, rather than for their own sake; moreover, they dedicate this merit together with all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s excellent intention regarding the perfection of generosity.

Furthermore, regarding the bodhisattvas’ insatiable intention when practicing the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline up to the *pāramitā* of wisdom: suppose a bodhisattva were to pass through as many lifetimes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and in each of these lifetimes lived for as many great eons (*mahākalpa*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; during this vast period, they were constantly deprived of all necessities of life and remained within a trichiliocosm filled with blazing fire, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down therein, yet were able to practice even a single moment of the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline, or even up to the *pāramitā* of wisdom—practicing them in such successive and differentiated ways until the entire aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom was ultimately fulfilled, whereby they would presently realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

When these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they remain unsatisfied with their cultivation of the aspirational intention regarding this accumulation of ethical discipline up to the accumulation of wisdom.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas practice these perfections, from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they proceed in continuous succession without a single moment of regression or interruption, until they finally sit upon the seat of enlightenment.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to great joy toward all sentient beings who are thereby gathered; yet, although those sentient beings experience joy because of being so gathered, it cannot compare to that of the bodhisattvas.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they regard all sentient beings included therein as having rendered great kindness to themselves, rather than seeing themselves as having rendered kindness to those beings, because those beings have assisted them in attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the benefits of practicing the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, although they generate vast merit of ethical discipline up to merit of wisdom for immeasurable sentient beings, they do not hope for gratitude or for future karmic rewards.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s unstained intention regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they bestow upon all sentient beings the karmic fruits obtained from their vast accumulations of ethical discipline up to their vast accumulations of wisdom, rather than for themselves; moreover, they dedicate this merit together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such an intention is called the excellent intention of a bodhisattva regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.

There are three kinds of reliance on the restoration through skillful means; that is to say, because one observes that the three spheres are entirely pure by means of non-conceptual wisdom. Why is this so?
By means of this expedient, all practices cultivated through mental attention are swiftly brought to fulfillment.
Furthermore, there are three types of cultivation based on mastery: namely, mastery over the body, mastery over conduct, and mastery over teaching.
Mastery over the body refers to the self-nature enjoyment body (*svābhāvika-sambhogakāya*) of all Tathāgatas.

Mastery over the activity of the two bodies refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Tathāgatas, because by means of this, they can manifest for all sentient beings every kind of practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding "speaking with mastery," it means being able to proclaim all the various distinctions of the six pāramitās without any obstruction.
What are these distinctions?
This refers to the manifestation of the distinctions of the six *pāramitās* by means of eighteen kinds of sustenance (*upastambha*).

What are these eighteen? They are: sustenance of the body; sustenance of the mind; sustenance of wholesome dharmas; sustenance of the wholesome; sustenance of awakening (*bodhi*); sustenance of compassion; sustenance of not abandoning sentient beings; sustenance of relinquishing inferior states of mind; sustenance of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); sustenance of skillful means regarding roots of virtue; sustenance of the perfect realization of roots of virtue; sustenance of the inexhaustibility of roots of virtue; sustenance of being free from weariness; sustenance of the fulfillment of all intended aims; sustenance of the activity of governing a community; sustenance of entering the stages (*bhūmi*); sustenance of eliciting the Buddha-nature; and sustenance of establishing the Buddha-activities.
The six types of giving, such as generosity and so forth, each have three distinctions, which are subsumed under three sets of three respectively.
As for the three kinds of giving, they are: the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

The three types of ethical discipline (*śīla*) are: the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

The three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are: the patience of enduring enmity and harm (*āghāta-niṣkrodha-kṣānti*), the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*), and the patience of discerning the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).
The three types of diligence are: the diligence of donning the armor, the diligence of skillful means, and the diligence of benefiting sentient beings.

The three types of meditative concentration are: the meditative concentration for dwelling in happiness in the present life, the meditative concentration for manifesting supernormal powers, and the meditative concentration for benefiting sentient beings.

Regarding the three types of wisdom, they are: wisdom that takes conventional reality as its object, wisdom that takes ultimate reality as its object, and wisdom that takes sentient beings as its object.
It should be understood that the gift of material wealth can sustain the body, because provisions such as food and drink benefit the recipient’s physical basis.
The gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*) is able to sustain the mind, because it comforts the minds of others by freeing them from sorrow and fear.
The remaining phrases should be understood accordingly according to their meaning.

As for the "inferior mind," this refers to the mind of bodhisattvas who, weary of the suffering of saṃsāra, share the same attitude as the followers of the two vehicles; it is only through being sustained by the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*) that they eventually abandon this mind.

The inexhaustibility of the roots of virtue means that until the very limit of saṃsāra, one constantly performs acts for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, not abandoning them even within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, because this is sustained by the diligence of benefiting sentient beings.

Regarding the activity of gathering the assembly: it refers to relying upon internal realization to provide instruction and admonition to those beings to be converted; causing those whose minds are not yet concentrated to attain concentration, and causing those whose minds are already concentrated to attain liberation, because this is sustained by the meditative absorption that benefits sentient beings.

"Entering the great stages" means that one who has previously gained faith-understanding (*adhimukti*) in the profound teachings and perfected the accumulations (*sambhāra*) is able to swiftly enter the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), by being sustained by the wisdom that takes conventional reality as its object.
The remaining points are easy to understand and thus are not explained again.
Furthermore, as for the distinctions, there are seven kinds of giving:
first, fundamental giving, which refers to the perfection of giving possessed by a bodhisattva in the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), because they practice giving based upon that lineage.

Second is the gift of the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), which refers to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) possessed by a bodhisattva at the stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), because they practice giving based upon having received the great vows.
Third is the gift of gathering (*saṃgraha*), which refers to the perfection of giving possessed by a bodhisattva at the stage of practicing for the benefit of oneself and others.

Fourth is the gift free from grasping, which refers to the perfection of generosity belonging to a Bodhisattva at the stage of contemplating the true meaning, because it is free from the conceptual grasping of such [distinctions] as "the giver" and so forth.

The fifth is the gift without appropriation, which refers to the perfection of generosity belonging to Bodhisattvas at the stage of majestic power (*vibhutva*). Although they do not appropriate external means of subsistence, by the power of samādhis such as the "Space Treasury" (*ākāśagarbha*), they raise their hands and wave them toward the sky, causing precious jewels and other objects to rain down according to their wishes.

Sixth is giving according to what is appropriate, which refers to the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva at the stage of maturation, because they practice giving in accordance with what is suitable for those to be converted.
Seventh is vast giving, which refers to the perfection of generosity at the stage of supreme enlightenment, because it is unsurpassed.
Just as there are seven kinds of giving, so it is for each of the perfections up to wisdom, according to their respective applications.
What is their summary?
It means that, for the purpose of summarizing the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, the perfections such as giving and the others are briefly explained therein.
This summary consists briefly of four types:
first, inclusion by lineage (*gotra*), which refers to knowing that [the perfections] such as the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) are associated with and accordant with that lineage;
second, inclusion by the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), because they are subsumed within the various arisings of that thought.
The arousal of the mind is of two kinds: namely, undifferentiated and differentiated.
The undifferentiated refers to the aspiration: "May I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Regarding the distinction: it means, "May my perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) be swiftly fulfilled, up to and including the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
It should be understood that within this context, the generation of the mind through its distinctions encompasses all the perfections, because these [perfections] are the causes thereof.

Third is the inclusion of the benefit of oneself and others: by means of the inclusion through giving, one acquires all wealth, happiness, and sovereignty; this is called the inclusion of self-benefit.
By means of this giving, one attracts and gathers material resources for the sake of benefiting others; this is called the inclusion of the benefit of others.
The remaining modes of inclusion should be understood according to their respective meanings.

Regarding the fourfold inclusion in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are many varieties; namely, it may be explained in terms of the *dharmadhātu*, because suchness (*tathatā*) is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of generosity and the other perfections.
Alternatively, it is explained in terms of the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*), because it serves as the vessel for accomplishing all-knowledge;
or it is explained in terms of the integration of wisdom, because it brings all-knowledge to full completion.
Alternatively, it is explained in terms of following through knowledge (*jñāna-anuvartana*), because the five *pāramitās* proceed in accordance with the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Alternatively, it is explained in terms of the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), because the *prajñā-pāramitā* is the very essence of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
Since this ultimate meaning has suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) as its essence, it is able to encompass generosity and the other perfections.
Based on this brief explanation, the remaining meanings of "encompassment" should be reflected upon according to reason.

Regarding that which is to be remedied: it refers to the six [perfections] beginning with generosity, which, in their respective order, have stinginess, transgression of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom as their respective objects of remedy.

Furthermore, all wholesome dharmas subsumed within the perfections (pāramitās), as well as their respective opposites and the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa), are all that which is remedied by the perfections.
Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*): it refers to all immeasurable and boundless praised benefits based upon the five fruits; these are called merit.
Specifically, the ability to permanently sever that which is to be countered by oneself constitutes the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) of these *pāramitās*.
In the present life, the fact that one benefits oneself and others through these [virtues] such as generosity constitutes the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
In future lives, their successive and progressive arising in ever-increasing excellence constitutes the fruit of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

To experience great wealth, rebirth in the higher realms, freedom from enmity and destruction, abundance of joy and happiness, being honored among sentient beings with an invulnerable body, and belonging to a vast and noble lineage—these, in their respective order, are the maturational fruits (*vipākaphala*) of the perfections such as generosity.
There are, in brief, three types of mutual determination: first, the means (*upāya*);
second, the distinctions (*prabheda*); and third, the demonstration of distinctions (*prabhedasaṃdarśana*).
Regarding the means, it refers to that which can be obtained within all forms of the means of giving.
The relinquishing of all internal and external bodies and wealth is the skillful means of giving;
when one relinquishes everything within this skillful means, it is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Within this very context, when the mind of compassion prevents all harm, oppression, and affliction directed toward others, that is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Within this very context, when one endures obstacles, harm, and exhaustion, that is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
In this very context, repeatedly giving rise to a courageous and diligent mind of generosity is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
In this very context, the mind being purely virtuous, focused on a single object without wandering outward, is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

In this very context, skillfully grasping the practice of giving as it truly is in terms of its causes and effects, without entertaining divergent views, is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
In this manner, up to the application of the perfection of wisdom, one should appropriately establish each according to what is fitting.
Because giving through fearlessness exists in all places, there are briefly four types of distinctions:
first, the distinction of its essential nature;
second, the distinction of its accompaniments; third, the distinction of its exhortation and praise; and fourth, the distinction of its cultivation.

Regarding the distinctions in the essential natures of the perfections such as generosity and so forth, they consist, respectively, of relinquishment, restraint, endurance, exertion, mental abiding, and discernment.

Regarding the distinction of companions (*sahāya-viśeṣa*): it means that within the skillful means of giving and the other perfections, all the remaining *pāramitās* function in concert, as explained extensively above.
Regarding the distinction of exhortation and praise (*samādāpana-praśaṃsana-viśeṣa*): it means to exhort, praise, rejoice in, and celebrate giving and the other perfections.
Regarding the distinction of planting [the seeds]: this refers to establishing the perfections (pāramitās), such as giving, within the mental continuums of others.

Among these, the perfection of giving consists of material gifts; the remaining five perfections constitute the gift of fearlessness; and all six are the gift of the Dharma, because they are all planted within the mental continuums of others.

Regarding "demonstration by way of differentiation," this refers to demonstrating the perfections (pāramitās), such as generosity and so forth, through their various distinctions, such as being of a single type and so on.
For example, it is as if someone were to ask:
"Is that which is the perfection of generosity also the perfection of ethical discipline?"

If one asks whether that which is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is also the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), this question should be answered by means of a "consequent" formulation (*paścāt-pādaka*): namely, all perfections of ethical discipline are indeed perfections of generosity, but there may be perfections of generosity that are not perfections of ethical discipline.

This refers to the perfection of generosity not subsumed under the perfection of ethical discipline; likewise, up to the point where the perfection of wisdom is contrasted with the perfection of generosity, one should apply the "subsequent clause" (anuloma-paścāt-pada) in all such cases.
The remaining [factors], when viewed in relation to one another, should also be considered according to reason.

In this context, for those who practice gradually starting from the stage of a beginner, it is taught that the subsequent necessarily depends on the preceding, while the preceding does not depend on the subsequent; therefore, all [subsequent factors] are formulated as "concordant with the subsequent" (*anuloma-paścātpādaka*).
If one has already become habituated [to them], the six types of simultaneous cultivation all mutually encompass one another, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Regarding the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), if one speaks according to the mutual assistance of the pure and mixed aspects of the six *pāramitās*, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.
Furthermore, is everything that constitutes giving necessarily a *pāramitā*?
Or is everything that is a *pāramitā* necessarily giving?
To answer this question, one should employ the threefold formula (*trikoṭika*).
There may be giving that is not a pāramitā, namely, giving that is practiced without being dedicated toward great enlightenment.
There may be both giving and a pāramitā, namely, giving and so forth that are dedicated toward great enlightenment.
There may be that which is neither giving nor a *pāramitā*, namely, excluding those factors previously mentioned.
In this manner, up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, one should apply fourfold permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) to each, reflecting upon them according to reason.
Furthermore, do all acts of giving produce the various types of merit belonging to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)?
This should be analyzed through four propositions.
The first proposition refers to the practice of giving that is not dedicated toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
The second phrase refers to exhorting, praising, rejoicing in, and feeling delight at the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
The third phrase refers to dedicating the performed act of giving toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those aforementioned characteristics.
In this manner, one should apply fourfold alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) to each of the perfections up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), reflecting upon them according to reason.
Furthermore, for what reason is the Vaipulya division said to be vast and profound?
It is because the nature of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is vast and profound.

That is to say, since the fruit of this attainment—the nature of omniscience—is most vast and profound, the cause receives the name of the fruit; therefore, the Vaipulya division is specifically described as being vast and profound.
Furthermore, for what reason do some beings fail to develop resolute conviction regarding the vastness and profundity of the Vaipulya section, but instead harbor fear?
It is because they are far removed from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), have not planted roots of merit, and are under the influence of evil friends.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) refers to the fact that the bodhisattva lineage is its very essence.

Because a portion of sentient beings lacks the bodhisattva lineage, their mental disposition is inferior; they are unable to develop resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward the vast and profound teachings, and therefore they experience fear.

Furthermore, although a portion of sentient beings possess the lineage of a bodhisattva, because they have not planted the various roots of merit such as the correct aspiration for great enlightenment, they lack resolute conviction in this matter and therefore experience fear.

Furthermore, although some sentient beings have already planted roots of goodness, because they are influenced by evil friends who slander the Mahāyāna, they are unable to develop resolute conviction in it; therefore, they experience fear.
Furthermore, for what reason do some sentient beings, despite generating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward the vast and profound teachings of the Vaipulya division, fail to attain liberation?
It is because they dwell deeply in their own adherence to views (*svadṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and constantly and firmly cling to the literal meaning of the words.
Those who dwell deeply in their own dogmatic views do not further seek out the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Those who always rigidly adhere to the literal sense of the words constantly and stubbornly cling to the sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).

Just as one might, upon hearing the statement that all phenomena are ultimately without intrinsic nature, dismissively negate the existence of the characteristics and natures of all phenomena, so too is it with those who stubbornly cling to the literal meaning of other sutras of provisional meaning.
Therefore, although one may have faith in the Mahāyāna, one does not attain liberation.
Because the Mahāyāna is taught through various intentional expressions (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), the Bhagavān, relying on this underlying intention, spoke these words in the *Mahādharmanirhāra-sūtra*:
"If bodhisattvas grasp the meaning according to the literal expression and do not discern phenomena according to correct reasoning, they will give rise to twenty-eight types of incorrect views."

What are called the twenty-eight types of incorrect views? They are: the view of signs; the view of deprecating designations; the view of deprecating conceptualization; the view of deprecating reality; the view of grasping; the view of transformation;

the view of innocence; the view of renunciation; the view of contempt; the view of provocation; the view of inversion; the view of production; the view of not establishing a thesis; the view of equivocation; the view of service; the view of stubborn ignorance; the fundamental view; the view of seeing non-existence within views; the view of abandoning skillful means; the view of non-renunciation; the view of obstructing increase; the view of producing non-merit; the view of no karmic fruit; the view of accepting humiliation; the view of slander; the view of being unfit for discourse; the view of vastness; and the view of overweening pride.

"Those who see according to appearances" refers to those who, upon hearing the statements in Mahāyāna sūtras that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), are without arising or cessation, are quiescent from the beginning, and are by nature in *nirvāṇa*, do not understand the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*). Instead, they merely follow the literal meaning of these words and develop a conviction (*adhimukti*), asserting that all phenomena spoken of by the Buddha definitely lack intrinsic nature, definitely lack arising, and so forth.
To cling to such characteristics as "the absence of intrinsic nature" and so forth is called the view of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadṛṣṭi*).

When one clings to such characteristics as the absence of intrinsic nature and so forth, one then slanders the three natures—namely, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) refers to the fact that foolish worldlings, with respect to the characteristics of form and so forth, engage in pervasive conceptualization and give rise to superimposed attachments, asserting: "This is form," up to "this is nirvana."
This grasped object has no reality and no essence; it exists only as that which is designated by names and words.

As for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it refers to this very form and so forth, which are merely the substance of false discrimination, and whose causal nature is either different or non-different [from its effect].
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

To give rise to acts of denial regarding these three natures constitutes the next three views: namely, the view that deprecates designation (*prajñapti-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*), the view that deprecates conceptualization (*vikalpa-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*), and the view that deprecates reality (*tattva-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*).
When he thus slanders all phenomena in every respect, in order to establish this false view, he further resorts to a limited portion of reasoning.
Furthermore, regarding all definitive sūtras that reveal the ineffable true nature of phenomena, they employ extensive skillful means to distort them entirely so that they conform to their own views.
These two types are the next two views, namely, the view of appropriation (*parigraha-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of transformation (*pariṇāma-dṛṣṭi*).
They further give rise to this view:
"If one practices wholesome or unwholesome deeds based on this view, they are certainly all without fault and without transgression."
All actions are directed toward the sublime good, and all previously accumulated obscurations and defilements are brought to liberation.
These two types correspond respectively to the next two views, namely: the view of blamelessness and the view of renunciation.

Having thus adhered to his own view, he then falsely conceives contempt and disparagement toward the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, which establishes the aggregates and other phenomena in a manner contrary to that view; furthermore, he gives rise to deep resentment and jealousy toward those Śrāvakas who do not believe in such false views.
These two types are precisely the next two views: the view of disparagement and the view of resentment.

Furthermore, they conform to their own evil and false views, asserting: "I shall establish emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as they truly are. Yet, regarding what is not those characteristics, they give rise to the perception of those characteristics, thereby establishing them erroneously.
Furthermore, one reflects as follows:
"If one can realize such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā), or cause others to enter it, all such acts give rise to immeasurable merit.
These two types correspond respectively to the next two views: namely, the view of perversion and the view of production.

If others should properly challenge the wrong views he has generated toward them, at that time he does not at all wish to establish his own position; instead, he resorts to mockery and fallacious reasoning to challenge the others.
These two types correspond to the next two views, namely, the view of not establishing a thesis and the view of evasive equivocation.
They further give rise to such overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming that if one practices in this manner, it constitutes true worship and reverence for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Such a view is called the "view of reverential service.

For those who have thoroughly mastered the non-erroneous nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), in order to cause them to abandon such evil views, one may employ various skillful means of reasoning based on reality to awaken them; yet they stubbornly cling to their ignorant views without any intention to relinquish them, asserting: "Only this is true; all else is false and delusory."
To view things in such a manner is called the "view of stubborn ignorance.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) associated with all the views mentioned above are termed the "root view."

In order to reveal the doors of the faults of the seventeen kinds of views mentioned above, he further explains other views, namely: the view of characteristics is called the "view of non-view regarding views."

This arises from the firm adherence to such characteristics as non-existence and the like; because one does not grasp at the conceptualization of any characteristic, it is called the view of abandoning skillful means, which consists of the view of deprecating designations, the view of deprecating discrimination, and the view of deprecating reality.

Because they revile the nature of all phenomena and conceive the notion that diligent application of effort is useless, they embrace the view of grasping and the view of transformation; this is called the view of non-emergence.
Because one cannot realize the fruit through practice that lacks skillful means, the view of sinlessness and the view of renunciation are termed the "view of increasing obstacles.
Because one's conduct is deviant and there is no possibility of exhausting these obstacles, the view of disparagement and the view of resentment are termed the "view of producing non-merit."

Because the gateway of misconduct arising from the True Dharma and fellow practitioners of the holy life leads to great ruin, namely the view of perversion and the view of origination, these are called the views of fruitlessness.

Because that which is established as being of a non-Dharmic nature cannot lead either the teacher or the recipient to realize any superior fruit, the view of not establishing a thesis and the view of evasive equivocation are termed the "view of humiliation."
Because one who engages in irrational debate cannot possibly achieve victory, this is the view of "reverential service" (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), which is termed the "view of slander" (apavāda-dṛṣṭi).
Because one forcibly superimposes what should not be spoken, this is the view of "stubborn ignorance," which is termed the "view of being uncommunicative" (anālāpya-dṛṣṭi).
One should not engage in discourse with those who perversely cling to emptiness, for their prolixity is ultimately of no benefit.
This constitutes the fundamental view, termed the "vast view" (*vipuladṛṣṭi*), because by means of it, various categories of evil views will increase and expand in the future.
The twenty-seven views mentioned above are all termed views of overweening pride (*adhimāna-dṛṣṭi*), because they can all give rise to false and unsubstantial overweening pride.
How is this known?
For it is stated immediately following that sutra: "In this way, these seventeen views are ten, and ten are seventeen; twenty-seven are one, and one is twenty-seven."
Furthermore, as stated in the Vaipulya section, all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
With what underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) was this said?
It means that they lack an inherent nature (*svayambhū-svabhāva*) and lack an essential nature (*ātma-svabhāva*).
Because it has no abiding intrinsic nature, and because it lacks the nature of characteristics as apprehended by foolish commoners.

Regarding the absence of a spontaneous nature (*svayambhāva*), it is called "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) due to the absence of such spontaneity; it is not said to lack intrinsic nature because it precludes a nature that depends on conditions.
Regarding "the absence of intrinsic nature": because this very intrinsic nature that previously existed can no longer exist, it is said to be "without nature."
Regarding that which has no abiding intrinsic nature: although its substance is presently existing and has not yet reached the state of disintegration, it must necessarily perish next.
Because its substance lacks the meaning of abiding, it is said to be without intrinsic nature.

There is no such thing as the nature of the marks grasped by foolish people; for instance, those foolish people who have not yet seen the Truth rely on the gateway of the habitual tendencies of verbal designations and conceptual proliferation to falsely grasp the natures and marks of all phenomena.
Because it is far removed from such an apprehended intrinsic nature, it is said to be "without nature.
Furthermore, with respect to the imagined intrinsic nature, there is the absence of nature in terms of characteristics;
with respect to the dependent intrinsic nature, there is the absence of nature in terms of arising.

Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is ultimately without intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is stated that its meaning of being without intrinsic nature is further revealed through alternative formulations.

Furthermore, "all phenomena" refers to the three natures: namely, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
