The nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) definitely lacks its own characteristic; because it lacks its own characteristic, it is called "the naturelessness of characteristics" (lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā), and because it is the naturelessness of characteristics, it is called "naturelessness.

The nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva) arises in dependence upon various conditions and does not arise spontaneously; because it lacks the nature of spontaneous arising, it is called "the naturelessness of arising" (utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā), and because it is the naturelessness of arising, it is called "naturelessness."

Because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the object of pure cognition, because its self-essence is manifested as being devoid of the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and because it has the ultimate (*paramārtha*) as its essence and is manifested by the absence of intrinsic nature, it is called "the absence of nature in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*); since it is the absence of nature in the ultimate sense, it is termed "absence of nature."
By this principle, the Tathāgata has therefore taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
It is not that they are said to be "without nature" because their characteristics and modes of being are entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, it is said:
"All phenomena are without arising and without cessation; they are quiescent from the beginning and by nature in nirvāṇa.
With what underlying intention was this said?
As there is no intrinsic nature, so too is there no arising.
As there is no arising, so too is there no cessation.
As there is neither arising nor cessation, so too is there primordial tranquility.
As it is originally quiescent, so too is its intrinsic nature nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of intentions; by means of these intentions, one should correctly discern all the intentions of the Tathāgatas within the Vaipulya section.
What are the four? They are:
the intentionality of equality, the intentionality of another time, the intentionality of another meaning, and the intentionality of the inclinations of sentient beings.

Regarding the intentionality of equality: for example, when it is said, "At that time, I was named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin," this is because there is no difference between him and my own Dharmakāya.

The intention regarding another time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*) is as follows: for example, it is said that if there are those who aspire to be born in the world of Sukhāvatī, they shall all attain rebirth there;
or that if one even briefly hears the name of the Tathāgata Vimalacandraprabha, one will certainly never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Statements such as these are intended for another time. Regarding the intention of a distinct meaning:
it is like the statement that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; such statements cannot have their meaning taken literally.
Regarding the intentions and inclinations of sentient beings: with respect to a single root of virtue, at times one praises it in order to inspire them to practice with joyful vigor;
at other times, one disparages it in order to prevent them from becoming complacent upon attaining a mere modicum of goodness.

For those whose temperament is dominated by greed, he praises the richness, bliss, and adornment of the Buddha-fields. For those whose temperament is dominated by pride, he praises the various Buddhas as being superior or preeminent.

For those who constantly suffer from remorse and are thus hindered from practicing virtue, he speaks these words: "Even if such beings commit acts of disparagement toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they will nonetheless be reborn in the heavenly realms."

For those of indeterminate lineage, in order that they may abandon the inferior disposition of the śrāvakas, [the Buddha] prophesied that the great śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood, and further taught the One Vehicle (ekayāna) as being without a second.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of secrets; by means of these secrets, all the secrets of the Tathāgatas within the Vaipulya section should be understood according to their definitive meaning.
What are these four? They are:
the secret of entry, the secret of characteristics, the secret of counteractive measures, and the secret of transformation.
These four types briefly encompass all the principles of the Tathāgata’s secret teachings within the Mahāyāna.

"Causing entry into the secret" means that within the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is taught that all phenomena such as form possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), in order to cause those who might otherwise feel fear to gradually enter the holy teaching.
The "secret of characteristics" refers to teaching that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising, and are without cessation, with respect to the three natures.

The "secret of antidotes" refers to the Tathāgata’s proclamation of various secret teachings in order to subdue various faults; for example, he taught the Supreme Vehicle as an antidote to the eight kinds of obstacles.
What are the eight? They are:

disparaging the Buddha and the Dharma, indolence, being satisfied with little merit, giving rise to complacency, the conduct of greed and pride, remorse, lack of a settled nature, and differentiation.
The detailed explanation of specific instances is provided according to what is appropriate, as in the teaching on the four intentions (*caturabhiprāya*).
Regarding the secret of transformation (*pariṇāmābhisandhi*), this refers to the cryptic terminology employed in the sūtras.
As it is said:
"Perceiving the non-solid as solid, dwelling deeply in perversion, and being tormented by extreme afflictions, one attains supreme enlightenment.
The intended meaning here is that one gives rise to a firm and superior realization regarding the absence of distraction.
Why is this so? "Firmness" has two meanings:
first, solidity; second, agitation.
Because this distraction causes the mind to become rigid and unruly, it is also termed "firm.

Regarding those who dwell deeply in perversion (*viparyāsa*): this refers to inverting the four perversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity into impermanence and so forth; therefore, they are called "perversion."
Because one does not regress from this, it is called "dwelling deeply.
Regarding those who are "extremely afflicted by afflictions," this refers to being oppressed by extreme fatigue due to long-term diligent practice of asceticism.
Regarding those who attain supreme enlightenment: if they possess the three matters described above, they will certainly and swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, within the Vaipulya section, how is the characteristic of a bodhisattva skilled in the samādhi of phenomena (*dharmasamādhi*) to be known?
It is said to be due to five kinds of causes: first, the moment-to-moment elimination of the basis of all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);

second, the emergence from various conceptualizations to experience the joy of the Dharma; third, the realization of the immeasurable light of the great Dharma characterized by non-conceptuality; fourth, the constant presence of non-conceptual characteristics that accord with the side of purification; and fifth, the ability to sustain the causes for the complete accomplishment of the Buddha-body, which becomes increasingly superior and excellent.

These five kinds are explained based on the three types of praised qualities of bodhisattvas: namely, the praised quality of śamatha, the praised quality of vipaśyanā, and the praised quality of that which partakes of both.
There are further two kinds of praise for the merits of śamatha:

first, the moment-to-moment progression toward pliancy (praśrabdhi) is uninterrupted because it pervades the basis [of the body], and thus, moment by moment, it eliminates all bases of coarse heaviness (dausthulya).
Second, through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one contemplates all teachings as being without distinction because they are of a single flavor.

One becomes free from the conceptualizations of the various characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and attains the joy of the Dharma—the delight in the sūtras and other scriptures.
The merits praised for vipaśyanā are also of two kinds:

first, because there is no interruption or deficiency in the phenomena being investigated and they are not forgotten, one illuminates and realizes through wisdom the immeasurable and non-conceptual characteristics of the Dharma, such as the sūtras, by means of mindfulness.

Regarding the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), all preceding forms and images appear constantly before one, free from conceptual construction and free from effortful application.

As for the fifth type, which is the Dharma-body praised as possessing both aspects, it refers to that which is comprised within the transformation of the basis resulting from the permanent abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is called "perfection" at the tenth stage and "accomplishment" at the stage of a Tathāgata.

Because it causes the dharmakāya to be swiftly perfected and accomplished, it cultivates and establishes outflowing habitual tendencies that become increasingly superior and excellent; therefore, it is termed "appropriation."
Based on these five kinds of causes, it is shown that five types of cultivation can attain five fruits.
What are the five? They are:
cultivation of the sign of cessation, harmonious cultivation, signless cultivation, effortless cultivation, and cultivation of the transformation of signs.
Question:
Since both the teachings of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka equally flow from the Dharmakāya,

why is it that when sentient beings offer incense, garlands, and the like to the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they generate a vast and boundless accumulation of merit, whereas this is not the case for the teachings of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka?
Answer:

Because the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the locus upon which the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings depend; because it is capable of establishing great purpose; and because it is the source from which the unsurpassed, immeasurable, and vast accumulation of merit arises.
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya, Fascicle Twelve;
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya, Fascicle Thirteen.
Compiled by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati as a commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: Attainment (*Prāpti*), Part One of the Third Section on Ascertainment (*Viniścaya*). What is the ascertainment of attainment?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds: the establishment of the *pudgala* (person) and the establishment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
The former is that which realizes, and the latter is what is realized.

Although the *pudgala* does not exist as a substantial reality, it is established for four reasons: because it facilitates verbal expression, because it accords with worldly convention, because it removes fear, and because it demonstrates the virtues and faults of oneself and others.

Regarding the ease of verbal expression: if one establishes a single conventional designation of a "sentient being" by aggregating an immeasurable variety of forms and so forth, and an immeasurable variety of conceptualized phenomena with distinct characteristics, then various verbal expressions such as calling, coming, and going will not be difficult to employ.

Those who conform to the world do not engage in conventional discourse based solely on the notion of "dharmas"; for the most part, they engage in discourse based on the notion of "sentient beings. Therefore, in order to transform the world, the Noble Ones must necessarily employ the same skillful means as them by provisionally establishing the *pudgala*.

Regarding those who are free from fear: worldly sentient beings have not yet realized the profound nature of dependent origination; if they hear that all sentient beings are without self, they immediately give rise to fear and refuse to undergo correct transformation.

To demonstrate the presence of virtues and faults in oneself and others: if one were to set aside the conventional designations of sentient beings and speak only of the defiled and purified characteristics of phenomena, then there would be no distinction whatsoever; it would be impossible to discern whether such faults have been abandoned or not abandoned within this body, or whether such virtues have been realized or not realized within this body. Therefore, the *pudgala* (person) is established.
How is it established?

Briefly, there are seven kinds: namely, by way of the distinction of afflictive conduct (*carita*), the distinction of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), the distinction of support (*upastambha*), the distinction of means (*upāya*), the distinction of fruit (*phala*), the distinction of realm (*dhātu*), and the distinction of practice (*pratipatti*).

Furthermore, there are seven types of distinctions in the conduct of afflictions: namely, those of greedy temperament, those of hateful temperament, those of deluded temperament, those of proud temperament, those of discursive temperament, those of balanced temperament, and those of attenuated defilements.
There are three distinctions of renunciation: namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.

There are three distinctions of sustenance: namely, those who have not yet accumulated the provisions, those who have both accumulated and not yet accumulated the provisions, and those who have already accumulated the provisions.
There are two types of distinction in skillful means: namely, those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma.

There are twenty-seven distinctions of fruition, namely: those liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*); the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattipratipannaka*), the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*); the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*); the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*). Furthermore, there are: those with seven more births at most (*saptakṛtparama*), those from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), those with one interval (*ekavicika*); those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*); and among the arhats: those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), those of the nature of reflecting (*cetanakadharman*), those of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those of the nature of abiding in the immovable (*sthitākampya*), those capable of being urged toward higher states (*prativedhanādharman*), and those of the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
Regarding the distinction of realms: this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As there are these three in the desire realm, so it is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas in the desire and form realms, as well as pratyekabuddhas in the desire realm and inconceivable Tathāgatas.
There are briefly five types of distinctions in spiritual practice:

first, the bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief; second, the bodhisattva practicing through superior intention; third, the bodhisattva practicing with signs; fourth, the bodhisattva practicing without signs; and fifth, the bodhisattva practicing without effort.
There are thus immeasurable distinctions among such *pudgalas*.

A *pudgala* of greedy temperament (*rāga-carita*) is one who possesses intense and long-lasting desire; for even toward inferior and attractive objects, they are able to give rise to a superior degree of greed, and once it arises, it persists for a long time without interruption.

As it is for those whose temperament is dominated by craving (*rāga-carita*), so it is for those whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarka-carita*); each should be explained accordingly, following their respective objects with intensity and duration.

As for the person of equal parts (*sama-bhāga-pudgala*), this refers to one who dwells in the state of innate afflictions (*svabhāva-avasthāna-kleśa*), being free from both intensity and dullness because they dwell in a state of equilibrium among the various afflictions; thus, the afflictions manifest according to the power of the objects encountered.
A person of weak defilements (*tanubhūmi-pudgala*) refers to one who abides in the state of their natural disposition with subtle and slight afflictions.
This is because, as previously described regarding the characteristics of afflictions in the state of natural disposition, these current afflictions are subtle and slight in comparison to them.
Although subtle afflictions may still manifest with respect to superior objects of focus, they are suppressed by the power of the excellent remedies previously cultivated.

A person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle refers to one who abides in the *dharmatā* of the Śrāvakas—whether of determinate or indeterminate nature—who possesses dull faculties, has personally sought liberation by making a vast and correct vow, cultivates the intention for renunciation and liberation from craving, takes the Śrāvaka-piṭaka as their object of focus, and through diligent practice of the "Dharma-conforming Dharma-practice," attains the end of suffering.

It should be understood that within this context, the Śrāvaka vehicle is described through the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), intention (*āśaya*), objective sphere (*viṣaya*), and the fruits of practice.

In contrast to the faculties and lineages of Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas, these [Śrāvakas] are said to be dull; were it otherwise, it would contradict the description of those who "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) and others as having sharp faculties.

A person belonging to the vehicle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhayāna-pudgala*) is one who abides in the *dharmatā* of a solitary realizer; whether of determinate or indeterminate nature, they possess middling faculties, have personally sought liberation by making a vast and correct vow, cultivate the intention for renunciation and detachment from craving as well as the intention for the realization of solitary enlightenment, take the Śrāvaka Piṭaka as their object of focus, and diligently practice the "Dharma in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).

Whether they have previously not yet produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) or have previously already produced them; whether they have previously not yet attained the fruits [of the path] or have previously already attained them—when they emerge into a world devoid of a Buddha, they bring the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) before them through internal contemplation alone, either dwelling solitarily like a rhinoceros horn or proceeding as a solitary victor in a group, thereby attaining the end of suffering.

If one has not previously aroused the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) nor attained the fruits [of the path], then one becomes a rhinoceros-like solitary dweller (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*); otherwise, one will become a member of the group-dwelling pratyekabuddhas.

A Mahāyāna *pudgala* refers to one who abides in the *dharmatā* of a bodhisattva—whether of determinate or indeterminate lineage—and who possesses sharp faculties. For the sake of seeking the liberation of all sentient beings, they have generated a vast and great vow; they cultivate the intention for non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, take the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as their object of focus, and diligently practice the "Dharma-conforming Dharma-practice. They bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, receive the great prophecy, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Those who have received the great prediction" refers to those dwelling in the eighth bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*), because they have realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Individuals who have not yet completed the accumulations" refers to those who take the superior dharmas of the truths as their object, giving rise to a weak degree of pure faith and resolute conviction, and accomplishing a weak degree of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*), but for whom the time of birth [in the higher realms] is not yet fixed.

Regarding individuals who have either completed or not yet completed the accumulations: this refers to those who take the superior dharma of the truths as their object, give rise to a medium degree of pure faith and resolute conviction, and achieve a medium degree of the factors conducive to liberation; they are at the stage where birth [in the higher realms] is already determined.

A person who has already completed the accumulations refers to one who, taking the Dharma predominant over the Truths as their object, gives rise to superior pure faith and resolute conviction, and achieves the superior stage of the factors conducive to liberation; this occurs at the very moment of that birth.

Furthermore, those who have not yet completed the accumulations (sambhāra) refers to those who take the superior dharmas of the truths as their object, who have attained the inferior degree of the patient acceptance of the investigation of dharmas (dharmavicaya-kṣānti) regarding the truths, and who have attained the inferior degree of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), but for whom the time of birth [in the next life] is not yet fixed.

Those who have already or have not yet fully accumulated the provisions refer to those who take the superior dharmas of the truths as their object, who have achieved the medium level of patient acceptance of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmavicāra-kṣānti*) regarding the truths, who have achieved the medium level of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and for whom the time of birth [in the next life] is already fixed.

"One who has already perfected the provisions" refers to one who takes the superior dharmas that have the truths as their object; such a person achieves the highest degree of *dharmavicāra-kṣānti* (receptivity to the investigation of dharmas) regarding the various truths and achieves the highest degree of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which occurs at the very moment of this birth.

These three types of individuals, by virtue of accomplishing the three grades each of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),

are— respectively in their order— those who have not yet reached certainty, those who have reached certainty, and those for whom it occurs in this very life, based on their ability to induce the factors conducive to penetration and the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
The superior characteristic of pure faith in the dharmas that are predominant with respect to the truths is the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
The characteristic of the patient acceptance of the investigation of these very dharmas is the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
These follow their respective order because faith is predominant in some and wisdom is predominant in others.

Among these, the three grades of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exclude the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), because the nature of the Supreme Mundane Dharma consists of only a single moment that necessarily does not continue; at the very moment it arises, one definitely enters into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), as this does not occur in the preceding stages.

From the lower and middle grades of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is the possibility of regression; however, this refers solely to the regression of active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and not to the regression of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). This is because those who have already produced roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) based on *nirvāṇa* do not produce them anew.
Based on these roots of goodness conducive to liberation of the inferior grade, the Blessed One said:
"If one possesses the superior grade of mundane right view, even after passing through a thousand births, one shall not fall into the three evil destinies."
Furthermore, there are four kinds of factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*):

first, the factors conducive to liberation based on reliance; second, the factors conducive to liberation through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); third, the factors conducive to liberation through joyful aspiration; and fourth, the factors conducive to liberation through realization.
All roots of goodness, from the desire for wholesome dharmas up to those sought for the sake of liberation, are termed the "factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) as a basis.

Among these, the roots of goodness associated with the corresponding teachings and accompanied by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) are termed the "resolute conviction factors conducive to liberation."

The roots of goodness associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that takes as its object the state of liberation through conditions, which are continuous, pure, and accompanied by joy, are called the "factors conducive to liberation characterized by delight" (*mokṣabhāgīya-nirveda*).

Those roots of goodness that definitely give rise to the "factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within this very life are called the "factors conducive to liberation leading toward realization" (*mokṣabhāgīya-abhimukha*).

Furthermore, there are six kinds of aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya): namely, the aid to penetration that accords with [the path], the aid to penetration of superior progress, the aid to penetration of thorough realization, the aid to penetration of subsequent transformation, the aid to penetration of a single birth, and the aid to penetration of a single sitting.
If the initial arising of wholesome roots that take the truths as their object and proceed in a lower degree is called the "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
then when these same wholesome roots develop into a middle degree, it is called the "superior advancement conducive to penetration," because it is more excellent than the preceding lower degree.

When these very roots of goodness increase to the highest degree, one becomes definitively capable of penetrating the principles of the Truths within this very life; this is called the "penetrating stage conducive to definitive discernment" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, within this very stage, those of indeterminate lineage who turn toward supreme enlightenment, as well as pratyekabuddhas who seek self-realized enlightenment without a teacher, proceed toward other births; these are called "other-directed aids to penetration" (*anyatva-nirvedhabhāgīya*).
If one is certain to attain penetration within this very life, it is called the "aids to penetration in one birth" (ekajāti-pratipannaka-nirvedhabhāgīya).
If one is certain to attain penetration in this very session, it is called the "aids to penetration in one sitting" (ekāsana-pratipannaka-nirvedhabhāgīya).

A person who follows through faith (śraddhānusārin) is one who has already fulfilled the provisions (sambhāra), possesses dull faculties by nature, and cultivates the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) in accordance with the instruction of others.

A person who follows through the Dharma (dharmānusārin) is one who has already fulfilled the provisions, possesses sharp faculties by nature, and spontaneously cultivates the clear realization of the truths in accordance with the superior Dharma of the truths.
A person of resolute belief (*śraddhādhimukta*) refers to one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and has reached the stage of fruition.
A person of attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) refers to one who follows the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) and has reached the stage of fruition.

A person who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin pudgala*) refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have already fully attained the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa-samādhi*); such a person is called one who has realized through the body because they dwell in the full possession of the eight liberations, having realized them through the body.
The eight liberations refer to such states as "possessing form, one perceives forms," and so forth, which will be explained in detail later.

A person liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta pudgala*) refers to one who has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) but has not yet fully realized the meditative absorptions of the eight liberations; this is because they have definitively severed only the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that are the objects to be countered by wisdom.

A person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta-pudgala*) refers to one who has already abandoned all outflows (*āsrava*) and has fully realized the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa-dhyāna*), because they have attained liberation from both the portion of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa-bhāga*) and the portion of the meditative hindrances (*samāpattyāvaraṇa-bhāga*).

A person who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka) refers to one who abides in the stage of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), as well as one who abides in the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

Herein, the intended meaning is that from the very first session of the aids to penetration until the fruit of the first stage has not yet been attained, all such persons are termed candidates for the fruit of stream-entry.
A person who has entered the fruit of stream-entry refers to one abiding at the moment of the sixteenth mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This very path of seeing is also called "entry into the certainty of rightness" (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*) and is also called "clear realization of the dharma" (*dharmābhisamaya*).
Question:
Who attains the first fruit at the stage of the final mind-moment of the path of seeing?
Answer:

If one who has not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm subsequently enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), it refers to the gradual practitioner (*anupūrvika*):

although they have partially abandoned desire, they are still termed "one who has not yet abandoned desire. Such a person subsequently enters the state of right determination and attains the fruit of stream-entry at the stage of the sixteenth moment of mind.
If one is "doubly detached from desire," they subsequently enter the state of right determination and attain the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

This refers to one who has first used the mundane path to sever six grades of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the desire realm; such a person is termed "doubly detached from desire."
Subsequently, upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), he attains the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) at the stage of the sixteenth moment of mind.
If he has already abandoned desire, he attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) upon subsequently entering the state of right determination.

This means that one who has first used the mundane path to sever the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the desire realm is called "one already detached from desire.

Such a person subsequently enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and, upon reaching the stage of the sixteenth moment of mind, attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
Question:

If one has already permanently abandoned all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing and thereby attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), why is it said that one attains the fruit of stream-entry only by permanently abandoning the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*)?
Answer:
Because they are subsumed by the most excellent; through these three types of liberation from hindrances, one attains what is most preeminent. Why is this so?

Because it is a cause for not setting out toward liberation; because even after having set out, it serves as a cause for a mistaken departure and a cause for an incorrect departure; and because, through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one clings to the five aggregates of grasping as "self" and "mine," one develops deep attachment to them, fails to feel revulsion toward this great mass of suffering, and lacks the resolve to set out toward supreme liberation.

There may be sentient beings who, although they have already set out toward liberation, nevertheless—due to the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), and because they perversely cling to false paths while doubting the true path—proceed toward a false deliverance and an incorrect deliverance.
Furthermore, these three fetters are the causes for delusion regarding the objects of knowledge, the causes for delusion regarding views, and the causes for delusion regarding the antidotes.

Why is this so? It is because, through the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is deluded regarding the objects of knowledge, falsely superimposing the characteristics of "self" and "mine" upon this great mass of suffering.

The clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) causes delusion regarding the vision of what is to be known, because one regards perverted views as the cause of purification and liberation.
Doubt (vicikitsā) causes delusion regarding the direct antidote, because one lacks certainty concerning the Three Jewels.

A person who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka) refers to one who, within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), has already abandoned five grades of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path. Why is this so?
Because, subsequent to the path of seeing, one has already abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm up to the medium-of-the-medium degree and abides in the path that abandons them;

a person who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) is one who, within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), has already abandoned the sixth category of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.
Why is this so? Because this [fruit] is established upon the ultimate completion of the path that has already permanently severed the middling and weak grades of afflictions.

A person (pudgala) who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) is one who, within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), has already severed the seventh and eighth grades of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.

Why is this so? Because after the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), one has already abandoned the weak-superior and weak-middle grades of afflictions of the desire realm, and it is established on the basis of abiding in that path of abandonment.

Regarding the person who has attained the fruit of non-returning: this refers to one who, within the path of cultivation, has already abandoned the ninth grade of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path. Why is this so?
Because this [fruit] is established based on the ultimate completion of the path that permanently abandons the soft-soft grade of afflictions of the desire realm.
Question:

If one has already permanently abandoned all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing, as well as all afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, thereby attaining the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), why is it said only that one attains the fruit of non-returner by permanently abandoning the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*)?
Answer:
Because it is subsumed by the most excellent.
What is meant by "most excellent"?
Because these five fetters serve as the predominant causes for rebirth in the lower realms and the lower worlds, they are called "supreme.
Why is this so? The "lower realms" refer to the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts.
The "lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because it takes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) as its predominant causes, it prevents sentient beings from transcending the lower destinies.
Because greed and hatred serve as the primary causes that cause sentient beings to fall further down into the lower realms.

A person (*pudgala*) who is a candidate for the fruit of Arhatship is one who has already permanently abandoned eight categories of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and abides in that path.

Regarding the person who has attained the fruit of arhatship: this refers to one who has eternally abandoned the ninth category of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and abides in that ultimate path.
Question:

If an arhat has eternally abandoned all afflictions of the three realms, why is it said only that by eternally abandoning all five higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana), one attains the fruit of arhatship?
Answer:
Because it is subsumed by the most excellent.
What is meant by "most excellent"?
Because these five fetters are the causes for grasping at the higher realms and the causes for not relinquishing the higher realms, they are called "supreme.

Why is this so? Because craving for the form and formless realms leads to grasping and the subsequent birth in the higher form and formless realms of the desire realm; because restlessness, pride, and ignorance do not relinquish birth in those higher realms; and because those who practice the higher dhyānas are tormented by craving, pride, and doubt.
The person who returns at most seven times (saptakṛtparama-pudgala) refers to the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Moving back and forth between the realms of humans and gods, receiving mixed births, they reach the end of suffering after at most seven returns.
A person who goes from family to family refers to a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) who,
whether among the gods or among humans, attains the end of suffering by passing from one household to another.

Why is this? Because one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry and proceeds toward the fruit of once-returning will, whether among gods or among humans, definitely come and go for at most two more existences before attaining parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the "ekavīcika" (one-interval) *pudgala*, this refers to one who is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner).
Alternatively, having received only one more existence in the heavenly realms, they will reach the end of suffering. Why is this so?

That is to say, having progressed from the fruit of once-returner toward the fruit of non-returner, or because they attain parinirvāṇa after experiencing only one more existence in the heavenly realms, there is only a single interval remaining to accommodate this one lifetime;
therefore, they are called "one-interval" (ekavicika).

A person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is one for whom the fetters of birth have already been severed, but the fetters of arising have not yet been severed; or, as soon as the intermediate existence (antarābhava) has arisen, the Noble Path manifests before them, whereby they reach the end of suffering.

Alternatively, once the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has arisen, as one is about to proceed toward birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), the moment a thought arises, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests, and one attains the end of suffering.
Or, having already directed the mind toward proceeding to birth-existence, before reaching birth-existence, the Noble Path manifests, and one attains the end of suffering.

This passage demonstrates three types of *antarāparinirvāyin* (those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state): those for whom the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that causes the continuity of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) as one proceeds toward the place of rebirth has been exhausted;
yet, by the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) alone, the aggregates (*skandha*) continue to arise after death, and these latent dispositions remain unexhausted.

Alternatively, as soon as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises, one may manifest the Noble Path through the power of habitual practice and sever the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), thereby entering *parinirvāṇa* at that very stage.

Or, once the intermediate state has arisen, upon merely forming the thought of proceeding to the next existence (*upapattibhava*), one manifests the Noble Path, severs the remaining latent dispositions, and enters *parinirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, having reflected, one may be on the way to a place of rebirth; before reaching that state of rebirth, the Noble Path manifests and severs the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), whereby one enters *parinirvāṇa*.

These three types are established based on the distinctions of stages—before setting out, just having set out, and having already traveled far—relative to the place of rebirth, in accordance with the *Saptapuruṣagatīsūtra*.

A person who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) refers to one for whom both fetters are as yet unsevered; immediately after being born into the form realm, the noble path manifests before them, whereby they reach the end of suffering.

A person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion refers to one who, having been born there, reaches the end of suffering through the manifestation of the noble path without relying on deliberate application.
One who does not rely on application is so called because the untainted noble path manifests spontaneously through the power of prior habituation, being effortless.
One who attains parinirvāṇa with application refers to one who, having been born there, manifests the noble path through the power of application and thereby reaches the end of suffering.
Regarding those who attain through application (*prayogika*), they are the opposite of the aforementioned.

As for the person who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*): this refers to one who, having taken birth in each successive stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), finally enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven; there, the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) becomes manifest, and he attains the end of suffering.
Furthermore, there are those who proceed even as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), where the Noble Path manifests and they attain the end of suffering.
This passage demonstrates two types of "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*): first, those who reach as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; second, those who reach as far as the Peak of Existence.

Regarding "reaching the ultimate limit at the Akaniṣṭha heaven": this refers to a person (*pudgala*) who is strongly attached to the flavor of meditative absorption. Because they repeatedly give rise to attachment toward the various grades of dhyāna, such as the weak and so forth, they take birth sequentially in each realm from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Finally, upon reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven, they enter parinirvāṇa.

Regarding "reaching the peak of existence": this refers to one who does not practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, but merely avoids the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; thus, proceeding through all stages in the aforementioned sequence up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), they finally attain parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are five grades of distinction in the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna:
first, inferior cultivation; second, middling cultivation; third, superior cultivation; fourth, superior-excellent cultivation; and fifth, supreme cultivation.
By means of this fivefold mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the five Pure Abodes in their respective order.

An Arhat of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman) is one of dull faculties; whether distracted or undistracted, whether reflecting or not reflecting, they are liable to fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life.
"One who reflects" intends to harm oneself;
"one who does not reflect" does not intend to harm oneself.
"Falling away from dwelling in happiness in the present life" refers to falling away from worldly meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and other concentrations.

The Arhat who preserves the Dharma through reflection (*cetanādharman*) is one of dull faculties; whether distracted or undistracted, and whether not reflecting or reflecting, he may fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
If one has reflected thus, one is able to avoid falling away.

As for the Arhat who protects the Dharma, this refers to one of dull faculties; if they become distracted, they may fall away from the blissful abiding in the present life, but if they do not become distracted, they are able to abide without falling away.

The "immovable arhat" refers to one of dull faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, is capable of not falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life, yet is unable to refine their faculties.
The cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) refers to transforming inferior, dull faculties into superior, sharp faculties.
For this reason, it is not said that those of the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) can cultivate their faculties, because their nature is already that of sharp faculties.

One who is "capable of reaching" (khaṇḍa) arhatship refers to one of dull faculties; whether distracted or undistracted, they are able to not fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life and are capable of refining their faculties.
An Arhat of immovable dharma refers to one of sharp faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, is capable of never regressing from the blissful dwelling in the present life.
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) refers to one who is born or has grown up in the desire realm and has not attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
A learner (*śaikṣa*) of the desire realm refers to one who is born or has grown up in the desire realm, has already attained the noble dharmas, yet still possesses remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the person who is a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): this refers to one who has been born or grown up in the desire realm, has already attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), and possesses no remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Just as there are three types in the desire realm, so too there are three types each in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); they should be understood accordingly.

A bodhisattva belonging to the desire realm or the form realm refers to one who, being endowed with the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that are dissociated from birth in the formless realm, dwells in the bliss of meditative absorption while being born either in the desire realm or the form realm.
Question:
For what reason does a bodhisattva not take birth in the formless realm?
Answer:

If a Bodhisattva who has already attained supreme majesty takes birth, it is solely for the purpose of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not a place where sentient beings can be matured.

"Those who have abandoned birth in the formless realm through meditative absorption" refers to those capable of dispelling all states of superior concentration that lead to birth in the formless realm.
"Those who abide in the bliss of meditative absorption" refers to those who do not fall away from meditative absorption.

Because this bodhisattva possesses skillful means in turning [the roots of virtue], in order to bring the sentient beings to be converted to maturity, he is born either in the desire realm or the form realm.

Regarding the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*) of the desire realm: this refers to one who, when no Buddha has appeared in the world, is born in the desire realm and spontaneously realizes the enlightenment of a solitary realizer.

The "Inconceivable Tathāgata" refers, for instance, to the manifestation within the desire realm—beginning from the initial appearance of dwelling in the wondrous jewel palace of Tuṣita Heaven, up until the manifestation of the Great Parinirvāṇa—and the manifestation of all the great practices performed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The conduct of all bodhisattvas refers to everything from manifesting in the Tuṣita heaven palace up to manifesting great supernatural transformations to subdue the armies of Māra.
The conduct of all buddhas refers to everything from manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment up to manifesting the great parinirvāṇa.

A bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*) refers to one who dwells within the stage of practice through resolute belief and has accomplished the lower, middle, and upper levels of patience (*kṣānti*).

Because they abide in the bodhisattva lineage, from the initial generation of the great aspiration for enlightenment until they have not yet entered the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and have not yet attained supramundane, internal realization of reality, they are called a bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief.

A bodhisattva who practices with superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) refers to all bodhisattvas within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because they have already realized the supramundane, internal realization of pure intention.

Bodhisattvas who practice with signs refer to those bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of the Joyous, the Stainless, the Luminous, the Radiant, the Difficult to Conquer, and the Manifest; for although they do not take delight in these six stages, they are nevertheless interspersed with various signs.

A bodhisattva who practices the signless refers to all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*); because by means of this stage, whether through deliberate effort or even according to their own inclination, they are able to prevent the manifestation of signs.

Bodhisattvas who practice without effort (*anābhoga-caryā*) refers to all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of Immovability (*acalā*), Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), and the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), because these bodhisattvas have already attained fully matured non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding what is called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) person, there are two types:
first, those who attain liberation gradually; second, those who attain liberation all at once.
Those who attain liberation gradually are as explained extensively above.

Regarding those who attain liberation all at once (*sakṛd-vyutthāna*): this refers to those who, having entered the direct realization of the truths (*satya-abhisamaya*), rely upon the *anāgamya* concentration to produce a supramundane path, thereby suddenly severing all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. Because they sever them category by category, only two fruits are established for them: namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).

Regarding the abandonment of each category individually: this refers to first abandoning the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness all at once, and so on, down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*).

Regarding the "sudden severance of the three realms," this refers to what is severed through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); it is not like the gradual, item-by-item severance of the various stages and levels as occurs on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
What serves as proof for this meaning?
As stated in the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*:

"Whatever form there may be, up to and including consciousness—whether past, future, or present; as explained at length, whether far or near—all this taken together is condensed into one part, one mass, one accumulation, and one heap."
Having thus summarized, one should contemplate that all things are impermanent and all things are suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
Based on such contemplation, only the first and last fruits can be established.

Because these two fruits, respectively, are manifested by the permanent and complete abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation within the three realms, the second and third fruits are not established [as separate stages].

Because these two fruits are manifested by the abandonment—either with remainder or without remainder—of only those defilements of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation by one who has already seen the truths.

Furthermore, for one who thus attains liberation all at once, the Tathāgata establishes the fruit of arhatship immediately following the fruit of stream-entry in the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*; such a person-gone (pudgala) generally achieves mastery over the noble intent either in the present life or at the time of death.
If one is unable to accomplish this, by the power of their vow, they will return to birth in the desire realm through that very vow-force;

even if they do not succeed, because they have not yet been able to leave all desires without remainder, they are born in the desire realm by the power of their vow so that they may swiftly realize parinirvāṇa.

The establishment of clear realization (abhisamaya) consists briefly of ten types: namely, the clear realization of phenomena (dharma-abhisamaya), the clear realization of meaning (artha-abhisamaya), the clear realization of reality (tattva-abhisamaya), the subsequent clear realization (pṛṣṭha-abhisamaya), the clear realization of the jewels (ratna-abhisamaya), the clear realization of non-activity (apravṛtti-abhisamaya), the ultimate clear realization (niṣṭhā-abhisamaya), the clear realization of the śrāvaka, the clear realization of the pratyekabuddha, and the clear realization of the bodhisattva.

The clear realization of the Dharma refers to having attained superior pure faith and resolute conviction regarding the supreme dharmas of the truths, and proceeding in accordance with that faith. Why is this so?

Due to the dominant influence of the sūtras and other teachings concerning the truths, through the power of the dominant condition consisting of hearing the voice of another, one has attained the superior degree of pure faith and resolute conviction, which is subsumed under the final roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
Because one has attained such pure faith and superior resolve, it is said that one realizes the truths through the realization of the Dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).

As for the realization of the meaning (*arthābhisamaya*), it refers to the patient acceptance of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*) regarding the objects of the truths, having already attained the highest degree [of understanding] within the dominant dharmas concerning those very truths.
This patience (*kṣānti*) resides within the stage of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Why is this so?

Because, through the dominant influence of correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward the aforementioned teachings, one attains the superior patience in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), which is subsumed under the final roots of goodness conducive to penetration regarding the objects of the truths, such as suffering.

This patience through the thorough investigation of phenomena (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti), being manifested by three kinds of appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra), further constitutes three grades: namely, the superior-weak, the superior-middle, and the superior-superior.
The "superior-mild" refers to the mild stage at the time of this very birth.
The "superior-medium" refers to the stages of *mūrdhan* (Summits) and *kṣānti* (Patience).
The "superior-superior" refers to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

True clear realization refers to the noble path possessed at the moment of the sixteen mental instants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as the conventional knowledge of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) obtained at the conclusion of the clear realization within the path of seeing.

Because the seeds of that [knowledge] are nurtured by the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of supramundane knowledge, it is said that one "attains" this knowledge even though it does not manifest; for during the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is no interruption, and thus there is no room for mundane consciousness to arise.
On the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) then manifests.

"Subsequent clear realization" (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) refers to the entire path of cultivation; for all mundane and supramundane paths following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are termed subsequent clear realization.
The "jewel clear observation" (*ratna-abhisamaya*) refers to verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) in the Buddha, verified confidence in the Dharma, and verified confidence in the Saṅgha.

This is because the noble disciples of the Buddha have attained decisive, verified, and pure faith toward the Three Jewels, namely: that the Bhagavat is the truly and perfectly enlightened one; that the Dharma-Vinaya is the truly well-expounded; and that the community of noble disciples are the truly pure practitioners.

Regarding those who do not practice the clear realization (*abhisamaya*): because they have already attained the discipline of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-saṃvara*), although they still abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), they think, "I have now exhausted the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; I am no longer capable of creating karma for the miserable destinies that would result in rebirth within those miserable destinies."
"One who has already attained the discipline of non-action" refers to one who has realized and attained the discipline subsumed by the "precepts cherished by the Noble Ones.
Because of attaining this, the ripening results in the hells and so forth—which are the objects to be countered by it—will certainly never occur again.
Because the hells and other realms of suffering have been permanently exhausted and no longer function, it is called the "non-functioning clear observation" (*apravṛtti-abhisamaya*).

Regarding the "ultimate clear observation" (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*), as explained in the context of the ultimate path within the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it refers to having stilled all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and having attained the acquisition of all disconnections (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*), and so forth.

The realization of the śrāvakas refers to the seven types of realization previously mentioned; because they are realized by hearing the voice of another, they are called the realization of the śrāvakas.

Regarding the clear realization of the Pratyekabuddhas: it refers to the seven types of clear realization previously mentioned; because they are realized without depending on the voice of another, it is called the clear realization of the Pratyekabuddhas.

The clear realization of a bodhisattva refers to when bodhisattvas, regarding the seven clear realizations previously explained, give rise to the patience of cultivation and accumulation but do not realize them directly; this is for the sake of attaining skillfulness in the means of training śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and out of compassion for sentient beings so as not to depart via the lower vehicles. Nevertheless, within the Bodhisattva Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they enter the bodhisattvas' determination of the correct nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*). This is called the clear realization of a bodhisattva.
The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) has already been explained; its distinctions shall now be discussed.
Question:
What is the distinction between the clear realization of the Śrāvakas and that of the Bodhisattvas?
Answer:

Briefly stated, there are eleven kinds, namely: the distinction of objective spheres, the distinction of support, the distinction of penetration, the distinction of vows, the distinction of renunciation, the distinction of gathering, the distinction of establishment, the distinction of retinue, the distinction of superior birth, the distinction of birth, and the distinction of fruit.
Regarding the distinction of objective domain (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*): it means taking the vast Mahāyāna as its object.
Regarding the distinction of sustenance (*dhāraṇa-viśeṣa*): it means that over the course of a full *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, the accumulations of merit and wisdom are brought to completion.

Regarding the distinction of thorough penetration: it refers to supramundane wisdom induced by the skillful means of the Dharma based on the principle of the selflessness of persons and phenomena, because it thoroughly penetrates both types of selflessness.

Regarding the distinction of the vow (*praṇidhāna-viśeṣa*): it refers to the ability to realize that all sentient beings are equal to oneself, and thus to vow to gather them in and benefit them as one would oneself.
Regarding the distinction of renunciation (*niryāṇa-viśeṣa*): it refers to renunciation by means of relying upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The distinction of "appropriation" refers to being appropriated by non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The distinction of "establishment" refers to the thorough cultivation and purification of the buddha-fields of all Buddhas.
The distinction of retinue refers to the fact that all sentient beings to be converted are gathered as one's retinue.
The distinction of superior birth refers to the manner in which a son conceived in the womb continues the paternal lineage so that it is not severed.
In this way, the bodhisattva succeeds to and upholds the lineage of the Buddhas so that it is never severed; this is because it is the characteristic of a true son of the Buddha.
As for the distinction of birth, it refers to being born within the great assemblies of the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the distinctions of the fruit, there are further ten kinds: namely, the distinction of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); the distinction of the perfection of qualities; the distinction of the five aspects; the distinction of the three bodies (*trikāya*); the distinction of nirvāṇa; the distinction of the attainment of the unified activity of wisdom; the distinction of the purification of hindrances; the distinction of the unified activity of karma; the distinction of the skillful manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and entering parinirvāṇa; and the distinction of the five kinds of deliverance.

Regarding the distinction of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): it refers to the permanent abandonment of all seeds of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) that serve as the basis for both defiled and non-defiled states, and the permanent transformation of the basis for all unsurpassed qualities.

Regarding the distinction of the perfection of merit: it refers to the eternal and complete fulfillment of boundless qualities such as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Regarding the distinction of the five aspects: it refers to the distinctions among the five aspects, beginning with purity (*viśuddhi*).
First is the distinction of purity, which refers to the permanent abandonment of all afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies.
Second is the distinction of perfect purity, which refers to the universal cultivation and purification of the Buddha-fields.
The distinction of the three bodies refers to the perfection of the *dharmakāya*.

The distinction of the enjoyment [body] refers to the fact that at all times and in all places, within great assemblies, it enjoys various forms of the great Dharma-joy together with all bodhisattvas.

The differentiation of the five activities refers to the arising of various transformations as appropriate, performing the deeds of a Buddha throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds in the ten directions.
The distinction of the three bodies refers to the realization of the perfect svabhāvakāya, sambhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya.

The distinction of nirvāṇa refers to the fact that within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, all qualities remain uninterrupted for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

Regarding the attainment of the distinction between the unified wisdom and its functional application: it means that because one has attained the single flavor of the most supremely pure dharma-realm, each and every function of the various kinds of sublime wisdom that depend upon it—the functional capacity of a single Buddha—is equal to the functional capacity of all Buddhas.
The distinction of the purification of hindrances refers to the permanent abandonment of all afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The distinction of the activity of harmonious cooperation refers to the fact that every action of guiding and transforming individual sentient beings is due to the sovereign power of all Buddhas.

Regarding the distinctions in the skillful manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and entering parinirvāṇa: this refers to the repeated manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth in all worlds throughout the ten directions, as appropriate for each case, until the end of time, in order to bring all beings to be converted to maturity and liberation.
Regarding the fivefold distinctions of deliverance, these refer to the five matters of deliverance from calamities and so forth.
First is deliverance from calamities: this refers to when the Tathāgata enters cities and towns, causing those who are blind, deaf, and so on, to regain their eyes, ears, and other faculties.
Second is rescue by means other than [the correct path], which refers to causing one to attain mundane right view so as to remain far removed from all false and evil views.
Third is rescue from the miserable destinies, which refers to causing one to be born into the Path of Seeing so as to transcend all miserable destinies.
Fourth is the rescue from the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*), which means causing [beings] to realize the fruit of arhatship and thereby become eternally liberated from the three realms.
Fifth is the rescue from the vehicles (*yāna*), which means causing all bodhisattvas not to take pleasure in the inferior vehicles.
Question:
As the sūtras describe the most excellent qualities such as the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), by which clear realization (*abhisamaya*) are they subsumed?
Answer:
It is comprised within subsequent clear observation (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) and ultimate clear observation (*nisthābhisamaya*). Why is this so?

Because such supreme qualities are produced by the noble disciples either on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or on the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*); therefore, they are comprised within these two types of clear observation.

What, then, are these? They are the immeasurables, the liberations, the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality, the absence of conflict, the knowledge of aspiration, the analytical knowledges, the supernormal powers, the primary marks and secondary signs, the purities, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the foundations of mindfulness, the ways in which he need not guard himself, the quality of never forgetting, the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the sublime wisdom of all modes. Such qualities as these, the Tathāgata has taught in various sūtras, either based on the Śrāvaka vehicle or based on the Mahāyāna.

These various merits are briefly displayed according to their respective natures through five categories: namely, the basis, the object, the mode of activity, the essential nature, and the accompaniments.
"Immeasurables" refers to the four immeasurables:
first, the immeasurable of loving-kindness; second, the immeasurable of compassion; third, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy; and fourth, the immeasurable of equanimity.
What is loving-kindness?

It refers to the concentration, wisdom, and the mental states and mental factors associated with them, which abide in the fulfillment of the altruistic intention to endow all sentient beings with happiness, based upon meditative absorption (dhyāna).

Herein, the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) is revealed: it takes meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) as its basis, sentient beings as its object, the wish for them to be endowed with happiness as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), and concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) as its essential nature. Since all virtuous qualities are subsumed within calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) serve as its attendants.
It should be understood that all virtues, such as compassion (*karuṇā*) and the rest, are likewise according to their respective applications.
What is compassion?

It refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*) present within one who dwells in the fulfillment of the intention to free all sentient beings from suffering; the rest is as previously explained, because its basis, essential nature, and accompanying factors are similar to those of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
What is joy (*muditā*)?

It refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*) present when one dwells in the fulfillment of a mental disposition that does not part from the desire for the happiness of all sentient beings; the rest is as previously explained.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

This refers to the concentration and wisdom—along with the remaining factors as previously described—present within the fulfillment of abiding in a benevolent intention toward all sentient beings while relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

"Benevolent intention" means that regarding sentient beings who are associated with happiness and so forth, one relinquishes attachment and other afflictions, and reflects: "I shall cause them to be liberated from their defilements."
Such an intentionality is called the aspect of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
When the aspect of the intentionality for the benefit [of others] is perfected, it is called "abiding in fulfillment.
As for "liberation," this refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), as explained at length in the sūtras.
What is the liberation of one possessing form who perceives forms?

It refers to relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wherein one has not yet suppressed the perception of forms internally, or where the perception of forms is currently established as being seen; while perceiving the forms that are seen, one dwells in their fulfillment. This includes the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) associated with them, up to the point of attaining liberation from the obstacles to transformation.
"Having form" refers to the fact that within one's own body, the perceiver has not yet relied upon the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) to suppress and eliminate the perception of form;
or it refers to the fact that the perceiver’s perception of form remains established and present before them.
"Contemplating all forms" means that one contemplates and perceives forms—whether beautiful or ugly—through mental resolve (*adhimukti*).
"Liberation" means being able to liberate oneself from all obstacles regarding the manifestation of transformations (*nirmāṇa*)."
What is the liberation consisting of the perception of external forms while being internally without the perception of form?

It refers to having already subdued the perception of form within oneself, or having established the perception of the formlessness of the perceiver; one contemplates the perceived forms and abides in their fulfillment. This includes both concentration and wisdom, as described previously for the remaining details.
"Internally having no perception of form" means that, regarding the internal body, one has already suppressed and eliminated the perception of form in the seer by relying on the formless attainments;
or it means that the perception of formlessness in the seer is established and made manifest.
This means that the designation "seer" (draṣṭṛ) arises as a mental image present before one; the rest is as explained previously.
What is the dwelling in the full realization through bodily witness of the pure liberation?

It refers to the fact that regarding internal pure and impure forms, one has attained the mutual correlative perception (*anyonya-apekṣā-saṃjñā*), the mutual interpenetrating perception (*anyonya-anupraveśa-saṃjñā*), and the perception of a single uniform taste (*eka-rasa-saṃjñā*).

Regarding that which has already been attained in its full perfection—whether it be meditative concentration or wisdom—the rest is as previously explained, up to [the removal of] the obstacle to the arising of pure and impure transformations for the sake of liberation.

In this context, it is shown that regarding pure and impure forms, by means of the perception of mutual dependence and the perception of mutual inclusion, one attains the perception of their mutual single flavor.

Why is this so? Because one regards certain pure forms as impure in relation to other forms, and regards certain impure forms as pure in relation to others; they do not exist independently of such mutual dependence.
Why is this? Because when one perceives only a single category, the cognitions of "pure" and "impure" do not exist.
Furthermore, within the pure, the nature of the impure enters as a concomitant; within the impure, the nature of the pure enters as a concomitant.
Why is this? Because within that which is commonly regarded as pure, being merely covered by thin skin, there currently exist thirty-six kinds of impure things, such as hair and body hair.
In this manner, one proceeds step by step to take all forms collectively and unify them into a single flavor of the perception of purity.

Having understood this, one who attains mastery over liberation regarding forms as desired is able to sever the obstacles to the transformation of pure and impure forms, as well as the obstacles to the arising of afflictions therein.
What is meant by "affliction regarding transformations"?
It refers to the application of effort toward the transformation of pure forms, which is contrary to the transformation of impure forms.
What is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space?
It refers to the concentration or wisdom present within the full attainment of dwelling in the sphere of infinite space that accords with liberation; the rest is as previously explained.

As it is with the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, so it is with the liberations of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Up to and including liberation for the sake of attaining the peaceful liberation that is free from the obstacle of impediment—these four types, when attained by a noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka), are able to accord with the untainted (anāsrava) and constitute a state of purity; only then are they called "liberation," because they are liberated from the relish of craving (tṛṣṇāsvāda).
"Peaceful liberation" refers to transcending the realms of form and formlessness; being pure therein is called "unimpeded.
Attachment to the formless is the obstacle to this.
What is the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling?

It refers to relying upon the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, transcending all other peaceful liberations, and dwelling in the full attainment of a state resembling true liberation; therein, the mind and mental factors cease, serving as the liberation from the obstacles to the cessation of perception and feeling.

This reveals that the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its basis; it lacks an object, mental aspect, or associates, because mind and mental factors are absent, and it has the cessation of mind and mental factors as its essential nature.

Furthermore, this liberation resembles true liberation and has fulfillment as its nature; for when a noble disciple has already attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) through the supramundane path, the various minds and mental factors do not temporarily manifest. This is because, in this state, there is ultimate tranquility and the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) does not function.
These eight liberations are also called the "noble abodes" (*āryavihāra*), because they are the dwellings of all noble ones (*ārya*).
Nevertheless, noble ones mostly rely on two of these abodes—namely, the third and the eighth—because they are the most excellent.
Therefore, when the sutras speak of "witnessing these two liberations with the body and dwelling in their perfection," they refer to these alone and no others.

Because these two types sever the obstacles to liberation regarding the form and formless realms respectively, leaving nothing remaining, and because one realizes the perfect transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), they are designated as "supreme."
Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), they refer to the eight spheres of mastery, as explained at length in the sūtras.
