The first four spheres of mastery are established by means of two liberations (*vimokṣa*), while the latter four are established by means of one liberation, because they flow forth from them.

Why is this so? It is because, perceiving forms internally, one contemplates external forms that are few—whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—and regarding those forms, one attains superior knowledge and superior vision, obtaining a perception in accordance with reality; this is the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having the perception of internal forms, one observes external forms that are manifold, whether beautiful or ugly; as explained at length, until one attains the perception of things as they truly are—this is the second sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These two spheres of mastery arise from the liberation of one possessing form who observes forms.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited; the full exposition continues until one attains the perception of things as they truly are—this is the third base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as vast; the full exposition continues until one attains the perception of things as they truly are—this is the fourth base of mastery.
These two spheres of mastery arise from the liberation consisting of the internal perception of formlessness while observing external forms;
therefore, the first four spheres of mastery are established by means of these two liberations.

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance—just like an *umakā* flower, or like a deep-dyed blue garment from Vārāṇasī, which is blue, blue in appearance, blue in manifestation, and blue in radiance.
Thus, with the internal perception of formlessness, one contemplates external forms; whether they are blue, or even blue light, it is likewise.
One attains superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, obtaining a perception of them as they truly are; this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are yellow, even unto yellow light—just like a *karṇikāra* flower or a deep yellow robe from Vārāṇasī. Extensively described as "yellow," up until the attainment of the perception of reality as it is, this is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are red, even unto red light—just like the *pāṇḍu-tiṣyaka* flower, or like a deep crimson robe from Vārāṇasī. Whether it be red, or as described at length up to "attaining the perception of reality as it is," this is the seventh stage of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are white, appearing white, manifesting as white, and emitting white light—just like the color of the star Uṣas, or like a very bright white cloth from Vārāṇasī, which is white, appears white, manifests as white, and emits white light.
Thus, with the perception of no internal forms, one contemplates external forms; whether they are white, appearing white, manifesting as white, or emitting white light—it is the same.
Having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, one attains the perception of reality as it is; this is the eighth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) arise from the attainment of the deliverance of the pure (*śubha-vimokṣa*), which is fully realized through bodily witness.

Herein, "deliverance" refers to the mental resolution (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the object, while "mastery" refers to the overcoming of the object. Regarding objects—whether small or large—one possesses sovereign control according to one's will, either by causing them to disappear or by transforming them at will.
"Small forms" refers to forms belonging to the category of sentient beings, because their magnitude is small.
"Abundant forms" refers to forms not belonging to the category of sentient beings—such as houses, forests, lands, and mountains—because their magnitude is large.
"Beautiful and ugly colors" are comprised of pure and impure manifest colors (*varṇa*).
"Inferior and superior colors" refers to humans and gods respectively; because among those various colors, the superior ones exercise mastery over them.
"Knowing" is by means of the path of śamatha;
"seeing" is by means of the path of vipaśyanā.
"Attaining the perception of reality as it is" refers to attaining a perception free from overweening pride regarding what has been mastered and what has not yet been mastered.
"Blue" is the general term.
"Manifestly blue" refers to innate blue.
"Appearing as blue" refers to composite blue.
"Blue light" refers to the fresh, pure blue light emitted by those two.
As it is with blue, so it is for yellow, red, and white, as explained at length.
The reason two similes are given for a single location is to manifest the two types of visible color: the co-emergent (*sahaja*) and the combined (*saṃyukta*).
Regarding "that which is blue," this generally refers to the two types of blue: that of the flower and that of the cloth.
"Blue as manifest" is spoken of in reference to the blue of the flower, because it is co-nascent [with the flower].
"Blue as appearing" is spoken of in reference to the blue of the cloth, because it is established only through combination.
Regarding "blue light," it is explained according to two aspects, because both possess a fresh and pure radiance.
Within these two similes, terms such as "blue" and "manifesting blue" should be understood according to their respective general and explanatory clauses.
As it is with blue, so it is with yellow and the others; the rest is as explained in the section on liberation (*vimokṣa*).
What is meant by "the rest"?
It refers to the internal perception of form while observing external forms, and so forth.
As with the cases such as "perceiving forms while having internal form," they should be explained according to their respective correspondences.
Having already explained the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and their superior objects of focus, the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are defined as follows:

within the state of dwelling in the perfection of pervasiveness, whatever concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the associated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are present, these are called the spheres of totality.
As for "pervading," its measure is vast, universal, and boundless.

This further consists of ten types, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness; all of these completely pervade.
Question:
For what reason are earth and the other elements established as the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities)?
Answer:

Because these spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) contemplate both the supported color-form and its support as being entirely pervasive, if one were not to establish the [elements] such as earth within them, then the spheres of totality would be devoid of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as their support; consequently, one would be unable to contemplate the derived color-forms, such as blue, as having the characteristic of pervasiveness.
Therefore, for the purpose of contemplation, one establishes the earth and other elements so that both the basis and the based are entirely pervaded.
The others are as appropriate, as explained in the section on liberation, namely the sphere of infinite space and so forth.

It should be understood that herein, one undertakes cultivation by relying on liberation, gives rise to skillful means by means of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and achieves fulfillment by means of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
If one attains fulfillment regarding these, then one reaches the ultimate consummation of liberation.
Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle 13; Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle 14.
Compiled by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati as a Commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

Section on Ascertainment, Chapter Three: Attainment, Part Two. Furthermore, regarding "non-contention" (*araṇā*): it refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the associated mental states and mental factors, which reside in the perfection of guarding against the arising of afflictions in others, based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Why is this? One who dwells in the state of non-contention (*araṇā-vihārin*), if they wish to go to where all sentient beings are to be seen, first uses the power of knowledge resulting from their vow (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) from their own dwelling place to observe whether afflictions will arise in relation to their own body for those sentient beings in the future.

Having observed in this way, if one knows that attachment, aversion, stinginess, envy, or other afflictions will arise toward me [upon going], one does not go; if they will not arise, then one goes to that place.
Because it is able to protect others from the arising of various afflictions and disputes, it is called "the absence of dispute" (*araṇā*).

Regarding "knowledge of aspiration" (*praṇidhijñāna*): it refers to the concentration and wisdom, along with their associated factors, that exist within the fulfillment of the aspiration to understand all that is to be known, based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); the rest is as previously explained.

Why is this so? Because one who has attained the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna) desires to thoroughly understand all objects of knowledge throughout the three times; thus, first directing a mind of right aspiration toward each respective object, they pray, "May I understand such and such things exactly as they are," and subsequently enter superior meditative concentration (adhiprajña-dhyāna).
Having arisen from that, one’s aspirations are fulfilled, meaning that one is able to comprehend all that ought to be known.
Regarding the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there are four:

first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); third, the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) refers to the concentration and wisdom—along with the remaining factors as previously described—that, based upon meditative absorption, are fully endowed with unimpeded mastery regarding the distinctions among the names of all phenomena.

Regarding the distinction of names: it refers to the unimpeded and complete mastery over the various designations such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth, in relation to "lack of knowledge," "lack of vision," and "lack of clear realization" (*anabhisamaya*), whether it be concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), and so on at length; this is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) refers to the concentration or wisdom present within the state of being fully endowed with unimpededness regarding all characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and intentions (abhiprāya); the remainder is as previously explained.
"Characteristics" refers to the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.
Regarding "intention" (*abhiprāya*), it refers to specific meanings and so forth.
If one possesses unimpeded mastery and fulfillment regarding these, it is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

Regarding the analytical knowledge of etymological expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), it refers to the concentration or wisdom possessed within the unimpeded mastery and fulfillment concerning various regional dialects and the terminology used to explain all phenomena; the rest is as previously described.
"Various regional dialects" refers to the diverse distinctions of speech arising according to the individual conceptions of countless countries and towns.

"Explanatory terminology for all phenomena" refers to such terms as "worldly" because it is subject to destruction, and "form" (*rūpa*) because it is subject to transformation and decay, and so forth.
If one attains unimpeded penetration regarding these, it is called the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), it refers to the concentration or wisdom present within the perfection of unimpeded differentiation among all phenomena; the remainder is as previously explained.
The differentiation of all phenomena refers to such categories as substantial existence, nominal existence, conventional existence, and ultimate existence.
To attain unimpeded mastery regarding these is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Supernormal powers (abhijñā) refer to the six supernormal powers:

first, the power of the base of psychic transformation; second, the power of the divine ear; third, the power of discerning the minds of others; fourth, the power of recollecting past abodes; fifth, the power of perceiving death and rebirth; and sixth, the power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya).

The supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) refers to the concentration (*samādhi*), the wisdom (*prajñā*), and the associated mental states and mental factors (*caitta-caitasika-dharma*), which, based upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), consist in the possession of various miraculous transformations and majestic powers.
"Endowed with various miraculous powers and majestic virtue" refers to being fully possessed of mastery over various miraculous transformations, such as transforming one into many and so forth.

"Divine ear supernormal power" (divya-śrotra-abhijñā) refers to the concentration and wisdom involved in being fully endowed with the majestic virtue of hearing various sounds as they arise, based upon meditative absorption (dhyāna); the rest is as previously explained.
"Various sounds" refers to the sounds of humans, devas, and so forth.

"Pervasive knowledge of the distinctions of mind" refers to the concentration or wisdom—whether in meditative absorption or otherwise—possessing the majestic power to discern the distinctions in the mental activities of other sentient beings by relying on dhyāna; the rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the penetration of the distinctions in the mental activities of other sentient beings: it refers to knowing, as they truly are, the distinctions in mental activities such as those possessed by desire and so forth.

Regarding the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*): it refers to the concentration and wisdom involved in the mastery of recollecting one's conduct in previous limits while relying upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); the rest is as previously explained.
"Recollection of past conduct" refers to recollecting the successive distinctions of names, clans, and so forth throughout past lives.

"Mastery over death and rebirth" refers to the concentration and wisdom possessed within the full mastery of observing the distinctions of the death and rebirth of sentient beings while relying on meditative absorption; the rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the observation of the differences in the death and birth of sentient beings: this means observing with the divine eye the deaths and births of sentient beings—their beautiful and ugly forms, and their future destinies as they are about to go to happy realms or evil realms.

The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) refers to the concentration and wisdom, along with their associated mental states and mental factors, that are fully endowed with the majestic power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows refers to the knowledge by which one thoroughly penetrates all the means for the exhaustion of outflows, as well as the excellence of the exhaustion of outflows; it is because this knowledge has been brought to fulfillment.

Regarding the "perfection of the secondary marks": this refers to the concentration and wisdom, along with their associated mental states and mental factors, as well as the resultant maturation (vipāka-phala) produced thereby, which manifest the perfection of the physical basis adorned by the primary and secondary marks while relying upon meditative absorption (dhyāna).

Why is this so? It is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, by the predominant power of meditative concentration and wisdom, and for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, manifests a physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not that very substance, because he is manifested by means of the Dharma-body.
If bodhisattvas are able to manifest in such a way, one should know that concentration and wisdom constitute their intrinsic nature.
As for those who are born in other great assemblies, their nature consists of the ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*) produced therein.
"Purity" refers to the four purities: first, purity of the basis (*āśraya-viśuddhi*);
second, purity of the object (*viṣaya-viśuddhi*); third, purity of the mind (*citta-viśuddhi*); and fourth, purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*).
These four kinds of purity in all aspects are attained only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have already acquired great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding "purity of the basis" (*āśraya-śuddhi*): it refers to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) upon which one relies; specifically, it consists of the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the associated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), within the fulfillment of taking up, abiding in, or relinquishing the basis according to one's desire.
One who is fully endowed with the powers of taking up, abiding, and relinquishing is able to take up birth immediately according to their wish;
once born there, they are able to remain for as long as they desire according to the measure of their life-force (*āyur-saṃskāra*);
and if they wish to relinquish those life-forces, they are able to relinquish them immediately.
In their respective order, there are three kinds of perfection.

Regarding the "purity of the objective sphere," this refers to the perfection of the wisdom that transforms objects according to one's wishes; it includes both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth, as explained at length.

One who is fully endowed with the knowledge of transformation (*nirmāṇa-pratibhāsa-jñāna*) is so called because: "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to the manifestation of forms and so forth that did not previously exist; "transmutation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the alteration of forms and so forth already produced into gold, silver, and the like; and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the realization of the distinctions among the characteristics of all types of objects.
In their respective order, there are three kinds of perfection.
Regarding the purity of mind, this refers to the mastery over the gateways of samādhi as one desires; it consists of either meditative concentration or wisdom, the rest being as previously explained.

Because one is able to enter an immeasurable variety of samādhis moment by moment according to one's desire, "purity of knowledge" refers to the concentration and wisdom involved in the full mastery of the retention doors (*dhāraṇīmukha*) as desired, based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); the rest is as previously explained.

Regarding "the gate of dhāraṇī being fully sustained": this means that by reflecting upon any single one of the forty-two syllables and taking this as the primary focus, one is then able to realize skillfulness in the conventional designations for the distinctions among all phenomena.
"Power" refers to the ten powers of the Tathāgata: first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible;

second, the power of knowing the ripening of one's own karma; third, the power of knowing the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; fourth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings; fifth, the power of knowing the various inclinations of beings; sixth, the power of knowing the various elements of beings; seventh, the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere; eighth, the power of recollecting past abodes; ninth, the power of knowing death and rebirth; and tenth, the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows.

The power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible refers to the concentration and wisdom, as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with them, which are fully perfected in the knowledge of all modes of what is possible and what is impossible, based upon meditative absorption.

The perfection of the knowledge of all aspects regarding what is possible and what is impossible refers to all samādhis and so forth within the unimpeded and unattached manifestation of the knowledge of all aspects concerning causes and non-causes.

The power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*) refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) present within the perfection of all-aspect knowledge of one’s own karma; the remainder is as previously explained.
It consists of the samādhis and so forth that function without attachment or obstruction within the all-aspect knowledge of one’s own karma.
In this manner, the remaining powers should be correctly established according to their respective applications.
What does "according to their respective applications" mean?

Regarding the power of knowledge concerning dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis: it refers to the perfection of knowledge regarding all aspects of dhyāna, liberation, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); whether it be meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), the rest is as previously explained.

This is because, within the unimpeded and unattached manifestation of the knowledge of all modes of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), all samādhis and so forth constitute its essence.

Regarding the power of knowledge concerning the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*), it refers to all samādhis and so forth within the unimpeded and unattached manifestation of the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties in every respect.

The power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*) refers to all the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and so forth present within the unimpeded and unobstructed functioning of the knowledge of the various distinctions among all types of inclinations.

The power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*) refers to all the samādhis and so forth that function without attachment or obstruction within the knowledge of the distinctions among all types of elements.

The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminīpratipaj-jñānabala*) refers to all the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and so forth that operate within the unattached and unimpeded manifestation of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere in all their aspects.

The power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of former abodes refers to all the samādhis and so forth involved in the unimpeded and unattached manifestation of the knowledge that recollects former abodes in every respect.
The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth refers to all samādhis and so forth that function without attachment or obstruction within the knowledge of all modes of death and rebirth.

The power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows refers to all samādhis and so forth that function without attachment or obstruction within the knowledge of all modes of the exhaustion of outflows.
"Fearlessness" refers to the four fearlessnesses: first, fearlessness regarding perfect enlightenment;
second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding obstructive dharmas; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the path leading to the transcendence of suffering.

The fearlessness of being a perfectly awakened one (*samyaksaṃbuddha-vaiśāradya*) refers to the concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the associated mental states and mental factors that arise when, relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one establishes oneself in the possession of the title of "perfectly awakened" regarding all aspects of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*) through the gateway of self-benefit.
As the Sūtra says:

"I am the Truly and Fully Enlightened One; even if there were any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, or Brahmās in the world who, relying on the Dharma, were to raise an objection or cause me to be reminded, saying that regarding these dharmas I am not truly and fully enlightened."
Regarding this matter, my right view is without basis.

Because my right view regarding this matter has no grounds, I dwell in peace, free from fear and dread; I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, or Brahmā in any world can turn.

Regarding the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*): this refers to the concentration and wisdom—whether meditative absorption or insight—by which, relying on dhyāna and through the door of one’s own benefit, one establishes and fulfills the proclamation of one’s own qualities regarding the destruction of all types of outflows; the rest is as previously explained.
As the Sūtra says:
"My outflows are forever exhausted," and so forth, as explained in detail previously.

Regarding the fearlessness in declaring the obstructing dharmas: this refers to the concentration and wisdom—along with the rest as previously described—by which, relying on meditative absorption and through the gateway of benefiting others, one establishes oneself in the perfection of proclaiming one's own qualities by declaring all kinds of obstructing dharmas.
As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, I have taught my disciples the obstructing dharmas; that which is defiled will necessarily act as an obstacle," and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding the fearlessness in proclaiming the path leading out of suffering: this refers to the concentration and wisdom, as previously described, by which one—relying on meditative absorption and through the gateway of benefiting others—establishes oneself as possessing the full perfection of the title of virtue in proclaiming the dharma of the path to liberation in all its aspects.
As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, I have taught the path of deliverance for my disciples; by practicing it, the Noble Ones certainly attain deliverance and certainly achieve penetration.

Should any śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, or Brahmās in the world, relying on the Dharma, raise an objection or cause one to reflect, saying that 'cultivating this path is not the correct deliverance, nor does it correctly exhaust suffering or realize the limit of suffering,' [the Noble Ones would remain unshaken]."
"In this matter, I have right view and am without [fear]; and so forth, as explained at length.
These four fearlessnesses, briefly stated, are twofold: namely, self-benefit and benefit for others.
The first two are for one's own benefit, due to the distinction between wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*);
the latter two are for the benefit of others, due to the removal of discordant factors (*vipakṣa-dharma*) and the cultivation of remedial factors (*pratipakṣa-dharma*).
Regarding the fearlessness of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi-vaiśāradya*), it is spoken from the perspective of one's own benefit through internal wisdom:

"I have attained perfect enlightenment regarding all aspects of the objects of knowledge, reaching the very limits of their distinctions; in the presence of the entire world, I proclaim my own title of virtue and establish the correct state free from challenge," including all that is extensively explained therein, concerning the concentration and wisdom involved.
It should be understood that the remaining fearlessnesses are likewise to be applied accordingly.
"The exhaustion of outflows in every respect" refers to the permanent extinction of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
"All obstructive phenomena" refers to all phenomena that are the objects of antidote to the various forms of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
The path of deliverance in all its aspects refers to everything from the path of skillful means up to the ultimate path.

As for the foundations of mindfulness, these are the three unique foundations of mindfulness of the Tathāgatas; that is, when presiding over a great assembly, the concentration and wisdom possessed within the perfection of the non-arising of afflictions in every respect, as explained in detail previously.
What are the three foundations of mindfulness?

They are as follows: the Great Teacher, out of compassion for all who seek their welfare and benefit, gives rise to great compassion and proclaims the essential Dharma to his disciples, saying to the bhikṣus:
"You should know this which brings benefit; this which brings happiness; and this which brings both benefit and happiness."

At that time, if there are disciples who listen with reverence, and having heard it, receive it attentively and abide in a mind intent on following the teaching, they will practice with diligence, performing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.

The Tathāgata does not give rise to a mind of joy nor does he leap for joy; rather, he gives rise to great equanimity, abiding in mindfulness and clear comprehension, providing exhortations and instructions according to what the assembly of noble ones should practice.
This is called the first unique application of mindfulness (*āveṇika-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, out of compassion for all who seek benefit and welfare, the Great Teacher gave rise to great compassion and proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma to his disciples, [stating] that it leads even to this: benefit and happiness.

At that time, if there are disciples who do not listen with reverence, and so forth, up to those who do not practice with diligence according to the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti), the Tathāgata does not give rise to anger or resentment toward them;
he does not abandon his protective care, nor does his mind feel regret or distress, but rather he gives rise to great equanimity (upekṣā), and so on, as extensively explained.
This is called the second unique application of mindfulness (*asādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, out of compassion for all who seek their own welfare and benefit, the Great Teacher gives rise to great compassion and proclaims the essential points of the Dharma to his disciples, [stating] that it leads even to this: the ability to bring about benefit and happiness.
At that time, one portion of the disciples listened with reverence and even practiced the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma with diligence;
another portion of the disciples did not listen with reverence and did not practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma with diligence.
The Tathāgata does not give rise to joy toward them, nor does his mind experience even the slightest resentment.

These three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) manifest the Great Teacher’s mastery over the assembly; they consist essentially of the concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth, which are fully endowed with the non-occurrence of all forms of afflictions—both those associated with attachment and aversion—as well as their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Regarding "non-protection," this refers to the three forms of non-protection.

This means that when the Great Teacher governs the assembly, he possesses the complete skillful means for providing instruction and admonition as desired; this includes both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth, as explained at length.
What are these three?
As the Sūtra says:

"The bodily actions of the Tathāgata are pure in their manifestation; there are no impure manifestations of bodily action that need to be concealed, such as [the thought], 'May others not know of my verbal or mental actions. The same applies to their manifestations."

Because that Great Teacher is free from fear and anxiety, he skillfully guides all the assemblies of those to be converted according to their inclinations; he is naturally endowed with powerful means for subduing, gathering, instructing, and teaching them.

The quality of non-forgetfulness refers to the concentration and wisdom—up to the full explanation—that consist in the possession of perfect mindfulness regarding all aspects of what has been done and what has been spoken.

In this context, it is shown that the samādhis and so forth present within the perfection of mindfulness regarding whatever is performed, by way of the gate of transformative activity, constitute the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*).

The permanent severance of habitual tendencies refers to the concentration and wisdom—up to the full elaboration—of an omniscient one regarding the non-manifestation of that which is not performed by an omniscient one, even while remaining fully endowed [with all qualities].

In this context, it is shown that for the Omniscient One, all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and so forth present within the perfection of the non-occurrence of any physical or verbal actions—whether they express the presence of residual afflictive or cognitive obscurations—are the permanent abandonment of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"Great Compassion" refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth as extensively explained, within the fulfillment of abiding in great compassion toward the object of the uninterrupted suffering of sentient beings.

Herein it is shown that all *samādhis* and so on within the fulfillment of abiding in great compassion toward the objects of every kind of uninterrupted suffering of all sentient beings throughout the three realms is called "great compassion."
The "unshared Buddha-dharmas" refer to the eighteen unshared Buddha-dharmas. What are they? They are:

the perfection of the purity of unshared bodily, vocal, and mental actions; the perfection of non-retrogression regarding the attainment of the basis, the fruit, and the faculties; the perfection of the manifestation of unshared activities; and the perfection of abiding in unshared wisdom—whether it be meditative concentration or insight—and so forth, as explained at length.
What are these eighteen? As the Sūtra says: The Tathāgata has no errors; he has no harsh or abrupt sounds;

he has no loss of mindfulness; he has no unconcentrated mind; he has no diverse perceptions; he has no equanimity lacking discernment; his aspiration does not regress; his vigor does not regress; his mindfulness does not regress; his concentration does not regress; his wisdom does not regress; his liberation does not regress; all his bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; all his verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; all his mental actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; he knows the past without attachment or obstruction; he knows the future without attachment or obstruction; he knows the present without attachment or obstruction.
The establishment of those characteristics is as explained at length in the Sūtra. Regarding the Tathāgata’s freedom from error:

although an Arhat Bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), when he goes out into towns and cities for alms, he may at times associate with or dwell among wild elephants, wild horses, wild oxen, or fierce dogs; or at times he may tread upon thickets of thorns or leap across pits with his feet; or at times he may enter the homes of women and engage in speech that does not accord with proper principle; or in forests and wildernesses, he may abandon the right path and travel along a wrong road; or he may associate with thieves and ferocious beasts.
Such errors and lapses still exist for Arhats, but they are forever absent in the Tathāgata.

Regarding the absence of "sudden or violent sounds": it refers to instances where an Arhat, while wandering through forests or wilds at some time, may lose his way; or enter an empty house and cry out loudly, producing a great and violent noise; or, due to the fault of non-defiled habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), expose his lips and teeth and manifest a loud laugh.
Such sounds of sudden outbursts still exist in Arhats, but in the Tathāgata they are forever absent.

Regarding "the absence of forgetfulness of mindfulness": this means that Arhats may still experience non-afflicted lapses in memory regarding what was done long ago or what was spoken long ago; in the Tathāgata, such forgetfulness is forever absent.

Regarding "having no unconcentrated mind": this means that while an Arhat must withdraw his mind for it to become concentrated, it becomes unconcentrated as soon as he emerges [from meditation]; the Tathāgata, however, has no unconcentrated state at any stage.

"Having no manifold perceptions in the mind" means that while an Arhat conceives a perception of aversion toward conditioned existence (*sa-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and a perception of tranquility toward unconditioned nirvana (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), the Tathāgata has no perception of distinction between cyclic existence and nirvana, because he abides in the foremost great equanimity.

"Non-abandonment without discernment" means that an Arhat does not abandon activities for the benefit of sentient beings without first employing wisdom to investigate them; since the Tathāgata is free from such occurrences, he has no non-discerning abandonment.

Furthermore, regarding the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), Arhats may still experience a falling away from what has not yet been attained; that is to say, they may experience a falling away from aspiration, a falling away from diligence, a falling away from mindfulness, a falling away from concentration, a falling away from wisdom, and a falling away from liberation. Such six types of falling away are forever absent in the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, an Arhat at one time engages in wholesome bodily karma, and at another time engages in indeterminate bodily karma; the same applies to vocal and mental karma.
Because the Tathāgata’s three types of action are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom, there is no indeterminate action.
"Having wisdom as a precursor" means that [action] is originated by wisdom.
"Following wisdom in its movement" means that it proceeds together with wisdom.

Furthermore, because an Arhat bhikṣu cannot give rise to the mind and immediately understand all knowable things across the three periods of time, his wisdom-vision has attachments; because he cannot understand everything completely, his wisdom-vision has obstructions.

When the Tathāgata momentarily directs his mind toward the objects of the three periods of time, he immediately and universally knows them all; therefore, his wisdom and vision are unattached and unimpeded.
Among the eighteen [unique qualities], the first six have as their essence the samādhis and so forth pertaining to the fulfillment of the purity of uncommon bodily, vocal, and mental actions.
Being free from error is spoken of in reliance upon the purity of physical action.
Being free from harsh or violent speech is spoken of in reliance upon the purity of vocal action.

Being free from loss of mindfulness, being free from an unconcentrated mind, being free from diverse perceptions, and being free from equanimity lacking discernment—these four are spoken of in reliance upon the purity of mental action.

The non-retrogression of aspiration up to the non-retrogression of liberation—these six have as their essence the samādhis and so forth present within the possession of non-retrogression regarding that which is not yet attained, namely, the basis, the fruit, and the faculties. The "basis" refers to aspiration; the "fruit" refers to liberation; and the "faculties" refer to diligence and the others.

All actions of body, speech, and mind are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom; these three constitute the essence of the samādhis and so forth present within the perfection of the manifestation of unshared karma.

Knowing the past, future, and present without attachment or obstruction—these three constitute the essence of the samādhis and so forth within the perfection of abiding in unshared wisdom (*āveṇika-jñāna*).

As for "the excellence of knowledge in all aspects" (*sarvākāra-prajñā*): it refers to the concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with them, which exist within the perfection of the nature of excellent knowledge in all aspects regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*).
What is the perfection of the nature of sublime knowledge in all its aspects regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases?

It refers to the fulfillment of the wisdom that reaches the ultimate limit by thoroughly penetrating all distinctions among the self-nature and specific characteristics of the aggregates and so forth.
How are such qualities as these brought forth?
It is said that they rely upon the four pure dhyānas.

Whether non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or bodhisattvas, when bringing forth the four immeasurables and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they for the most part rely upon the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*). As for śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas, when bringing forth the remaining qualities, they do so [by relying on all four dhyānas].
By what cause are such qualities induced?
It is by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and repeatedly contemplating the dharmas as they have been established.
Herein is shown the basis for inducing such qualities, as well as the person (*pudgala*) who can induce them and the means (*upāya*) by which they are induced.
How does one bring forth skillful means?
It refers to the repeated mental engagement with the modes of activity, through numerous acts of attention and a concentrated mind, directed toward the teachings as they have been established.

When wishing to induce immeasurability, one relies on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and repeatedly contemplates, with mental engagement associated with cultivated wisdom, the teachings on a mind accompanied by loving-kindness that is free from resentment and enmity.

When one wishes to bring forth supernormal powers and so forth, one relies upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and repeatedly contemplates, with attention associated with wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the teachings concerning such things as transforming one into many.
In this manner, one should repeatedly contemplate all aspects as they have been established, understanding them according to their respective correspondences.
Furthermore, such qualities are briefly of two kinds:
first, the actualization of one's own functional activity; second, abiding in one's own intrinsic nature.
If it manifests and initiates its own specific activity, it takes the conventional wisdom obtained subsequent to supramundane wisdom as its essence.
If it abides in its own nature, it takes supramundane wisdom as its essence.

Furthermore, "manifesting one's own functional activities" refers to the various deeds performed by the noble ones (*ārya*), such as the elimination of the obstacles to be abandoned, according to their respective capacities.

Abiding in one's own nature refers to dwelling in happiness in the present life through the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth, which are without objective referents and are subsumed within the most excellent, tranquil, non-conceptual wisdom.
Furthermore, what is the function of the immeasurables?

This means that by dwelling in compassion while abandoning the opposing obstacles, one is able to swiftly perfect the accumulation of merit and bring sentient beings to maturity without weariness of mind.
"Abandoning the opposing obstacles" refers, in their respective order, to the four immeasurables which are able to abandon ill-will, harmfulness, lack of joy, and affectionate resentment.
"Abiding in compassion" means that the four immeasurables function in accordance with the task of benefiting sentient beings.
Because one abides in compassion toward all sentient beings, one is able to swiftly fulfill the accumulation of merit.
Regarding "maturing sentient beings with a mind free from weariness": this is because, out of compassion for all sentient beings, one disregards one's own self.
What is the function of liberation?
It is said to be the elicitation of transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*), being without difficulty in manifesting either pure or impure transformations.
He is unimpeded regarding peaceful liberation and is able to abide in the foremost peaceful noble dwelling by means of resolute reflection.
Herein, it is shown that the first two liberations are capable of producing transformative manifestations.
By means of the third liberation, one encounters no difficulty in manifesting pure or impure transformations.
By means of the four formless liberations, one encounters no obstruction regarding the liberation of tranquility.
By means of the final liberation, one is able to abide in the foremost peaceful noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of resolute reflection" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), it clarifies that the meaning of such-and-such a form of resolute conviction is the meaning of liberation.
What is the function of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)?
It is that they enable one to exercise mastery over the objects of the three preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*), because they completely overcome those objects.
What is the function of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
It is said that it effectively accomplishes the objects of focus for liberation because it pervades and extends everywhere.
What is the function of the absence of conflict (*araṇā*)?
It is that whatever speech one utters is heard with faith and submission; for protecting the minds of others is supreme, as one utters speech in accordance with what is appropriate.
What is the function of the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)?

It is said that it is able to skillfully discern matters pertaining to the three periods of time and so forth; it is revered by the entire world because it is understood by all as that which the multitude looks up to and relies upon.
What is the function of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
It is said that they delight the minds of sentient beings by skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma, and they are able to sever all nets of doubt.
What is the function of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
That is to say, by means of physical action, verbal action, and the discernment of others' minds, he guides and transforms sentient beings, causing them to enter the holy teaching.
Having thoroughly understood all the mental activities and the past and future states of sentient beings, he provides instruction as appropriate, enabling them to achieve permanent transcendence.

This passage demonstrates the supernormal powers (abhijñā) from the power of miraculous feats (ṛddhi-viṣaya) and the divine ear (divya-śrotra) up to the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya). These function, respectively, to initiate physical actions such as emanations and guidance; for by means of the divine ear power, one understands the distinctions among all vocal sounds and is thus able to initiate verbal actions.
What is the function of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*)?
It is that they cause those who see them even for a moment to perceive [the Buddha] as a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), thereby giving rise to pure faith (*śraddhā*) in their minds.
What is the function of purity (*viśuddhi*)?

That is to say, by the power of this [merit], one takes up existence in birth; according to one's desire, one may remain for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon, or relinquish the formations of life, or exercise mastery over all phenomena, or exercise mastery over all meditative concentrations, or uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
This passage demonstrates that through the purification of the basis (*āśraya*), one attains mastery over the appropriation, maintenance, and relinquishment of the physical basis as one desires;

this comprises three points: namely, intentionally taking up birth in existence (*bhava*) and so forth; through the purification of the object (*ālambana*), one attains mastery in the sovereign functioning within all phenomena; through the purification of the mind (*citta*), one attains mastery in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and through the purification of wisdom (*jñāna*), one upholds the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
What kind of deeds does he perform?

It means that, in order to eliminate and abandon theories of no cause, theories of evil causes, and theories of attaining results without action, he unerringly proclaims the path to higher rebirth; he penetrates the mental activities of all sentient beings and correctly teaches their capacities as vessels for the Dharma, their dispositions, latent tendencies, objects of experience, and the provisions necessary for liberation.
According to what is appropriate for each case, he proclaims the definitive path to supreme victory and subdues all māras.
He is fully capable of providing answers to all inquiries and debates.

Herein, it is shown that the first two powers enable him to teach the path to higher rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*), while the remaining eight powers enable him to teach the path to definitive excellence (*niḥśreyasa-mārga*).
These two types of endowments demonstrate the deeds performed by all Buddhas.

Why is this so? Because the World-Honored One, through the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), subdues all proponents of non-causality and proponents of false causes in the world, and proclaims the unerring path to higher rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*).

Because various non-Buddhists regard higher rebirth as being either causeless or caused by such things as intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or a creator god (īśvara), their doctrines are termed "theories of no-cause or false causes."

By means of the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma, he subdues all those in the world who propound the theory that results are obtained without action; he correctly proclaims the right path to the happy realms.

The various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and others claim that results are naturally obtained without performing actions, and thus they are called proponents of the theory that results are obtained without action.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments, one penetrates the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Because these are the practices performed by the mind, they are called "mental activities."

By means of the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties, one enters into all those who are vessels for the correct teaching of the Dharma; for when the faculties such as faith are well-matured, they are capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma.
By the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations, one penetrates all superior and inferior dispositions.
By the power of knowledge regarding various elements, one penetrates the nature of all latent proclivities and afflictions that are susceptible to being destroyed.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere, one enters into the spheres encompassed by the teachings of all the Great and Lesser Vehicles.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives, one enters into all the accumulations.
The causes and conditions for the noble path accumulated in previous lives are called the provisions (*sambhāra*).
By means of the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth, one realizes and enters into all future functional capacities.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*), he realizes the transcendence of all three realms.
Having thus realized it, he proclaims the supramundane noble path of liberation as is appropriate for each case.
These ten are called "powers" because they are well able to subdue all māras and because they are well able to provide definitive answers to all questions and discourses.

Regarding the subduing of all māras: by means of these ten powers, one can subdue the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the celestial māra (*devaputra-māra*), and the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), as they are supreme.
Even though the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have been severed, they cannot act as an impediment; therefore, it is called "supreme.

Regarding the "prophetic declaration of all inquiries and treatises": this refers to the fact that in all matters—from what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) up to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)—all inquiries and treatises are prophesied without obstruction.
What is the function of fearlessness?
It is to establish oneself as the Great Teacher amidst the great assembly and to subdue all heterodox opponents who raise perverse challenges.
One is called the "Great Teacher" because one’s own welfare and the welfare of others are perfected through a multitude of virtues.

"Subduing heterodox opponents who raise erroneous challenges" means being able to subdue those heterodox opponents who raise erroneous challenges regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata for attaining perfect enlightenment and permanently severing all outflows that obstruct the path.
What is the function of the foundations of mindfulness?
It is to be able to guide the great assembly without defilement, because, through respectful listening and so forth, one is free from afflictions such as attachment and aversion.
What kind of activity does non-restraint perform?

It means being able to provide instruction and admonition to one's disciples without interruption, because there is no concealment or protection of one’s own faults for fear that they might be exposed.
What function does the quality of non-forgetfulness perform?
It means being able to never abandon any of the Buddha-activities. Why is this so?
Because of this, one is able to remain vigilant regarding the beneficial tasks to be performed for sentient beings before them, without transgressing for even a single moment.
What is the function of the permanent severance of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?

This means that being free from all afflictions, he does not manifest any activities resembling those performed by afflicted beings, unlike an arhat bhikṣu who still manifests such things as errors and lapses.
What is the activity of great compassion?
It is to survey the world throughout the six periods of day and night, observing in various ways who is declining, who is regressing, who is increasing, and who is progressing, and so forth.
What is the function of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)?
It is said that, through the purity of the actions of body, speech, and mind, and by attaining non-retrogression, whether walking or standing still, one outshines all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
These phrases, according to what was previously explained, should be interpreted accordingly in relation to the characteristics such as the fulfillment of the purity of the three uncommon karmas.
What is the activity performed by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
This means that it is able to sever all nets of doubt for all sentient beings, causing the eye of the True Dharma to remain for a long time.
By this, those sentient beings who are not yet matured are brought to maturity, and those already matured are led to liberation.
"One who has severed the net of doubt" means that their wisdom is unimpeded in all circumstances.

"Causing the eye of the True Dharma to endure for a long time" means that, at various times and in various places, they proclaim diverse distinctions of Dharma gates in order to sever the doubts of those sentient beings to be converted.
The compilers of the canon compiled it in successive order so that it would not perish.
Relying upon this Dharma-eye, they cause sentient beings who have not yet reached maturity to mature quickly, and those already matured to attain liberation swiftly.
Furthermore, at the various stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), when one realizes the progressively superior paths, one abandons the previously attained inferior paths.

For example, upon realizing the path subsumed under a particular fruit, one simultaneously abandons the path subsumed under its preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*), because the latter no longer manifests.

Furthermore, at this very time, there is the realization of the abandonment of the aggregates; for, upon attaining the fruit, one brings about the permanent elimination of the latencies (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions that are the objects of abandonment, leaving nothing remaining, and thereby realizes the superior transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Furthermore, within the realm of nirvana without remainder, all noble paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are abandoned through instantaneous relinquishment, whereas this is not the case for bodhisattvas; therefore, it is said that only bodhisattvas possess inexhaustible roots of goodness and inexhaustible merit.
"To abandon that which is to be abandoned all at once" means the abandonment such that it never manifests again in the ultimate sense.
It is not that the noble paths attained by Bodhisattvas involve such an abandonment, for they act out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings so that they may all attain nirvāṇa.
For this reason, the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa Sūtra* and other scriptures state that bodhisattvas possess inexhaustible roots of goodness and inexhaustible merits.
Furthermore, for what reason are the "unanswered" (avyākṛta) matters established?
This is because his question was not based on correct reasoning (*yoniśas*).
Why was the question not based on correct reasoning?
Because it avoided the sphere of reflection upon cause and effect, as well as defilement and purification.

In this context, it is shown that regarding matters such as whether the world is eternal or non-eternal as inquired about by the various non-Buddhists, the Tathāgata establishes fourteen points as "unanswerable" (avyākṛta), because those questions do not accord with correct reasoning and lead to what is unbeneficial.
What kind of inquiry leads to meaningful benefit?
It refers to all inquiries based upon the Four Noble Truths, because such inquiries are subsumed under the spheres of reflection concerning cause and effect, as well as defilement and purification.
Furthermore, for what reason is a bodhisattva who has already entered the bodhisattva stage of "surpassing and transcending birth" (abhisamayāntika) not considered a stream-enterer (srotāpanna)?
It is because, by attaining the non-abiding path (*apratisthita-mārga*), they do not achieve the state of being exclusively a stream-enterer.
For what reason is he also not a Once-returner?
Because he undergoes immeasurable births within the various realms of existence.
For what reason is he also not a Non-returner?
Because they abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) yet are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, once Bodhisattvas have attained the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), they cultivate only the path that serves as the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) across the ten stages, and not the path that serves as the antidote to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When they attain enlightenment, they suddenly sever both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), suddenly becoming Arhats and Tathāgatas.

Although these Bodhisattvas have not yet permanently severed the afflictions, these afflictions are like poisons suppressed by mantras or medicines; they do not give rise to any of the faults of the afflictions, and throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*), they are like Arhats who have already severed the afflictions.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas should cultivate skillfulness regarding the objects of knowledge; they should cultivate skillfulness regarding various expedient means; they should cultivate skillfulness regarding false conceptualization; they should cultivate skillfulness regarding non-conceptualization; and from time to time, they should cultivate the refinement of their faculties.
The objects of knowledge are, in brief, of six kinds:

first, the deluded; second, the basis of delusion; third, the basis of non-delusion; fourth, that which is both deluded and non-deluded; fifth, the non-deluded; and sixth, the outflow of the non-deluded.
"Delusion" refers to the grasping at subject and object.

"The basis of delusion" refers to that which is the domain of noble wisdom; its essence consists solely of the characteristics of activity and false conceptualization. Because this exists, all foolish worldlings undergo the turning of delusive grasping.
The basis for non-delusion refers to suchness, because it is the locus upon which non-conceptual wisdom relies. Regarding delusion and non-delusion:

this refers to all wholesome dharmas, such as the wisdom derived from hearing, which accord with supramundane wisdom; they do so by conceptually discerning the objects of knowledge while remaining in conformity with non-conceptual wisdom.
Non-delusion refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The outflow of non-delusion refers to the wholesome dharmas attained subsequent to the noble path (*ārya-mārga*).
Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is, in brief, of four kinds:

First, skillfulness in maturing sentient beings; second, skillfulness in fulfilling the Buddha-dharmas; third, skillfulness in swiftly realizing supernormal powers; and fourth, skillfulness in the uninterrupted continuity of the path.
Skillfulness in maturing sentient beings refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), because by means of them one gathers others and establishes them in wholesome dharmas.
Skillfulness in fulfilling the Buddha-dharmas refers to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to bring to perfection the perfection of generosity up to the nature of the sublime wisdom of all aspects, they should train in the perfection of wisdom."

Regarding "swiftly realizing the skillfulness of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*)," this refers to the confession of all evils, the rejoicing in merit, the invitation of the Buddhas, and the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) during the six periods of day and night, as explained in detail in the *Ārya-maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
Skillfulness regarding the non-interruption of the Path refers to the nirvāṇa without abode.

Because it is repeatedly perfected and uninterrupted, it pervades all worlds throughout the ten directions, manifesting all the practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas according to those who are to be transformed.

False conceptualization is, in brief, of ten kinds: namely, fundamental conceptualization, conceptualization of signs, conceptualization of the manifestation of signs, conceptualization of the transformation of signs, conceptualization of the transformation of the manifestation of signs, conceptualization induced by others, irrational conceptualization, rational conceptualization, conceptualization of attachment, and conceptualization of distraction.
Fundamental discrimination refers to the ālayavijñāna, because it is the seed of all discrimination.
Discrimination of characteristics refers to the consciousnesses of the body, the dwelling place, and that which is experienced, because these are the grasped characteristics.
Furthermore, these appear in their respective order, taking as their characteristics the material sense-faculties, the physical world, and the objects such as form.

As for the "manifestation of characteristics," this refers to the six groups of consciousness and the mind (*manas*), because they manifest in accordance with the characteristics of the grasped objects as previously described.
The discrimination of the transformation of characteristics refers to the arising of the transformation of characteristics of the body and so forth, as previously described.

The discrimination of the manifestation of characteristics refers to the arising of the manifestation of characteristics of visual consciousness and so forth, in their various distinctions of states such as suffering and pleasure, as previously described.
Regarding "that which is derived from discrimination," this refers to the characteristics of the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes (nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya) comprised within the teachings.
This, in turn, is of two kinds:
first, that which has as its essence poorly expounded doctrine and discipline; second, that which has as its essence well-expounded doctrine and discipline.

By the power of this predominance, there are successively induced two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely, improper conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) and proper conceptualization (*yoniśo-vikalpa*).
"Conceptualization of attachment" refers to all conceptualizations arising from improper conceptualization that are subsumed under the sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭi-gata*).
Distracted conceptualization refers to all conceptualizations characterized by the grasping at non-existence and so forth, which arise from conceptualizing in accordance with reality.

This, moreover, is of ten kinds: conceptualization of non-existence, conceptualization of existence, conceptualization of superimposition, conceptualization of denial, conceptualization of identity, conceptualization of difference, conceptualization of intrinsic nature, conceptualization of specific differences, conceptualization of meaning according to the name, and conceptualization of name according to the meaning.
These ten kinds of conceptualization are taught based on the initial section of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
As the Sūtra says:
"O Śāriputra!"
This bodhisattva truly exists as a bodhisattva, yet they do not correctly perceive a bodhisattva.

They do not correctly perceive the name "bodhisattva"; they do not correctly perceive the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); they do not correctly perceive awakening (bodhi); they do not correctly perceive practice; and they do not correctly perceive non-practice.

Why is this? It is because name is empty of intrinsic nature, not empty of emptiness; form is empty of intrinsic nature, not empty of emptiness; and so on, up to consciousness, which is empty of intrinsic nature, not empty of emptiness.
Why is this? This emptiness of form is not identical to form, nor is there an emptiness that exists apart from form.
Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form; this applies likewise up to consciousness.
Why is this? Because these exist only as names— namely,

"this is the name of a bodhisattva," "this is a bodhisattva," "this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," "this is awakening (bodhi)," and so on, up to "this is form (rūpa)" and "this is consciousness (vijñāna)."

Because their intrinsic nature is without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purity, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they correctly do not observe arising, nor do they correctly observe anything up to and including purity.

Why is this? Because one conceptually designates adventitious names for those various phenomena that are being deliberated upon; based on these adventitious names, one engages in verbal expression, and following such and such verbal expressions, one gives rise to such and such attachments.
The bodhisattva does not correctly observe any of these names; because he does not correctly observe them, he does not give rise to attachment.
In this sutra, the following statement—"this bodhisattva truly exists as a bodhisattva," and so forth—is spoken in order to counteract the discrimination of non-existence.
Because the term "truly existent" carries the meaning of "having an intrinsic nature," in order to counteract the conceptualization of such an intrinsic nature, it is said:
"One does not correctly perceive a bodhisattva, and so forth, up to one does not correctly perceive non-practice."
Because of the elimination of the two natures of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*),
and in order to counteract the conceptualization of superimposition (*samāropa*), it is said as follows: Why is this so?
It is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), because it negates the unreal, imagined intrinsic nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
To counteract the conceptualization of denial (*apavāda-vikalpa*), it is said as follows:
It is not emptiness.
Because of this name, the thoroughly imagined nature is absent, yet its nature exists at all times.
To counteract the conceptualization of it as a single entity, it is said:
This emptiness of form is not identical to form, and so on, up to this emptiness of consciousness, which is not identical to consciousness.
This is because their intrinsic natures are distinct. Why is that?
Because form and so forth are the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while emptiness is the nature of the perfected (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
the following statement was made to counteract the conceptualization of difference:
"Emptiness does not exist apart from form," and so on, up to "emptiness is itself consciousness."
Because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is devoid of characteristics, and because its non-existence cannot be apprehended apart from those [characteristics],
in order to counteract the conceptualization of intrinsic nature,
it is said: "This is merely a name," namely, "this is form" (*rūpa*), up to "this is consciousness" (*vijñāna*), and so forth.
Because there is no determinate intrinsic nature of the signified apart from the signifier,
in order to counteract the conceptualization of distinctions, it is said:
"Because that intrinsic nature is unarisen," and so forth, up to "one does not correctly perceive purity."
Because it eliminates specific characteristics such as arising and so forth, and in order to counteract the conceptualization of objects according to their names, it is said:

"Regarding those various phenomena that are conceptually constructed, one provisionally establishes adventitious names; based on these adventitious names, one engages in verbal expression," and so on.
To counteract the discrimination that follows names according to their referents, it is said:
"In all such names, the bodhisattva correctly does not engage in contemplative observation; because he correctly does not engage in contemplative observation, he gives rise to no attachment."
Because one does not see or grasp at names according to their referents, there are briefly three kinds of non-conceptualization:
first, non-conceptualization through contentment; second, non-conceptualization free from inversion; and third, non-conceptualization free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
These three types—ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas—should be understood according to their respective order.
Among them, ordinary beings, having reflected thoroughly upon any single dharma-nature such as impermanence, become satisfied and content.

This means that one recognizes this matter as inevitable and has no further expectations; this is called non-conceptual contentment, because at that time all discursive thoughts and conceptualizations have ceased.

When the śrāvakas, in order to counteract the inversions such as the notion of permanence regarding the aggregates, correctly investigate that there are only phenomena such as form, they thereby attain supramundane wisdom that penetrates the nature of selflessness; this is called non-inverted non-conceptuality.

Once bodhisattvas have realized that phenomena such as form are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), they are able to eliminate and dissolve all marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). They thereby attain the most ultimate, supramundane wisdom that penetrates and pervades true suchness (*tathatā*); this is called non-proliferated non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañca-nirvikalpa*).

This non-conceptual wisdom is further distinguished by being free from five characteristics; that is, it is called "non-conceptual" because it is not due to a lack of mental attention, not due to transcendence, not due to tranquility, not due to intrinsic nature, and not due to the application of effort toward an object of focus.

Why is this so? If non-conceptuality were defined merely by the absence of mental attention (*manasikāra*), then states such as deep sleep or intoxication would have to be considered non-conceptual wisdom, because in those states one does not contemplate the characteristics of phenomena.

If it were called "non-conceptual" simply because it transcends [vitarka and vicāra], then all stages from the second dhyāna upward would have to be non-conceptual wisdom, since they transcend vitarka and vicāra.
If that were so, the statement that the mind and mental factors of the three realms constitute the essence of conceptualization would be contradicted.

Furthermore, if they are called "non-conceptual" because they have ceased, then the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) should be non-conceptual wisdom, since the conceptual mind and mental factors have ceased therein.
If that were so, then cognition (*jñāna*) would also have to be non-existent.

If it is called "non-conceptual" by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then form (*rūpa*) and other such phenomena would also have to be non-conceptual wisdom, because they too lack a conceptual intrinsic nature.
If it were called "non-conceptual" simply because one applies effort toward an object of focus, then the nature of conceptualization itself would have to be non-conceptual wisdom.
If you claim this is indeed non-conceptual, then the very characteristic of such application is itself the characteristic of conceptualization.
Therefore, non-conceptual wisdom does not possess those five characteristics.
If that is so, how should one contemplate the characteristic of non-conceptuality free from conceptual proliferation?
It means that no volitional application arises with respect to the object of focus.

What, then, is this? If bodhisattvas, having transcended the teachings of conformity, investigate all phenomena and find that neither their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are real;

and because they are sustained by the power of familiarity with this investigation, they—without relying on further effort—attain internal mental composure within the realm of reality as it is, the non-conceptual sphere (*niṣprapañca-dhātu*) which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. This is what is called non-conceptual wisdom free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas are by nature of sharp faculties, why must they still practice the refinement of the faculties?
It is because they are caused to induce the middling-sharp faculty based on the soft-sharp faculty, and then to induce the superior-sharp faculty based on the middling-sharp faculty.

It has already been stated that all bodhisattvas by nature possess sharp faculties; yet, it is further stated that they should cultivate the refinement of their faculties from time to time. This is called "refining the faculties" because, within their own category, there exist three grades—mild and so forth—in which each subsequent grade is induced by the preceding one.

If it were otherwise, individuals belonging to the lineage of those with sharp faculties would possess faculties of only a single category, and the distinctions among the categories of faculties for bodhisattvas and others would be impossible to find.
Nevertheless, there are those who may attain it; for this reason, there are further distinctions among those of sharp faculties.
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle 14; *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle 15.
The Commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* compiled by Bodhisattva Sthiramati, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang under Imperial Decree. Part 4:
The Chapter on Discussion (*Vāda-viniścaya*). Section One of the Fourth Chapter on Discussion within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*: What is the determination of discussion?

Briefly stated, there are seven kinds: namely, the determination of meaning, the determination of explanation, the determination of analytical exposition, the determination of formal debate, the determination of compendium, the determination of the rules of discussion, and the determination of the secret.
The determination of meaning refers to the undertaking of a definitive analysis based on six types of meaning.
What are these six meanings? They are:
the meaning of intrinsic nature, the meaning of cause, the meaning of fruit, the meaning of activity, the meaning of association, and the meaning of progression.
The meaning of "intrinsic nature" refers to the three intrinsic natures, namely the imagined and so forth.
The meaning of "cause" refers to three causes:
first, the cause of arising; second, the cause of transformation; and third, the cause of accomplishment.
The cause of origination refers to the four conditions, such as the causal condition, because by means of these, all conditioned phenomena are produced.
