The cause of transformation refers to how those phenomena proceed in succession; for example, ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to the cessation of suffering, because through this sequence, defilement and purification proceed.

Regarding the "probans" (*hetu*): it refers to what is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is not so apprehended, and so forth, as subsumed under formal statements; for by means of this, one can establish a probandum (*sādhya*) that was previously unknown.
Regarding the meaning of "fruit," it refers to the five fruits.

What are the five? First, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*); second, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*); third, the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); fourth, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); and fifth, the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*).
The ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) refers to the ālayavijñāna and so forth.
The flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) refers to the various wholesome dharmas within one's own continuum that arise subsequently from the wholesome dharmas produced in previous lives.
The dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), which is perceived through the dominant power of the collective karma of all sentient beings.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) refers to things such as crops and agriculture.
The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) refers to the permanent extinction of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by means of the Noble Path.
Regarding the meaning of "action" (*karman*), there are five types of action:
first, the action of appropriation; second, the action of function; third, the action of exertion; fourth, the action of transformation; and fifth, the action of realization.
The meaning of these five types of karma is as explained previously in the section on the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*).
Regarding the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*), it refers to five kinds of association. What are these five?
First, association by aggregation; second, association by following; third, association by connection; fourth, association by state; fifth, association by transformation.
"Association by accumulation" (saṃnipāta-saṃprayoga) refers to the presence of wood, stones, and so forth within a house or similar structure.

"Association by persistence" (anubandha-saṃprayoga) refers to causes such as latent dispositions (anuśaya); because these exist, one says that [the mind] is associated with afflictions even when those afflictions are not manifesting.
Regarding "correspondence through connection" (*saṃbandha-saṃprayoga*), this refers to the mutual correspondence among relatives and the like.

Regarding "correspondence through state" (*avasthā-saṃprayoga*), this refers to the continuous states such as receiving benefit; because of these states, it is said that one is currently "in correspondence with pleasure," and so on, up to "in correspondence with neither-pain-nor-pleasure."

Regarding "correspondence through transformation" (*pariṇāma-saṃprayoga*): this refers to the manifestation of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) and so forth; because these exist, it is said that [the mind] corresponds with greed and so forth, or with faith and so forth.
As for the meaning of "transformation," there are five types of transformation: first, transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*);

second, transformation of abiding (*sthiti-pariṇāma*); third, transformation of inversion (*viparyāsa-pariṇāma*); fourth, transformation of non-inversion (*aviparyāsa-pariṇāma*); and fifth, transformation of differentiation (*viśeṣa-pariṇāma*).
Transformation by characteristics refers to the three conditioned characteristics, such as arising and so forth, because they evolve through their distinct characteristics.
Transformation by abiding refers to the fact that the supported phenomena abide and evolve within the supporting [basis].
"Reversal through inversion" refers to the fact that defiled phenomena do not proceed according to reality.
"Non-reversal through non-inversion" refers to the fact that purified phenomena proceed according to reality.
"Differentiated transformation" refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) transform according to distinctions such as past, future, present, internal, external, and so forth.
"Exegesis of the definitive analysis" refers to the ability to explain the essential tenets of various sūtras and to elucidate their meanings.
Furthermore, what are these?

Briefly, there are six kinds: the object to be fully known, the meaning to be fully known, the causes and conditions for full knowledge, the intrinsic nature of full knowledge, the fruit of full knowledge, and the realization of that fruit.
Because these six meanings are used to explain all sūtras exhaustively according to their respective applications, they are called the "Explanatory Determination" (Viniścaya).
The objects to be thoroughly known are the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
the meanings to be thoroughly known are impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth.
Thorough knowledge of causes and conditions refers to pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), guarding the sense doors, and so forth.
Thorough knowledge of intrinsic nature refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Thorough knowledge of the fruit refers to liberation (*vimukti*).
That realization and experience refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, there is an analytical determination explained through fourteen gates.
What are these fourteen?

These are: the gateway of comprehensive explanation, the gateway of comprehensive categories, the gateway of general and specific divisions, the gateway of successive unfolding, the gateway of prohibition, the gateway of the transformation of syllables, the gateway of disintegration and non-disintegration, the gateway of establishing the person (pudgala), the gateway of establishing distinctions, the gateway of principles, the gateway of thorough knowledge and so forth, the gateway of power and lack of power, the gateway of individual inducement, and the gateway of elicitation.

The Door of Compendium of Exegesis (*viniścaya-saṃgraha-mukha*) refers to those instances where the reasons for the dependent origination of various sūtras are proclaimed, along with the sequential meaning of the phrases, the underlying intentions, and the resolution of difficulties.

The Door of Compendium of Subjects (*vastu-saṃgraha-mukha*) refers to those instances where various sūtras are analyzed and explained by way of the subjects of training (*śikṣā-vastu*), the subjects of the Noble Truths (*ārya-satya-vastu*), and so forth.

As it is said: "Commit no evil, practice all that is good, and thoroughly subdue your own mind; this is the holy teaching of all Buddhas. In this verse, such points are explained in accordance with the three trainings.

Regarding the classification by way of general and specific sections: this refers to instances where a passage first presents a general summary in a single phrase, followed by a detailed explanation of its components in subsequent phrases.

For example, in the *Sūtra on the Collection of the Twelve Freedoms*, it first states the two phrases "one's own perfection" and "the perfection of others," and subsequently provides a detailed explanation of each in five phrases respectively; such cases are included here.

Regarding the "gate of successive opening and leading": it refers to those instances where [the teachings] are displayed as the basis for successive opening and leading; therefore, these dharmas are explained in this specific order.

Just as with the sequence of the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, one must first have faith and acceptance before exerting diligence; having exerted diligence, one then establishes mindfulness; once mindfulness is established, the mind attains stability; and once the mind is stable, one then knows things as they truly are—and so on.
The door of prohibition refers to those instances where, based upon a certain matter, that very matter is prohibited.
For example, in the *Sakalikā-sūtra*, based upon the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), four types of individuals (*pudgala*) are prohibited:

first, those who remain outside the True Dharma; second, those who remain within the True Dharma but become complacent merely by attaining hearing and reflection; third, those whose minds become timid and weak regarding the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*); and fourth, those whose accumulations (*sambhāra*) are not yet fulfilled.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I know, I see, and I declare the destruction of the outflows"—this passage of scripture precludes the first [type of person].
"Those who do not apply themselves with diligence to the cultivation of contemplative practice"—this precludes the second.
The analogy of the axe-handle is taught to refute the third [position].
The analogy of the raft is taught to refute the fourth.

Regarding the "gate of the transformation of syllables" (*akṣara-parāvṛtti-dvāra*), this refers to instances where it is shown that the manifest meaning of one set of syllables is transformed into another meaning; examples include verses such as those concerning lack of faith and ingratitude, which will be explained later.
Regarding the gate of ruin and non-ruin: it refers to those instances where the loss and non-loss [of the roots of goodness] are revealed, along with their respective means and distinctions.
As stated in the *Sujāta-sūtra*:
"Loss" refers to being defiled by and attached to internal and external bases of existence.
The internal basis has the five aggregates of grasping as its characteristic, while the external basis has the four dwellings, wife, children, and so forth as its characteristic.
"Non-disintegration" refers to being free from these two kinds of defiled attachment.

The failure of the means refers to not going forth into homelessness; or, even though one has gone forth, practicing with negligence so as to fail to attain the destruction of the outflows. That which is contrary to this constitutes the non-failure of the means.
The Buddha told Sujāta: "Noble son!
There are two matters that are both excellent and sublime: either shaving off the beard and hair, or even going forth into the homeless life."
If one has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and even declares for oneself that one will not undergo further existence,
this correctly reveals non-destruction and its means, while simultaneously revealing destruction and its means, because they are the opposites of these characteristics.
Regarding the distinction of non-destruction, it is as revealed in the verse: "The bhikṣus are exquisite, tranquil, and free from all outflows.
This reveals both renunciation and the exhaustion of the outflows.

To further clarify the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), other phrases are spoken: namely, freedom from desire, freedom from bondage, the nirvāṇa without appropriation (*anupādāna*), sustaining the final body, and subduing those who are the emissaries of Māra.

This demonstrates that through the mundane path one becomes free from desire, while through the supramundane path one eternally abandons the fetters conducive to the lower realm, eternally abandons the fetters conducive to the higher realm, and eternally abandons the internal basis for existence.

This is a brief explanation of the exhaustion of the cause and the exhaustion of the result, which also incidentally clarifies the distinctions regarding loss and ruin, as they are the opposites of these characteristics.
Regarding the establishment of the gateways for the *pudgala* (person): this refers to those instances where such statements are made based upon a certain number of *pudgalas*.
As stated in the *Jalopama-sūtra*, three and four types of distinctions are taught based on two kinds of *pudgalas*.
What are these two? They are the ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*) and the worldling who has seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya-pṛthagjana*).
There are three distinctions: namely, the absence of white dharmas, few white dharmas, and many white dharmas.
There are four distinctions regarding the vision of the truths (dṛṣṭisatya), namely, abiding in the four fruits: three of those in training (śaikṣa) and one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Regarding the door of establishing distinctions (*vyavasthāna-prabheda-mukha*): this refers to instances where the meaning of questions formulated as fourfold alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) and so forth is demonstrated.
As stated in the *Anityatā-sūtra*:
"Does one who observes correctly observe all forms?"
If one contemplates form, is it always correct contemplation?
One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first proposition refers to not superimposing the inversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, or self upon the other four aggregates such as feeling, and further contemplating them as that which should be known and abandoned.

The second phrase refers to the superimposition of the inversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self upon the aggregate of form, as well as regarding it as something not to be known and not to be abandoned.

The third phrase refers to the absence of the superimposition of the inversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self upon the aggregate of form, as well as regarding it as something to be known and to be abandoned.

The fourth phrase refers to the superimposition of the perversions of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self upon the four aggregates beginning with feeling, as well as regarding them as neither to be known nor to be abandoned.
Just as the fourfold formulation was established based on form (*rūpa*), so too should it be explained in detail for all instances, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest,
up to the statement:
"If one has accomplished what was to be done, does everyone consider themselves to no longer undergo future existence?"
If one claims for oneself that there will be no further existence, has one accomplished all that was to be done?
This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, until the end of their lives, constantly practice sublime conduct.
The second phrase refers to those who hold the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
The third phrase refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The fourth phrase refers to those other than the aforementioned characteristics.
The "Gate of Principles" (naya-mukha) refers to those instances where the meaning of six principles is revealed.

What are these six? First, the principle of true reality; second, the principle of realization; third, the principle of instruction; fourth, the principle of avoiding the two extremes; fifth, the principle of the inconceivable; and sixth, the principle of intentionality.
Regarding these six types, the first three should be understood through the subsequent three in their respective order.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus in the *Rasavāda-sūtra*:
"In regard to form, there is gratification," and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, it is shown that through the approach of avoiding the two extremes of superimposition and denial, one definitively realizes the approach to the true meaning.
The statement that there is "taste, fault, and renunciation" demonstrates the avoidance of the extreme of denial.
Regarding "from form up to consciousness," this reveals the avoidance of the extreme of reification (*samāropa-anta*).
This is because it demonstrates that defilement and purification depend solely upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and not upon a self (*ātman*).
...up to the point where he addressed the bhikṣus:
"By means of this, I have personally realized and known, up to the point that I have already awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This reveals the principle of realization attained through the definitive resolution of the inconceivable principle.
This reveals that it is the true realization personally experienced within;
thus, all such sūtras are the mode of the teaching, which should be understood through the mode of the intended meaning (*ābhiprāyika-naya*).

This means that this sutra was spoken with the intention of realizing and experiencing the objects to be fully known, the meanings to be fully known, the full knowledge itself, and the fruit of full knowledge.
"The objects to be fully known" refers to form and so forth.
The meaning of "that which is to be fully known" refers to the presence of gratification and so forth.
By means of these specific distinctions, one fully knows the phenomena such as form.
"Full knowledge" refers to knowing, as it truly is, the five aggregates of clinging through these three modes of turning.
The fruit of thorough knowledge refers to the liberation, even unto ultimate liberation, attained by all beings from this world of gods down to humans and celestial beings alike.
Its realization and experience refers to one’s own direct realization and knowledge: "I have realized and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Regarding the "gates of thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) and so forth: this refers to those passages which, based on the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), reveal the meaning of the characteristic of thorough knowledge, the characteristic of permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa*), the characteristic of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and the characteristic of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Furthermore, they reveal the meaning of the distinctions among the categories of these characteristics of reality; the meaning of the relationship between the dependent and the basis; the meaning of the characteristics of factors that obstruct thorough knowledge and so forth; the meaning of the characteristics of factors that are conducive to thorough knowledge and so forth; and the meaning of the faults and virtues associated with the lack of thorough knowledge and its attainment. This is also explained in detail in the *Rasavighāta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Relish of Craving).
The characteristic of reality refers to the characteristic of the truth of suffering as comprised within the aggregates of clinging.
The characteristic of thorough knowledge refers to knowing, as it truly is, the presence of gratification and so forth regarding that very [suffering].

The characteristic of permanent abandonment and the characteristic of realization refer to attaining liberation from all worldly realms, because one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) through the permanent abandonment of all hindrances.
The characteristic of cultivation refers to dwelling in the frequent practice of a mind free from inversion.
Regarding the characteristic of differentiation by category, there are five types of differentiation within the characteristic of reality, namely: form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Regarding the characteristic of thorough knowledge, there are three types of differentiation, namely: savoring (*āsvāda*); because of savoring, and so on, up to renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*); and because of renunciation, knowing it as it truly is.
The characteristic of permanent abandonment and the characteristic of realization each have two types of distinctions, namely: liberation from afflictions and liberation from suffering.
The statement that "from this world of gods and humans, including both gods and humans, all attain liberation" clarifies liberation from afflictions.
In order to clarify this specific meaning, the term "renunciation" (niḥsaraṇa) is subsequently stated. Why is this?
Because another sutra says:
What is renunciation?
It refers to that state wherein craving is eternally extinguished, craving is eternally severed, and one has transcended craving.
Thus, because the afflictions that give rise to future suffering have attained dissociation, one is also liberated from suffering.
To clarify this meaning of distinction, it is next stated that there is "freedom from bondage" and "ultimate liberation.
There are two types of distinctions regarding the characteristics of cultivation: namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The "mind free from inversion" indicates the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); "abiding through extensive cultivation" indicates the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the characteristic of the relationship between the supported and the support, this means that the characteristics such as reality (*tattva*) and so forth are shown to serve as the basis for each subsequent stage.
The characteristic of factors that obstruct thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and so forth refers to not knowing, as it truly is, these three turnings.

The characteristic of factors conducive to thorough knowledge and so forth refers to observing the characteristics of gratification (*āsvāda*) and so forth within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), as they have been established.

Regarding the characteristics of faults such as non-thorough knowledge: this refers to not being liberated, up to and including not realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
That which is contrary to these is called the characteristic of virtues such as thorough knowledge.

The gate of power and lack of power refers to those instances where it is demonstrated that every single word possesses functional efficacy; for if even one word were not spoken, the meaning would remain uncomprehended.
As stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*:
"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises," namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth.
Each of these phrases possesses its own functional efficacy, as explained previously in the section on the characteristics of dependent origination.
The "Gate of Individual Induction" refers to instances where a single phrase from a sutra is first presented and subsequently explained at length through immeasurable interpretive methods.
For example, as the sutra says:
"If a bhikṣu accomplishes six dharmas, he could even blow apart the high and vast king of mountains, the Snowy Mountains, with the breath of his mouth, let alone a corpse of ignorance."
What are the six? They are:
when monks possess skillfulness in generating the mind, up to and including skillfulness in means.
What is a monk’s skillfulness in generating the mind?

That is to say, a bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, dwells having fully attained up to the fourth dhyāna; such a bhikṣu possesses skill regarding the arising of the mind.
What is a bhikṣu’s skill in the stability of the mind?

It refers to the fact that, through diligent cultivation, a bhikṣu transforms meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that belong to the category of decline into those that belong to the category of stability; such is a bhikṣu’s skill in the stability of the mind.
What is a bhikṣu’s skill in the arising of the mind?

It is when, through thorough cultivation, a bhikṣu transforms meditative absorption that belongs to the stage of abiding into one that belongs to the stage of progress; such is a bhikṣu’s skill in the arising of the mind.
What is a bhikṣu’s skill in the cultivation and increase [of wholesome qualities]?

It refers to a bhikṣu who employs skillful means to give rise to wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, and so forth, as extensively explained in the two right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). In this way, a bhikṣu possesses skill in the cultivation and increase [of wholesome qualities].
What is a bhikṣu’s skill in diminishing?

It refers to a bhikṣu who employs skillful means to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen, and so forth, as extensively explained regarding the two right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*). This is a bhikṣu’s skill in diminishing.
What is a bhikṣu’s skill in means?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, desiring the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration through desire and the cultivation of the formations of abandonment, practices the four bases of psychic power, and so forth, as explained at length. This is a bhikṣu’s skill in means.

The "gate of elicitation" refers to a place where, within each individual phrase, four propositions are proclaimed; and each of those individual phrases is further divided into four propositions, thus proceeding in an infinite succession of elicitation.

As the Buddha’s sūtras state: "Bodhisattvas have four methods for purifying the cultivation of bodhi: first, skillfully cultivating emptiness; second, having a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings; third, constantly gathering and benefiting the assembly of bodhisattvas; and fourth, extensively offering the gift of Dharma with an undefiled mind."
These four dharmas purify the cultivation of bodhi through the gates of benefiting oneself and others, for the purpose of counteracting four types of opposing obstacles.
What are these four?
First, attachment to the flavor of meditative concentration; second, ill-will; third, pride; fourth, attachment to gain and offerings.
Furthermore, there is a distinction: the first reveals the antidote for abandoning afflictions, while the others reveal the distancing from inferior vehicles.
Bodhisattvas distance themselves from the inferior vehicle by means of three causes and conditions:

first, by embracing all sentient beings; second, by bringing to maturity those who have already entered the Dharma; and third, by causing those who have not yet entered the Dharma to enter the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a distinction: the first reveals the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), while the others reveal the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*).
This threefold distinction consists in gathering and maturing [beings] so that they may enter the three gates, for each is capable of generating superior merit.
Furthermore, there are two distinct conditions:
first, by way of intention, which means being accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness;
second, by way of correct practice, which refers to the two practices of teaching and realization.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas who accomplish four dharmas are able to cultivate emptiness:

first, the absence of mental fluctuation within; second, being sustained by the power of discernment through faith and understanding; third, penetrating all phenomena as they truly are; and fourth, liberation from all hindrances.
These four dharmas reveal the basis for cultivation and the distinctions within cultivation.
What serves as the basis?
It is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
What are the distinctions in cultivation?
First, by means of the path of ordinary beings, which is sustained by the power of hearing and reflection;
second, by means of the path of training, which is the realization of the true nature of all phenomena.
Third, by means of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), which refers to being liberated from all obstacles.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas who accomplish four qualities have minds free from obstruction toward all sentient beings:
first, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); second, not disparaging right practice; third, not discriminating signs (*nimitta*); and fourth, enduring toil and hardship.
These four dharmas reveal the distinction between the basis and the unimpeded mind.
What serves as the basis?
It is the loving-kindness cultivated during past lives.
What is the distinction of the unimpeded mind?

It means that toward those who abide in wrong conduct, the mind harbors no resentment or hostility; toward enemies, one does not conceptualize them as such; and for the sake of benefiting others, one exerts oneself with tireless diligence.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas who accomplish four qualities are always able to gather and benefit the assembly of bodhisattvas:
first, not evaluating themselves; second, providing correct instruction and guidance; third, being gentle and easy to dwell with; and fourth, diligently serving and making offerings.
These four dharmas demonstrate the distinctions between the basis and the benefit.
What is the basis?
It is the subduing of pride.
What is the distinction of gathering and benefiting?
It refers to the three phrases explained later, applied respectively to the three types of bodhisattvas: those who are inferior, equal, and superior.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas who accomplish four dharmas are able to extensively provide the gift of Dharma with an undefiled mind:

first, skillfully understanding obstacles and difficulties; second, being well able to dispel ignorance and mental depression; third, joyfully accepting and gathering [disciples]; and fourth, loving and delighting in the Dharma as their refuge.
These four dharmas demonstrate the basis [of the teaching] and the distinctions in the extensive opening of the gift of Dharma.
What is the basis?
It is the thorough realization that gain, honor, and respect are obstructive and difficult conditions.
What is the extensive opening of the distinctions of the gift of Dharma?
It consists of demonstrating, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening.

"Demonstrating" refers to those who are submerged in ignorance; "instructing and encouraging" refers to those who are attached to negligence or who disparage themselves as inferior; and "gladdening" refers to those whose correct practice is perfected, because they naturally delight in the Dharma.
Thus, within each of the first four statements, four further distinctions are induced; such as these are called the "gates of induction" (*ākṣepa-mukha*).

Regarding the "analytical determination through detailed exposition," this refers to the application, as appropriate, of single-phrase, antecedent-phrase, subsequent-phrase, two-phrase, three-phrase, four-phrase, affirmative, and prohibitive formulations to the phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) as they have been described.

As for "one by one," this refers to the method of inquiry: having first asked about one dharma in relation to each of the other dharmas, and having set aside that dharma, one then asks about a second dharma in relation to the others; in this manner, one asks about every single dharma one by one.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"If one accomplishes the sense-base of the eye, does one also accomplish the sense-base of visible form?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the sense-base of visible form, does one also accomplish the sense-base of the eye?"
This should be answered by following the preceding formulation.
If one possesses the eye base, does one also possess the ear base?
This should be answered with a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭi).
In this manner, it should be stated accordingly up to the sense-field of the mind (manāyatana).
If one is endowed with the sense-field of the eye, is one also endowed with the sense-field of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
This too should be answered by means of the "prior clause" (pūrvapada).
If one accomplishes the sense-base of form, does one also accomplish the sense-base of the eye?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the sense-base of the eye, does one also accomplish the sense-base of form?
This should be answered by means of a *pṛṣṭhottara* (subsequent) formula.
If one accomplishes the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), does one also accomplish the sphere of the ear (*śrotrāyatana*)?
This too should be answered by means of a *paścātpādaka* (consequent) formula.
Thus, it should be explained accordingly up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
If one accomplishes the ear-base (*śrotrāyatana*), does one also accomplish the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*)?
This should be answered by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The same should be stated accordingly, up to the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*).
In this manner, each successive category is gradually reduced; the same principle should be applied accordingly to all other cases as appropriate.

Regarding the "conformity with the preceding term" (*pūrvapādaka*): it refers to taking any two phenomena from among all phenomena and posing questions to one another, answering the question by relying upon the preceding phenomenon.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"Is that which is knowledge also that which is known?
And conversely, is that which is known also knowledge?"
This should be answered by following the preceding formula:
All knowledges are also objects of knowledge;
there are objects of knowledge that are not knowledges, namely, all other phenomena.

Regarding the "conformity with the subsequent term" (*paścātpādaka*), this refers to two dharmas being questioned in relation to one another, where the answer to the question is given by relying on the subsequent dharma.
For example, it is like asking:
"Is that which is the grasped also the grasper?"
If that which is the grasper is also the grasped?
This should be answered with a "consequent-to-the-subsequent" formula:
whatever is a grasper is also the grasped; however, there are things that are the grasped which are not graspers.

There are things that are objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) but not subjects of apprehension (*grāhaka*); these refer to the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*), and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), excluding those associated with consciousness.
Regarding the "two phrases," this refers to answering a question with two alternatives, and no more than that.
For example, based on the establishment [of categories] by way of the aggregates (*skandha*) and based on the establishment by way of the elements (*dhātu*), one might ask:
"Is that which is counted among the aggregates also counted among the elements?
Or, is that which is counted among the elements also counted among the aggregates?"
This should be answered with two propositions:

either it is reckoned among the aggregates (skandha) but not among the elements (dhātu), namely the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha). Why is this so?

There is no single *dhātu* that entirely subsumes the characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), nor one that entirely subsumes the characteristics of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Alternatively, there are *dhātus* whose number does not correspond to the number of aggregates; this refers to the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the "three propositions" (*trikoṭika*), it refers to answering a question with only three propositions.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"If something is counted among the aggregates (skandha), is it also counted among the bases (āyatana)?
And if something is counted among the bases, is it also counted among the aggregates?"
This should be answered with three propositions:
either it is reckoned among the aggregates (skandha) but not among the bases (āyatana), namely the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha);
or it is reckoned among the bases but not among the aggregates, namely the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Some are counted among both the aggregates (*skandha*) and the bases (*āyatana*), namely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*).
Those that are neither are definitely not found among the aggregates and bases.
Regarding the "four alternatives" (*catuṣkoṭi*), this refers to answering a question by means of a fourfold formulation.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"If one possesses the eye faculty, does one also possess the ear faculty?
Conversely, if one possesses the ear faculty, does one also possess the eye faculty?"
This should be answered by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first proposition refers to one who is deaf and whose eye-faculty has already arisen and is not abandoned.
The second proposition refers to one who is blind and whose ear-faculty has already arisen and is not abandoned.
The third phrase refers to the faculties of the eye and ear having already arisen and not being abandoned.
The fourth phrase excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "expressing assent," it means answering a question in accordance with it; one expresses assent to the question by using such words.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"Are all things that are impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
And if they are conditioned phenomena, are they all impermanent?"
One should respond by affirming:
"The question is thus.
As for the phrase of negation (*pratiṣedha-pada*), it refers to answering a question with "it is not so," thereby negating the question with the words "it is not so."
If someone were to ask:
"How many truths (satya) include those formations (saṃskāra) that exist outside the aggregates (skandha)?
one should answer by way of negation:

Regarding the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, which states that there are no formations apart from the aggregates: this refers to the method of resolving all points of truth and falsehood through questions and answers based on the eight interrogative particles (*kathaṃ*).
As for these eight interrogative particles, for example, one might ask:
Who is it that has nothing to be attained?
It refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has already attained the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
What is it that they have nothing to attain?
That is to say, regarding the characteristics of the apprehended and the characteristics of the apprehender:
by means of what is there non-apprehension?
It is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is there nothing to be attained?
It is because one seeks to rescue and liberate all sentient beings, causing them to dwell in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By what means is there nothing to be attained?
That is to say: encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world, hearing the true Dharma, applying correct mental attention, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
What is it that is not apprehended?
It is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
In what is there non-apprehension?
It is said: from the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) up to the tenth bodhisattva stage.
To what extent is there non-apprehension?

This refers to eleven kinds: first, that which has already arisen and already ceased; second, that which has not yet arisen; third, that which is present before one; fourth, that which is produced by the power of causes; fifth, that which is produced by the power of virtuous friends; sixth, the non-apprehension of all phenomena; seventh, the non-apprehension of emptiness; eighth, the presence of the conceit of "I"; ninth, the absence of the conceit of "I"; tenth, not having yet completed the accumulations; and eleventh, having already completed the accumulations. Thus, these eleven are non-apprehensible.
One should understand them in their proper order according to all that exists—past, future, and present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near.

As it is with the subject, so it is with the object; that is to say, whether it be the non-apprehension of the agent, the non-apprehension of the object, the non-apprehension of the instrument, the non-apprehension of the purpose, the non-apprehension by means of, the non-apprehension of that, the non-apprehension within, or the non-apprehension to such an extent—one should understand all such instances in this same way.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of principles for the definitive resolution of equal discourse: namely, refutation, establishment, severance, and awakening.
Regarding "refutation," this refers to the negation and dismantling of another's position, stating that their flawed exposition is not a virtuous matter.
"Establishing" refers to establishing one's own position, declaring that this well-spoken teaching is truly a virtuous matter.
"Severing" refers to being able to resolve the various doubts raised by others.
One who is capable of awakening refers to one who enlightens the ignorant mind and causes it to understand the profound meaning.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of reasoned analysis for determining principles, as stated in the verse:
"Essential nature, basis, consciousness, purity, and means, etc."
One should know that each of the five [objects] has six [aspects], as one contemplates all dharmas that are objects of knowledge.
Regarding the six [factors] such as intrinsic nature: first, intrinsic nature; second, cause; third, object; fourth, aspect; fifth, immediate antecedent; and sixth, predominant condition.

The six factors beginning with the "basis" are: first, the basis; second, the support; third, inclusion; fourth, association; fifth, accomplishment; and sixth, defilement. The six factors beginning with "consciousness" are:
first, consciousness; second, sensation; third, perception; fourth, attention; fifth, knowledge; and sixth, thorough understanding.
The six [aspects] beginning with purity are: first, purity; second, terminology; third, renunciation; fourth, profundity; fifth, the gateways of liberation; and sixth, entry into all phenomena.

The six [aspects] beginning with skillful means (*upāya*) are: first, skillful means; second, penetration (*prativedha*); third, cultivation (*bhāvanā*); fourth, perfect realization (*pariniṣpatti*); fifth, culmination (*niṣṭhā*); and sixth, elicitation (*ākṣepa*).
There are four kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), namely: substantial intrinsic nature, nominal intrinsic nature, conventional intrinsic nature, and ultimate intrinsic nature.

There are four kinds of causes: namely, the cause of production (*janana-hetu*), the cause of establishment (*upastambha-hetu*), the cause of transformation (*pariṇāma-hetu*), and the cause of reversal (*pratyāgamana-hetu*).

There are seven kinds of objects: namely, the object with signs (*nimitta-viṣaya*), the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa-viṣaya*), the object of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-viṣaya*), the object of stability (*sthiti-viṣaya*), the object of augmentation (*samāropa-viṣaya*), the object of diminution (*apavāda-viṣaya*), and the object of mastery (*vaśitva-viṣaya*).

There are five types of modes of activity (*ākāra*): namely, the mode of analytical investigation, the mode of differentiation, the mode of correct understanding, the mode of observation, and the mode of performance and subsequent performance.

There are nine kinds of immediate succession (*samanantara*): namely, immediate succession of its own kind, immediate succession of a different kind, immediate succession of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), immediate succession of retrogression, immediate succession of arising, immediate succession of contiguity, immediate succession of separation, immediate succession of origination, and immediate succession of cessation.

There are seven kinds of predominance: namely, predominance of appropriation, predominance of arising, predominance of abiding, predominance of the defilement of enjoyment, predominance of purification, predominance of the field, and predominance of grasping.

There are eight kinds of bases: namely, the basis of the realms, the basis of the destinies, the basis of the continents, the basis of villages and fields, the basis of persons, the basis of freedom from illness, the basis of ethical discipline, and the basis of adornment.

There are five kinds of dependence: namely, dependence on requisites, dependence on virtuous friends, dependence on the Dharma, dependence on mental attention (*manasikāra*), and dependence on meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

There are eleven kinds of inclusion: namely, inclusion by element (*dhātu*), inclusion by characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), inclusion by category (*jāti*), inclusion by stage (*avasthā*), inclusion by accompaniment (*sahāya*), inclusion by time (*kāla*), inclusion by direction (*deśa*), inclusion by totality (*sakala-bhāga*), inclusion by partiality (*ekadeśa-bhāga*), inclusion by mutual relation (*anyonya*), and inclusion by ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

There are ten types of association (saṃprayoga): namely, association by way of other-nature, non-contradictory association, universal association, non-universal association, association with that which is to be remedied, association with the remedy, association through prior habituation, association not through prior habituation, inferior association, and vast association.
There are three kinds of accomplishment: namely, accomplishment of seeds, accomplishment of mastery, and accomplishment of manifest activity.
There are four kinds of affliction: namely, affliction of defilements, affliction of karma, affliction of birth, and affliction of hindrances.
There are six kinds of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
There are three kinds of feeling, namely: suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

There are twenty kinds of perceptions (*saṃjñā*), namely: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of danger, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of impurity, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a dismembered corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a corpse being devoured, the perception of a blood-stained corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of a skeleton, and the perception of the contemplation of emptiness.

There are seven kinds of mental attention (*manasikāra*): namely, mental attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*), mental attention of detachment (*prāvivekya*), mental attention of delight in withdrawal (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*), mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), mental attention of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*), and mental attention of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).

There are ten kinds of knowledge: namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising.

There are nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*): namely, the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin pertaining to the desire realm; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin pertaining to the form and formless realms; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation pertaining to the desire realm; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation pertaining to the form and formless realms; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of the path pertaining to the desire realm; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of the path pertaining to the form and formless realms; the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm; and the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm.

There are seven kinds of purity: namely, purity of virtue, purity of mind, purity of view, purity through the overcoming of doubt, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the progress along the path, and purity of knowledge and vision regarding the final cessation of the path.
There are eight kinds of interrogative particles (*kathaṃ-vastu*), namely the eight "how" particles; and there are eight kinds of conditional particles (*yadi-vastu*).

There are six kinds of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*): namely, worldly renunciation, the renunciation of the Śrāvakas, the renunciation of the Pratyekabuddhas, the renunciation of the Mahāyāna, non-final renunciation, and final renunciation.

Profundity is of ten kinds, namely: profundity of characteristics, profundity of affliction, profundity of purification, profundity of dependent origination, profundity of karma, profundity of gnosis, profundity of birth, profundity of awakening, profundity of the Buddha, and profundity of the teaching.
There are three doors of liberation, namely: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*).

There are eight aspects for entering into all phenomena (*dharma*): that all phenomena have desire as their root, are produced by mental attention (*manasikāra*), are gathered by contact (*sparśa*), are drawn in by feeling (*vedanā*), have concentration (*samādhi*) as their precursor, have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their excellence, have liberation (*vimukti*) as their firmness, and have renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) as their finality.

There are seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*), namely: the skillful means of maintenance, the skillful means of yoga, the skillful means of signs, the skillful means of discernment, the skillful means of skipping, the skillful means of immediate succession, and the skillful means of immediate succession with skipping.

There are five kinds of thorough penetration: namely, thorough penetration of signs and words; thorough penetration of the contained and the container; slow thorough penetration; swift thorough penetration; and thorough penetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

There are four kinds of cultivation: namely, cultivation through acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation through removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*), and cultivation through antidotes (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).

There are four kinds of perfect realization: namely, perfect realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*), perfect realization of detachment (*vairāgya-sākṣātkriyā*), perfect realization of the fulfillment of faculties (*indriya-paripūri-sākṣātkriyā*), and perfect realization of qualities (*guṇa-sākṣātkriyā*).
Ultimacy is of six kinds: namely, ultimacy of knowledge, ultimacy of abandonment, ultimate ultimacy, non-ultimate ultimacy, inferior ultimacy, and vast ultimacy.
There are twenty kinds of production, namely: the production of the immeasurables, up to the production of the sublime knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
*Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Fifteen; *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle Sixteen.
The Commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* compiled by Bodhisattva Sthiramati, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang under Imperial Decree.

Part Two of Chapter Four: The Section on Determination (*Viniścaya-vibhaṅga*), "The Treatise" (*Śāstra*). Regarding the "real intrinsic nature" (*dravya-svabhāva*), it refers to the truly existent nature of all phenomena.
The nature of designation refers to the designated existence of all phenomena.
The conventional nature refers to the conventional existence of all phenomena.
The ultimate nature refers to the ultimate existence of all phenomena.
The productive cause refers to the four conditions, beginning with the causal condition.
The evidentiary cause refers to the three means of valid cognition:
first, direct perception; second, inference; and third, verbal testimony.
The "transforming cause" refers to dependent origination in its forward order (*anuloma*).
The "returning cause" refers to dependent origination in its reverse order (*pratiloma*).

"Objects with signs" refers to the five objects, such as form, which are the objects of the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness; this is because that which arises from perceiving these [objects] possesses only non-conceptual signs (*nirvikalpa-nimitta*).
The object of conceptualization refers to the objects perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because conceptualization arises by taking these objects as its basis.
The object of counteraction refers to those objects which, when taken as a basis, cause one to abandon defilements, because they serve as effective antidotes.
The object of abiding refers to that which, when taken as an object, enables the arising of the noble, celestial, and Brahma-abodes, because it is that in which the various noble ones abide.
The object of augmentation refers to that which, when taken as an object, enables further progress and advancement, because it is the cause for increasing excellence.

The object of diminution refers to that object which, when taken as a focal point, allows one to enter the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); it is so called because it is the cause for the diminution of mind and mental factors.

The object of mastery refers to that object which, when taken as a focal point, gives rise to superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); it is so called because it is the cause of mastery.
The analysis of modes refers to the analysis of phenomena according to their various categories, such as those with form and those without form, those visible and those invisible, and so forth.

Regarding the aspect of differentiation: this refers to the meaning of the differentiation among phenomena, such as the single characteristic of faith, which may be termed "purity of mind," "delight," or "acceptance," and so forth.

The aspect of correct comprehension refers to correctly comprehending the object of focus through various aspects; for example, that which has the aspect of discernment is called consciousness (*vijñāna*), that which has the aspect of grasping images is called perception (*saṃjñā*), and that which has the aspect of experiencing is called sensation (*vedanā*). Such are the cases.

Regarding the aspects of observation (*ākāra*), these refer to the sixteen aspects: namely, the four aspects of impermanence and so forth; the four aspects of cause and so forth; the four aspects of cessation and so forth;

and the four aspects of the path and so forth. Alternatively, there are the six mundane aspects: namely, the aspect of coarseness (*audārika*), the aspect of hindrance (*āvaraṇa*), the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*), the aspect of tranquility (*śānta*), the aspect of excellence (*praṇīta*), and the aspect of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Regarding the aspect of "acting in accordance with what has been done": this means that after having performed a task, one further acts in accordance with it; for example, just as one has already well-guarded by means of a certain practice, one subsequently initiates other practices of guarding in accordance with that initial one.

Regarding "immediately preceding [condition] of its own kind" (*sabhāga-samanantara*): this means that immediately after greed, greed arises again; the same applies to hatred and so forth, because they arise as the immediate antecedent of their respective distinct types.

Regarding "immediately preceding conditions of different categories" (*visabhāga-samanantara*): this refers to cases such as anger arising immediately after greed, the form realm arising immediately after the desire realm, and the formless realm arising immediately after the form realm, and so forth.

Regarding "the immediate succession of samāpatti" and so forth: this refers to the arising of states immediately following a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). For example, immediately after a wholesome state of the desire realm, one enters the first *dhyāna*; immediately after the first *dhyāna*, one returns to a state of the desire realm.
In this same manner, one should understand the second dhyāna and so forth, as well as the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), according to reason.
Regarding "immediately following from falling away" (*hāny-anantaram*), this refers to that which arises immediately upon falling away from the dhyānas and so forth.
"Arising as immediate" (*samanantara*) refers to that which arises immediately at the time of birth, such as when one is born from the desire realm immediately into the form realm and so forth.
"Adjacent immediate" (*anantara-samanantara*) refers to the successive arising of various minds and mental factors without interruption; because within this interval, the mind is not severed.

Regarding "separated by an interval" (vyavahita-anantara): this refers to occasions such as when emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), because there is an interval between the preceding moments of mind and mental factors and the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors.
"Arising as immediate antecedent" means that when this dharma has ceased, that dharma arises in immediate succession.

"Cessation as immediate antecedent" means that when this dharma has ceased, that dharma ceases in immediate succession; for example, when the mind and mental factors have ceased in immediate succession, one either enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), or enters the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
"Predominance in grasping" refers to the fact that the faculties such as the eye possess a predominant power with respect to the apprehension of their respective objects.
"Predominance in production" refers to the fact that the male and female faculties possess a predominant power with respect to the production of conception and gestation.
Regarding the predominance of abiding: this refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) having the power of predominance over the abiding of the body and so forth.
Regarding the predominance of the defilement of enjoyment: this refers to the five feeling-faculties (*pañca-vedanendriyāṇi*) having the power of predominance over that which is enjoyed.

Furthermore, because they are underlain by greed and the other [afflictions]: that is to say, pleasure is underlain by greed, pain is underlain by hatred, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure is underlain by delusion.

Regarding the predominance of purification: this refers to the five faculties, such as faith, and the three faculties, such as "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,'" because they possess predominant power with respect to both mundane and supramundane purified phenomena.
Regarding the predominance of the field (*kṣetra-adhipati*): this refers to the fact that collective karma possesses a predominant power over the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Regarding the predominance of appropriation (*upādāna-adhipati*): this refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in relation to derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
The basis of the realms refers to the body comprised within the desire realm and so forth.
The basis of the destinies refers to the body comprised within the five destinies.
The basis of the continents refers to Jambudvīpa and so forth.
The basis of the village field refers to that which exists depending upon this village field, taking it as its very basis.
The basis of the person (pudgala) refers to that which exists depending upon this person, taking it as its very basis.
That which is the basis for health means that if something exists in dependence upon health, then that very [health] is used as its basis.
That which is the basis for ethical discipline (*śīla*) means that if something exists in dependence upon ethical discipline, then that very [discipline] is used as its basis.
That which is the basis for adornment refers to whatever various monastic adornments give rise to the various meritorious qualities; these are then taken as the basis.
That which is the basis for requisites refers to the four reliances, namely clothing and so forth.
The basis of the spiritual friend refers to that which, when relied upon, gives rise to the wholesome and so forth.
The basis of the Dharma refers to the twelvefold teaching, such as the sūtras and other divisions.
The basis of mental attention refers to the seven types of mental attention, namely, the mental attention that discerns characteristics and the others.
The basis for *samāpatti* refers to the seven meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
As the Sūtra says:
"I declare that by relying on the first *dhyāna*, one can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*); this applies likewise up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)."
Regarding inclusion by element (*dhātu-saṃgraha*): this refers to the seeds of the various elements, by which they are able to include the phenomena produced from those seeds.
Regarding inclusion by characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha*): this refers to the fact that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena are able to include themselves.
Inclusion by way of category refers to being subsumed under the ten bases of form and the aggregate of form based on their categorical nature, and so forth.
Inclusion by way of state refers to being subsumed under states such as those conducive to pleasant feeling.
Regarding inclusion by accompaniment (*sahāya-saṃgraha*): this refers to being included within the five aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) because they are its attendants, and so forth.
Regarding inclusion by time (*kāla-saṃgraha*): this refers to the past and so forth including the past and so forth.
Spatial inclusion refers to the fact that whatever aggregates and so forth exist within a particular space are included within that very space.
Total inclusion refers to the way that all forms—those of the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted—are subsumed within the category of "form."
"Inclusion by way of a single part" refers to the inclusion of the aggregate of form within the eye-faculty, and so forth.
"Mutual inclusion" refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases including one another.
Regarding inclusion by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-saṃgraha*): it refers to all phenomena being included within suchness (*tathatā*) as impermanent, suffering, impure, empty, and non-self.
Regarding association with other-nature (*parabhāva-yoga*): it refers to being associated with other-nature rather than with its own nature.

Regarding "conjunction through non-contradiction": this refers to cases where, although there is conjunction with another nature, they are not contradictory and do not exclude one another—such as greed and hatred, or pleasure and pain, and so forth.

Regarding those associated with universal occurrence: contact, feeling, perception, volition, and attention are present in all minds; the four afflictions—ignorance, the conceit of "I am," self-love, and the view of a personal identity—are present in the afflicted mind.
Regarding association with non-universal [factors]: this refers to greed and so forth, as well as faith and so forth, excluding the universal factors.
Regarding association with the objects of counteraction: this refers to the mutual association of the various afflictions.
"Correspondence through remediation" refers to the mutual correspondence of wholesome phenomena subsumed under the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
"Correspondence through prior habituation" refers to all corresponding phenomena, with the exception of supramundane phenomena and those obtained subsequent to the supramundane.
"Those not previously practiced" refers to the various associated dharmas excluded previously.
"Inferior associations" refers to the various associated dharmas subsumed under the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding "vast correspondence" (vaipulya-yoga), this refers to all the corresponding dharmas possessed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The characteristics of the accomplishment of the various defiled consciousnesses up to the seven kinds of purity have already been explained; they shall not be further expounded here.

Regarding the eight interrogative pronouns: they are "who believes," "what is believed," "by what is one believed," "for what purpose is one believed," "through what is one believed," "whose belief is it," "in what is one believed," and "how much is believed."

Eighth, regarding "terms" (*pada*): this refers to that which is capable of being believed, that which is believed, the act of believing, that for the sake of which one believes, that by means of which one believes, that which is believed, that in relation to which one believes, and the extent to which one believes.
All such immeasurable dharma-gates possess these eight aspects.
That which is not ultimate deliverance refers to that by way of the mundane path;
that which is ultimate deliverance refers to that by way of the supramundane path.
The first four are easy to understand, so they are not explained again.
"Profound characteristics" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
"Profound defilement" refers to how true suchness (*tathatā*) can be defiled yet remain undefiled.
The profundity of purity refers to how it is that very suchness (tathatā) is both pure and yet not pure.

The profundity of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) refers to how there is no dharma that possesses a real functional activity toward its own arising, yet those various dharmas nonetheless arise in manifold ways, and so forth.
Furthermore, although there is in reality no self, it appears as if there were a self.
Profundity of karma means that while there is karma and its maturation, an agent cannot be found.
Profundity of wisdom means non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
How is it that this wisdom, being non-conceptual, is yet able to clearly perceive the nature of *tathatā*?
Regarding "giving rise to the profound," it means that all bodhisattvas manifest birth not through the power of karma or afflictions.

Regarding the profundity of bodhi: within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the bodhi of all Buddhas cannot be established as having a single nature, because it is realized by immeasurable continuities;
nor can it be established as having diverse natures, because its basis is without differentiation.

The profound nature of all Buddhas means that within a single great assembly, there are immeasurable and boundless Buddha-Bhagavāns with various bodies and various intentions, yet it is not said that there is any distinction between self and other.
Furthermore, the transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) does not abide in the marks of a Buddha, yet is able to perform various buddha-activities.

"Teaching the profound" refers to the various distinctions of secret intentions (*abhiprāya*) within the Mahāyāna teachings, as well as the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) and all dharmas.
The characteristics of desire as the root and so forth have already been explained and need not be further elaborated.
Regarding the skillful means of sustenance, this refers to all the skillful means pertaining to the accumulations (*sambhāra*).
The skillful means of yoga refers to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The skillful means of signs refers to all the skillful means regarding the signs of tranquility (śamatha), exertion (pragraha), and equanimity (upekṣā).
The skillful means of decisive resolution refers to all the skillful means within the stages conducive to decisive resolution (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The skillful means of intermittent application refers to the skillful means of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*).
The proximate expedient means refers to the expedient means of definitive discernment (*viniścaya*).
The expedient means of immediate succession and separation refers to the two types of expedient means: namely, yoga and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Within the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), they are termed "proximate" (*sāmantaka*); within the application of skillful means (*upāyasaṃdhāraṇa*), they are termed "remote" (*vyavahita*), because they are distant from the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
As for the cultivation of thorough comprehension and its perfect realization, these have already been explained elsewhere, and thus are not further expounded here.
The culmination of wisdom refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The culmination of abandonment refers to the permanent and complete eradication of all afflictions without remainder.
The ultimate culmination refers to that which is achieved by means of the supramundane path.
That which is not ultimate and final refers to the mundane path.
Inferior culmination refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Vast culmination refers to the buddhas and bodhisattvas.
The culmination of a bodhisattva refers to the final stage.
The culmination of all Buddhas refers to the moment when unobstructed wisdom arises, like the simultaneous appearance of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of suns.
The twenty kinds of inducements have already been explained at length.
Regarding the "compendium of determinations" (*viniścaya-saṃgraha*), it refers to the fact that all determinations are subsumed under ten topics.
What are these ten topics?

These are: the discernment of what is to be accomplished, the discernment of entry, the discernment of the supreme, the discernment of reasoning, the discernment of treatises, the discernment of thorough penetration, the discernment of purification, the discernment of elicitation, the discernment of the differentiation of phrases, and the discernment of the accomplishment of all meanings through a momentary mental attention that does not require effort.
The "Determination of Accomplishment" refers to the ability to determine and accomplish various worldly means of livelihood and so forth.
The "Determination of Entry" refers to the ability to examine which of the three vehicles one should enter.
How does one cause others to also enter [the path]?

Regarding "ascertainment through superior resolve," this refers to giving rise to superior faith and understanding based on the teachings as they have been heard, by means of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Regarding "ascertainment through reasoning," this refers to weighing the underlying intent of what was previously and subsequently taught, by means of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The determination through treatises (*śāstra-viniścaya*) refers to the principles of inquiry and discourse established according to what has been heard and reflected upon, for the purpose of enabling others to successively enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
Thorough penetration and determination (*prativedha-viniścaya*) refers to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because it is able to thoroughly penetrate the principle of the truths (*satya*).
The discernment of purification refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it is able to purify all afflictions without remainder.
The discernment of accomplishment refers to the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*), because it is able to bring about superior qualities.

Regarding the determination of the distinctions among phrases: this refers to the teaching of the distinctions among the infinite meanings of the Dharma by means of introductory gateways that differentiate between two, three, four, and so forth, up to many phrases.

Regarding the "ascertainment that all objects are accomplished by merely directing the mind for a moment without effort": this refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom; because, free from prior effort, when he momentarily directs his attention toward any object, his unhindered and unattached wisdom and vision proceed.
Regarding the determination of the methods of debate (*vāda-vidhi-viniścaya*), there are briefly seven types:

first, the essence of debate; second, the locus of debate; third, the basis of debate; fourth, the adornments of debate; fifth, the points of defeat in debate; sixth, the departure from debate; and seventh, the dharmas that are of great utility in debate.
Skillfulness in these seven gates is called the "Determination of the Rules of Discourse" (*vādanyāya-viniścaya*).
As for the essence of discourse (*vāda*), there are further six types:

first, formal discourse (*pravāda*); second, contentious discourse (*vivāda*); third, disputatious discourse (*apavāda*); fourth, abusive discourse (*upavāda*); fifth, compliant discourse (*anuvāda*); and sixth, instructional discourse (*avavāda*).
Discourse refers to all worldly speech.
Sophisticated discourse refers to those discourses followed and heard by the world, so called because they are esteemed by worldly wisdom.
Contentious discourse refers to speech in which the positions established by each party are mutually contradictory.
Abusive discourse refers to the utterance of coarse and malicious words arising from mutual anger.
Harmonious discourse refers to decisive speech that accords with pure knowledge and vision.

The treatise on instruction refers to all discourse intended to guide sentient beings, such that those whose minds are not yet concentrated bring their minds to concentration, and those whose minds are already concentrated attain liberation.

Regarding the locus of debate: one initiates the discussion either in a royal court, or in a court of law, or before those who are honest and capable of serving as authorities, or before virtuous companions, or before śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are well-versed in the meaning of the Dharma.
"Those belonging to the royal family" refers to those in a place where the king himself has descended.
"Those who uphold justice" refers to those in a place where royal affairs are adjudicated.
"Those who are honest and fit to be authorities" refers to merchants and the like.
"Having good companions" means that among one's associates, neither the proponent nor the opponent oversteps their respective words.
"Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who well understand the meaning of the Dharma" means those who have thoroughly mastered both the literal expression and the meaning within various treatises.
Regarding the basis of the treatise (*śāstrāśraya*), it refers to that upon which the treatise is established; briefly, there are two kinds:
first, the thesis to be established (*sādhya*), and second, the means of establishment (*sādhana*).
There are two types of the thesis to be established:
There are two [aspects]: first, the essential nature; second, the distinctions.

There are eight types of means for establishing [these], namely: first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*); sixth, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); seventh, inference (*anumāna*); and eighth, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). These are the means by which things are established.
"Self-nature" refers to the establishment of whether the self-nature of the self or the self-nature of phenomena exists or does not exist.

"Particularity" refers to the particularities of the self and the particularities of phenomena—such as being all-pervasive or not all-pervasive, permanent or impermanent, having form or being formless—and other such infinite varieties of distinction.

The "formulation of a thesis" (*pakṣa*) refers to proclaiming to another the meaning one intends to establish and which one accepts for oneself, so as to cause that other person to understand it. Why is this?
If one did not specify "that which is to be established," then even stating a position already established by oneself to another would have to be called the formulation of a thesis.
If one does not state the meaning accepted by oneself, then stating a meaning that ought to be established for another's school would have to be called "formulating a thesis" (*pakṣa-sthāpanā*).
If one does not mention the other [party], then merely uttering this statement alone should be called "formulating a thesis."
If one does not say "proclaiming," then expressing this meaning through the body should be called "formulating a thesis" (*pakṣasthāpana*).
If one does not say "causing another to understand," then when the listener has not yet understood this meaning, it should be called "formulating a thesis."

If, because there are no excessive faults in the manner established, one establishes the intrinsic nature of the self and phenomena as either existent or non-existent, or their distinctions such as being pervasive or non-pervasive, and if these possess the aforementioned characteristics, this is called "formulating a thesis" (*pakṣa*).

Establishing the reason (*hetu*) refers to correctly stating, regarding the very meaning to be proven that has not yet been clearly understood, such characteristics of conviction as being perceptible or imperceptible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The characteristic of conviction is the sense of the reason for conviction.

Why is this so? Because by correctly explaining the characteristics of what is perceptible and what is imperceptible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), conviction arises regarding the meaning to be established that has not yet been clearly understood; therefore, the correct exposition of those characteristics is called "establishing the reason" (*hetu*).
That which is perceptible or imperceptible by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) refers to what is spoken of in terms of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for establishing an analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), it refers to the correct explanation that brings together the aspect already seen with the aspect not yet seen.
The "aspect already seen" refers to the portion that has been manifested.
The "aspect not yet seen" refers to the portion that has not yet been manifested.
A correct exposition that uses the manifested portion to manifest the unmanifested portion so that their meanings are equal is called an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"Application" (*upanaya*) refers to citing other instances of the same category so that they may be brought into accord with the correct principle of this teaching.

That is to say, after the meaning previously established has been proven by means of the three members [of the syllogism], one further cites those meanings to establish other instances of the same category; thus, one brings them into accord with the correct reasoning of this teaching—this is called "application."
"Connection" (*saṃdhi*) refers to the correct teaching regarding that which reaches the ultimate goal.
Because it is perfectly established by this principle, this matter is definitively without variation in its connection to the ultimate; thus, it is called "connection."
The characteristics of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth have already been explained; now they shall be briefly illustrated by way of actual examples.
For instance, a proponent of non-self (*anātman-vādin*), regarding this very matter, first states to a proponent of self (*ātman-vādin*) that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self.
This statement constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Next, it says, "Because four faults would be found if [the self] were designated in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*).
This statement constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
