Why is this so? If one were to designate a real self in relation to the aggregates, would this conceived self be identical with the characteristics of the aggregates,
or would it exist within the aggregates?
Is it established in some other location?
Or is it designated as something that does not belong to the aggregates (*skandha*)?

If it is designated as having the very characteristics of the aggregates, then since the aggregates lack self-mastery and arise from a multitude of conditions, they are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
If the self were identical to those characteristics, the self would not be established; this is called the first fault.

If it were designated within the aggregates, then since the aggregates which serve as its basis are impermanent, the self which depends upon them would also have to be impermanent; this is the second fault.
If the designation "self" were applied elsewhere apart from the aggregates, the self would have no cause and would serve no purpose; this is the third fault.

If it were designated as not belonging to the aggregates, the self would exist independently and be liberated by its own nature, such that seeking liberation further would render one's efforts futile; this is the fourth fault.
Next, it is explained how the past is designated based on the present;
this statement serves as an illustration. Why is that?
If one designates the past as truly existent by means of its being identical to present characteristics, then is this conceived past identical to the present characteristic itself,
or does it exist within the present?
Is it established in another location?
Or is it established without depending on the present?

If it is established by means of the characteristics of the present itself, then since "having already arisen but not yet ceased" is the characteristic of the present, the substance of a past dharma would also have to take "having already arisen but not yet ceased" as its characteristic; this is the first fault.

If it were designated within the present, it would be designated within that which has not yet ceased; since this is incompatible with the nature of cessation, it is not logical—this is the second fault.

If one were to designate [a phenomenon] elsewhere apart from the present, then since nothing else—apart from the present—that is substantially existent can be found even in the slightest degree, how could one designate it there?
This is the third fault.
If one were to designate [a dharma] without depending on the present, then one would also have to designate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as belonging to the past; this is the fourth fault.
However, because the characteristics of the past have perished and ceased, the meaning of "signlessness" (animitta) is established.
If it were designated as being identical to the present, four logical fallacies would ensue; therefore, the characteristics of the past are not established.

The same applies to the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): if one were to designate a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), four faults would ensue; therefore, the meaning of selflessness is established.
Next, having thus refuted the inversion of a self, it follows by this very reasoning that permanence and so forth are likewise non-existent.
These words constitute the application (*upanaya*).
The subsequent statement— that by this reasoning, the five aggregates are all impermanent, and so forth, up to being selfless—
constitutes the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) means that which is correctly and clearly manifest to oneself, free from delusion.
The phrase "correctly and clearly manifest to oneself" indicates that it correctly apprehends its own object, such as when the eye correctly apprehends visible forms and so forth.

This statement is intended to distinguish [the object under discussion] from worldly things such as jars that are currently perceived, which are commonly accepted as being of a nature obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); since those [jars and the like] are merely conventional (*prajñapti*), they are not actually obtained through direct perception.
The term "clearly cognized" (*abhrānta*) is used to exclude objects that do not appear before one due to causes such as obstruction;
the term "non-erroneous" (*avibhrānta*) is used to exclude such things as the circle of fire produced by a whirling torch, illusions, and mirages.
Inference (*anumāna*) refers to the conviction arising from what remains after direct perception.
What does this mean?
It means that, setting aside what is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is a definitive concomitance regarding other non-manifest phenomena.
Having previously seen its accomplishment, when one now perceives a portion of it directly, a correct faith and understanding arises regarding the remaining portions.
This is because they must certainly exist therein, due to their simultaneous occurrence.
Just as when one sees smoke from afar and knows that there is fire there, this is called inference preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣapūrvaka-anumāna*).
Scriptural authority (*āptāgama*) refers to teachings that do not contradict these two means of valid cognition.

What is this? It refers to all teachings that do not contradict either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), which are absolutely unchanging and certainly worthy of trust and acceptance; therefore, they are called authoritative scripture (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*).

Regarding the adornment of discourse (*vādālaṃkāra*): it refers to initiating a discussion based on the correct principles of treatises in such a way that it is profoundly excellent; this is called the adornment of discourse.
This further comprises six types:
(1) proficiency in one's own and others' tenets, (2) perfection of speech and tone, (3) fearlessness, (4) eloquence, (5) gravity and dignity, and (6) being worthy of offerings.

"One who is skilled in their own and others' tenets" refers to one who possesses a pure, mature, and clear understanding of both the literal text and the meaning of their own and others' systems, without interruption from beginning to end.

"One whose speech and sound are perfect" refers to one who, being well-versed in the science of phonetics (*śabdavidyā*), initiates the discourse only after ensuring they are free from faults in the sounds and syllables of what is to be said, such that the uttered speech is not confused or disordered.

"Fearlessness" means that when one is in the midst of a great assembly, even though surrounded by countless individuals of exceptional talent who harbor deviant attachments and have conspired together, the words one utters are composed and free from fear.
Eloquence means that one’s speech is without impediment.
Sincerity and gravity mean that one’s speech is not abrupt or violent; rather, one observes the opponent's discourse until it reaches its conclusion before then speaking.

"One worthy of offerings" (arhat) refers to one who is established in a virtuous and harmonious nature, whose speech is gentle and good, and who employs skillful means to accord with the mind of the opponent in debate.
"Defeat in debate" refers to abandoning the argument, being outwitted in speech, or committing an error in speech.
Due to these three types [of defeat], proponents fall into positions of defeat and suffer subjugation by their opponents.

"Abandoning the argument" refers to speaking for oneself and admitting the failure of one's own thesis while praising the merit of the opponent's thesis, such as saying, "I am not skillful; you are skillful," and so forth.

"Yielding" refers to withdrawing by resorting to expedient means under the pretext of other matters; or abandoning one's original position by discussing extraneous affairs; or manifesting anger, arrogance, concealment, and so forth, as explained at length in the sūtras.
"Using other matters as a pretext to withdraw by means of a skillful device" refers to using other matters to distract from the meaning of what is being said.
As the Sūtra says:
"The Elder Cāṇakya engaged in debate with various non-Buddhists; he would either refute the thesis he had established, or establish a thesis after having already refuted it."
Regarding faulty speech, there are briefly nine types:
first, confused; second, harsh; third, unintelligible; fourth, limitless; fifth, inconsistent with the meaning; sixth, untimely; seventh, indecisive; eighth, obscure; and ninth, incoherent.
"Confused" refers to abandoning the subject under discussion to speak at length on other matters.
"Rough and crude" refers to speech that is impetuous and violent due to outbursts of anger.
"Indistinct" refers to the meaning of the doctrine being expounded such that it is not understood by the assembly or the opponent.
"Immoderate" refers to the redundancy of words, wherein the expressed meaning either increases or decreases [from what is necessary].
There are, briefly, five types of "incoherence with the meaning":

first, meaninglessness; second, contradiction of the meaning; third, subversion of the principle; fourth, identity with the thesis to be proven; and fifth, the sense of inviting faults and difficulties. These are categorized as such because [the former] cannot be established, because the meaning is inconsistent, because it is not determinate, because the reasoning used to prove it must itself be proven, and because all such discourse is pursued by what is irrational and untrue.
"Untimely" means that what should be said is presented out of sequence.
"Indeterminate" means that having established a point, one subsequently refutes it, or having refuted it, one establishes it again; because of such rapid shifting, it is difficult to comprehend.
"Unclear" means that one answers without grasping the characteristics of the *śāstra* being expounded, or uses a mixture of formal and colloquial language in a disordered manner.
"Incoherent" means that the flow of speech is interrupted in the midst of it.

Regarding "withdrawal from debate": this refers to observing the merits and faults [of the discussion] so as to withdraw from the debate or refrain from engaging in it altogether, fearing one might fall into a position of defeat; or, if the debate is indeed commenced, being able to bring it to a successful conclusion.
Furthermore, if one knows that the opponent is not a fit vessel for the Dharma, the assembly lacks virtue, or one lacks skill oneself, one should not engage in debate.
Only if one knows that the opponent is a fit vessel for the Dharma, the assembly possesses virtue, and one possesses skill oneself, may one engage in debate.
"Those who oppose the teaching and are not vessels for the Dharma" refers to those who cannot lead others out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
"The assembly at that time lacked virtue" means they were not sincere and pure, but instead delighted in perverse attachments and harbored partiality and factionalism.
"One who lacks skill" refers to one who has not attained proficiency in the body of the treatise up to its ornaments.
The opposite of this is called a "proponent of the counter-argument," such as those who possess the "Dharma-vessel" and so forth.
Regarding the factors that contribute much to the process of debate, there are briefly three types of requisites necessary for initiating a debate.
What are these three?
First, being well-versed in one’s own and others’ tenets; by means of this, one is capable of engaging in debate universally, as one engages in debate regarding all matters of discourse.
Second is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), by which one is capable of initiating discourse while standing before all assemblies.
Third is eloquence (*pratibhāna*), by which one is capable of skillfully answering all difficult questions and challenges.
Furthermore, if one desires to seek one’s own benefit and happiness, one should thoroughly master the principles of various treatises and should not engage in contentious debate with others.
As the Bhagavān stated in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-sūtra*: "If bodhisattvas wish to apply themselves with diligence to cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities;

wish to practice the authentic 'dharma-conforming-dharma' (dharmānudharmapratipatti); wish to skillfully gather and benefit all sentient beings; and wish to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), they should correctly contemplate the phenomena of the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana) and should not engage in contentious debate with others."
What are the twelve?
First, when the subtle Dharma that realizes the unsurpassed meaning is proclaimed, those who possess faith and understanding are extremely rare to find.
Second, those who cultivate a mind intent on receiving the teaching and pose questions are extremely rare to find.
Third, it is extremely rare to find an assembly that skillfully observes virtues and faults.
Fourth, it is extremely rare for those who engage in debate to be able to avoid the six faults.
What are these six? They are:

the fault of adhering to false doctrines; the fault of evasive speech; the fault of speaking at an inappropriate time; the fault of retreating from one's position; the fault of harsh speech; and the fault of mental resentment and anger.
Fifth, it is extremely rare for one who initiates a debate not to harbor fierce malice.
Sixth, it is extremely rare for one who initiates a debate to skillfully protect the minds of others.
Seventh, when engaging in debate, it is extremely difficult to skillfully protect a concentrated mind.
Eighth, when engaging in debate, it is extremely difficult to have a mind that wishes for oneself to be inferior and for the other to be victorious.
Ninth, it is extremely rare for one who is inferior to find their mind free from affliction when facing a superior;
tenth, it is extremely rare for one whose mind is already afflicted to attain abiding in peace and security.
Eleventh, it is extremely difficult to find those who, not dwelling in peace, constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas.

Twelfth, for those who do not constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas, it is extremely difficult to find those whose minds have not yet attained concentration but can quickly attain it, or whose minds have already attained concentration and can quickly achieve liberation.

Since this sutra has already explained that one should cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities through desire, diligence, and vigor, why does it further state that one should practice the "steadfast and true Dharma" and the "practice in accordance with the Dharma"?
It is for the purpose of manifesting the purity of one's underlying intention (*āśaya*).
Why is this? Because they do not cultivate the various categories of wholesome qualities, such as hearing and reflection, for the sake of gain, honor, and the like.
Those who wish to properly gather and benefit sentient beings distinguish their practice from that of the śrāvakas and others, because for bodhisattvas, the practice of benefiting others is supreme.
When a bodhisattva has thus fulfilled the practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning and intent of the various passages in this sutra: when engaging in debate, the nature of the Mahāyāna Dharma is supreme and profoundly deep; it is difficult enough to understand it with a non-contentious mind, let alone through contentious rivalry.
Whenever they initiate a debate, although they may pose questions, they have no intention of seeking understanding but merely seek out faults.
Furthermore, their supporting witnesses are not upright in heart; they are unskilled in the Gate of the School and delight in clinging to perverse attachments.
Generally, all discourse is characterized by many of the six faults. Why is this so?

When engaging in debate, one may harbor private attachments to false doctrines; or employ deceptive means to seek out the errors of others; or interrupt before the speaker has finished to raise disorderly speech; or, when the opponent’s words accord with correct principle, instead respond with slander and denial; or use coarse language to vex the opponent and the minds of the assembly; or harbor resentment and anger toward them. Thus, such discourse is frequently possessed of these six kinds of faults.

Furthermore, when engaging in debate, it is extremely difficult for the body and mind to remain tranquil; because they are not tranquil, two matters cannot be accomplished: namely, skillfully protecting the minds of others and skillfully protecting one's own mind.
By means of this, one causes others' minds to attain pure faith, and through right effort and skillful means regarding the state of liberation, one brings one's own mind to concentration.
Furthermore, when engaging in debate, such a mind frequently arises:
"How may I achieve victory, while causing my opponent to fall into defeat?"
If one’s wishes are not fulfilled, one immediately harbors burning affliction (*paridāha*).

Because of this, one does not dwell in peace and happiness; consequently, one is unable to cultivate wholesome qualities without interruption. Therefore, regarding those superior realized dharmas, there is a falling away from what has not yet been attained.
The "Secret Determination" refers to the transformation of the sets of names, phrases, and syllables that express one meaning in order to further reveal another meaning.
As it is said in a sutra:
"Having killed one's father and mother, And the King, as well as two who are learned..."
"To slay a kingdom and its followers—this person is said to be pure.
In this verse, words that express the most grievous evils commonly recognized by the world are transformed to secretly reveal other meanings of purity.
What are the most grievous crimes recognized by common worldly consensus?
They are the parricides and matricides, as well as the harming of venerable persons and the great assembly.
There are two kinds of venerable persons:
First, the distinct; second, the common.
The common is further of two kinds:
first, that which protects the world; second, that which is worthy of offerings.
There are also two other types: namely, the father and the mother.
Those who protect the world are the kings.
Those worthy of veneration are the learned brahmins, for they are collectively recognized by the world as being most pure.
If one kills and harms [the victim] in its entirety, it is called "an offense against a venerable person.
If one slaughters the people of a nation along with their accompanying animals, it is called "harming a great multitude.
That which makes this meaning manifest is called the "words that express the most grievous evils recognized by common worldly consensus."
How does this transformation of words secretly reveal the meaning of purity?
It is because expressions such as "killing one's father and mother" are transformed to secretly reveal other meanings, such as the permanent severance of craving and so forth.

Why is this so? Because craving, karma, the appropriating consciousness, the two types of grasping—namely, adherence to precepts and views—and the six sense bases such as the eye, along with their respective objects, are designated as "mother," "father," and so forth, according to their sequence, due to the similarity of their functions.
Craving is the cause of origination, and karma is the cause of birth; by means of these, one is able to plant the seeds of habitual tendencies, acting as the father of the world.
Through these two causes, consciousness accompanied by grasping flows on without interruption.

Although one seeks liberation while in the state of saṃsāra, the attainment of liberation is obstructed by two types of non-expedient methods: namely, false conceptualization and [the pursuit of] what is merely pure and supreme.
The two types of grasping—grasping at precepts and views—are like the learned brahmins of the world who constantly and falsely cling to what they consider supreme purity.
The six sense bases, which serve as the support and object for this consciousness accompanied by grasping, are like the kingdom and its retinue in the world.
If one can forever sever such dharmas as these, it should be known that this person is most pure.
Furthermore, as a sutra says:
"Lacking faith and ungrateful, / Severing intimacy so there is no room for it..."
"Constantly eating what others have spat out, he is the supreme man.
In this verse, while the literal meaning proclaims something extremely base and inferior in the world, the transformation of the words cryptically reveals another, supreme meaning.
There are four kinds of inferiority in the world, namely: inferiority of mental action, inferiority of bodily action, inferiority of verbal action, and inferiority of enjoyment.
There are two further types of inferior mental action:
first, that which is contrary to the arising of faith, such as not believing in future lives and so forth, and consequently failing to practice giving and other virtues.
Second, because they are ungrateful and give rise to non-virtue, disregarding past kindness and violating worldly principles by committing all manner of evil deeds such as harming their mothers.
Regarding the inferiority of their physical actions: it refers to engaging in thievery, breaking through walls, and other secret acts that are most contemptible for the sake of making a living.
Inferior verbal karma refers to such acts as lying, which are most contemptible because they are not tolerated within virtuous assemblies.
Inferior enjoyment refers to things such as ghosts, dogs, and birds, who prefer to eat what has been vomited.
To clarify this meaning, it is called "the words that express the most inferior sense of the world.
How does one transform these words to reveal the unsurpassed meaning?
It is by means of the transformation of terms such as "lack of faith" (aśraddhā) to secretly reveal other superior meanings.
"Lack of faith" refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation, because it is personally realized.
"Not knowing gratitude" refers to the wisdom of *nirvāṇa*.
Conditioned phenomena are called "gratitude," while unconditioned phenomena are not.
Because one knows that [the Buddha] was not a benefactor, it is called "unknowing gratitude.
"Severing the secret" means permanently severing the afflictions that serve as the cause for the continuity of future existence.
"Having no place of containment" means that one will no longer be born within the various realms of suffering in future lives.

Regarding "one who eats vomit": this refers to one who, although temporarily sustaining the body through the power of provisional requisites within this present life, does not give rise to delight or craving for life or wealth.
If one can act in this manner, they are a supreme person.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"Perceiving the non-solid as solid, Abiding well within perversion,
And being tormented by extreme afflictions— One attains supreme enlightenment."
This is as previously explained.
However, regarding its essential nature: it refers to the various bodhisattvas who, relying upon samādhi, realize great enlightenment through the two paths of vision and cultivation.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes five dharmas, the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) will be swiftly fulfilled.
What are these five?"

First, increasing the nature of stinginess; second, becoming weary of giving; third, loathing those who beg; fourth, not giving even the slightest amount; and fifth, being far removed from the practice of giving.

Regarding the increase of the dharma-nature of stinginess: this refers to the realization of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) within that dharma-nature-tathatā, by means of the permanent eradication of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of stinginess along with their residual impressions (vāsanā).
"Being weary of giving" means that for the sake of practicing generosity, one has vowed to undergo difficult ascetic practices over a long period of time.
"Hating those who beg" means desiring that they take what they need themselves, out of a distaste for their begging.
"Having no slight or momentary giving" means giving all things at all times.
"Being far removed from giving" means being constantly free from giving with the expectation of a reward and so forth.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who accomplishes five dharmas is called a practitioner of the Brahma-faring (brahmacārin) and has accomplished the foremost pure Brahma-faring.
What are these five?"

First, constantly seeking to leave desire through desire; second, abandoning and severing the dharmas of desire; third, immediately becoming firmly attached when desire and greed have already arisen; fourth, fearing the dharmas that counteract desire; and fifth, repeatedly meeting in pairs.
The accomplishment of the foremost pure holy life refers to the supramundane path.
"Constantly seeking to leave desire through desire" means that one eternally abandons that [desire] by means of this very suchness of universal knowledge (*yathābhūta-parijñā*).
This "thorough knowledge as it truly is" refers to the wisdom that is able to penetrate this suchness (*tathatā*).
"Abandoning and severing the dharmas of desire" refers to constantly observing the means for abandoning and severing non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*).
"Immediately firmly grasping at sensual desire that has already arisen" means that when sensual desire has already arisen internally, one immediately firmly grasps it and casts it out externally.
"The Dharma for treating the fear of sensual desire" means teaching sentient beings the perils of sensual desire to instill fear in them, and establishing the path of antidotes to rescue them all.

Regarding "repeatedly realizing through enumeration": this refers to the repeated realization, through both mundane and supramundane paths, as well as through the two paths of śamatha and vipaśyanā, of the four noble truths which distinguish the causes and effects of affliction and purification.
For what reason is this treatise titled the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya*?
Briefly, there are three meanings: namely, because it is that which is equally collected, because it is that which is universally collected, and because it is that which is correctly collected.
This question is posed to clarify the origin of its name through the principle of etymological interpretation.
"Compiled by those who are equal" means that it was collectively compiled by the great bodhisattvas who have realized the direct vision of reality (*tattvābhisamaya*).
"Comprehensively collected" means that it universally encompasses all the points of investigation found within the Mahāyāna Abhidharma sūtras.
"Correctly collected" means that through the skillful means of unerring compilation, it leads up to the attainment of the Buddha's bodhi.
